1.1: 1.1 Here begins. AUGUSTINE. This book is entitled among the Hebrews the Book of Hymns, for this reason: a hymn is where there are words and praise together with song, which is found in the psalms. According to some it is also entitled the Book of Soliloquies; this seems to be so because what someone searches out within himself, and learns from no one except from the truth presiding inwardly over him, is called a soliloquy. For example, just as blessed Augustine investigated within himself the nature of the soul and the nature of God, in the same way the Prophet can be said to have investigated within himself the incarnation of the Son of God and the restoration of the human race. King David, also a prophet, while he reigned prosperously and wished to magnify the worship of God, when he was at last bringing back to Jerusalem the ark, which the Philistines had returned and which had wandered a long time in uncertain resting places, went before it unclothed, with a harp (2 Samuel 6). He had also chosen four thousand men to sing psalms not only with the voice but also with musical instruments, and set over them four: Asaph, Jeduthun, Heman, Ethan, or the sons of Korah, who, falling away from their father's crime or sacrilege (whom fire had consumed, Numbers 16), remained most devoted in the worship of God. JEROME. The psaltery is a musical instrument fashioned in the shape of a letter, and the present work took its name from that musical instrument by which it was sung. The psaltery is called nebel among the Hebrews, ... among the Greeks, and organum among the Latins. Many say that David did not make all the psalms, because some of them are entitled in the person of others. But, as blessed Jerome says, they are not to be heard in this. For David composed all the psalms; he also appended titles, in which he had many helpers, over whom he set four, namely Heman, Ethan, Asaph and Jeduthun. It was done by divine counsel that the psalms were entitled in the persons of others, either only because of the interpretation of the names, or because of the matter at hand, or because of both. Only for the interpretation of the names, as in the person of Jeduthun; for the matter at hand, as in the person of Haggai and Zechariah; for both, as in the person of Solomon. Jeduthun, Asaph, the sons of Korah and others of this kind were not the authors of the psalms, but were set over the artists who sounded the psalms in three ways: either with the human voice, or with musical instruments, or commonly in both ways. And this in two ways: either the instrument after the voice, or the voice after the instrument. Hence their names are inserted in the titles, so that they might receive honor from their ministry, chiefly for the signification of the matters. A psalm is the sound of an instrument; a canticle is the singing of the human voice in praise of God. It is a 'canticle of a psalm' when the voice comes after the instrument, and a 'psalm of a canticle' when the instrument comes after the voice. CASSIODORUS. It is usually asked why the psalms, rather than other Scriptures, are read in the Church. This is because anciently this custom was in the temple of God among the Hebrews. Or because the psalms contain more mysteries than the other Scriptures, and say many things briefly, in which the whole law and the prophets and the Gospel consist. CASSIODORUS. Prophecy is a divine inspiration or revelation, which announces the outcomes of events with unchangeable truth, either through deeds or through words; hence prophecy is a vision, and a prophet is one who sees. This grace has been given in many ways: either through the works of men, as was the ark of Noah and the sacrifice of Abraham and the crossing of the Red Sea; or through births, as Esau and Jacob, who signified things to come; or through speaking angels, as they spoke to Abraham, Lot and others; or through visions, as to Isaiah and Ezekiel and the rest; or through dreams, as to Solomon, Joseph and Daniel; or through a cloud and a voice from heaven, as to Moses; or still in other ways. David, however, was taught inwardly by none of these but by heavenly inspiration, filled with the Spirit speaking in him, as in 1 Samuel: 'The Spirit of the Lord was directed upon David' (1 Samuel 16). And the Lord says: 'If David in the Spirit calls him Lord, how is he his son?' (Matthew 22). The Holy Spirit was given to the prophets in such a way that sometimes he withdrew because of sins and returned when appeased; and as Peter says: 'Prophecy was never brought by human will, but holy men of God spoke inspired by the Holy Spirit' (2 Peter 1). Nor are those foreign to the office of prophecy to whom the ability to understand or interpret the Scriptures has been given. JEROME. There are many kinds of anointed ones (christs): the patriarchs were called christs, as in 'Do not touch my christs' (Psalm 104); in Proverbs all who came out of Egypt are called christs. The chrism is made in Exodus, whence the priests are anointed; there is another ointment with which kings are anointed; but this is in two ways: if it is David and Solomon, that is, one of strong hand and one peaceable, he is anointed from a horn; if Jehu and Hazael, from a small flask, which is an earthen vessel. But Cyrus too, king of the Persians and Medes, who released Israel, is a christ, according to the verse: 'Thus says the Lord to my christ Cyrus' (Isaiah 45), which the following words do not allow to be taken of the Savior, as some think. There is the prophetic ointment, with which Elijah is commanded to anoint Elisha as prophet (1 Kings 19); above all is the spiritual ointment, which is called the oil of gladness, with which Christ was anointed above his fellows, who have the chrism of baptism. If anyone loses this, let him not despair; for concerning the chrism to be set apart it is written in Leviticus (Leviticus 13) that when someone's leprosy has been cleansed, the priest is to put oil in his left hand, and the other things said there, and he himself is to be called a christ of God. What remains is that the same man is frequently anointed, lest there be an occasion of ruin for the negligent. For it suffices for the leper that, after the first ointment is lost, he be anointed a second time; but he is often anointed who always advances: and from the oil of the leper he comes to the ointment of the people; from there to the priestly; from that to the chrism of the high priest; from the high priest to the king; from the king to the patriarchs; from the patriarchs to Christ. CASSIODORUS. Just as prophecy occurs in different ways, so also at different times. There is therefore one concerning the present, as Elizabeth: 'Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come?' etc. (Luke 1). Concerning the past, as Moses: 'In the beginning God created heaven and earth' (Genesis 1). Concerning the future, as: 'Behold, a Virgin shall conceive,' etc. (Isaiah 7). Again, one prophecy is according to the foreknowledge of God, which must be fulfilled in every way, as: 'Behold, a Virgin shall conceive,' etc. Another is according to a threat, as: 'Forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown' (Jonah 3). It is to be noted, therefore, that the prophet sometimes speaks indiscriminately of future things as though present; sometimes of past things, sometimes also properly of future things. This happens because he says all things as the Holy Spirit dictates, to whom all things, whether past or future, are known as though present. REMIGIUS. This book consists of one hundred and fifty psalms, not without a reason of deeper mystery. For this number is most celebrated in mysteries. It consists of eighty and seventy, whose beginning and signification come from the eight and the seven. The eight signifies the eighth age of resurrection: for since there are six ages of the living, the seventh will be of the dying, the eighth of those rising again. By the seven, the time of this life is signified, which is passed in the repetition of seven days. Rightly, therefore, was this book composed with such a number of psalms, because it teaches us so to work and live in the sevenfold span of this life that in the eighth, of the resurrection, we may obtain the robe of glory. Or because the New Testament is signified by the eight: for the fathers of the New Testament serve the eighth day, observing the eighth day of Christ's resurrection, that is, the Lord's Day, the octaves of the saints, awaiting the eighth of the resurrection of the dead. By the seven, the Old Testament: for the fathers of the Old Testament served the hebdomad, that is, the seven, observing the seventh day, the seventh week, the seventh year and the fiftieth, which is woven of seven weeks of years, that is, the jubilee; hence Solomon: 'Give portions to seven, and also to eight' (Ecclesiastes 11). Well, therefore, was this book of psalms produced with this number, whose parts contain the teaching and commandments of both Testaments. AUGUSTINE. Again, through the three fifties there is a threefold division of the psalms, to signify the three states of the Christian religion: the first of penance, in which the first fifty of the psalms also ends, namely 'Have mercy on me, O God'; the second of justice, in which the second fifty also ends: 'I will sing to you of mercy and judgment'; the third state of eternal life, in praise of which the third fifty concludes, namely 'Let every spirit praise the Lord.' THE SAME. There is one Book of Psalms, not five, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles: 'As it is written in the book of Psalms' (Acts 1). Jerome, however, says five books, that is, five divisions made by 'so be it, so be it.' The order of the psalms disagrees with the order of the history, because David first sinned with the wife of Uriah and sang of penance, 'Have mercy on me, O God,' before his son persecuted him and he sang, 'Lord, why are they multiplied'; but they are believed to have been so arranged by the prophet Ezra at divine prompting. The subject matter is the whole Christ, bridegroom and bride. The intention is to conform to Christ, the new man, men who were deformed in Adam. The manner of treatment: sometimes he deals with Christ as head, sometimes as body, sometimes as both. As head, in three ways: either according to the divinity, as 'With you is the principle,' etc.; sometimes according to the humanity, as 'I slept,' etc.; sometimes by transference, as when he uses the voice of the members, as there: 'Far from my salvation,' etc. Likewise of the Church in three ways: sometimes according to the perfect, sometimes according to the imperfect, sometimes according to the wicked, who are in the Church in body, not in mind; in number, not in merit; in name, not in nature. Blessed is the man who has not walked, etc. AUGUSTINE, Enarrations on the Psalms, vol. 3. The order: Adam walked away when he departed from God; he stood when he was delighted by sin; he sat when, confirmed in pride, he could not return except by being freed through this one, who had none of these. Adam walked away when he consented to the persuasion of the devil; he stood while he ate the fruit; he sat while he excused himself: 'The woman whom you gave me deceived me' (Genesis 3). It is like exiles, who are more easily called back while they are on the road, with more difficulty when they are already standing, and most difficultly when they have become masters and lords there. REMIGIUS. Sin is committed by thought, by deed, and by words in teaching. CASSIODORUS. The impious one is such toward God, the sinner toward himself, the pestilent toward his neighbor. In the chair, giving an example of sinning. CASSIODORUS. The throne belongs to kings, the tribunal to judges, the chair properly to teachers. Ibid. It is as if he said: You who have fallen through the first Adam, be conformed to this second one: for blessed is the one contrary to the first
1.2: 1.2 But in the law. AUGUSTINE. CASSIODORUS. Here he is shown to be full of every good in himself. AUGUSTINE. It is not perfect praise to flee what is blameworthy unless what is praiseworthy follows. In the order in which they grew in the first verse, they are removed from the second. In the law. Ibid. He who is in the law acts according to the law; he who is under the law is acted upon according to the law: the former is free, the latter a servant. Ibid. AMBROSE. The law that is written for the one who serves is one thing; the law that is beheld by the mind of one who has no need of letters is another. Will. CASSIODORUS. So that there may be no weariness of labor, nor idleness, but he will meditate always. The will of the sense is under the law; of reason, in the law; of divinity, above the law.
1.3: 1.3 And he shall be. Ibid. Here he is shown to be useful to us, giving the fruit of life, and leaves, and overshadowing. Blessed is the man. But in the law. And he shall be. A full definition of the blessed man. All these things befit not every blessed man but Christ alone. Like a tree. Ibid. After the likeness of the tree of life that is in paradise, from which the obedient man would have eaten. Tree. Ibid. In paradise there is the tree of life, a tree for life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Of waters. AUGUSTINE. The waters are the Holy Spirit, according to the verse: 'He who believes in me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water' (John 7), and it is against the heat of vices. CASSIODORUS. Or by water is meant the wisdom of God, by which the inner man is refreshed, so that he thirsts for water. AUGUSTINE. Or the mortal race, as in Job: 'Many waters, many peoples,' because they flow down into death as waters into the sea. It will give. Ibid. To give belongs to a rational sense and to the will of the one offering. And the leaf. Ibid. As leaves cover the fruit, so the words of the Lord guard his promises. And all. Ibid. What is meant by 'all' in each case.
1.4: 1.4 Not so the wicked. Here he terrifies his adversaries with the punishment of the wicked; fear of this makes the preceding promises more welcome. From the face of the earth. AUGUSTINE. Of eternal stability, because just as this earth nourishes and sustains man, so that earth does the inner man.
1.5: 1.5 Therefore the wicked shall not rise again. Because the wind casts them away, that is, therefore, because they have been given over to a reprobate mind: therefore they do not rise in the first resurrection, so as to judge themselves in counsel, so as to put the wills of God before their own. Or in the council, that is, in the harmonious multitude of the just, the impious idolaters or apostates. Sinners, false Christians: either they do not rise in the future so as to judge, or so as to rest, once judged, in the council, that is, in the assembly of the just. In judgment, etc. In the judgment there will be four orders: some will judge and not be judged, as the most perfect; others will neither judge nor be judged, as the condemned unbelievers; others will be judged and be saved, as the moderately good; others will be judged and perish, as wicked believers. In the council. AUGUSTINE. In the eternal good, which it was for the saints to follow by counsel. Or in the council, in the judgment, so as to judge with them; for there is judgment when different sins are punished with different penalties; and from this likeness it is so called. They rise. Which resurrections: of the soul, from sins in the present; of the body, from death in the future, by which it will become impassible and immortal.
1.6: 1.6 For the Lord knows, etc. That is, these do not rise in soul, because God does not approve their works, but only those of the just.
2.1: 2.1 A psalm. The modulation made by the touch of ten strings is good action, which is done by the observance of the ten commandments. David. CASSIODORUS. 'Strong of hand' or 'beautiful to look upon' is Christ, who overcame the powers of the air, and upon whom the angels also desire to look. Why have the nations raged, etc. CASSIODORUS. This psalm is second in order, first in its title; hence in the Acts of the Apostles it is called the first. First he rebukes and threatens the persecutors, predicting as a prophet. Vain things. Ibid. To hold him in death; or, lest the world go after him.
2.2: 2.2 Kings. Ibid. The former, Herod who killed the infants; the latter, Pilate who consented to the death of Christ. Kings and princes. Ibid. According to Ambrose, he could also speak in the plural of one. For only King Herod and the prince Pilate are reported, by Peter's voice in the Acts of the Apostles, to have conspired against Christ.
2.3: 2.3 Let us break asunder. AMBROSE. Or they came together saying: Let us break asunder the reasonings of them, the Lord and his Christ, or of Christ and his disciples, by which they want to bind us to themselves. AUGUSTINE. And though it could be said otherwise, it more plainly fits those who do not wish the yoke of Christ to be placed on them. Bonds. The promises of eternal life and the threats of Gehenna, by which they want to subject us to themselves. Let us cast away. Having destroyed the reasonings, let us shake off his dominion from us. Ibid. The yoke, that is, the law: but he who dwells in heaven.
2.4: 2.4 Shall laugh. Ibid. As when, after guards were posted, he rose: He shall deride, when they were scattered through the world. The derision of God is the power of foreknowledge which God gives the saints, so that, seeing the name of Christ to be in all nations, they understand that those men meditated vain things.
2.5: 2.5 Then shall he speak to them. Ibid. He opens it more plainly when he says, he shall trouble. The wrath of God is the movement that occurs in a soul that knows the law of God, when it sees it passed over by evil, a movement by which many things are avenged; or, the wrath of God is the darkening of the mind of the transgressors of the law.
2.6: 2.6 But I. CASSIODORUS. Second, he introduces his words about his omnipotent kingdom and his ineffable generation, where we learn of his divinity and humanity. King. THE SAME. So also the kings of the earth are established by him. Preaching upon Sion, so also the prophets; Son, so also Israel; I have begotten you. This belongs to Christ alone.
2.7: 2.7 The Lord said. The person of the one who reigns. My Son. AUGUSTINE. Therefore I give you the nations as an inheritance rather than to any obedient one, because you are Son by nature, and consubstantial by ineffable begetting. Today. Ibid. Although it can be taken of the day on which he was born according to the man, yet because 'today' signifies presence, let it be taken of the eternal generation of the Wisdom of God.
2.8: 2.8 Ask. AUGUSTINE. It pertains to the assumption of the man: things done for the salvation of men, according to which he intercedes for us. Inheritance. CASSIODORUS. Inheritance (hereditas) from the master (herus), because in it he rules with free power.
2.9: 2.9 You shall rule them. AUGUSTINE. Partly you shall rule, partly you shall break, according to the verse: 'Behold, this one is set for the fall and for the resurrection of many' (Luke 2), so that 'he who is just may be justified still, and he who is filthy may be filthy still' (Revelation 22). Rod of iron. CASSIODORUS. The power of Christ is the iron rod; the sinner is the potter's vessel, which is of clay and easily broken.
2.10: 2.10 And now, O kings, understand. 'Now,' that is, through the things that have been said. CASSIODORUS. Third, in view of these things made manifest, he admonishes all to obey humbly, and persuades them from what is useful, lest they perish, and from what is honorable, because blessed are all who trust in him. In this he speaks after Christ as an Apostle. AUGUSTINE. Or: I having been established as king, do not be sad, you kings of the earth; for it is expedient for you to be under him, from whom come understanding and instruction, so that you may not rule rashly but serve the Lord of all, and rejoice in blessedness.
2.12: 2.12 Lest at any time he be angry. Ibid. A doubt not according to the prophet but according to those very persons, who think of God's anger with doubt. From the just way, that is, Christ having been taken away, or from good action.
2.13: 2.13 When his wrath shall be kindled. CASSIODORUS. Now it does not burn when he chastises as a father, but in the future it will burn, because in the future there will be no patience. In a short time his wrath. Because he examines not each of these separately, but all at once.
3.1: 3.1 A psalm, AUGUSTINE, on the passion and resurrection of Christ: the son Judas, from whom he fled, withdrew with the others to the mountain with him as he departed; or rather when the wisdom of God abandoned his mind, so that he might be wholly the devil's, which desertion is called flight on account of its swiftness. Hence: 'What you do, do quickly' (John 13). To him Christ showed peace, as David did to his wicked son, whence it is called the peace of the father: but Judas, like Absalom, perished hanged. He sets forth two opposing parties. The voice of Christ, as if marveling, when he came to save: Lord, why, etc.
18.10: 18.10 The fear of the Lord. Ibid. The fear of the world is not holy, because it is not profitable, and changes with times. The fear of the Lord is without any disturbance, because love is mingled with awe, because if he fears the judge, he knows him to be merciful. AUGUSTINE. Fear, not that penal fear for earthly things, for love of which the soul is afraid, but chaste fear, by which, the more she loves, the more she takes care not to offend the bridegroom, and therefore it is not cast out but remains. Judgments. The judgments of God need no other's authority.
18.11: 18.11 Desirable. Ibid. Or, much to be desired, or much gold and stone; or much precious. Desirable above gold, etc., up to whose will he puts before his own, and they are sweeter than he is to himself. Above gold, that is, everything that is sought, for riches, or power, or pleasure. Honey. The food of God is honey; that is, one already loosed from the world; and the honeycomb, that is, because he is still wrapped about, who needs the pressure of the squeezing hand of God, that he may go into life.
18.13: 18.13 Sins, who. Ibid. Third, he asks to be purged from vices, that he may be worthy as the Psalmist to relate these sacraments. To the mind that sees, truth is sweet, judgments pleasant; to one not seeing, what sweetness? but why is it not seen? because of sins: nor is it a wonder: 'Sins, who understands?' CASSIODORUS. Sins: all of them, for some are known. Mine defile, others' afflict, and now spare, drive away the persuader. From hidden. He includes all sins in two, etc., up to by which man was seduced; and by consenting made it his own. AUGUSTINE. There is no greater sin than to apostatize from God, which is the beginning of pride: and pride is the beginning and cause of all sin.
19.1: 19.1 Unto the end. CASSIODORUS. A figure of working, what is to come the Prophet sings. Ibid. The Prophet out of excessive charity wishes things to turn out prosperously for the Church, which through Christ he saw to come.
19.2: 19.2 May he hear: what in the time of tribulation he wishes to be done for him. In the day of tribulation, in which we pray to God with greater desire. The God of Jacob, that as to him, so to you he may give the grace of blessing, and set you before the Jews.
19.3: 19.3 May he send: the Father. Help, by sending the Son.
19.4: 19.4 May he be mindful. He speaks as of a priest about to sacrifice and a king about to fight. Of sacrifice. Ibid. He foresaw the sacrifice of the Church, not of cattle, but of the blood and body of Christ.
19.5: 19.5 May he grant. Diapsalma, which in the time of glory he wishes and affirms. All. AUGUSTINE. Not only in that you laid down your soul for the life of many; but also in that blindness in part has happened to Israel, and so all Israel would be saved.
19.6: 19.6 We shall rejoice. Ibid. Therefore this prayer, because we shall rejoice and be magnified, shows that he is one of the Church so long beforehand.
19.7: 19.7 In powers. AUGUSTINE. Our powers are the salvation of his favor when even out of tribulation he gives help, because vain is the salvation of men, which is of the left hand, whence pride is also born. The salvation of the right hand. Ibid., that is, spiritual grace, etc., up to those who presume on earthly dignity.
20.1: 20.1 Unto the end. The third psalm, on the two natures in Christ, describes the heavenly king, so that the world may believe by hearing him whom the Jew despises when seen. He makes the discourse demonstrative in praise of God.
20.2: 20.2 O Lord, in your strength the king shall rejoice. CASSIODORUS. He sets out the sum, namely, merit and reward.
20.4: 20.4 For you have prevented him. CASSIODORUS. Diapsalma; he describes his powers and glory, etc., up to as a crown for the head. Crown. Ibid. Because the circuit of the Apostles surrounded the teacher, or the whole circle of the world, that is, the universal Church.
20.6: 20.6 In your salvation: glory and great beauty, etc. CASSIODORUS. By the Word of the Father, what glory comes from there. Glory from judgment, because he will judge in the Godhead. Beauty in majesty, which will then appear. Glory and great beauty, etc. Glorious, like Peter, by whose shadow the sick were healed; and beauty is upon him, besides whom there is no other foundation. Therefore upon him, for you will give.
20.7: 20.7 In joy with your countenance. For the king hopes in the Lord, and in mercy, etc. THE SAME. That is, concerning this, that his own will rejoice with your presence, when you will be all in all.
20.9: 20.9 Let your hand be found, etc. THE SAME. On the punishments of the enemies, as above on the praises of Christ.
20.11: 20.11 Their fruit you will destroy from the earth, and their seed. There will be for them no fruit of blessedness in the land of the living.
20.13: 20.13 For you will set. CASSIODORUS. Things said about the future, etc., up to so that when they thought to kill, salvation came about.
20.14: 20.14 Be exalted. THE SAME. The conclusion.
21.2: 21.2 God, God. CASSIODORUS. A complaint of abandonment is put first, and also a prayer, as in all the psalms on the passion. AUGUSTINE, CASSIODORUS. God, God: he doubles it from affection, or God of all by the power of creation, my own properly by worship. AUGUSTINE. When he said this on the cross, he indicated that this psalm was written of him. Look upon me. CASSIODORUS. This is not in the Hebrew but was added by the Septuagint translators. Why have you forsaken me? AUGUSTINE. This is marvelous, since God was also with him; but it is for us, who are in him his body. Far from my salvation, that is, of my old man, because salvation is far from sinners, and these are words not of justice but of sins. Or, far from salvation are the words of my sins, which are to be taken away.
21.3: 21.3 I will cry. AUGUSTINE. He says it of us, his body, as when he says: 'Let this cup pass from me,' that is, he is thought to have feared to die; but he said this for his weak ones who fear to die, so this too is the voice of the members: I will cry and you will not hear. By day, and you will not hear, and by night and not to folly. CASSIODORUS. Because there is no darkness in him, and yet he is not heard unto bodily safety.
21.4: 21.4 You dwell in the holy place. AUGUSTINE. And so it is marvelous, because you delivered the fathers; but I am a worm. CASSIODORUS. You dwell in the holy place, because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. The praise of Israel, AUGUSTINE. that is, of one who sees you, not of him who wished to hide himself from your sight.
21.5: 21.5 In you our fathers hoped, they hoped. CASSIODORUS. Great beauty, while he repeats 'they hoped.'
21.7: 21.7 But I, etc. AUGUSTINE. Up to here Christ in the person of the old man, here now he speaks properly in his own person. But I. Now properly Christ: I was born without seed, that I might be beyond men in man, in whom I was made a reproach, so that even thus the pride of man might imitate the humble. A worm and no man, a reproach. CASSIODORUS. So basely trampled, etc., up to a worm, born without intercourse, mortal, humble and vile, creeping in silence.
21.9: 21.9 He hoped in the Lord, etc. CASSIODORUS. Saying: Hope in the Lord, etc. The irony of the Jews, behold as it were a historical narration, not prophecy, that there may be no excuse, no ambiguity.
21.10: 21.10 From the breasts. Not from the time I began to nurse, etc., up to but you were my God. From the womb.
21.11: 21.11 From the womb. AUGUSTINE. Not only of the mother, which is the law of birth for all; but from the darkness of the Synagogue, in which he is unfaithful, not yet born in the light of Christ, who trusts in those carnal observances of the sabbath and circumcision.
21.12: 21.12 Depart not from me, you who have already begun. You drew me out: not a man, lest the Virgin's childbirth be doubted; it was done by the power of God. My hope from the breasts: true humanity and great perfection; for from the breasts he does what a mature man hardly does. On you I was cast, not into the sins of man. Others are cast into Adam, from which they are guilty. From my mother's womb, you are my God. CASSIODORUS. Neither was the conception without God, nor in sin, as man's; whence the Angel: 'The Holy Spirit shall come upon you.'
21.13: 21.13 They have surrounded. THE SAME. The passion is described, which the prayer ends; to convict the Jews he relates things to come as past.
21.14: 21.14 They have opened. THE SAME. Like beasts wishing to swallow, their mouth, not opened to wisdom. Like a lion. AUGUSTINE. As a lion seizing they surrounded, as roaring they opened the mouth.
21.15: 21.15 Like water. When water is poured out, etc., up to whence, leaving him, they fled. CASSIODORUS. As water is the sacrament, the washing away of sins, etc., up to and it was made solid. Like wax. He rightly compares the mysteries of the law to wax, etc., up to for they have surrounded. In the midst of my belly. AUGUSTINE. The belly signifies the weak in the Church, or the memory of the Church.
21.16: 21.16 My strength is dried up like a potsherd. CASSIODORUS. Not like hay, but like a potsherd, which is made firmer by fire. My tongue. AUGUSTINE. Those through whom I was to speak kept my precepts to themselves: and through them I was led into kinship with those who were the dust of death.
21.17: 21.17 They dug. THE SAME. The Gospel narrative. Even if this is literal, the digging of the hands signifies that they did not believe his works; of the feet, that they tore the Apostles. CASSIODORUS: they dug. The dug earth bears fruit; so Christ wounded gave the fruit of life.
21.18: 21.18 They have numbered all my bones. CASSIODORUS. The punishment of the cross is properly described. So they numbered the bones, that is, the Apostles; they sought to extinguish them lest they grow to a greater number. They looked upon me. THE SAME. With diligence and delight, though the eyes are accustomed to turn away from a cruel sight. See how obstinate, nothing done by chance, nor was the heart softened by so many miracles.
21.19: 21.19 They parted my garments among them, etc. AUGUSTINE. His sacraments could be divided through heresies, but not the tunic from above, that is, given by God; this is charity or unity, which no one can divide. CASSIODORUS. But perhaps it also comes to some by the gift of God, etc., up to like the olive branch brought by the dove to the ark. AUGUSTINE. Or, through the single soul, head and body, which as one rejects diversities.
21.22: 21.22 From the unicorns, my lowliness, etc. THE SAME. The Jews, seeking only earthly things: or, boasting of the worship of God as theirs alone, or being proud as the only ones, even after the servants having killed the son.
21.24: 21.24 You who fear the Lord, praise him, etc. CASSIODORUS. Human fear produces not praise but blame.
21.25: 21.25 Let all the seed of Israel fear him, for he has not despised, etc. He opens whom he called the seed of Jacob, adding: of the poor. AUGUSTINE. Not of him who cries out in the words of sins about a vain life, but of one not swollen with the pomps of the world.
21.26: 21.26 With you is my praise in the great Church, etc. THE SAME. He places praise with God, who teaches that one should not presume in man.
21.27: 21.27 They shall praise the Lord who seek him: they shall live. THE SAME. The poor praise God, the rich themselves: therefore the poor, because they praise God in order to seek him, and he himself is the riches of the poor. Their hearts shall remember for ever and ever and shall be converted to the Lord. THE SAME. Because he is the food of the heart.
21.30: 21.30 They have eaten and have adored. THE SAME. Let him not forbid the steward to eat, but warn the exactor to fear. In his sight they shall fall. CASSIODORUS. The Church receives both, but he himself sees and discerns.
21.32: 21.32 It shall be declared, etc. THE SAME. Or to the angels who offer the prayers of men to God, not for instruction but for ministry. CASSIODORUS. Note that the psalms on the passion end in great hope of Christians, that it may be known that salvation comes from the passion.
22.1: 22.1 A psalm of David. CASSIODORUS. The prophet foretold the return of the people from Babylon. The Lord rules me. A psalm of mercy, enumerating ten graces, so that all may hope in the mercy of God. AUGUSTINE. The Church speaks of Christ.
22.2: 22.2 In a place of pasture. CASSIODORUS. The first grace, the place of pasture, that is, the divine word, which fattens those who meditate. Beside the water. The second grace, the water of refreshment.
22.3: 22.3 My soul. THE SAME. The third grace, etc., up to but first he led me beside the water of refreshment, but first he converted my soul. He led. THE SAME. The fourth, that he led over the precepts of charity. In the paths. AUGUSTINE. The stricter commandments and more perfect counsels, as few just men walk in paths, as paths are narrower than roads.
22.4: 22.4 For though. CASSIODORUS. The fifth, that in the shadow of death he fears no evils. You are with me. AUGUSTINE. In the heart through faith, so that after the shadow of death I may be with you. Your rod. CASSIODORUS. The sixth, correction; or the rod is strictness, which turns vices around. The staff is governance, which sustains the faithful.
22.5: 22.5 You have prepared in my sight. CASSIODORUS. The seventh, the table of the Lord, the blessed banquet, the fullness of faith, heavenly food, of which the Apostle says: 'He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself.' In my sight a table: though not of the impious. Of this it is said: 'But these at the table of the rich man,' that is, of Christ, know that you too ought to prepare like things, that is, to suffer as he did. You have anointed: the eighth, the anointing of the head, namely Christ, which was dried up by no aridity of sin, whence the other members rejoice, because from the head the ointment goes down to the beard, the beard of Aaron, and to the hem of his garment. And my cup. The ninth, the cup, the blood of Christ, which so inebriates as to make sober. Mine, because I receive. Or, yours, because you give. The table and the cup, flesh and blood, though they are one sacrament, yet under different species, because both are taken, are placed here separately.
22.6: 22.6 And mercy. CASSIODORUS. The tenth, mercy following for guarding what preceded for conferring grace. And that I may dwell. JEROME. This is joined to all the above. As if: you placed me, brought me up, led me, etc., and this so that I may dwell.
23.1: 23.1 A psalm of David. AUGUSTINE. On the first day of the week the world was made, on the same man was restored through the resurrection of Christ: CASSIODORUS. whence it admonishes to receive the victor with triumph. The earth is the Lord's. First he says that the whole world is God's, etc., up to but who on his mountain, except the innocent?
23.2: 23.2 And upon the rivers. AUGUSTINE. As rivers into the sea, so the covetous slip into the world; and the Church overcomes even them, who, desires conquered, is prepared for immortality.
23.3: 23.3 Who shall ascend? He determines with what virtues those in the Church are endowed.
23.4: 23.4 Who shall stand? JEROME. For many ascend who do not remain. THE SAME. Innocent: toward his neighbor, in hand and heart, and he who is innocent to himself, etc., up to may they desire presence and knowledge. Who has not received. AUGUSTINE, JEROME. That is, who has not assigned his soul to things that do not abide, but sensing it to be immortal will desire eternal things, and therefore has not sworn deceitfully. In vain. JEROME. That is, who has stained it with no dregs of sins after baptism.
23.7: 23.7 Lift up. Diapsalma. The Christian religion having been declared, etc., up to which were set by the prince, the devil. And be lifted up. Against the gates of death. Eternal gates: all the grace which was given at the coming of Christ.
23.8: 23.8 Who is? He asks. The Prophet, to convict the faithlessness of the Jews, and by commending him further to invite others.
23.10: 23.10 The Lord strong is described through powers as by a proper name. Strong, AUGUSTINE. though you took him with swords. Mighty, though you handed him over to Pilate. Mighty in battle, lest you think you overcame him in the fight. Powers. JEROME, AUGUSTINE. The ministering ones, going before Christ in the ascension, cry to the other heavenly ones to open the way for the Lord coming: who, astonished at him clothed in flesh by a new mystery, ask, who is he? Lift up. CASSIODORUS. The doubling, etc., up to who gives all good things to all, or of the heavenly powers, that is, of the angels.
24.1: 24.1 Unto the end. JEROME. Here one scourged and repenting is set before others, lest they murmur in adversities: having experienced in himself, he coaxes through mercy, terrifies through justice. To you, O Lord, I have lifted up. AUGUSTINE. A psalm against the adversities of the world, etc., up to who not through all, the less perfect. CASSIODORUS. First he asks to be taught the ways of the Lord, because he is lifted up toward God. THE SAME. To contemplate you; he easily despises earthly things who beholds the divine.
24.2: 24.2 I trust. THE SAME. Having experienced my weakness in evils, I will not be ashamed before enemies. Neither let my enemies deride me: and I am certain that he fails in nothing who endures patiently. Without cause. THE SAME. Because all things are vain and fruitless that are alien from God. Show me your ways, O Lord. CASSIODORUS. The ways concern the order of life, etc., up to: Direct, pertains to life, teach to knowledge.
24.5: 24.5 Teach. AUGUSTINE. The very truth, that I may understand what I believe, because I have waited, and if this is not enough: Remember. God my savior. CASSIODORUS. There are two things that make men good: that we believe God to be savior, and that we patiently await his recompense.
24.6: 24.6 Remember. THE SAME. About former sins and those that are done daily, he prays through the mercy shown to the ancients, and because he fears the true judge. Of your compassions. Compassion properly lies in the bestowal of good things. Which are from of old. AUGUSTINE. That is, are from the beginning of the age: therefore let it not fail in me.
24.7: 24.7 Sins. CASSIODORUS. They are when the way of equity is left. Of youth. Not for age, but for the boldness of precipitation, which is when the heat of mind exceeds modesty. Ignorances. We do things which we do not know to be evil. Or the sins of ignorance in little ones, who are held by original sin. JEROME. Of youth. Before I went out from the house of the unjust father. Remember me, you. AUGUSTINE. Whose work it is to show mercy and forgive sins. According to your mercy. That is, your mercy is ample. Mercy toward the wretched, goodness toward anyone. God does good both when implored by the wretched and led by his goodness: none is good but God.
24.8: 24.8 Sweet. THE SAME. Because he forgives all former things, where grace is without merits. Upright. Because after mercy, etc., up to Sweet, because he gives pleasant things; upright, because he corrects. Therefore. CASSIODORUS. Because he is sweet and upright; not from cruelty but from kindness. In the way. That is, in faith, or the precepts of God. Or in the way of this life, where one must live rightly, he will give the law.
24.9: 24.9 In judgment. While he punishes, he will direct to better things. But let those who are rebuked be meek: as wild creatures tamed, so that they bear it. Because if they are mild, that is, of gentle mind, as having this naturally: he will teach them the precepts, for neglect of which the scourges came.
24.10: 24.10 Mercy and truth. AUGUSTINE. But what ways he will teach, etc., up to and then he guards against the severity of the judge. Testament. CASSIODORUS. The New, which is excellently called a Testament, where there is a clear and certain promise of inheritance which is also confirmed by death. And Testament. Of the old law, where the Prophets were witnesses of the promises.
24.11: 24.11 For your name's sake, O Lord. AUGUSTINE. That is, your glory, etc., up to and they are interpreted as the clean, who assert that they are clean of all sin.
24.12: 24.12 Who is the man? CASSIODORUS. Here he treats of eternal things; how they are held, laboring and praying that both he himself and all Israel be freed from these evils.
24.13: 24.13 Soul. THE SAME. and if not at once, etc., up to whatever others do, etc. Seed. JEROME. It is good, whence fruit is gathered. Is a support. AUGUSTINE. Fear seems to belong to the weak, but the Lord is a support to those who fear him, and makes his Testament manifest to them. Eyes. SOLOMON. The eyes of the wise man are in his head, that is, in his heart.
24.16: 24.16 Only-begotten. THE SAME. The only one is loved more, the poor man is grieved over more.
24.17: 24.17 From my necessities. That is, from adversities, which are necessary for all who wish to live piously in Christ.
24.19: 24.19 Look. AUGUSTINE. The perdition of so many men cannot be without sorrow, and therefore he prays for them.
24.21: 24.21 The innocent and the upright have adhered. THE SAME. The wicked were tolerated; they did not adhere.
24.22: 24.22 Israel. AUGUSTINE. The people whom you have prepared for your vision.
25.1: 25.1 A psalm. CASSIODORUS. This psalm admonishes to avoid the company of the wicked and to be joined to the just, because manners are formed by living together. Judge. AUGUSTINE. Because after mercy, etc., up to are carried off by the wind of pride. CASSIODORUS. Judge: this is not the presumption of the just man but the certainty of God's mercy, which he shows there hoping in the Lord; then, I shall not be weakened. In innocence. AUGUSTINE. Not of angels, but such as is of men.
25.2: 25.2 Prove me. CASSIODORUS. That is, first examine my strength, etc., up to not merits, but I attend to the mercy which made me such. CASSIODORUS. Prove me. But you, prove in temptations, lest any sin remain, etc., up to lest anyone murmur about them. Burn my reins. THE SAME. With the fire of your word, the heart with the heat of the spirit. The heart for thoughts, the reins for delights.
25.3: 25.3 Mercy. CASSIODORUS. Which does not allow one to be tempted beyond his strength, or the burning itself is mercy, not harshness. I have been pleasing in truth. AUGUSTINE. To whom his own lie is displeasing, and he himself is pleased with truth and in it.
25.4: 25.4 I have not sat. CASSIODORUS. I have been pleasing in truth, because I have not sat. I hated, which is to avoid evils. And I will wash, which is to do what is right. Vain. CASSIODORUS. The vain are those who labor over perishable things; the impious are heretics, who pervert the Scriptures: the former seek superfluous things, the latter poisonous ones.
25.5: 25.5 Of the malignant. THE SAME. Who do evil to their neighbors.
25.6: 25.6 I will wash. AUGUSTINE. By doing penance. And the altar, I will adorn the mind with virtues, or faith, because there is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church. Among the innocent. AUGUSTINE. Dwelling; that I may hear from them, that is, that I may learn with what voice you are to be praised; or, that I may hear: 'Come, you blessed of my Father.'
25.7: 25.7 The voice of praise of the Holy Spirit, who teaches to praise you.
25.8: 25.8 Lord. CASSIODORUS. He asks not to be mingled with the wicked in judgment, because he does not agree with them but with the house of God. I have loved the beauty. CASSIODORUS. I will do these things because I have loved to make for you a beautiful house, and a place where you may dwell gloriously, that I may take something of the glory and essence of God.
25.9: 25.9 Destroy not. CASSIODORUS. Even if now you allow us to be together, do not destroy together. CASSIODORUS. Do not destroy in the future with the impious, with whom I have no communion here.
25.10: 25.10 Their right hand, AUGUSTINE, that is, if they do any good, etc., up to may mercy accompany in all things, which you owe, because:
25.12: 25.12 The foot, that is, the affection, which easily slips, has stood immovable against all scandals, stretching forward, and persisting straight. And because you thus redeem in the Churches, I will bless. It has stood. CASSIODORUS. Though shaken or confounded by scandals on every side.
26.1: 26.1 Unto the end. AUGUSTINE, CASSIODORUS. First, David chosen, etc., up to whence in the sacrament groaning and laboring, so as to rejoice in the reality. The Lord is my light, etc. CASSIODORUS. He speaks here of the first anointing, by which the second is made certain. The Lord is the protector of my life. AUGUSTINE. He gives the life of virtues, which he also protects, without which all his gifts are lost. Of whom shall I be afraid? THE SAME. Whom shall the flesh fear, when it has put on incorruption.
26.2: 26.2 Those who harm me. THE SAME. That they may put themselves before me in insulting: which God turned to the better, that with a slanderous tooth they consume not me but carnal desires. Or let them eat, that is, let the cruelty of the enemies delight in my death, flesh; they cannot the soul. They were weakened. THE SAME. When Christ took flesh, they became wavering, and afterward subjected themselves wholly to the faith. CASSIODORUS. Or, weakened little by little they came to the ruin of the soul.
26.3: 26.3 Camps. CASSIODORUS. Endeavors, battle, conflict. In this I. AUGUSTINE. I have hope of victory in the Lord, of eternal reward.
26.4: 26.4 One thing I have asked. AUGUSTINE. This is the one eternal house, in which one always remains, where the days are eternal; why there? that I may contemplate the delight of God, which is the true good. All the days of my life. AUGUSTINE. That as long as I live, etc., up to I will manifest the work. That I may see. THE SAME. Another reading: That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord, that is, to the end that at last it may appear, etc., up to and therefore I do not rashly ask one thing, though a sinner.
26.5: 26.5 In the hidden place: AUGUSTINE. as there are many parts, etc., up to whom he soon calls a rock.
26.6: 26.6 I have gone about. AUGUSTINE. Because he offered himself to me as leader, etc., up to that I might fulfill all his wills. JEROME. Or I have looked around at all created things, or the examples of the saints. AUGUSTINE. I have gone about all created things in mind, etc., up to the more ardently he seeks.
26.7: 26.7 Hear, O Lord, my voice, etc. CASSIODORUS. What labor, what groaning! A prayer before the second anointing, that he may have what he promises himself by the spirit of prophecy.
26.8: 26.8 To you my heart has said. CASSIODORUS. The heart, reason taught by you, converses with you about the one thing, and turns over nothing other than what you teach.
26.9: 26.9 Turn not away. AUGUSTINE. One person here asks temporal goods from God and rejoices in what is given; this one asks only one thing. Another, having them, fears God angry lest he take them away; this one does not consider it anger unless he turns away his face, even if he punishes something in him; he could have said nothing more divine. Decline not. AUGUSTINE. He does not decline in anger when he turns his face away from sins; or, decline not, so that you let me slip in anger, that is, that you punish; but that our weakness may become more cautious. My savior, etc. AUGUSTINE. As if: in vain you created and recreated, etc., up to was chosen by the Lord through Samuel.
26.10: 26.10 For my father, etc. He made himself a little child to God, he made him his father: because he commands, calls, founded, and rules. Mother, because he cherishes, contains, nurses together, and nourishes; but the world is the father, or the devil, the mother Babylon, that is, the society of the impious.
26.12: 26.12 Of those troubling me. CASSIODORUS. Such as Saul and his helpers, etc., up to because false.
26.13: 26.13 I believe to see. AUGUSTINE. But amid all dangers, God directing, I believe to see. The good things. THE SAME. The good things, which are true, eternal. They persuade to a happiness on this earth, which is that of the dying.
26.14: 26.14 Wait. CASSIODORUS. As I am certain about that, etc., up to endure what you suffer.
27.1: 27.1 A psalm to this. By David is sometimes understood the head, that is, Christ; sometimes the body, that is, the Church; at times both together, that is, the whole Christ is understood, as here. CASSIODORUS. The third psalm, which briefly treats of the passion and resurrection. THE SAME. Here Christ is set forth as, though so worthy, not trusting in himself but asking everything from God; a useful example to the just. To you, O Lord. THE SAME. A prayer made at the time of the passion. Be not silent. There is less in the Hebrew, etc., up to and the raising from death. Be not silent, etc., and I shall be like, etc. JEROME. Because the Word is always united to me, I am not such a man as the rest, who are born into the deep misery of the world. AUGUSTINE. Where, as it were if you are silent, your word is not known.
27.2: 27.2 Toward the temple. CASSIODORUS. According to the custom of the Jews, who were commanded to pray, wherever they were, toward that side where they knew Jerusalem to be: which Jesus too did, fulfilling the law. Or toward heaven, whence we hope for help.
27.4: 27.4 Give them. Ibid. It is a prediction, not a wish, according to what they intended, not according to what resulted from it: or he wishes the justice of God to be preserved in this.
27.5: 27.5 Because they have not, etc. THE SAME. Even if works were lacking, this would suffice for condemnation, that they did not understand through the law and the Prophets what God works invisibly through me, nor even the visible things. You will destroy. AUGUSTINE. That nothing may harm me, nor afterward your Church, or mine. Blessed. CASSIODORUS. Heard in the resurrection, he gives thanks, adding about the salvation of believers. The Lord. THE SAME. The same who is my helper, and protector is the strength of the people who trust in him, and protector lest they be harmed, and you, O Lord:
27.9: 27.9 Save. Behold how great the hope of believers, when he prays for them: having suffered for them he is judge and advocate. And rule them, etc. THE SAME. Lest they turn aside to crooked things. Lift them up, etc., from earthly things to seeking eternal, and by understanding of the Scriptures, and good work through this whole age until the end.
28.1: 28.1 A psalm of David at the consummation. THE SAME. The ark brought back from the Philistines, etc., up to that they may offer themselves to such a consummator. Bring to the Lord. THE SAME. First he admonishes to offer sacrifices. Sons of rams. AUGUSTINE. Because assault is not lacking, etc., up to and the seventy-two disciples sent to preach are signified. The voice of the Lord. CASSIODORUS. The preaching of Christ terrified minds within, that is, gave the spirit of fear to Jews and Gentiles. GREGORY. This one ascends from the lowest, that is, from the spirit of fear to the spirit of wisdom, etc., up to that is, spiritual understanding, these the Lord shakes. JEROME. As a farmer a barren land, etc., up to and will give strength, and will bless the same in eternal peace.
28.3: 28.3 The voice of the Lord upon the waters, etc. CASSIODORUS. On the establishment of the Church, where he enumerates the powers of the Holy Spirit with great proclamation. Of Lebanon. Lebanon is interpreted 'whitening.' The cedars of Lebanon, that is, tall men exalted in earthly things, whom God by breaking will crush, that is, bring back from pride to himself through the beloved son: and by this spirit of fortitude he will crush, as a captured unicorn is crushed.
28.7: 28.7 The desert. CASSIODORUS, AUGUSTINE. The Jewish people, etc., up to from which living water flows.
28.10: 28.10 The Lord. He shows what is to happen to the established Church. 'I have given you,' he says, 'power to tread upon serpents.' And as it is unheard of for stags to strike every kind of wild beast with the horn, so the Apostles, unlettered, refuted all philosophy. The flood. CASSIODORUS. The waters of baptism, which purges the crimes of the world.
29.1: 29.1 A psalm of a canticle at the dedication. AUGUSTINE. Above, concerning the consummation of the tabernacle in time of war: but this is a psalm of gladness, because the house is dedicated, that is, confirmed, which will remain in eternal peace: the body renewed not only of Christ but also of the whole Church. The whole Christ speaks in this psalm, because some things befit the head, some the body, some both. THE SAME. A psalm briefly on the passion and resurrection: so that the passion does not terrify those whom the hope of resurrection gladdens. The house of David. CASSIODORUS. The whole Christ the bridegroom, etc., up to the second, future state when one rests in it. CASSIODORUS. First he treats of his own dedication: and commands the saints hoping for the same to speak praises.
29.3: 29.3 O Lord my God, I cried to you, etc. AUGUSTINE. Christ, etc., up to but not in the dedication.
29.4: 29.4 Into the pit. JEROME. That is, from the pit of hell, where the souls of sinners are, lest, like them, I fall headlong into death.
29.5: 29.5 Give praise, etc. AUGUSTINE. Because out of his own goodness and holiness, not ours, he was mindful of us.
29.6: 29.6 For wrath. THE SAME. That is, vengeance, with which he avenged on us the first sin, which you loosed by death. Toward evening. THE SAME. Because wrath, etc., up to that is, in the time of grace after the time before the law, and under the law. JEROME. Toward evening. Because when the Lord had suffered and been buried, the Apostles and the women remained in weeping and groaning. And in the morning gladness. Because coming in the morning to the sepulcher, they received from the Angels the glory of the resurrection. Weeping. CASSIODORUS. Will tarry for men looking to the evening, when Adam declined and went out of paradise: but gladness will be for those looking to the morning, when Christ rose.
29.7: 29.7 But I. How he acted before the dedication and merited it. AUGUSTINE, CASSIODORUS. It makes evening. But I, while I was in paradise with abundance, said: I shall not be moved from this good, believing the devil saying: 'You shall not die the death' (Genesis 3). But, O Lord, in your will you gave strength to my beauty; that is, I was not good and strong from myself but from you. To show this: You turned away your face, that is, you sent me outside paradise: but now placed here I will cry to you, etc.
29.8: 29.8 You turned away. CASSIODORUS. God turned his face from Christ, by exposing him to passion and death; and so Christ was troubled: 'My soul is sorrowful even unto death' (Matthew 16). Troubled. AUGUSTINE. Recalling this time of trouble and misery, and placed in it, I hear the voice of the head about to die for me, saying: To you, O Lord, I will cry.
29.10: 29.10 What profit is there in my blood. THE SAME. He shows the necessity through which he does not allow him to descend into corruption. While I descend into corruption. For if I do not rise at once and the body is corrupted, I will announce to no one, I will gain no one. Confession is twofold, let us never be without it: when it goes ill with us in tribulations, let us confess our sins; when it goes well, in the exultation of justice let us confess praise to God.
29.11: 29.11 The Lord heard. CASSIODORUS. How he received it, namely the dedication, he treats. He said: I will cry, I will entreat, but the Lord heard me entreating.
29.12: 29.12 You have rent my sackcloth. THE SAME. Sackcloth is a rough garment, allowed for use in labor or in time of sadness, as for the Ninevites, that is, human flesh, which was rent in dying: and the grain of the glorious resurrection, or of divinity, came forth. Or, the punishment of sin, which being destroyed in the resurrection, the divinity previously hidden was brought forth: as what a whole sackcloth conceals, a rent one reveals. AUGUSTINE. Sackcloth from goats or kids, mortality; which Christ drew or received from sinners; whence: 'When they were troublesome to me, I was clothed with haircloth' (Psalm 34), that they might not see what was within.
29.13: 29.13 That I may not be pricked. THE SAME. That I may not die now unto the end. O Lord my God, I will give praise to you for ever. What is it: I will give praise to you for ever? I will praise you for ever.
30.1: 30.1 Unto the end, a psalm. AUGUSTINE. 'Ecstasy' here is taken as the dread of the troubled people over the persecution of all nations and the failure of faith throughout the world. CASSIODORUS. Against dread, hope and prayer are put first, etc., up to: 'They shall be two in one flesh' (Genesis 2), therefore also in one voice. AUGUSTINE. First the Redeemer speaks, then the redeemed, giving thanks. Then for a long while the voice of the Prophet on the disturbance is interposed near the end, and at the end. Here the humiliation of Christ and the martyrs is described: whence the exaltation follows.
30.2: 30.2 In you, O Lord, I have hoped, etc. THE SAME. There is an eternal confusion, from which he asks to be freed: and there is a temporal one for an hour, namely which is profitable.
30.3: 30.3 Hasten. THE SAME. In things to be done, in releasing souls and the like, that you may deliver on the third day, not delaying to the common resurrection; that this may be, be to me a protector as great as it befits God to be. Be to me. He said: Give justice, etc., up to he affirms deliverance.
30.5: 30.5 You will bring me out. CASSIODORUS. From death to the heights, so that the counsels of the Jews are in vain. Out of the snare which they hid. AUGUSTINE. Through two gates the devil tempts, etc., up to whence: You will bring me out of the snare.
30.6: 30.6 Into your hands. CASSIODORUS. Note that he speaks here who uttered the same words in the passion. AUGUSTINE. Into your hands. From these words which he said on the cross, he admonishes that he spoke in this psalm.
30.8: 30.8 But I, in the Lord, etc. CASSIODORUS. On joy, because he hopes in the Lord, who hates the vain. I will exult and be glad. To exult is to rejoice with great eagerness of mind; to be glad, with tempered affection. My lowliness. He takes it both for weakness and for the very virtue of humility. Necessities. AUGUSTINE. The necessities are infinite, etc., up to and in the future fully.
30.9: 30.9 In a spacious place. CASSIODORUS. The spacious place for going freely to the fatherland of virtues is charity: but because the flesh is weak and evils press: Have mercy on me, O Lord. Now the dread is recounted, that is, how many and how great are the things that disturb, against which there is prayer, I am troubled. AUGUSTINE. When before he said: 'You have set my feet in a spacious place,' etc. But to some the spacious place comes from the joy of deliverance; to others from tribulation, straitness. Troubled. He is angry for the sins of the chaff, etc., up to for the life of the perfect is the progress of others. The eye in anger. In the anger of the persecutors, etc., up to that God may be sought from all ranks. CASSIODORUS. Or the understanding is disturbed, and the mind is confounded, etc., up to neither in mind nor in body can any presumption of man be. AUGUSTINE. Anger through vice blinds the eye of the mind; anger through zeal disturbs: because this too, the mind being shaken, scatters contemplation, which is only in a quiet mind; but afterward in a little while it profits more for seeing.
30.11: 30.11 In poverty. THE SAME. Or want. I lack health of body, and the torments are not spared. I lack dissolution, and death is spared; and in this my confidence is weakened.
30.12: 30.12 Above all my enemies. THE SAME. They live worse than pagans and Jews, etc., up to for whom they fear and are known, lest all be such. CASSIODORUS. Or among all enemies, or held in greater reproach than those who deserve it; and to neighbors, kinsmen, or those about to believe; and to acquaintances, friends.
30.13: 30.13 They who saw me outside. JEROME. Outside, Christ, that is, who thought him a mere man. I am given over to oblivion as one dead from the heart. CASSIODORUS. Or I have fallen from their heart, like one dead whose memory is buried with the body, of whose restoration there is despair. A lost vessel, the dead Jesus is thought to be cast away.
30.14: 30.14 The blame of many. AUGUSTINE. They are blamed, etc., up to not any man. Round about. In him while they came together. CASSIODORUS. Of errors, etc., up to that is, by desire of temporal things.
30.16: 30.16 My lots. THE SAME. Or the times of life. AUGUSTINE. Because when you will, we live or die: therefore deliver. Even if just, and the hidden order of election is with you, I yet, etc., up to which, without merits, chooses whom he wills.
30.17: 30.17 Make to shine. CASSIODORUS. Make your goodwill manifest upon me, that as they despair of me dying, so they may trust in me rising. AUGUSTINE. Make to shine. Let it appear who belongs to you when there is now confusion; hence elsewhere: 'Distinguish my cause' (Psalm 41); yet lest he seem to justify himself, he adds: Save me in your mercy, not in my justice.
30.18: 30.18 I have called upon. THE SAME. You call upon God when you call him into yourself, and when you invite him into the house of your heart.
30.19: 30.19 Let them be made dumb. CASSIODORUS. Who here are talkative while they do not fear judgment. Dumb in punishments, in hell. Which speak. Aptly he opposes iniquity to the just man. In pride and in abuse. CASSIODORUS. Because the creature acts against the creator, and by the perverse use of God's benefits, he who, among other things, came on their account.
30.20: 30.20 How great. CASSIODORUS. What goods of God against the aforesaid evils, which lighten the evils themselves. AUGUSTINE. Seeing and marveling at these things the Prophet exclaims, etc., up to but in the future it will be revealed.
30.21: 30.21 From the disturbance. AUGUSTINE. So that he no longer suffers any human disturbance, even those now in tribulation, entering in mind to the face of God, are not disturbed. You will protect. CASSIODORUS. Lest the promise of the future alone disturb, he adds this: you will protect, lest they be harmed.
30.22: 30.22 Blessed. THE SAME. As if, what more? He concludes with praise the fullness of the benefit, comparing it with his own weakness. And the Prophet speaks, or the faithful people. He has made wonderful. AUGUSTINE. By sending the Spirit, he filled the whole world, etc., up to whence: 'Your name is ointment poured out.' CASSIODORUS. Or, God the Father made wonderful his mercy, etc., up to according to that: 'He rested in the heart of the earth.'
30.23: 30.23 I said in my excess. AUGUSTINE. The type of our fear, etc., up to: Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer. AUGUSTINE. In excess of mind. Or, with mind rapt he saw the height from which he feels himself cast very far: or he went out of reason by fearing. From the face of your eyes. If I were in your face, etc., up to but I accused my heart.
30.24: 30.24 Love the Lord, all, etc. CASSIODORUS. An oratorical or hortatory conclusion, for obtaining what was said. AUGUSTINE. Having now experienced the aforesaid, he exhorts us; as if: I was in tribulation, I feared, I cried, I was not confounded: so you too. His saints, whose part it is to love God, because they do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world; the friend of this world is made an enemy of God. Learn therefore not to love the world, that you may learn to love God: turn away, that you may be converted; pour out, that you may be filled. The Lord will require, etc. Even here at times, if he did this to no one, divine providence would not seem to watch, if divine patience were not preserved for all. To those who act abundantly. Who do not quickly repent. Pride. For every vice, because it is the root of all.
30.25: 30.25 Act manfully, etc. The strength of the whole psalm, that the frailty of the flesh not fear so many evils of the world.
31.1: 31.1 Understanding of David. AUGUSTINE. A psalm on the grace by which we are Christians, as the Apostle says (Romans 4). This psalm therefore begins with forgiveness, acting against the vice of men who do not know their sins or defend them and boast of merits. CASSIODORUS. Against the vice of men, therefore, this psalm is set, etc., up to in which standing he confirms them. Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, etc. AUGUSTINE. Not those in whom he has not found sin, but to whom he has forgiven. Iniquities. He speaks of the tinder of sin, namely concupiscibility, etc., up to but that sin may be no more. JEROME. Iniquities, before faith and baptism: sin, after faith and baptism.
31.2: 31.2 Blessed is the man. JEROME. To whom God forgives, for it is not through himself. He covers, lest it be revealed in judgment; and thus it will not be imputed to punishment. There is no guile in one who accuses himself: he holds in the heart what he confesses here with the mouth. Blessed: because formerly, not confessing to God, I fell into sin, while I cried out, if I did anything good.
31.3: 31.3 I was silent. AUGUSTINE. He who does not wish to confess sins labors without cause in the defense of sins: in which, when he even boasts of merits, his strength fails the more. CASSIODORUS. Blessed is he to whom he has not imputed. To some, who have grave sins, God imputes; to others through mercy he does not impute, even if they have some, namely those who do not proclaim themselves just when they are wicked but, acknowledging themselves, make satisfaction; now I profess this, but formerly: Because I was silent, etc. AUGUSTINE. Or, I was silent, with the voice of sin, while I cried out all day: while the punishment of sin, or interior blinding, showed me to be a sinner, or while my wicked life, I being silent, cried out, if I did anything good. While I cried out all day, etc. Even if one is not conscious to himself, he is yet not just: for who understands sins? Whence: 'There is a just man who perishes in his justice.' And the Apostle: 'I am conscious of nothing against myself,' etc.
31.4: 31.4 The thorn is fixed. CASSIODORUS. The thorn, which raises the whole body upright, that is, pride. AUGUSTINE. Likewise hardship, etc., up to: in the hands of a drunkard.
31.5: 31.5 My sin. Diapsalma. Confession, whence pardon, as above, of ruling, the growing old. I have made known. CASSIODORUS. For I said before, etc., up to and God hears.
31.6: 31.6 For this shall pray. THE SAME. Diapsalma. Commending penitence, he says it is common to all the saints; which the various sects reject, against whom he flees to God. AUGUSTINE. For this. Thence every saint prays, because you have forgiven; otherwise he would not be a saint. In a seasonable time, etc. The time is of grace, the law pressing, convicting the guilty, compelled them to cry out, grace heals. But in the flood, etc. AUGUSTINE. Although the saint prays, etc., up to the saint will pray, saying: You are my refuge. To him. God; for he changes the person as often. They do not come near who say fate makes them sin, or fortune, which rules all things, or the race of darkness, which rebels against God.
31.8: 31.8 I will give you understanding. THE SAME. Diapsalma. The penitent is answered: I will give you understanding, etc. Behold the psalm of understanding, lest the suppliant be thought neglected, God being witness. You, deliver. CASSIODORUS. You who promised, I will give you understanding. Or Christ answers the penitent: A joyful end, God gives understanding: whence he exhorts others to the same.
31.9: 31.9 Be not like the horse and the mule, etc. AUGUSTINE. Having received understanding, this penitent turns to the proud defending sins: therefore you, whom I invite, etc. The horse, the untamed Gentile; the mule, the Jew slow to believe. CASSIODORUS. The horse, without discrimination of riders; the mule takes whatever loads, etc., up to that is, boasting of their strength. Jaws. Or, the jaws with which they chew, that is, more sparingly, give provisions, that compelled by necessity they may return. AUGUSTINE. Or here you will break, and in the future there will be many scourges. Or: Be not like the horse, because many are the scourges here and in the future. Who do not draw near to you. CASSIODORUS. For there are those who, if they sin through weakness of the flesh, do not withdraw from pious prayers.
31.10: 31.10 Many are the scourges of the sinner, etc. AUGUSTINE. After the bridle scourges are added for taming, lest it be as with those unpunished ones to whom for now a wandering license of their way is given: so this one said above that he was tamed.
32.1: 32.1 Unto the end. CASSIODORUS. Here the prophet enumerates the power and deeds of God, and so invites to the praise of God; first, he admonishes the just and upright to praise, because we cannot exult in him except by praising: 'praise,' he says, 'befits the upright.' Rejoice, etc. AUGUSTINE. The crooked man praises God when it is well with him; blasphemes when it is ill: the upright always, like Job.
32.2: 32.2 Harp. THE SAME. It sounds from below, and is from the earth, whence let us praise, that is, prosperity and adversity, which are for us from him. On the psaltery. While you attend to the higher things he has given you, the heavenly doctrine. By the harp the flesh, by the psaltery charity is understood: to which the ten precepts of the law pertain: three in the first table toward God, seven in the second toward the neighbor.
32.3: 32.3 Sing to him, etc. As if: what more shall I say? rejoice especially over the incarnation. A new canticle. CASSIODORUS. Because it is not enough, unless your justice abound more than that of the Scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 5). Sing a new canticle. Of the incarnation, over which the world exults, of which the Angels sang.
32.4: 32.4 For the word is right. He has set out the manner of praise: now why he is to be praised? And all his works. AUGUSTINE. Lest anyone think he came to faith by merits, since all works which God loves, that is, rewards, are in faith, THE SAME. because he works only in the faithful; whence: 'Your faith has made you whole' (Matthew 10). Or, all works are right, etc., up to because the wicked remains, and therefore the more wicked, because he sees the just man favoring him. In faith. As if in outward things, if one has been faithful for the cause of justice, he whom he feared without knowing him will add inward faith; whence: who will not give him what is his own, who has been faithful in another's? AUGUSTINE. God is faithful, giving man what he promised: man is faithful, believing the one who promises; from the promise God is truly our debtor.
32.5: 32.5 The earth. THE SAME. The Church everywhere on earth.
32.6: 32.6 By the word. That is, the wisdom of God the Father. The heavens. The Apostles were fully instructed, by living with him even bodily: and afterward all their strength was strengthened by the spirit of the Son; through the heavens made firm he gathers and consolidates in the unity of faith, hope and charity. The wineskin, the Church, in which is dead flesh. Even the depths, that is, the deep places of the darkness of vices, he places among those who are a treasure, from which wisdom enriches others. AUGUSTINE. The earth. The heavens do not need mercy, etc., up to what he works. Their power. When they were among wolves, etc., up to license.
32.7: 32.7 As in a wineskin. CASSIODORUS. Literally: as the sea by shores, he shuts in the Church the surging peoples; and in the treasures of his wisdom he places the deep heights, to prove who inquires into the Scriptures with zeal of piety.
32.8: 32.8 Let all the earth fear. THE SAME. The Church from the sea, etc., up to but let the earth fear the Lord. Let it fear, or rather let them be moved by the hand of mercy, by the likeness of one sleeping. By him, because he created: and therefore he administers usefully, because something is also moved by the devil, but what is moved usefully by God is therefore by him. Let them be moved. AUGUSTINE. Not by the terrors of men, etc., up to power only from God.
32.9: 32.9 He spoke and they were made. It notes creation and formation together. He commanded the re-creation.
32.10: 32.10 The Lord scatters the counsels. CASSIODORUS. That counsels against him may not take effect, as those of the Jews, and against his own. Of the nations. When he destroyed idolatry. Of the peoples. Of the Jews, whose will, though fulfilled, was nevertheless reproved by the resurrection. Of princes. Of tyrants or demons.
32.11: 32.11 But the counsel of the Lord, etc. THE SAME. The secret of the incarnation in which he took counsel for man. Remains for ever. Because it is to obtain eternal salvation for us. Thoughts. Predestination, in which all things are laid up, which also so remain as they were foreseen.
32.12: 32.12 Blessed the nation. CASSIODORUS. He calls blessed the one who has come to the worship of God: which happens in Christian times, in which the nations were converted; these are the just and upright whom praise befits. AUGUSTINE. All blessedness is in the soul, etc., up to the people blessed by God their possessor.
32.13: 32.13 From heaven. AUGUSTINE. By the man Christ. He looked forth at the coming of the Son and saw mercifully, not the sins, CASSIODORUS. from which he turned away his face; but he saw all the sons of men, that is, all who wish to be born again to a new life. AUGUSTINE. How did he choose? etc., up to he inspired every good will.
32.15: 32.15 He fashioned. AUGUSTINE. He formed by the hand of grace. Singly, giving to each certain things. JEROME. Whence nevertheless the unity of the body, that is, of the Church, comes about. Singly, that is, not from Adam, as some say the soul from the soul, and he knows all at once, and all their acts.
32.16: 32.16 The king is not saved. So the just are made, but even when made they are not saved by their own strength. Not only spiritual things are from God, but also outward ones. JEROME. No one has anything except from him, because neither the powerful like a king nor the strong, etc., up to even if he is in much abundance of strength.
32.17: 32.17 The horse is a vain thing. AUGUSTINE. An animal in whose swiftness or strength one trusts; figuratively any greatness of the world over which one is proud: but the higher you are raised in it, the more heavily you fall. CASSIODORUS. Or, the horse is the body of man, however beautiful and well formed, yet it is deceptive for bodily and spiritual safety. AUGUSTINE. Or, the horse is worldly happiness, which carries men, and while it hastens too much, the horse falls and ruins the rider. The horse, human wisdom. The giant, some proud man exalting himself against God.
32.18: 32.18 Behold the eyes. No one is saved by his own strength, but: Behold whence salvation comes, the eyes, etc. The eyes, the regard of the divinity which will protect them. Those who fear him. CASSIODORUS. To fear the Lord and always to hope are joined.
32.19: 32.19 To deliver, etc. THE SAME. These are the two prayers of the faithful: that in the judgment he be snatched from death, and that here he be fed with spiritual things, where is their need.
32.20: 32.20 Our soul waits for the Lord. What he thinks of the aforesaid, as a conclusion.
32.21: 32.21 For in him. AUGUSTINE. Because to those absent he sent his name through faith. We have hoped. We who are to come to God, not by our merits. CASSIODORUS. Because in him, lest anyone murmur about patience, he adds the gift, namely that he rejoices here in the Lord. And we hope in the name of Christ, whom the Prophet joyfully awaited as to come: We have hoped. It notes continuous time, because it is not right to cease, whence the weary soul can always be restored. Let your mercy be upon us, O Lord, etc. He desires the incarnation to be completed, that he may be able to be perfect. In you. He says this that all superstition and perversity may be excluded.
33.1: 33.1 A psalm of David. AUGUSTINE. Christ speaks, and in him the Christian: he teaches humility while commending the body and blood. When Christ changed his countenance, that is, the sacrifice, before the Jews, who are the kingdom of their father David, according to the verse: 'And the Lord will give him the throne of David'; the Church is the kingdom of the Father.
33.2: 33.2 I will bless. CASSIODORUS. The second psalm by an imperfect alphabet, etc., up to is glorified with him.
33.3: 33.3 In the Lord shall my soul be praised. THE SAME. For its praise is the proclamation of its Lord, as a good servant glories in the good fame of his Lord. The meek. Not the learned, not those who fast, because they are proud: but the meek, because they have temperance in all things. The meek, not being proud of their own intelligence; not bearing the yoke of God in the manner of the untamed.
33.4: 33.4 Magnify the Lord. Spiritual grace does not wish to do alone what profits many; so he calls others: Magnify, so as to draw those invited, he says what good things came to him from it: I sought the Lord. Out of all. It cannot be said in detail how great things he obtained who sought nothing other than God. Come. CASSIODORUS. Now in detail he admonishes the saints about the new countenance. As if: Magnify: and if at first, come to the joyful. Or, Magnify, and in what order? behold: Come by faith. AUGUSTINE. Come by clinging in faith, and running with the two feet of twofold charity. CASSIODORUS. The praises having been put first, he exhorts to communion. Be not confounded. AUGUSTINE. Whatever happens to the just man here, he is not ashamed, because he is always superior before God: but the proud man in adversity blushes, because he has not come to God.
33.7: 33.7 The poor man. CASSIODORUS. This one is the spiritual man here, because he comes near and is enlightened, and will not be ashamed; because, when he cries out, he is delivered from all the straits of the world at death, when he already passes to God.
33.8: 33.8 The Angel will send. Come, and as this poor man cried and was heard, in the same way he will send the Angel, etc. AUGUSTINE. He will send the Angel. Other interpreters have translated thus: 'The Angel of the Lord encamps round about those who fear him.' An angel from heaven, or a man, who is the minister of the will of God. Faulty codices have: The Lord will send the Angel.
