33.9: 33.9 Taste and see. Here openly of the sacrament which he carried in his hands. Taste the flesh and blood of Christ. Sweet is the Lord. THE SAME. And pleasant: because he is life to the one who receives, driving away all troubles in the future, that is: Hope through this for eternal life. CASSIODORUS. And because God is life, the flesh which he united to himself is life-giving.
33.10: 33.10 All his saints. CASSIODORUS. No one, however well deserving, should desist from this, nor presume security. For. AUGUSTINE. The Lord fed him who despised him, and will he forsake him who fears? He promises not superfluous things but necessary ones. There is no want. Because even in the present they have as much as nature requires.
33.11: 33.11 The rich have wanted and have suffered hunger. CASSIODORUS. Because they have not faith. They have hungered, because they are not satisfied with the body of the Lord. For what do they have who do not have God? Or, the rich have wanted, that is, they will lack the highest good, although they hunger, that is, desire. But those who seek with all zeal will have without diminution the good, which is every good.
33.12: 33.12 Come, children, hear me. Diapsalma. The sacraments of the Church having been treated, he admonishes those outside, who are receiving the first rudiments of the faith, lest the name of fear be dreaded, he adds: I will teach you, children, the fear of the Lord, as a useful thing. CASSIODORUS. Now he also warns beginners what to abstain from.
33.13: 33.13 To see good days. Because all confess that they wish to.
33.14: 33.14 Restrain. THE SAME. Note that he first says the tongue is to be restrained, since, when we wish to speak, we first move the lips, which soon follow the movement of the tongue. Restrain, you who desire life. Behold how they ought to fear.
33.15: 33.15 Turn away from evil. CASSIODORUS. This avoids guilt, etc., up to otherwise in the future he will not be caught.
33.16: 33.16 The eyes of the Lord, etc. THE SAME. On the retributions of the good and the wicked, lest in dangers the just man grow soft through some doubt. The eyes of the Lord. And do not distrust from your weakness, because the eyes. To their prayers. THE SAME. The swiftness of hearing, since the hearer dwells in them.
33.17: 33.17 The memory. AUGUSTINE. So that not even mention, etc., up to which they committed.
33.19: 33.19 The Lord is nigh. He has delivered: for he is inclined to this, because he is nigh; or, it is an allusion to the cry.
33.20: 33.20 Many are the afflictions of the just. As also in the New Testament, he is nigh, and will save, which is necessary, because many are the afflictions. CASSIODORUS. Many: from the devil, from envious men, and from themselves. He will deliver. AUGUSTINE. Not bodily, but by giving them patience: or, he will deliver spiritually.
33.21: 33.21 Bones. THE SAME. Virtues. And one, etc., so that patience may not perish.
33.22: 33.22 Worst. THE SAME. Not merely evil, even if it ends amid riches, and perfumes, and the lamentations of men, yet it is worst, because in sins it drags to hell. Those who hate. Whose? Not of all, because sinners; but of those who hate the just man, who justifies, that is, Christ, through whom he who is not reconciled perishes: but he will redeem souls, according to which the death is worst.
34.1: 34.1 Judge, O Lord. CASSIODORUS. He begins with a prayer for both sides of the fight, with a recalling of guilt, and it was for each what he deserves, showing how much he bore from adversaries, and the punishments that are rendered to them for iniquity.
34.2: 34.2 Arms and shield. JEROME. With arms he strikes enemies, with the shield he protects us. Elsewhere he calls the shield 'of good will'; the arms are we, because as we are armed by him, so he himself is armed from us. AUGUSTINE. Or, the soul of Christ, which overcame the enemies, which does nothing unless God fights through it. Take hold of arms. Make me have arms, doctrine, miracles. Shield. Constancy. Arise. Make me use what I have received.
34.3: 34.3 Pour out. Me, who am now in obscurity, glorify so evidently that you shut in and convince, that they may have nothing to bark at: and say to my soul so that all may know that its salvation is, against what they say: 'There is no salvation for him in his God' (Psalm 3). Sword. AUGUSTINE. The sword is the soul of the just. When the just abound, the sword is poured out, while the life flashes: hence the enemy is shut up, having nothing to say ill of us. THE SAME. It is a prophecy not a wish, or this concerns those to be converted.
34.5: 34.5 Let them be. THE SAME. A prophecy: or in the manner in which God does it, by just judgment, not with a bitter mind. As dust before the face of the wind. CASSIODORUS. Dissolved by God, so that they do not cohere with one another, whom divine grace does not moisten.
34.8: 34.8 Let the snare which he knows not come upon him. CASSIODORUS. Or in a good sense, the snare of the truth, which the sinner does not know. And the catch which he hid. That is, the hidden death, namely of Christ. Let it take hold of them. Namely, that they not be left to their own crimes. And into the snare let him fall. A good by which they are restrained from evils. Into the same. That is, from death itself. Into the same. AUGUSTINE. Not into another, but into him, which they set. For no wicked man does not first harm himself.
34.9: 34.9 But my soul shall rejoice. CASSIODORUS. Hope of good and joy having been put first, he relates how maliciously they act toward the kind. In the Lord. AUGUSTINE. Than whom nothing is sweeter: nor did he who made all things fail: seek him, therefore, and in him you will have all.
34.10: 34.10 All my bones shall say. The carnal have no word of praise and confession, because the weak things are utterly silent before you; but the strong praise you as great and tremble. THE SAME. All my bones. All the strength of the mind, because another cannot say this, namely: O Lord, who? etc., as though no one, because he alone delivered: The needy from the hand. CASSIODORUS, AUGUSTINE. The human race is needy, because mortal; poor, because in sweat it seeks bread; a beggar, because, cast down from pure wisdom, it has a thin and shadowy reason.
34.11: 34.11 Unjust witnesses rising up. CASSIODORUS. The calamities of man having been told, lest Christ himself seem a stranger to them, he sets out his passion. Things I knew not. AUGUSTINE. They are sins, etc., up to but not by committing.
34.12: 34.12 They repaid. THE SAME. When I had brought fruitfulness, they repaid barrenness: I life, they repaid death; I honors, they insults; I medicine, they wounds. Barrenness. The Lord cursed the fig tree, where when he sought fruit he found none but leaves: so in the Synagogue words without deeds; whence: 'You who preach not to steal, steal.'
34.13: 34.13 Haircloth. THE SAME. The flesh, haircloth, on account of the likeness of the flesh of sin. My prayer. CASSIODORUS. As he said: 'Your peace shall return to you' (Matthew 10); so his prayer, not accepted by the Jews, returned to him. In my bosom. AUGUSTINE. The bosom is the secret place, in which we are commanded to pray. The secret place of Christ is the divinity, to which the humanity prays.
34.14: 34.14 As a neighbor and as a brother, etc. Case for case. As: of our neighbor and brother, thus I was pleased, that is, I rejoiced in the kinship of those who pursued me. Behold grace for hatred, benefit for injury. AUGUSTINE. As a neighbor. This is fitting for one drawing near to God, and rejoicing, who is pleasing to God as a brother and neighbor. As one mourning. CASSIODORUS. Other interpreters: 'as a mother mourning her son, I bowed down over them.' As one mourning. Though I did all this, they still did not wish to be converted; and yet when they would not be converted, I was thus humbled, that is, I grieved, like a father mourning a son.
34.15: 34.15 And against, etc. When I grieve piously, the Jews rejoice impiously.
34.16: 34.16 They were scattered. CASSIODORUS. Dissolved, the miracles in the passion having been seen, yet not pricked for hardness. Or scattered through the whole world: yet they were not pricked, that is, did not repent. Or scattered, that is, divided: some say he is good, others not. They tempted me. AUGUSTINE. What was done to the head on the cross is done to the body everywhere. They gnashed. The custom of savagery, when reason fails, is to gnash the teeth: and what it wants, silent, it shows. He ends this in prayer:
34.17: 34.17 Lord, when will you look? THE SAME. When shall we see vengeance on those who insult us. My only one. CASSIODORUS. The only one is the soul of Christ, which alone is free from sin.
34.18: 34.18 I will give thanks to you. AUGUSTINE. Now from the fruit he puts forward the confession of the whole Church: then he prays, with recalling of guilt, for the confusion of the persecutors and the exultation of the faithful.
34.19: 34.19 Let them not rejoice over me. THE SAME. He repeats of the passion, to add about their punishment. They wink. CASSIODORUS. Because in turn by silent nods they admonish one another to deceive and tempt.
34.20: 34.20 Speaking. CASSIODORUS. That is, while they spoke peaceably. In anger. That is, deadly. For one thinks deceit who does not wish to kill: but these thought so because they wished to put to death.
34.21: 34.21 And they opened wide. THE SAME. First winking, thinking deceits, they opened wide their mouth, with free and open voice crying death: 'Crucify, crucify.'
34.22: 34.22 You have seen, O Lord. THE SAME. This is said when we wish to call something to memory: you have seen that they are cruel, be not silent, do not delay to give sentence.
34.23: 34.23 Attend. THE SAME. By giving the name above every name, that I may be intent, undeserving. To my cause. Ibid. The punishment is like for a crime, but not the cause: for it is not the punishment that makes a martyr but the cause.
34.24: 34.24 Your, O Lord God. THE SAME. Which is in itself, or which he gave to him. Let them not rejoice. CASSIODORUS. Let them rather weep than rejoice to have accomplished evils.
34.25: 34.25 We have devoured him. AUGUSTINE. Those incorporated are devoured.
34.26: 34.26 Let them be ashamed and fear together. CASSIODORUS. Rather let them be ashamed in the glorification of the resurrection, and fear, that is, dread the punishments. Be ashamed. He who is ashamed condemns his acts by his own estimation: but one can be ashamed who has no reverence; therefore he adds: reverence, to note conversion. Reverence is the fear of the Lord with love. Let them be clothed with confusion and reverence. With shame, as with the haircloth of penance and a mournful garment. Shame, against the boldness which they had in their raging; reverence, against the shamelessness of falsehood, that by these they might cure that.
34.27: 34.27 Let them rejoice and be glad. THE SAME. In great hope the end of the faithful, as others on the passion. Let them rejoice and be glad. Those say 'well done' to their own soul whose gladness flees, these turn their wishes not to their own soul but to God, and place their gladness, which is perpetual, in his praises, not in themselves.
34.28: 34.28 And my tongue shall meditate your justice. AUGUSTINE. Let this be, and my preachers will out of zeal announce you as just, who have fulfilled the promises, and all things universally in which you are to be praised. CASSIODORUS. My tongue. His tongue meditated justice when he preached the New Testament to the peoples.
35.1: 35.1 Unto the end, a discourse. CASSIODORUS. Here he treats of the error of certain persons, etc., up to which nevertheless threatens all. There is no fear before the eyes: because of guile, that is, because he obeys the flesh and not God, when reason suggests otherwise, since God sees even if no other does: or, what the unjust man himself sees, he knows from God, so that it may be found by him that his iniquity is to be hated before God and all men. THE SAME. First, he asserts that evils are from man.
35.2: 35.2 The unjust man has said, etc. CASSIODORUS. There are two kinds of sinners: for either through weakness of the flesh they cannot follow the commands of the law; or they are blasphemers who sin freely, as though God did not care for this; hence: He has said, etc. AUGUSTINE. A description of the unjust man. There is no fear of God. CASSIODORUS. Because guile did not wish to study the law, by which he would be excused through ignorance.
35.3: 35.3 For he has dealt deceitfully. AUGUSTINE. Many inquire into their iniquities, etc., up to nor are they excused by ignorance.
35.4: 35.4 Words. THE SAME. He shows the iniquity, etc., up to that he might act well.
35.5: 35.5 On his bed. That is, in the heart, in which evil works please him; and this is, he stood in every way, with zeal and delay: he found indeed, and knew them to be evil, but yet did not hate. He would not. AUGUSTINE. Not that he could not; he acts more perniciously against himself who does not will what he can. For there are some things that men, even if they wish, can fail to understand, such as 'In the beginning was the Word,' and yet they can understand how to act well. On his bed. THE SAME. That is, the heart, where the Lord commanded to pray with the door shut, etc., up to wisdom, namely of the flesh, which is the enemy of God.
35.6: 35.6 O Lord, in heaven. CASSIODORUS. Good things from God through mercy. As if to say: Evils are from man, but goods from mercy. O Lord, in these who are heaven, that is, knowing secrets, is your mercy: and that they themselves are clouds is from you. AUGUSTINE. Or in heaven, that is, mercy, etc., up to announces, truly, his truth having been sent. Unto the clouds. That is, the preachers, through whom God thunders in announcing, flashes with miracles, rains with doctrines. They are also the mountains, whom the sun first clothes with light, which afterward, from them though not by them, descends to the lowest of the valleys: for they are ministers of doctrine, but God enlightens.
35.7: 35.7 Your judgments. AUGUSTINE. That you have mercy on these, you blind those; to none are they at all searchable: yet you save both, these only bodily, those also spiritually, in which is great mercy.
35.8: 35.8 Men, etc. He shows that even temporal things are from God.
35.9: 35.9 They shall be inebriated. THE SAME. The thing cannot be expressed, but by this likeness he intimates that, filled, they lose their mind, so that they no longer recognize their fathers, sons, and other friends. Or, then in reality drunk, who now hope. Torrent. As if: There will be a rush of grace and mercy to inebriate. THE SAME. Torrent. Not that the blessedness is transitory, but copious. Or, your will in man breaks all obstacles. Or, the wisdom of Christ is a torrent, because sudden and rapid.
35.10: 35.10 For with you is the fountain of life. CASSIODORUS. With you, Christ, is the fountain, that is, the beginning of all good; and in your light, because through his preaching we see the light of the Father and the Holy Spirit, and therefore extend it, that in this age one may walk more safely.
36.1: 36.1 A psalm of David. This psalm is as it were the garment of Christ, which covers his whole body with precepts, and protects from adversities, and cherishes as with a bosom of counsel. A potion against those who murmur at the flowering of the wicked, the labor of the good, as though all things happen by chance, so that, God despised, they cling to the world. The Church therefore warns that no one imitate the malignant, but whatever good is hoped for be asked of the Lord, who gives profitable and eternal things.
36.2: 36.2 The green herbs. AUGUSTINE. Now it is winter, etc., up to because it has not yet appeared what we shall be. AUGUSTINE, CASSIODORUS. Herbs not of gardens but of the field, that is, the most worthless, which spring up of themselves in the fields. Hay, the noble, who easily prosper; herbs, the middling: but those too quickly wither, and these fall.
36.8: 36.8 Cease. AUGUSTINE. Anger is sudden, fury lasting; but both are to be abandoned, through which sin is committed. CASSIODORUS. This is said to one who is still weak, etc., up to by doing so flourishes for a time.
36.10: 36.10 And yet a little while, etc. AUGUSTINE. After this short life, etc., up to nor did he feel the worm of the gnawing conscience.
36.12: 36.12 He will watch, etc. CASSIODORUS. Having said that the good ought not to envy the wicked, etc., up to endeavors to kill.
36.13: 36.13 But the Lord, etc. THE SAME. So let us too, seeing them about to perish, laugh even at the present ones, a great consolation.
36.14: 36.14 The sword, etc. THE SAME. If he will not act by flatteries or threats, he attacks by punishment. If not even so he succeeds, he lies in wait with deceits, when by speaking well he intends evil.
36.16: 36.16 Better is, etc. THE SAME. A little before of malice and endurance: here of riches and poverty.
36.17: 36.17 But he strengthens, etc. AUGUSTINE. Most of all by the example of his cross. For the cross of Christ ended in punishment and remains in glory: from places of punishments it passes to the brows of emperors.
36.18: 36.18 In the days of famine. CASSIODORUS. That is, in this life, etc., up to the more they are lifted up, the sooner like smoke they vanish.
36.21: 36.21 He will borrow. THE SAME. He hears the word of God, does not repay it by works. And will not pay. That is, does not repay by works what he received by hearing. He shows mercy and will repay, etc. Of those things which he receives, etc., up to generosity follows.
36.23: 36.23 Steps. THE SAME. Which by themselves are crooked, because born in sins. His way. AUGUSTINE. The way of the earth is not hard but full of robbers: or, God will will the way of man.
36.25: 36.25 I have been young, etc. THE SAME. He treats here that the just man is never forsaken, mingling the rewards of the good and the punishments of the wicked with interspersed exhortations. AUGUSTINE. The Church speaks as one man, who in the first times was younger, at the end of the age has grown old, in a fruitful old age, because spread through all nations. THE SAME. I have been young. A boy in Abel; in the prophets and patriarchs a youth; in the time of the martyrs as an old man; at the end of the world as in decrepit age. CASSIODORUS. Younger, when I received the beginnings of the law in Adam; I grew old, when in an honorable age at last I received Christ.
36.26: 36.26 All the day he shows mercy. Or, he speaks of almsgiving, which begins from mercy, and afterward opens the hand: or, of spiritual things.
36.28: 36.28 He loves judgment and will not forsake his saints. CASSIODORUS. Therefore: you too love it, that you may rejoice in your goods.
36.31: 36.31 They shall be supplanted. THE SAME. To supplant is to place snares of pits under one's feet.
36.33: 36.33 But the Lord. THE SAME. The consolation of the just man. In his hands. AUGUSTINE. The earth of Job was handed into the hands of the impious one, that is, the flesh: but God leads out the soul unconquered, lest it yield. When he is judged. CASSIODORUS. Or, he does not permit the just man to be condemned when he is judged by the impious; or, to that impious one, namely to his evil.
36.34: 36.34 And he will exalt. THE SAME. Because only when exalted can one dwell in heaven. You will see. THE SAME. What you now believe; he notes the joys of the good in two ways: first, because then they will perceive in how great delights they are. Then, because they will see the punishments of the wicked, whence the blessedness is more welcome to those freed from such evil.
36.35: 36.35 I saw the impious exalted. THE SAME. Against this, etc., up to whose place for harming, having been bound, is taken away.
36.36: 36.36 I passed by. The world, tending to God by better conduct: and I saw that nothing was possible, since all are nothing in which man glories. I sought. I called to mind: because the good then grieve more over the impious, that they are separated from them, when they are changed for the better. Place. Their world, which will also be dissolved. I passed by. AUGUSTINE. He passes by who does not attend to the present but the last things, etc., up to to whom this virtue belongs, is put in the place of the blessed.
36.37: 36.37 The remains. The good things that will be left after this life, or good memory after death.
36.39: 36.39 But the salvation of the just is from the Lord. All these things for the just, yet all from God, and he gathers it up in sum.
37.1: 37.1 A psalm of David in remembrance of the sabbath. AUGUSTINE, CASSIODORUS. That we may always keep in memory sin, which we cannot altogether flee, so as at least to restrain ourselves from it, here he introduces the torment of penance in many ways, so that he seems to propose Job himself to beginners as an example, that they may embrace torments, lesser in merits indeed, by which we are freed from eternal punishment. AUGUSTINE. The sabbath is the rest of eternity, which the one conscious of sin fears to lose, and desires to have when gravely afflicted.
37.2: 37.2 O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury. First, he seeks mercy concerning punishments in summary. Rebuke me. CASSIODORUS. That the punishment may be from mercy for correction, not from anger for vengeance.
37.3: 37.3 Arrows. AUGUSTINE. The vengeances you threatened to Adam, saying: 'In whatever day you eat, you shall die the death.' Because he ate, they are fixed in us too; and not for an hour, but you confirmed it, that it be until the end of the age. AUGUSTINE, CASSIODORUS. For the arrows. He numbers what he suffers, etc., up to because it can be lightly harmed.
37.4: 37.4 There is no soundness, etc. AUGUSTINE, CASSIODORUS. From the pressure of vengeance exerted on Adam. Or, he is terrified by fear of future wrath, so that there is no soundness in the flesh: after the manner of the bashful, who is already afflicted by scourges to come. Or, from the face of wrath, because I foresaw the face of wrath, that is, what you threaten, lest I see wrath. There is no peace. Grave sorrow comes to the inward parts from the face of sins, because the holy man, beyond the bodily punishments, is afflicted by sins, thinking he deserves graver. There is no soundness. CASSIODORUS. Here he seeks mercy from the power of the judge and from the weak person. There is no peace to my bones. He takes bones for flesh. And he explains what he had said, adding another thing: namely from the face of sins.
37.5: 37.5 They have gone over. AUGUSTINE. Or have lifted up, that is, because iniquity raised the head of the proud against God, God weighed it down, as with a burden, and pressed it down that it may not now be raised.
37.6: 37.6 They have putrefied. CASSIODORUS. A narration, in which the miseries are enumerated. My scars. AUGUSTINE. Or my bruises; another reading, that is, my sins. He is not sound who has scars that have putrefied and stink: that, turned away from them, we may adore the sabbath, and groan: Running with the bridegroom after the odor of the ointments.
37.7: 37.7 I am become miserable. THE SAME. Having said how his iniquities went over him, he says how they weighed him down.
37.8: 37.8 For my loins. CASSIODORUS, AUGUSTINE. I sin not only by my own weakness, but also by the devil, who afflicts the body and wearies the soul with vain imaginings; and through this there is again no soundness, as also above through the arrows. AUGUSTINE. Loins, or, the soul is filled, etc., up to when we shall see the truth as it is.
37.9: 37.9 I roared with the groaning. CASSIODORUS, AUGUSTINE. Groaning is of the heart, roaring of the voice: by the likeness of beasts, to which he compares himself: to show a stronger groaning: it is the virtue of patience that it bursts forth into groaning, not into words.
37.10: 37.10 Before you all. CASSIODORUS. Such is what deserves to be before you, because he asks for sins. AUGUSTINE. and therefore it is not hidden but the groaning is heard, because it is pious for the freeing of the soul: God does not care for others. My desire. THE SAME. This is prayer, nor does he ever cease to pray who does not cease to love: charity is a cry.
37.11: 37.11 My heart is troubled. CASSIODORUS. He sets out the sorrows of the mind, because the virtue of patience has left. Troubled, because the mind has succumbed to its suffering. The light, that is, reason, lately disturbed, which he does not have with him because of the enormous troubles.
37.12: 37.12 My friends and neighbors. THE SAME. And for these two consolations humanity rejoices, but for this one they are the heap of the passion. AUGUSTINE. My friends. So far he has confessed what he suffers from himself within, etc., up to and this also befits anyone living among men.
37.14: 37.14 As a deaf man I did not hear, and as a dumb man not opening his mouth. CASSIODORUS. Not opening to the iniquity of those advising, etc., up to he roared against the pains of the body.
37.16: 37.16 For in you, O Lord, have I hoped, etc. THE SAME. Because amid so many evils he hoped in the Lord, he affirms that he is to be heard in the recalling of amendment. I have hoped. A saving medicine against evils, to hope, not to fail. In you, O Lord, who change sad things into glad.
37.17: 37.17 For I said: Lest at any time my enemies rejoice over me. AUGUSTINE. Again the head speaks of the weak feet, though it is in heaven. It does not abandon what it has on earth. While my feet are moved. CASSIODORUS. If they are sometimes moved by human weakness, the impious laugh at what grieves the pious.
37.18: 37.18 I am ready. THE SAME. Knowing that I have offended. Sorrow, because he has offended: the impious defends himself; the just is angry against himself.
37.19: 37.19 For my iniquity. THE SAME. The two ways of perfect penance, confession and amendment, through tears, almsgiving, and the like.
37.20: 37.20 They live. AUGUSTINE. They enjoy the world, strengthened in worldly things, and daily they become more numerous.
37.22: 37.22 Forsake me not. THE SAME. Absolved of past things, with thanksgiving professing God the author of salvation, he joyfully cries out that he not now be left. CASSIODORUS. Because the offense is graver after pardon. AUGUSTINE. An exultant conclusion, so that there may be certain hope for those imitating. Depart not from me. How then above: 'Why have you forsaken me?' That is the voice of the old man who was crucified with him, but here he speaks in his own person.
38.1: 38.1 Unto the end. AUGUSTINE. Because this is about eternal blessedness, for which it is pleasant to leap across, even if it is heavy to the flesh. It teaches, however, to cross over from the world to God. But the one crossing over always draws upon himself the envy and calumny of the wicked from his good reputation: whence he deliberates to be silent among the wicked, lest he say anything ill. Jeduthun. THE SAME. Leaping over them, that is, those remaining in the world. CASSIODORUS. First, on the restraint of the tongue among blasphemers and calumniators: whence he also desires to know the end, where these things are not.
38.2: 38.2 I said: I will guard my ways, etc. AUGUSTINE, CASSIODORUS. This psalm admonishes, among blasphemers, the wicked, and calumniators, the restraint of the tongue, to suppress contests and quarrels: for this silence is very useful. CASSIODORUS. I said: I deliberated in my heart: where the wise deliberate before they speak. Ways. JEROME. That is, actions and words. That I may not sin by foolish or idle things. With my tongue. AUGUSTINE. Not in vain is the tongue in the word: because it slips easily. I have set to my mouth. After I passed beyond earthly delights, etc., up to teaching us to beware of this and not imitate it. CASSIODORUS. I set it to the point that I became dumb, etc., up to him who seeks a cause of contention.
3.2: 3.2 Lord, why. CASSIODORUS. The first psalm of those that treat the passion and resurrection briefly, against those, and especially the pagans, who do not think that the glory of majesty can descend to lowly things.
3.3: 3.3 Many say, etc. AUGUSTINE. Or each one says this who is assailed by vices and desires. They say to the soul: There is no salvation, etc. By the heaping up of vices, despair of health creeps in, as though the vices were mocking the soul; or even the devils and his angels, by their suggestions.
3.4: 3.4 You are my protector. CASSIODORUS. In Christ. The head, Christ, or the mind that serves the law of God. You have struck all. Rightly in predestination it is said of the devil and his angels. Upon the people. That is, each one of us. THE SAME. Or the Church and her head speak this, established throughout the whole world amid the storms of persecutions. Many say, desiring to extinguish the Christian name, There is no salvation. Otherwise they would not hope to destroy the Church that is spreading far and wide. Protector. Because taken up in Christ and exalted with him. The head himself, who first ascended into heaven.
3.5: 3.5 And he heard me from his holy hill, etc. That is, the prayer of the Church, or justice, is heard by Christ.
3.6: 3.6 I slept: according to the verse: 'Arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you' (Ephesians 5). It is no wonder that the Savior says these things, since he did much greater things for the salvation of souls during the time he was absent from the body, which are recounted in the Catholic epistle of Saint Peter: 'When he went and preached to the spirits that were in prison, who had once been unbelieving' (1 Peter 3).
3.7: 3.7 I will not fear thousands, who try to extinguish the name of Christ
3.8: 3.8 For you have struck, etc. Now that the Church is reigning, the enemies have been struck with confusion. The teeth of sinners, namely, slanderous words; or the princes come to destruction. Therefore believe, O men, that salvation is of the Lord, and, O Lord, may your blessing be upon your people. With my voice. This is fitting for me because with my voice. He who is good and asks good things cries out with his own voice; with another's voice, that is, one not in harmony with his life. I slept. The end of the matter, whence he proposes that there is nothing to fear. I, with emphasis; as if to say: they rage, but I would not sleep unless I wished to. Or, I slept by consenting; I was lulled by working evil; I arose by abandoning sins. For. AUGUSTINE. He does not look back, nor does he save beyond this because he struck: but from this the teeth were crushed, because he struck; that is, the slanderous words were brought to nothing; or, teeth are those who cut off some from the number of the saints and incorporate them with the wicked.
4.1: 4.1 Unto the end. AUGUSTINE. 'End' is said in two ways, when something fails, or when it is perfected. Ibid. A canticle indicates gladness. Psalms are those sung to the psaltery, which the Prophet used in a great mystery. A psalm, concerning conduct for action, that false gods and the vanities of the world be abandoned; of a canticle, because mention is made of eternal joy.
4.2: 4.2 When I called upon, etc. CASSIODORUS. By his own example he rebukes unbelievers about false things. You have enlarged for me. Ibid. You led me from the narrowness of sadness into the breadth of joy. 5. We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation, etc. (Romans 5). First he indicated that he was heard; now, as one having God in his heart, he speaks to him. Have mercy on me. Having mercy on justice and delay. Again, have mercy against the miseries of this life. My prayer. Concerning the good things to be asked. And while it is so with me, O sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?
4.3: 4.3 Why do you love vanity, etc. CASSIODORUS. By desire you embrace, by labor you seek vain idols and lies, which are not God; or earthly things, which do not do what they promise.
4.4: 4.4 And know, etc. Having set forth the new man, he commands them to put off the old. AUGUSTINE. Note that 'And' is placed at the beginning to join the words spoken with the vision that is in the heart, so here, as: Do not love vain things. And know. But the diapsalma forbids joining it so. Diapsalma, according to Jerome, always; the Hebrews say Selah, that is, always, in confirmation of the preceding part. Sympsalma, that is, the conjunction of the psalm. The Lord will hear. Of rest thus, and you: and therefore cry out, thus worthy of being heard.
4.5: 4.5 Be angry. If a movement of the mind arises which is not in our power, let reason not consent to it. CASSIODORUS. The movement of the mind is not in our power, but by God's grace we can temper it; what therefore belongs to habit he permits; what belongs to fault he forbids. JEROME. The Apostle teaches this: 'Let not the sun go down upon your anger' (Ephesians 4), so that to be angry at all, even lightly, is a sin; but it is justice to mitigate anger by swift repentance. In your hearts. AUGUSTINE. Concerning the things you discuss in the heart, which God knows: that is, consent; and concerning what you turn over in your beds, that is, the delight of the flesh, in which reason is held captive, as a wild beast in its lair. Be pricked with compunction, by repentance; or the beds are the thoughts of the fierce. CASSIODORUS. Anger is venial which is not brought to effect. Diapsalma. Offer sacrifice. CASSIODORUS. With the old man laid aside, we are commanded to be offered in sacrifice, since we are certain of good things. AUGUSTINE. The sacrifice of justice is a troubled spirit, so that punishing itself it may slay itself to God; or, just works after repentance, which the diapsalma marks, so that one passes from the old life to the new, and thus hope for good things. But because there is hardly anyone who loves inner goods, he adds:
4.6: 4.6 Many say: Who shows us good things? Namely, the future ones, about which they doubt and despair. Answering this he shows briefly what good things are to be sought.
4.7: 4.7 The light of your countenance is signed upon us, etc. AUGUSTINE. This light is the whole and true good of man, by which he is signed, as a denarius by the image of the king. Light. AUGUSTINE. Light, that is, a shining countenance, and one illuminating us, the image by which you are known. CASSIODORUS. Or: the cross has been impressed on us, as the sign of our king, which is the light of the countenance, because God shines in such things. The image of creation is reason; of recreation, grace; of likeness, the whole Trinity. In my heart. AUGUSTINE. Not outside in vain things, but within, where God dwells, gladness is to be sought.
4.8: 4.8 From the fruit. CASSIODORUS. Because they think the complete good is in these. These three, as more suited to human uses, he puts in place of all riches.
4.9: 4.9 In peace in the selfsame. CASSIODORUS. But I will sleep in peace of mind, here forgetful of the world, and I will rest in the future: because already in one hope, not in the multiplicity of the world. In peace I will sleep and I will rest. AUGUSTINE. From all the things of the world, when this mortal puts on immortality: and this will truly be, because there is already hope: and this is: For you, O Lord; and surely what is hoped for will be.
5.1: 5.1 For her who obtains the inheritance. Because here the one is honored to whom the inheritance is affirmed, from which the rival is excluded. It is the Church that receives the inheritance, that is, eternal life, God himself, which speaks here of the inheritance that she seeks for herself, and asserts that the rival is said to be excluded. BEDE. That is, for the Church, which, with Christ rising, received the gifts of spiritual goods, and which is herself sometimes called the inheritance of the Lord, purchased by his precious blood; hence it was said: 'Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance.' The whole psalm, then, is uttered from the person of the Catholic Church, who in the first section asks that her prayer be heard, proclaiming that heretics and schismatics are to be excluded from the Lord's gifts. In the second section, through the understanding of the divine Scriptures, she begs to be directed by the right path to that happy homeland, asserting that the faithless are completely alien from it. Finally, recalling the rewards of the blessed, so that by one preaching it might both turn the wicked by the foretold punishment and rouse the just by the promised rewards.
5.2: 5.2 My words. CASSIODORUS. Here the prophet intimates that a threefold prayer is to be made. For there are three principal vices in prosperity, three in adversity: against which we ought to make a threefold prayer. In prosperity, against the concupiscence of the flesh, against the concupiscence of the eyes, against the pride of life. In adversity, against fear of death, of danger, of loss. Ibid. A threefold prayer: words, the psalmody of the mouth; cry, the affection of the heart; therefore: You will hear. Behold, three times about the same thing. To the ears. The ears of God are power and clemency. Power, by which he is able; clemency, by which he is willing to hear; for if there were not clemency, he would hear the prayers of no one.
5.3: 5.3 To the voice. That prayer has a voice which is worthy to be heard. King. AUGUSTINE. Properly the Son; rightly first 'king,' because through him one goes to the Father, whence he adds: And my God: and yet he does not say 'attend' in the plural, but attend, because God is one.
5.4: 5.4 For, etc. AUGUSTINE. So far, the prayer that it be heard, etc., up to and this in the morning, as soon as it leaves the darkness.
5.5: 5.5 In the morning I will stand. CASSIODORUS. Or, in the morning when eternity shall begin, and then I will see fully that iniquity does not please: because then the impious one will not dwell but will be taken away, that he may not see the glory of God (Isaiah 26): and then they will not remain, even if they had his mercy.
5.6: 5.6 Nor shall the unjust abide. Those who do evil. For you hate those who work it, not those who have worked it.
5.7: 5.7 You will destroy all who speak a lie. AUGUSTINE. Because this is contrary to truth. Truth is concerning what is. A lie is not a substance or nature, but concerns what is not, and deservedly he is destroyed who turns aside from what is to what is not. Ibid. To lie is to speak against what is perceived in the mind. Ibid. There are certain lies for the sake of safety, etc., up to I had not thought that a raging man could ...
5.8: 5.8 But I. AUGUSTINE. Third, he says that he will be the future house of God, and now draws near in fear before the consummation, which casts out fear. I will enter. CASSIODORUS. By this I will enter, because I will worship. Ibid. He asks against the things which the rival brings in: whence she herself will perish.
5.9: 5.9 Lord, lead me. AUGUSTINE. Fourth, advancing amid obstacles, he prays to be helped inwardly, lest he be turned aside by deceitful tongues. In your justice. CASSIODORUS. Because you receive the penitent and suppliant. In the sight. AUGUSTINE. Where man does not see; he is not to be believed when he praises or blames, because he does not see in the conscience, in which the way to God is directed. Therefore he adds: For there is no truth in their mouth.
5.10: 5.10 For there is not, etc. Not only is there no truth in the mouth, but it is a sepulcher: because they bring forth foul things to corrupt, and if they do not succeed by these, they act deceitfully, that is, they not only plot but accomplish.
5.11: 5.11 Judge them, O God. Let them fall from their thoughts. He does not wish it but predicts what will be. He falls who is disappointed of a good hope. And let them rejoice. CASSIODORUS. After the retributions of the wicked he adds the rewards of the good, so that, as the punishment terrifies, the rewards may incite.
5.13: 5.13 As with a shield. CASSIODORUS. In one word he indicates the free benefits of God. The will that calls is a defense against all things, and a crown, and a shield. Fitted to the head it is a crown, to the heart a defense.
6.1: 6.1 The eighth is the coming of the Lord, in which the sinner fears to be reproved, and therefore repents. AUGUSTINE. Some call the eighth the coming of the Lord, etc., up to whence the Church, fearing, prays here.
6.2: 6.2 Lord, rebuke me not in your fury. BASIL. Confession is a prayer of entreaty, which avails with God. First there is the exordium, in which he seeks goodwill through the power of the judge, through his own weakness, through the custom of sparing: because he does not wish to be asked by the dead, but by the living. Reprove. AUGUSTINE. To be reproved is graver than to be accused, whence condemnation is feared. To be corrected is milder, that is, to be amended or instructed. They are reproved in judgment who have no foundation. They are amended, that is, purged, who have built upon that foundation wood, hay, stubble. He says here, therefore: Heal, lest there be need of that there, whence he adds: Have mercy.
6.3: 6.3 Weak. AUGUSTINE. The soul is made weak by guilt, from which heal it, because the bones, that is, the mind, are troubled at the presence, and the soul, that is, sensuality: therefore how long do you delay, as if to say: What remains but that you heal? How long. AUGUSTINE. He intimates that he has long struggled with vices. God's delay, however, is not cruelty, but is to persuade the soul into what evils it has cast itself. For it does not yet pray so perfectly that it be told: 'While you are yet speaking I will say, Behold, I am here' (Isaiah 65). So that from the difficulty of healing he may be the more careful for himself, and to show what punishment awaits the unconverted if there is such difficulty for the converted, whence: 'If the just man shall scarcely be saved, where shall the impious and the sinner appear?' (1 Peter 4).
6.5: 6.5 Turn. CASSIODORUS. You who had turned away, or from vengeance. Deliver, from imminent death. Or deliver the soul bound by sins. Save me, etc., by giving virtues.
6.6: 6.6 For there is not. CASSIODORUS. Therefore here I hasten to be forgiven, because after death and in hell confession is not received. In hell. AUGUSTINE. The rich man who saw Lazarus confessed, though from the depths, in comparison with which he was compelled to confess his evils, so much so that he asked his brothers to be forewarned of them: but after the judgment, in deeper darkness, they will see no light of God to whom they might confess. Or, he calls sin death, in which he is forgetful of God who despises his commandments.
6.7: 6.7 I have labored. CASSIODORUS. He recounts the hardships by which the penitent are turned away; he groans while he sees what he has done and what punishment is to come. Bed. The conscience, which for some is rest, for some torment. Couch, sensuality; I will make fertile what was dry. Or, the bed is the delight of the body, in which man is dissolved. The couch is the heap of sins like garments, which when loosed, by the rain of tears a new harvest of virtues may grow.
6.8: 6.8 From fury. AUGUSTINE. From wrath, either of God, which is in the judgment, etc., up to lest anyone despair on account of the gravity of sins, he adds: Depart, etc. CASSIODORUS. A rebuke, that he be separated from those in whose company he sinned, and persist in the commandments of God. Enemies, AUGUSTINE. that is, vices, or wicked men, who are truly enemies to those who turn to God, from whom every good man is separated, not in place, but in mind. Because such labor of penance is not in vain, signifying that he has been heard, he adds: Depart.
6.9: 6.9 The Lord. Three times 'the Lord,' because it shows that the Trinity was present at the prayers: He began with tears, heard he rejoices. The Lord has heard. CASSIODORUS. He gives an example that those who pray faithfully are heard.
6.11: 6.11 Let them be ashamed and troubled. CASSIODORUS. As in a conclusion, now free from sins and rejoicing, he prays for his enemies, that they may be converted, that, like himself, they may obtain pardon. AUGUSTINE. Let them be ashamed. This is not here, where rather they mock those who leave all things, and make the weak ashamed, but in the judgment.
7.1: 7.1 Unto the end, a psalm. AUGUSTINE. Cush, who went over to the side of Absalom, etc., up to for it was not to be hidden from those for whom it was done. AUGUSTINE. This psalm can be understood in the person of Christ; if anything is said humbly, let it be referred to our weakness, which he bore. First he asks to be delivered from all tribulations.
7.2: 7.2 Lord my God. CASSIODORUS. This is the first psalm of those in which, through the acts of David, the future mysteries of the Lord are signified. The mystery of the incarnation was silence to the Jews; as David from his son, so Christ endured persecution from the people whom he had nourished. Deliver. AUGUSTINE. As if, all the war of the vices having been overcome, now surely nothing remains but the envious devil.
7.3: 7.3 Lest he seize, etc. Redeem, etc. CASSIODORUS. The words are proper: it is the Lord's to deliver, the lion's to seize. The order: first he puts the persecutors, then the lion. For being cleansed of all spiritual wickednesses, he is freed from the devil.
7.4: 7.4 Lord, if I have done this. Ibid. Literally of David and Absalom. If I have done this, that is, if this evil has befallen me through a past fault. Or if now there is iniquity in my hands, that is, in my works. Or, if I have repaid those who did evil to me, etc., which among men is called equity; deservedly, even if it does not appear so to men, let me fall empty from my enemies, from the fruit of meekness. AUGUSTINE. If I have done this, or, the universal sin, which he said without naming, which is pride, the root of all evils. Or, as follows, if there is iniquity, which is taken of every sin. If I have repaid. Ibid. That is, if I have not imitated you in just silence, that is, in patience, which you worked for me. Let me deservedly fall from my enemies. Ibid. He does not imprecate this on himself by oath, but says what befalls those who avenge themselves: he prophesies, therefore, he does not swear by imprecation, which is the gravest kind of oath. Made empty by vain and proud joy, as though he could not be conquered: Solomon, 'Better is he who conquers his anger than he who takes a city' (Proverbs 16).
7.6: 7.6 Let him trample, etc. Ibid. The soul of the sinner, of which it is said, 'You are earth, and into earth you shall return' (Genesis 3), is the food of the serpent, to whom in the curse it was said, 'You shall eat earth,' that is, of the devil, because it is earth, that is, earthly. And therefore he says here: Let him trample my life into the earth, that is, reduced to earth let him incorporate it into himself, and let it be despicable there. My glory. Ibid. Which ought to be in the conscience, where God sees, and firm in the Lord, as: 'He who glories, let him glory in the Lord' (1 Corinthians 1). Let him bring down into dust, that is, into pride and boasting, so that I might wish to glory before men. Let him bring down into dust. Dust which the wind casts away. Ibid. The boasting of the proud. He wishes, therefore, that his glory be firm within, where God sees: for it is dust if one glories before men; see how pride is to be avoided.
7.7: 7.7 Arise, O Lord. He asks that the glory of Christ's resurrection come to his aid. In your wrath. For this perfect man does not pray here against men but against the devil, that he may lose his possession, namely the sinners and impious, who are his possession. And because the taking away of man is a punishment to the devil, it is called the wrath of God against him. Or, he prays here for the resurrection of Christ, as in the preceding for his incarnation: that O Lord my God, etc. In the borders. The world, or hell, are the borders of the devil. And arise, O Lord. The proud devil, because he is conquered by iniquity, he adds: Or, Arise, that is, make yourself known in the whole world, by rising again. In the commandment, that you may cause the commandment of humility to be fulfilled: and this follows from it, because the Synagogue of various peoples, or specially of the Jews, will surround you, by loving or by persecuting: On account of this, that is, the loving one, return, that is, make them know your omnipotence, you who came down that they might see you; or on account of this, that is, the persecuting one, in which you find no place, return on high, that is, withdraw from those who persecute you. Synagogue. Ibid. The congregation of the people, etc., up to the Lord judges, concerning the judgment of the one who returned, that is, Christ. Innocence. Ibid. Because I have not repaid those who did evil to me. Upon me. Ibid. Justice and innocence are upon me, because they are not from me but from God.
7.10: 7.10 Searching the hearts. Ibid. What each one thinks. Reins. What delights each one; because the end of care and thought is delight, to which one strives to come. Men can see our works in words and deeds, but with what mind they are done, and what they desire to reach, God alone sees; who, when he sees the heart to be in heaven, and not delighting in the flesh but in the Lord, that is, when the thoughts are good, directs the just man toward their ends, and not only directs but helps the just man.
7.11: 7.11 Just is my help. Ibid. There are two offices of medicine, namely to heal sickness and to guard health. According to the first he said in another psalm: 'I am sick, heal me, O Lord.' According to the second, the perfect man says here, my just help is from the Lord. Both that medicine and this save: but that one brings from sickness to health, this preserves in health itself. That one provides a remedy for escaping disease; this, a remedy lest one fall back into disease. By that we are healed when sick, by this we are guarded when healthy.
7.12: 7.12 God the judge. CASSIODORUS. Here he terrifies by fear of the future judgment and promises hope to those who return. Is he angry. AUGUSTINE. Another reading: 'Does he bring on wrath every day?' In the Greek, 'brings on wrath' is more meaningful: because the wrath by which he punishes is not in himself, but in the angels of wrath, through whom he punishes: who, not on account of the justice in which they do not rejoice, but on account of malice, delight in human punishment: whom he does not gather every day for vengeance, but by patience invites to repentance.
7.13: 7.13 His sword. AUGUSTINE. Another reading: 'He has made his broadsword gleam.' CASSIODORUS. His sword, he will exercise manifest vengeance, and this is not said unequally, because he has bent his bow, he threatens, lest his patience be thought relaxed; he has prepared it, so that he may be thought about to send the arrow soon. His bow. Ibid. By comparison. For as one who has bent a bow threatens, so through sacred Scripture he threatens the wicked, lest God's patience be thought relaxed; and he has prepared it, so that he may be thought about to send the arrow soon: as someone prepares a bow to send an arrow. He has bent his bow, AUGUSTINE. tempering the Old Testament by the New Testament: He has prepared it, by explanation. Ibid. Or, he has prepared. God prepares and arranges, etc., up to but to those burning with zeal, arrows.
7.15: 7.15 Behold. As if: God has prepared these things in the Scriptures. Ibid. Whence it seems to man to be a cause of condemnation. But behold that it is not from God but from man, because he opened a pit, etc. He conceived sorrow, Ibid. that is, by desire of temporal things. He brought forth, accomplished, sent forth: and in the iniquity sent forth is the pit, that is, a precipice for others. Whence he adds:
7.16: 7.16 He opened a pit. And so he is comparable to one who opens a pit: for he opens it by conceiving fraud; he digs it by laboring, by pressing on the work of fraud; he falls in by bringing forth fraud, namely by carrying it out.
7.17: 7.17 His sorrow shall be turned, etc. The head is the soul, the crown of the head is reason: over which sins have dominion and remain above: and they will come down upon it when they thrust it down into punishments.
7.18: 7.18 I will give thanks to the Lord. CASSIODORUS. The conclusion, as though gathering all things into a sum, he says he gives thanks with eagerness.
8.1: 8.1 Unto the end, for the winepresses, etc. For the winepresses, that is, the Churches, etc., up to flow out into the rest of the soul.
8.2: 8.2 O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is your name! etc. CASSIODORUS. First, the praises of God, his majesty, and his lofty work are described. In all. Ibid. Therefore let not the Jews or any others claim for themselves what belongs to all, which is the intention. Above the heavens. AUGUSTINE. Literally, or the Scriptures: because it exceeds the utterances of all the Scriptures; or, above the heavens. Continuing with what follows, that is, into the Scriptures, which he stoops to infants, on account of the enemies of the cross: who are destroyed when the Scriptures are seen, that is, understood, brought down to infants; and when through them they are nourished to strength, and raised to the height of understanding.
8.3: 8.3 Out of the mouth of infants. Ibid. Of the unlearned, to whom the Apostle gave milk, whom those signified who praised the Lord, against whom the Lord uses this testimony. From these he perfected praise, because if only the perfect were in the Church, the human race would not be provided for; as now, when even the least, not yet capable of knowledge of spiritual things, are nourished by faith in temporal history. The enemies are all who speak against the dispensation accomplished through the Crucified. Heretics seem to be defenders of the faith, philosophers of wisdom, though the former attack faith and the latter true wisdom. Of sucklings, CASSIODORUS. not in age, but as Peter says, 'as newborn' (1 Peter 2), who cannot yet take food but milk; and it is, you are proclaimed not only by the perfect but also by the unlearned. Or, he calls the apostles infants and sucklings, who were simple and unlearned men; whence: 'God has chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the strong' (1 Corinthians 1). The praise is more perfect. Or, out of the mouth of infants and sucklings, that is, from the words of the Hebrew children you have perfected praise, which seemed to be done childishly, on account of the enemies, so that it might not seem human wisdom but divinely given. Your enemies. The pagans. The enemy. The Jew, who is an enemy of God while he defends the Father alone: because he who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father, or an enemy by desire.
8.4: 8.4 For I will see. Before the Jew, in spirit. Your heavens, the apostles, I will see present in posterity; this fits the earliest ones well. The works of your fingers. Because perfected by the cooperation of the Trinity, which is signified here by the three fingers, as there: 'Who weighs the mass of the earth with three fingers' (Isaiah 40). And through them, the moon and the stars which you have founded. Not those.
8.5: 8.5 What is man. Ibid. Second, he says that the nature of man, once corrupted, has been exalted in Christ above all things. For before he had shown the omnipotence of the Deity. By 'man,' sinners; by 'son of man,' the spiritual. Ibid. Man, any lowly one, of whom God is mindful by showing mercy; Son of man, Christ the man: for through him you visit him, when the Word was made flesh, in whom the physician came to the sick. Or the son. AUGUSTINE. The disjunction implies there is a difference between man and son of man. Every son of man is man, but not conversely, as Adam. Every man, therefore, bears the image of the earthly one; the Son of man is the heavenly one, and rightly the new man is the son of man, because the new one is made from the old by a certain change. AUGUSTINE. Why, leaving the higher things, does he speak of these lowest? But sheep, etc., up to who by the seed of the word of God make the hearts of men bear fruit.
8.8: 8.8 Moreover the sheep. He notes that the wicked are subject to Christ, which seems less so: for these are carnal men, dwelling in the breadth of the field, that is, in the wideness of pleasures, not on the mountains of virtues. The beasts of the field. Ibid. Those who live in the flesh, where they climb nothing steep: but the broad way to which they cling is the one that leads to destruction: hence Abel too is slain in the field.
8.9: 8.9 The birds of the air, the proud: of whom, 'They have set their mouth against heaven' (Psalm 72). Their head says: 'I will ascend into heaven and exalt my throne, and I will be like the Most High' (Isaiah 14). The fishes of the sea that walk the paths of the sea, the curious. These three, pleasure of the flesh, pride, curiosity, include all vices, which are the concupiscence of the flesh, the ambition of the world, that is pride, and the concupiscence of the eyes; through the eyes curiosity especially prevails.
9.1: 9.1 Unto the end, for the hidden sons. Nor is it added whose; by excellence it is the only-begotten of God. Hidden. Because other things of his are manifest, etc., up to and about the punishment by which he judges, purging, converting, blinding.
9.2: 9.2 I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, etc. The prophet sings joyfully, because the worship of the devil is destroyed by the coming of Christ: and Christ reigns, judges, helps.
9.4: 9.4 When my enemy is turned back, etc., they shall perish, etc. AUGUSTINE. Because when you turned the devil backward, his members are weakened so that they can do no harm, and they shall not be; or, they will be destroyed completely by your assault, when you say, 'Depart, you cursed' (Matthew 25); or, they will perish when God takes iniquity away from them.
9.5: 9.5 You have done my judgment and my cause. Ibid. Because they served me to my advantage, because you sat. You judge. JEROME. The Father, that Christ might die for the human race. AUGUSTINE. Or, Christ will judge at the end, to whom the Father has given all judgment.
9.6: 9.6 For ever and ever. Ibid. 'Age' is this present one which rolls on: the 'age of the age' is eternal, of which that is the image. Or it is a qualification, so that you not take it of this present one.
9.7: 9.7 Swords. CASSIODORUS. The power of the devil will be destroyed at the end of the age. Cities. His peoples. With a noise, that is, a very great outcry, as happens when prosperous affairs are closed by a grievous end. But on the contrary the Lord remains. The end, AUGUSTINE. is the sword which he will brandish at the second coming, judging openly, he who now judges secretly, up to which the enemy's swords avail something, but then they will utterly fail. Their. CASSIODORUS. In the plural, though above he said 'enemy' in the singular, because the demons are many but, being alike in malice, are as one. With a noise. AUGUSTINE. That is, both the din and the tumult of impiety have perished: or, when impiety is overthrown, a din is made, because no one comes to the highest peace who has not fought with vices with great din. His throne. CASSIODORUS. The judicial power; he who was judged in humility will judge in majesty.
9.10: 9.10 And he is made. How great it is that he who is judge should be the refuge of the poor man, who desires nothing of the world. In due times. AUGUSTINE. Man is not more opportunely turned away from the world than when labors and sorrows are mingled with these pleasures.
9.11: 9.11 Let them hope. AUGUSTINE. When they cease to hope in the things of the world. To those turned away from the world, seeking where to fix their hope, the knowledge of the name comes. The name is known when he whose name it is is known. His name is the Lord, which he knows who gladly serves him, or, he who is, and therefore let no one hope in transitory things, which have nothing but 'was' and 'will be.' For what is to come in them, when it has come, at once becomes past; it is awaited with desire, lost with sorrow, not held with certainty. For you have not forsaken. The Prophet provokes the faithful to praise, looking at the benefits of the present and future time.
9.12: 9.12 Sion. Ibid. A watchtower, which is now being done, so that we may come to the vision of peace, that is, from Sion into Jerusalem: but any zealous watching turns to error unless the Lord dwells in it. Studies. JEROME. That is, his commandments, which are to be studied.
9.13: 9.13 For requiring. Ibid. But as though those who were sent to evangelize were to say, no one believes us, and we are being killed, he answered: not without fruit, because requiring their blood in vengeance, in the judgment, where there will be glory for the slain and punishment for the slayer: he has remembered, etc. Ibid. not after forgetfulness, but after a long time, according to the feeling of the weak, who think him forgetful because it does not happen as quickly as they want: to whom add also, indeed he is not forgetful as you think: and if I said 'remembered,' this is against those complaining, who because of the delay think him forgetful.
9.14: 9.14 Have mercy. CASSIODORUS. In his own person he says what each one asks. See. Ibid. The look of God is help, and when it comes, light puts darkness to flight: from the pride of the enemy the humility of the sufferer is measured, because these are humbled as much as those are exalted.
9.15: 9.15 You who lift me up from the gates of death, etc. AUGUSTINE. That is, from all the desires by which one goes to death: death is already the very gladness in enjoying what is desired; hence the Apostle: 'The widow who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives' (1 Timothy 5). In the gates of the daughter of Sion. They are all the best pursuits, etc., up to which eye has not seen, nor ear heard. CASSIODORUS. Gates against gates, because these are of death, those of life. Sion. Ibid. He begot all the Churches of the world, because there Christ was born, whence faith began.
9.16: 9.16 I will rejoice. AUGUSTINE. Up to here the cry; from here the Church that is afflicted says, I will rejoice in Jesus. CASSIODORUS. For she is saved by hope. In the snare. Ibid. The hidden snare is deceitful thought: the foot is the love of the soul, which, if it is perverse, is called cupidity, if upright, charity. For the soul is moved by it as to a place to which it rejoices to have come through love. In the snare, therefore, that is, in fraudulent counsel: the foot, that is, the love that by fraud comes to vain joy, has been caught, because that delight binds them, so that they dare not tear their love away from it and turn to useful things. For if they try, it is painful to abandon what delights, and that pain does not let them depart.
9.17: 9.17 He shall be known. CASSIODORUS. Or concerning the future judgment, etc., up to as some falsely think.
9.18: 9.18 Let the sinners be turned. AUGUSTINE. This is the canticle of the diapsalma, as a hidden gladness of separation: which here occurs not in place but in affection, between the good and the wicked. CASSIODORUS. To sinners with Antichrist he predicts the end of evils; as though this for the time being, but at last they will be turned, lest they rejoice in their own. Into hell, lest they think they are to be sent elsewhere.
9.19: 9.19 Patience. AUGUSTINE. Patiently; for this especially God will be mindful of the poor, namely for their patience.
9.20: 9.20 Arise. AUGUSTINE. He prays for the future judgment. CASSIODORUS. Speaking of the end of the age, the prophet foresaw the coming of Antichrist; hence as though terrified he cries: arise.
9.21: 9.21 Let them know. That is, let them know by torment that they were foolish men.
9.22: 9.22 Why. AUGUSTINE. Diapsalma, because that Antichrist will be allowed to do such great things that he will be thought God: he adds as it were the voice of those groaning and asking about the delay of the judgment. CASSIODORUS, AUGUSTINE. Why. He discusses the evils of that time, etc., up to but in due season, namely so: While the wicked is proud.
9.23: 9.23 The poor man is set on fire; they are caught in the counsels which they devise. AUGUSTINE. Wonderfully the providence of God works from evils, etc., up to thus the wicked are condemned, the just are saved.
9.24: 9.24 For the sinner is praised. Therefore he is proud or is caught, because he is praised by his own, in the fulfillment of the desires of his sensuality. AUGUSTINE. The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins: for it delights them to do things in which not only is a reprover not feared but a praiser is even heard.
9.25: 9.25 In the wrath of his. CASSIODORUS. Of Antichrist, because he will do all things turbulently and cruelly: or, of God, he will not seek God by repenting; or, God will not seek him, to avenge himself here, but in the future will punish more gravely.
9.26: 9.26 Defiled. CASSIODORUS. The cause of wickedness is that he does not have God before his eyes, and therefore his ways, that is, his thoughts and works, are filthy. At all times. AUGUSTINE. His own, namely of his life, etc., up to and because he will lord it over all his enemies.
9.27: 9.27 He has said, etc. I will take possession of all nations, but not without evil, that is, sin, which is proper to him. Or I will always be without evil: this he promises himself, whose mouth is full of cursing, etc. I shall not be moved. AUGUSTINE. Or, he will think that by evil arts, and not otherwise, he will come from mortal generation into the eternal, as Simon Magus also thought.
9.28: 9.28 Under his tongue. CASSIODORUS. That is, his thoughts are about the labor of the saints and bodily sorrow, which is evident in the martyrs. Or, the labor of the saints and the sorrow which is in the pains of the body is under his tongue, that is, lighter than his tongue, which does harm inwardly: that pain, namely, is outside. Or, under the tongue, because words are feared more and will harm more than blows, by which the soul is cast down and will perish.
9.29: 9.29 In hidden places, etc. AUGUSTINE, that is, in ambiguous ones, where it is not easily seen what is to be asked and what not.
9.30: 9.30 His eyes are upon the poor, etc. Ibid. He sets out the snares; the eyes, as with mercy and affection; or, he deceives others in such a way that his eyes look cruelly upon the poor in spirit. The lion in his den, etc. Because in him there is force and guile, etc., up to through heretics and false brethren.
9.31: 9.31 He will bow down. CASSIODORUS. When, with excessive prosperity, he has let his mind slacken into ease, he will fall by sudden destruction: and the Lord will slay him with the spirit of his mouth. Unto the end. They deny that God sees, etc., up to he rouses the Lord, Arise, O Lord.
9.33: 9.33 Arise, O Lord God, and let your hand be exalted, forget not, etc. Ibid. He prays for the judgment, that these things, which are so great that no one would wish the time in which they happen to be prolonged, may soon be ended here. Arise. As if suddenly, that they may be crushed, while your own are exalted with you and glorified.
9.34: 9.34 Wherefore has the wicked provoked God. AUGUSTINE. Now understanding and rejoicing also about that judgment, he says, wherefore? that is, what does it profit to do such great evils? For God has said in his heart, etc. Ibid. This sense calls for pronunciation, etc., up to lest they labor or be angry. AUGUSTINE. Christ tolerated Judas and sent him to preach, and gave him the Eucharist, to show that the gifts reach those who receive the faith, such as Judas was.
9.35: 9.35 For you see the labor and sorrow. You have already ordained it, where you will deliver them into your hand. To the orphan, etc. AUGUSTINE. To him whose father, the world, through whom he was carnally begotten, dies, so that he may say: 'The world is crucified to me, and I to the world.'
9.36: 9.36 Break the arm. He terrifies with punishments, he soothes with good things. It shall be sought. AUGUSTINE. When it is still necessary for purging us, as above, while the wicked is proud, etc.; but because it shall not be found, that is, because there is now nothing in which there may be a place for his sin, there is no need of the file for smooth iron.
9.37: 9.37 The Lord shall reign for ever and for ever and ever. This kingdom will be the more welcome because of the evils that run together, which will come when Antichrist is destroyed; from this kingdom you nations shall perish, but the poor shall have it, because the desire of the poor, etc.
9.38: 9.38 The preparation of their heart. CASSIODORUS. Or, the desire, which is where something is sought more ardently with all the powers of the soul. Or, this, which God himself prepared in their hearts. Or, which they wish to ask immediately, may God hear. The ear, etc. AUGUSTINE. When the members are named which in us are visible and bodily, in God the powers of operations must be understood. To judge for the fatherless and the humble, etc. The second coming will be manifest, etc., up to the author of evils will be condemned with his people.
10.1: 10.1 Unto the end. AUGUSTINE. A psalm of David the prophet, teaching to resist heretics.
10.2: 10.2 In the Lord I put my trust. AUGUSTINE. About the heretics who wish to turn Catholics to their own perversity. Ibid. In the Lord I put my trust. As to the letter it can be read of the passion, and Christ says it according to the man, as he is wont against the terrors of the Jews, In the Lord I put my trust. In the Lord I put my trust. When sinners wish to shoot the upright. For behold. Ibid. These are the terrors of those threatening us concerning sinners, so that we may pass over to them as though to the just. For they say: The sinners have bent the bow, the Scriptures, from which they send poisoned arrows, which they prepare in the secret of the heart.
10.3: 10.3 In the dark. CASSIODORUS. Those living in a simple sense, or in their own ambiguous opinions, not that Scripture is able to do this, but because:
10.4: 10.4 For the things which you have perfected. He turns his speech from these to God, as if: Why do they say, migrate? Why is he terrified about sinners, who aim to shoot the upright? Because the things you have perfected they have destroyed in their assemblies, where they kill with poisons the little ones, who were to be nourished with milk, from whose mouth praise is perfected. But the just man, what has he done? AUGUSTINE. According to each part, etc., up to harms his own soul, not the just man, who believes in God.
10.6: 10.6 The Lord questions, etc. But the just man. He threatens judgment, through fear of which they may abandon falsehoods. Questions. Ibid. That is, tests, because the good are not wearied by obscure things but exercised in knowledge: they are not puffed up but confirmed. Which you have perfected. That is, you have perfectly brought forth, or by fulfilling what was foretold. They have destroyed, by expounding badly. Ibid. In the dark. Or on a dark moon. There are two opinions about the moon, etc., up to who then speaks holy sacraments, when they are given through holy ones.
10.7: 10.7 He shall rain upon. He shows what he will render to the wicked
10.8: 10.8 Justices. Ibid. In the plural, that you may take it of the just, in whom there are many justices, though God's is one. His countenance beheld equity. Equity was seen in the face, that is, in knowledge of him: for his face is the knowledge of him, that is, the power by which he will be made known to the worthy. Or he saw, because he does not give himself to be known to the wicked but to the good, which is equity.
11.1: 11.1 For the eighth. CASSIODORUS. For the eighth, because here the prophet asks that the iniquity of the world be destroyed, so that he may come to the truth of the promise to come. AUGUSTINE. The eighth for the day of judgment, as was said in the sixth psalm.
11.2: 11.2 Save me. He calls back from the falsehoods of the world to the words of God, where there is salvation; he asks to be saved from the perversity of the world. For the holy man has failed. CASSIODORUS. He sets out the many things he feared: gathering them into one so that the force may be greater. Holy. Ibid. God, who is everywhere present, has failed as far as concerns men, who do not believe in him.
11.3: 11.3 Neighbor. AUGUSTINE. Every man is a neighbor, when no evil is to be done to anyone: every man is a neighbor by the condition of first birth; friends and kinsmen by kinship of flesh; anyone who does good by comparison of mercy. Heart, etc. The sprouting signifies a double heart, in which the deceitful man is described, whence: 'A double-minded man is inconstant in all his ways.' The good have one heart and one soul.
11.4: 11.4 May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips, etc. CASSIODORUS. That is, let them perish everywhere, who agree in one perversity. The tongue that speaks proud things. Ibid. That is, the proud: these are the hypocrites, having an appearance in speech to deceive men, and not subject to God. REMIGIUS. Or, philosophers.
11.5: 11.5 Who have said: our tongue. CASSIODORUS. They boast of the power of their lips, as though they had not received it from God.
11.6: 11.6 Of the needy and the groaning of the poor. AUGUSTINE, CASSIODORUS. The needy, the Gentiles, who had neither law nor prophets; the poor, the Jews. Now. Which was not so in the former people. I will arise. I will appear in the Son. I will set. The consolation of the poor. Confidently. Powerfully, whom nothing resists.
11.7: 11.7 The words of the Lord. Ibid. Against the evils of the world, Christ sent by the Father, whose words are true, those of the impious false. Chaste. Against what was said above, they have spoken vain things
11.8: 11.8 You, O Lord. CASSIODORUS. Turning to the Lord, he shows the usefulness of the divine words.
11.9: 11.9 On every side. The conclusion on both parts. AUGUSTINE. On every side, that is, by desire of temporal things, which revolve in seven days and do not come to the eighth, that is, the eternal: whence 'a wise king scatters the wicked, and brings the wheel over them' (Proverbs 20), that is, the circuit of things that turn. You have multiplied the sons of men. Ibid. There is also a multiplication in temporal things that turns away from the unity of God: but the just are multiplied in height, when they go from virtue to virtue.
12.1: 12.1 Unto the end. CASSIODORUS. A psalm on the charity of Christ, etc., up to according to that verse: 'I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ' (Philippians 1).
12.2: 12.2 How long. CASSIODORUS. The great ardor of one who endures, etc., up to because hope is drawn out. Counsels. AUGUSTINE. There is no need of counsel, etc., up to grieving and praying for eternal things.
12.3: 12.3 How long shall my enemy be exalted, etc. CASSIODORUS. He says that before the coming of Christ the devil held men captive. Or over me, that is, my cruelty, because he is worshipped in the whole world, and he weeps because the world is thus perishing.
12.4: 12.4 Consider. Ibid. After the complaint, a prayer that he may be enlightened, lest he yield to the frauds of the enemy, who trusts in mercy. Consider. AUGUSTINE. Send him whom you are going to send. Hear me. CASSIODORUS. For all, for whom he asks in general. Enlighten. If not with the body, let us see with the mind. Lest I sleep. When, the light of faith being buried, they are shut in by carnal delight. In death. That is, in the sin which is against the Holy Spirit, of which John says: 'There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it.'
12.6: 12.6 They shall rejoice. AUGUSTINE. Not only to enlighten me, but lest the enemy rejoice. I have hoped. CASSIODORUS. Even if he hastens, yet he is patient: because even if it is delayed he is firm in hope, and inwardly, already seeing, he rejoices in him whom he desires to see in the flesh: hence he who before complained now says that good things have been given to him. He has given. He will not give: the great power of faith already has what is to come. My heart shall rejoice. If he so desires, if he so serves what is to come, what is to be done when it has been received?
13.1: 13.1 The fool has said. CASSIODORUS. A rebuke of the Jews, their malice described. The first psalm on the rebuke of the Jews, etc., up to this man is not God.
13.2: 13.2 The Lord from heaven. Ibid. But from that they are inexcusable, because the Lord looked down, that is, he stood out from human nature. AUGUSTINE. From heaven, that is, he looks through holy souls: for in himself nothing is hidden from him. Or, from heaven, through holy souls, which are the heaven and seat of God. Or, the Lord the Father from heaven, that is, from the secret of the divine mind. CASSIODORUS. Or from the equality of God the Father. If there is any that understands. Or he saw whether there is any that understands, and found that someone does not understand: because he does not seek but turns aside, for: 'All have turned aside,' etc.
13.3: 13.3 A sepulcher. Ibid. Thus made useless to others, because their throat is a sepulcher, etc. A sepulcher. These three verses, which run to the second division, at 'Shall they not know,' etc., are said not to be from the Hebrew, etc., up to he does not have them. Destruction. AUGUSTINE. Thus they have been made useless to themselves, etc., up to and unhappiness in the future. CASSIODORUS. The way of the impious, etc., up to: The fear of God before their eyes, etc.
13.4: 13.4 Shall they not know. He threatens judgment to the impious.
13.5: 13.5 The Lord they have not, etc. AUGUSTINE. For they do not truly call upon him, who love what displeases God.
13.6: 13.6 The counsel of the poor man. CASSIODORUS. An invective against the Jews, etc., up to that is, proceeding from the Jews, etc.
13.7: 13.7 Who will give out of Sion, etc. CASSIODORUS. Lastly the conversion of the Jews is foretold, which will take place when the fullness of the Gentiles shall have come in. When he shall have turned away. For the Jews also the Apostle cites this testimony of Isaiah: 'He shall come out of Sion who turns away the captivity, or the impiety, from Jacob.'
14.1: 14.1 Lord, who? CASSIODORUS. This psalm is properly instructive of morals, a restraint of presumption: where the unity of the present Church and the future rest are treated. First the prophet asks, like a priest standing before the face of the Lord, and seeks answers; wishing to know whom God judges worthy of his Church.
14.2: 14.2 He who. Ibid. The answer of the Lord, etc., up to as Christ the lamb without breaking of limbs, who properly entered the temple, not to be expiated like the others but without stain. Works justice. As when he cast the sellers and buyers out of the temple.
14.3: 14.3 Who speaks. Here he pursues it more fully. It is truth when a thing is as it is said: Christ did this properly. In his heart, who at times was silent to the unworthy who sought him deceitfully. He has not done guile. Guile is in the tongue when one thing is said and another is in the breast. Or, he did no guile, because all that he heard from the Father, without any addition or suppression, he made known to his neighbors, that is, the disciples; to the Jews, his neighbors according to the flesh. Nor has he done evil to his neighbor. But he prayed for them; he did not hold reproach against his neighbors, as is plain from the fact that he did not tear Judas with biting rebuke.
14.4: 14.4 To nothing, etc. AUGUSTINE. This is perfection, that the malignant one has no power in man, and that he is in his sight, that is, that he surely knows that no one is malignant except one who turns from the Creator to created things.
