The malignant one, that is, the devil, is despised; as when he said: 'Get behind me, Satan,' etc. On the contrary, he glorifies those who fear the Lord. He swore, when to the apostles he promised with the most certain truth: 'I will not now call you servants but friends.'
14.5: 14.5 He who swears to his neighbor, etc. Ibid. These three are not great, etc., up to when in the preceding conclusion he has put the past, he is brought to nothing. Money. Either earthly, which is utterly forbidden to be given at usury, which the Lord handed over to Judas to distribute to the poor, not at usury. Or spiritual, which is commanded to be given at usury, that is, preaching to instruct men. And gifts against the innocent. Christ does indeed receive gifts, as from the Magi, and daily pious offerings; but not against the innocent; indeed he gave his life for them. He who does these things shall not be moved. Behold the complete answer to the one who asks: he says 'does,' to invite us to action, not only to singing these things. He who does these things shall not be moved. CASSIODORUS. Conclusion. Likewise he who does these things will rest on the mountain.
15.1: 15.1 Inscription of the title. CASSIODORUS. This title is taken from the Gospel, not from the Old Testament. What the title noted, that is, victory and kingdom, fits Christ, which is treated here.
15.2: 15.2 Preserve me, etc. The second psalm, which touches briefly on the passion and resurrection; first, Christ, showing the one nature of man, asks that he be preserved, saying that all he endured was brought to the glory of his inheritance. AUGUSTINE. Christ speaks here according to the man, concerning whom the royal title stood out in the passion: Jesus of Nazareth, king of the Jews
15.3: 15.3 To the saints who are in the earth. Ibid. Christ has already explained how he prayed; he now relates what good things God did for him. AUGUSTINE. To the saints, etc., up to and power that I might rise. He has made wonderful. CASSIODORUS. As if: I said these things to the Lord; but the Lord has made wonderful, that is, has made wonderful wills; these are wonderful while, obeying them, men become heavenly from earthly.
15.4: 15.4 Multiplied. Ibid. By which he made wonderful, etc., up to which agree in one sound, by which his wills are shown.
15.5: 15.5 The portion of the inheritance. AUGUSTINE. Let others choose other things, etc., up to but those who choose God as their portion. CASSIODORUS. Or, the Lord is the portion, that is, the share and reward, of my inheritance, that is, of the saints. And the portion of my cup, that is, the reward of the passion. For the inheritance pertains to the Gentiles, the cup to the passion, which when drunk gives resurrection. But let no one think himself an heir unless he is outstanding.
15.6: 15.6 Lines, etc. Ibid. As a lot, in which there is divine election, as the lot fell upon Matthias, and each takes according to his measure. In the glorious. That is, in the saints.
15.7: 15.7 I will bless the Lord. Ibid. He gives thanks to the Father for the understanding, and for the passion, in which with his favor he conquers, and for the resurrection, and confession, and these are the things through which the inheritance is restored, that he may be king of the Jews, as the title says. Understanding, etc. AUGUSTINE. By which this inheritance can be seen and possessed. Moreover, etc. That is, above the understanding. Even till night, etc. That is, death, my lower part, the assumption of flesh, has instructed me, to expel the darkness of mortality which that understanding does not have, because on account of them it could neither be troubled nor fail. Reins. From whom according to the flesh I came forth, namely kindred: they rebuked me with injuries, with temptation and passion.
15.8: 15.8 I set the Lord before me. Ibid. Draw from this an example by which sins are avoided: for he who always beholds God with the eye of the mind is not inclined to sins.
16.1: 16.1 The prayer of David. CASSIODORUS. The prayer fits the person of the Lord, with the Church joined, who is his body. Hear, O Lord. Ibid. This psalm makes us attend to the true nature of his humanity. The prayer of Christ is the instruction of the faithful: as by weeping for Lazarus he taught us to have charity for our neighbor, he fled persecutors to take from us the boldness of thoughtless rashness. First, he asks that it be repaid to him according to justice. Not in deceitful lips. As one who is unjustly condemned; or as one who says: 'Lord, Lord,' and does not do the works. AUGUSTINE. Or, may my judgment come forth from your countenance, not in deceitful lips, so that in judging I may bring forth nothing other than what I understand.
16.2: 16.2 From your countenance. CASSIODORUS. That is, according to what you know in me, who have no sin. Judgment. By which the judgment of him who was judged is seen to have come forth. From your countenance, not from the disposition of the Jews, which is evident in the resurrection. Or, judgment, by which he discerns all things.
16.3: 16.3 You have proved. CASSIODORUS. By the likeness of a furnace, etc., up to you know that I am pure.
16.4: 16.4 Hard ways. Ibid. Namely the works of men: namely, those which the works of men deserve. Or those which men ought to imitate, for whom the way of vices is easy, of virtues hard. Or, it was not found, so that he does not speak, that is, that I may not say these things boastfully, or, that I may not sin with the tongue, which is a work of men. AUGUSTINE. Or, the hard ways of the robber, etc., up to after I walked the hard ways and completed my steps.
16.5: 16.5 Perfect. CASSIODORUS. Even to the end: before that there is only a beginning. Steps, that is, human actions, so that those who wish to imitate are not moved from you, or the footprints from them.
16.6: 16.6 I have cried. Ibid. Second, he prays that his purity be freed from the snares of the Jews. I too have cried, as if you were to say, this befits only the just man, who prays confidently, because he knows he is heard.
16.7: 16.7 Make wonderful. AUGUSTINE. Wonderful are the things that are new: these are the things that took place in the flesh, to the amazement of the Jews.
16.8: 16.8 The pupil. It is very small, and yet through it the sharpness of sight is directed, by which light and darkness are distinguished, as through the humanity of Christ the divinity discerns between the good and the wicked.
16.10: 16.10 Fat. CASSIODORUS. By the likeness of animals that are swollen with fat, that is, they have retained pride, not lean, that is, not humble; or fat, that is, they have retained the carnal sense, or, fattened with crimes, they have lost true understanding, so that what remains is to speak proud things. Their mouth has spoken pride. Not the heart, because often the wicked condemn in the heart what they defend with the mouth.
16.12: 16.12 They have taken me, etc. Ibid. Whence did they have this opportunity? I answer, they took me from God, whose disposition it is, or, from the betrayer, or, they received eagerly from the judge. Like a lion ready, etc. AUGUSTINE, CASSIODORUS. The princes are to be compared to the lion, the devil, at whose instigation they act: the people are the lion's whelp, that is, the son of the devil, dwelling, remaining in ambush, because it is the custom of the wicked to hide their intentions so that they may accomplish them secretly.
16.13: 16.13 Arise, O Lord. CASSIODORUS. A prayer concerning retributions. Prevent, etc. Ibid. By the likeness of a runner: everyone sins first against himself before against another. Supplant him: by the likeness of a wrestler, that is, make them ineffectual and cast them down. Deliver my soul from the wicked. AUGUSTINE. By raising me from the death inflicted by the impious. Sword. My soul is the sword; which your hand, that is, your power, has taken up, that by it he may subdue the kingdoms of iniquity and divide the just from the impious. Divide them, etc., CASSIODORUS. that is, the Jews divided, etc., up to misery, as deservedly: because, from your hidden things. From your hidden things. That is, from uncleannesses, etc., up to that is, they will share in evils even to satiety. From hidden things. AUGUSTINE. Not only is this visible punishment theirs, but from hidden things, that is, sins which are hidden from the light of your truth, their memory is full, so that they forget God.
17.1: 17.1 I will love you, O Lord, my strength, etc. CASSIODORUS. Christ says this, as does the Church, that is, the whole Christ. Ibid. First, the prophet, gathering up the sum, gives thanks for deliverance.
17.3: 17.3 Refuge. Ibid. When there was need of counsel, David fled to him and found it. Deliverer, so that if he is powerful, he frees the one held captive by enemies. Protector, AUGUSTINE. because I did not presume on myself, as though raising a horn of pride against you; but I found you the height of salvation, and that I might find it you took me up.
17.4: 17.4 Praising I will call upon. CASSIODORUS. After all things he does not boast in exaltation but attributes everything to God: and therefore is safe; for he who does otherwise, left to himself, perishes, even if he seemed to have conquered.
17.5: 17.5 They have surrounded me. Ibid. In the person of the just before the coming of Christ, etc., up to who were troubled by rushing iniquities.
17.6: 17.6 The sorrows of hell. The Gentiles, to be tormented in hell with deserved sorrow. The snares of death prevented me, it follows:
17.8: 17.8 Moved. Behold how, etc., up to and this which mortality and possibility anticipated. From his temple. CASSIODORUS. Either from heaven, or from the body of Christ to come. Moved. AUGUSTINE. Thus, Christ having been glorified, the sinners were moved and trembled. The foundations, etc. CASSIODORUS. The presumptions of the proud, that is, riches and such things on which they leaned: for the hope of the world has perished, which God hates.
17.10: 17.10 The heavens. Ibid. That is, he bowed the preachers from contemplation to ministry, and to bearing troubles. He came down, etc. He himself suffered in them, and into the knowledge of some. Darkness: the dark ones, who even persecute, are under his power; or, those who believe simply are subject to him.
17.11: 17.11 And he ascended. For he makes some full of knowledge, in whom he stands supereminent, whose swiftness of understanding he transcends: but he uses the dark ones secretly: hence, 'Assyria is the rod of my fury,' but he himself did not know, but his own know. He flew upon the wings of the wind. The winds, than which nothing is swifter, his fame surpasses, as when, soon after he was born, he was announced by a star.
17.12: 17.12 Darkness. AUGUSTINE. The obscurities of the sacraments, or, in these shadows, where we walk by faith and not by sight (Matthew 2). Not through the heavens. CASSIODORUS. He came down and ascended (2 Corinthians 5), but through ethereal clouds, as in the Hebrew, that is, through the prophets in whom the teaching is obscure, but through clouds not of the ether, that is, the Apostles, who are most radiant in the knowledge of him, that is, contemplating more closely.
17.13: 17.13 Hail. AUGUSTINE. Rebukes, which strike hard hearts; but if the fire of charity dissolves them, in a gentle mind they become satisfying [elsewhere: leaping] water. And coals, because by that fire dark hearts, set alight, revive.
17.14: 17.14 He thundered. CASSIODORUS. Literally, as when thunder was perceived, God saying: 'I have glorified, and I will glorify again.' He gave his voice: as when he did not say: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.'
17.15: 17.15 And he sent. Ibid. The Lord thundered, and the Lord sent: for the passage to the Gentiles was not always certain nor of reasonable habit.
17.16: 17.16 And the fountains of waters appeared. At Christ's coming, what the obscurity of the divine utterance was covering became plain. At the rebuke. Conversion to God: as with thanksgiving, because through preaching he rebuked sinners, and inspired them to fear the wrath to come. He sent. Ibid. So far of the Lord's coming; from here, of the Christian times. The Father sent Christ. He took me. The Church, the bride. Out of many waters. Ibid. Of baptism. Or he sent the Spirit, who is the gift. From on high, because equal to the Father and the Son. He took, as a fugitive. He lifted up, to the height of virtue and good work.
17.18: 17.18 From my enemies. AUGUSTINE. That is, vices, which harm more than all enemies. And from those who, etc. That is, outward enemies, namely men and also demons, which is necessary, because they were strengthened in a certain respect. Behold they prevailed, that is, they were stronger. By this he delivers the more, because they are strengthened; for when the Church is afflicted, she grows more.
17.20: 17.20 Into breadth. Ibid. Through the savagery of the wicked the Church grows in number and merit. He saved me, in that I came to faith. Because he wished me. AUGUSTINE. That is, he chose me freely.
17.21: 17.21 And he will reward me according to the justice of a good will. And according to the cleanness of my hands. Ibid. The works that come after the first benefits of God, namely faith and charity, which God provides freely without any preceding merit.
17.22: 17.22 For I have kept. Ibid. Or thus, continuing with the preceding verse, etc., up to and as I have begun, so I shall be unspotted, wherefore in the future he will reward.
17.24: 17.24 With him, to him, clinging. And I will observe, lest I fall again. From iniquity, which is the death of the blessed man.
17.25: 17.25 And he will reward. CASSIODORUS. God rewards in two ways: here in the present, that the just man may be justified, and he who is filthy may be filthy still, hence here he says: With the holy you will be holy, etc., and in the future a reward to the good and punishment to the wicked, hence there: 'For you will save the humble people,' etc., as though thus here: because in the future you will save the humble people. AUGUSTINE. And he will give: now not only on account of the breadth of faith which works through love, but on account of longanimity he will reward me. In the sight: this befits the just, that as they always behold God, so God continually looks upon them.
17.26: 17.26 With the holy. CASSIODORUS. He had said, to be rewarded according to justice, etc., up to because you, O Lord, will save the humble people. And you will humble the eyes of the proud. AUGUSTINE. There is also a hidden depth, by which you are understood to be holy with the holy, because you sanctify. For you light. What he announced about the elect and sanctified, he now prays for others.
17.29: 17.29 A lamp. Ibid. There were preachers in whom there was light, that is, knowledge of the truth, with which they enlightened others, hence: 'We have this treasure in earthen vessels.' Darkness. AUGUSTINE. Those who are still in darkness. My. By predestination.
17.30: 17.30 In my God. CASSIODORUS. For my God is the way by which one goes to heaven, undefiled. Or, the way by which the holy and immaculate Virgin came into the world. And whatever he said has been examined by the Holy Spirit, that is, is useful and honorable: as a wise man first judges within himself whatever he says. I shall pass over. Ibid. Man cannot utterly tear down, but with the help of God he passes the wall, the obstacle of sins.
17.31: 17.31 My God. Ibid. And continuing it follows: You will deliver me from the contradictions of the people. The rest he interposes as commendation. The words. They are proved by the fire of examination. Of all. Ibid. No one is excepted, except one who does not wish to hope.
17.32: 17.32 For who. Ibid. I say God: for who is another God, except him who is also Lord over things? And because he is known in Judea, not the gods of the nations; this is against the pagans, who devise many for themselves.
17.33: 17.33 God who. Ibid. Still beyond the common things, he commends through special ones, because third, Christ is commended for his virtue and power. Girded. Ibid. That is, armed. Or by the likeness of a runner. Or, it notes dignity and strength, which befits one who by his power will judge the people, or the world. Unspotted, without sin. The stag leaps over thorns and gaping places, so Christ the thorns and pits of sins: and as the stag the high places, so Christ ascended above all creatures.
17.35: 17.35 Who teaches: I make cautious against imminent snares. Hands, works or wills. To battle, against the devil. As a bow, etc., by the likeness of a thing that does not exist, that is, unrelenting strength. Arms. Christ's prophets and apostles, through whom he works: who are a bow of bronze, because in preaching they do not grow soft but, always strong, hurl the words of salvation.
17.36: 17.36 The protection of salvation. Not that I suffer nothing, which yet is for progress. Tribulation is correction, and teaching, and enlargement, and confirmation.
17.37: 17.37 You have enlarged. AUGUSTINE. Lest carnal narrowness hinder, because you have made charity broad, working cheerfully even concerning those things which are under me, namely mortal things and members.
17.38: 17.38 I will pursue. CASSIODORUS. By reproving, by wearing them out with various afflictions.
17.43: 17.43 And I will crush them small. AUGUSTINE. Behold the same operation of the Father and the Son. Above he said: 'You have destroyed, Father,' and now he says I will crush small, that is, I will take away their strength, so that afterward they yield to every wind of doctrine.
17.44: 17.44 You will deliver. CASSIODORUS. About them the wrath: But you will deliver me, the abasement of the Jews and the exaltation of the Gentiles.
17.46: 17.46 The sons. The Jews whom I nourished, become strangers: They have lied to me, to my honor. They have grown old and limped from their paths, following their own traditions rather than God's.
17.47: 17.47 The Lord lives. Ibid. Fourth, the Church rejoicing praises in summary the gifts of God. Or he lives, because he gives life. Blessed, because he blesses all things. And let the God of salvation be exalted. AUGUSTINE. May I not think of the God of my salvation in an earthly way, nor of salvation itself as earthly, but I will hope in him on high.
17.48: 17.48 Vengeance. CASSIODORUS. A pious vengeance, while the rebel is brought into subjection. From the wrathful. It is greater glory to deliver from burning evils.
17.51: 17.51 Magnifying, salvation. God who magnifies: Doing, God who does.
18.1: 18.1 Unto the end. CASSIODORUS. A psalm about the first coming, whence the tyrant falls, man is absolved; here the prophet looks to the end, that is, Christ, or to the last times.
18.2: 18.2 The heavens declare. Ibid. First, speaking of the incarnation, he commends the preaching of the new law. AUGUSTINE. The heavens, the apostles, of the glory of Christ in which he is equal to the Father. CASSIODORUS. Or the heavens, which sent the star. Glory. Ibid.: That God freely forgives sins. Works. AUGUSTINE. Those which are according to the man, etc., up to and they themselves become night to the same, to the dark, the knowledge which concerns human things. CASSIODORUS. And this so wonderfully, in that it is in all tongues; and so widely, in that it is in every part of the circuit of the earth.
18.3: 18.3 Day to day. CASSIODORUS. He speaks demonstratively. AUGUSTINE. Day to day. The Spirit utters to spiritual men the fullness of wisdom, etc., up to this teaching is continued by days and nights to posterity.
18.4: 18.4 Speeches. CASSIODORUS. Public persuasions. Words. Common narrations. Of which not. He would say more plainly, in which their voices are not heard, or, the voices of all speeches are heard: he does the same through the relative. AUGUSTINE. The Spirit made the first ones speak in all tongues, who was to gather all nations into one, one man then for all, so now one Christ, head and body.
18.6: 18.6 In the sun. CASSIODORUS. What he praises others for having done, he himself does, he preaches the incarnation. Or in the sun, in the open of the world, or in labor. The sun burns, shines, and varies the seasons. His tabernacle. AUGUSTINE. As a military dwelling, that is, the dispensation of his incarnation, in which he came to overcome the errors of the world. Or the tabernacle, the Church, in the open, not in secret, to be hidden. Bridegroom. CASSIODORUS. So often promised by the prophets, a great likeness of the sacrament: therefore born of a virgin, that he might join a virgin Church to himself. From his chamber. AUGUSTINE. That is, from the virginal womb, where God was joined to human nature as a bridegroom to a bride. Behold humble mercy, but strong in majesty. A giant to run. CASSIODORUS. Undisturbed, irrevocable, surpassing human nature in power. From the highest. Here the Trinity is shown, etc., up to it notes the unity of the Trinity. Nor is there anyone who hides himself, etc. AUGUSTINE. The Word made flesh did not permit anyone to excuse himself from the shadow of death: because the heat of the Word penetrated even that. Or, the heat is the Spirit, whom he sent when he returned, who is law, testimony, justice, precept, fear and judgments, because he does these things.
18.8: 18.8 The law of the Lord. CASSIODORUS. Second, he praises the precepts of the New and Old Testament. Ibid. The law given through Moses, correcting all its words by distinction, and sending to the grace of Christ. Converting. AUGUSTINE. By liberty, to imitate himself, not pressing with the yoke of servitude. Souls. Wills, not only hands, as the Old Testament. Testimony. Whatever testimonies he gave to Israel are full of truth, and gave wisdom to the humble. Wisdom: about divine things.
18.9: 18.9 The justices of the Lord. Ibid. All are right in him, who did not teach what he did not do, so that those imitating might rejoice in them, doing freely with charity, not slavishly with fear. CASSIODORUS. Justices, the law that justifies; whatever it commands is just.
72.16: 72.16 It is a labor before me. Augustine: It stands in my way like a wall, etc., up to: he sees them condemned in judgment.
72.17: 72.17 The sanctuary. Augustine: Christ, who as God discerns the merits of each. Or the sanctuary, the Holy of Holies, that is, the secret of the divine ordering.
72.18: 72.18 Nevertheless. Augustine, Cassiodorus: Behold what he learned in the sanctuary: that the wicked are deceived here, and afterward at the end will be forsaken by all. He himself was freed from that evil, since he too sought earthly things, but from God. Here he says that in this world the wicked are neither exempt nor unpunished, because even if happy, they still carry guilt and frequently fall into ruin. Nevertheless, that is, but: even here you have set before them this flower and abundance of temporal things, on account of their deceits, etc. On account of deceits. Augustine: Or, near a slippery place. As if to say: You acted with them in a deceitful manner, giving evils under the appearance of good. Or, near a slippery place, as temporal things are, where those who are near them through love fall; for when a deceitful man wishes to cast another down, he sets him near a slippery place.
72.20: 72.20 Like a dream. The same: The comparison is plain. With eyes closed we see goods that we do not find as soon as they are opened; in this life it is a dream, in death they awake, knowing what it is. In your city. In the sight of your people, or, while your city is being established. Jerome: Or in the heavenly Jerusalem, their image, the likeness of the deformities which they make for themselves: one a lion in ferocity, another a boar in the filth of lust. Cassiodorus: Or the glory of this time, which is not true glory but a likeness of glory; for when the truth fails them, the image will perish, and they will not keep even the likeness, who will have nothing of blessedness; therefore you will destroy them, because through them,
72.21: 72.21 My heart was inflamed. That is, envious of the happy. And my reins were changed. In which the state, that is, the steadiness of mind, was loosened so that I loved prosperity; it is a grave fault to give others an occasion of sinning. I was brought to nothing. Clinging to vain things, I was made unjust toward God. I did not know. It is a great and deep ignorance not to know that you are sinning. Cassiodorus: In your city, the image. Or this can be understood of heretics, etc., up to: or above the heavenly Church. For my heart was inflamed. Augustine: Behold the conversion of this Asaph, etc., up to: were changed into spiritual ones.
72.24: 72.24 When, etc. The same: Because earlier I was brought to nothing, that is, I descended to things that are nothing, because I did not know that they were nothing; and afterward I became gentle like a beast of burden, bearing the load, and I will be with you always. Beast of burden. Cassiodorus: Before God, those who think against God are in the place of cattle; and yet, though erring in these things and not knowing the judgments of God, I was in some way always with you, a stranger to idols, believing in you, and you held me. You held my hand. Augustine: Because although a beast, it did not depart from God. You held my hand, that is, the power of the right hand, that is, you covered me, because I am always with you, because I am a son. For he gave power to become children of God to those who believe in his name. On the left, the beast, loving these temporal things. Or the right hand. Cassiodorus: Not the left. God holds the right hand when he directs us to good works and frees us lest we sink, as with Peter. The same: Having seen the evil of the wicked and his own good, he rebukes himself for his former ways, because he sought earthly things from God, and he invites to the opposite. Augustine: He compares the heavenly reward with his earthly pleasure, and rebukes himself. Forever, etc. I shall never again be separated from him. Those who fornicate away from you, etc. Opposed to this fornication is chaste fear, which loves him freely, in whom it has all things.
72.28: 72.28 In the gates of the daughter of Sion. Augustine: In public, or in the concord of the Apostles, who are the gates of the Church. For preaching that is apart from the unity of the Church is empty. Or, by her virtues the Church is the daughter of Sion, that is, of contemplation.
73.1: 73.1 Understanding of Asaph. Augustine: Of the Synagogue, etc., up to: so that the hardness of the Jews might either be frightened or softened by calamities. Cassiodorus: He admonishes us to leave the figures behind and pass to the truth. Why, O God. The same: Describing the irreparable overthrow of Jerusalem, he asks the cause, wondering and lamenting; and he prays for the rejected people, and for vengeance on the destroyers, which is indeed useful to them, and has already been accomplished. You have cast us off. The same: As if strangers to your defense. Unto the end. Not even the temple is spared. He signifies the destruction and captivity brought by Titus and Vespasian. He calls them sheep, to move the mercy of the devout shepherd. Of your. We take vengeance more mildly on those whom we remember to have once been ours.
73.2: 73.2 You have possessed. Cassiodorus: Or, you have created; although he creates and orders all, yet the Jews especially, to whom he gave the Law and the Prophets. You have redeemed. Jerome: You by a price, that is, through you the price. Mount. Augustine: Eminence; Sion is contemplation, in which, in which thing, you have dwelt. Or the word is idle in it. Jerome: The mount, or of Mount Sion, or in it. Thus far the deeds of the true Testament, which the truth promised follows. By Sion he signifies Jerusalem, in which the presence of Christ dwelt, and therefore he begs that he not give it over to desolation. The rod of your inheritance. Augustine: The congregation itself is called the rod of inheritance; when Moses wished to take hold of this rod, it was turned into a serpent, but when he seized it by the tail it returned to a rod. Jerome: Because death entered the world by the persuasion of the serpent, the rod in the serpent is Christ in death. Hence also he who looked at the serpent, that is, believes in Christ dead, is healed from serpents, that is, from eternal death. Moses was afraid and fled, as the Apostles did when Christ was dying. With the tail held, that is, the hinder parts, it becomes a rod, because first he was slain, afterward he rose. The tail is also the end of the age, in which we return to the hand of God and are made firm, we who have slipped through death as through a serpent. Augustine: But because this concerns the Gentiles also, he expresses of whom he speaks: Mount Sion. That is, not of the Gentiles. Or, this Mount Sion, which you have inhabited in itself: Lift up your hand against their pride, of those by whom Jerusalem was overthrown, that is, the kings of the Gentiles. Unto the end, because they too already know Christ.
73.3: 73.3 Lift up. Cassiodorus: Your power, that you may turn their pride to humility, leading them to the end, that is, Christ, which has also been fulfilled, since at Rome the Christian religion has flourished. Lift up, because from being very superstitious it has become most holy. How great evils the enemy has done, etc. Augustine: The priests and the ministries of the temple were plunder. The whole nation was either slain or taken captive. The enemy, the Roman army; he sent this ahead by anticipation of theirs.
73.4: 73.4 They have gloried. Augustine, Cassiodorus: In their victory. Behold what they did without good zeal. They gloried; though repentance usually follows a crime, these turn it to glory; those who hate you, servants of demons, who are in no way to be tolerated. In the midst of your solemnity. Not in an outer place, but in the middle of the court. Another reading: they committed sacrileges. In the holy place. Cassiodorus: In the sanctuary, by contempt of the holy temple, where the Godhead seems to be despised, he stirs up indignation against the presumptuous. Signs, etc. Augustine: Eagles, etc., up to: that is, through the lofty places.
73.5: 73.5 As at the going out. Cassiodorus: Or as at an egress from above, that is, they did not know that this license went out from God. As in a forest, etc. Cassiodorus: Before it was built, he prophesies the overthrow of the temple. With axe and hatchet they have polluted the tabernacle of your name, etc. Augustine: The axe cuts beams; the hatchet pursues more finely. By this, then, he says that both great things and the smallest were cast down, so that the city was utterly devastated, first cut up, then fire devoured everything.
73.7: 73.7 In the earth, etc. Even to the ground they threw down the heights raised to the praise of God. He heightens the crime so that it may be avenged more severely. Cassiodorus: Or the whole can be read in the person of the despairing Jews, etc., up to: who among these things do not repent. Augustine: They said these things, but how long do you endure the reproaches of the Jews? He did not say this because he wishes them to perish, but to be changed. Unto the end of the world, that is, the evening, when the Jews will be converted.
73.9: 73.9 We have not seen our signs. Augustine, Cassiodorus: As if they were saying: These evils have rightly befallen us, because we did not see the signs; as if he were saying: We saw, but did not understand; and truly we saw, because this is the sign, that there is no prophet, or priest, or anointing; hence: When the Holy of holies comes, your anointing will cease (Dan. 9). And no prophet will know us any more, nor God through a prophet; that is, he will not announce Christ as coming, because he has already come. Any more. The same: Or he will not yet know, namely until the Jew acknowledges him.
73.10: 73.10 How long? etc. Cassiodorus: And as if he had suddenly known. How long, he supposed, will the adversary provoke? As if to say: He will reproach as long as the adversary, that is, the Jew, provokes your name. Why do you turn away. Augustine: After the sign of the rod, the sign of Moses' hand was added; this is the people of God: sent out from him it is unclean, but being called back it returns to its own color. He says therefore: How long do you not call back your hand, that it may acknowledge the Savior? Your hand and your right hand, that is, the Jews.
73.12: 73.12 But God is our king. Cassiodorus: With the signs destroyed, he shows the thing itself, namely, that in the coming of Christ salvation has been wrought everywhere. Augustine: But God. Asaph says with understanding, etc., up to: if therefore it has not gone before, let it at least follow. In the midst of the earth. Cassiodorus: Having become man, Jerusalem is said to be in the middle.
73.13: 73.13 You have strengthened. Augustine: The passage of the Red Sea made firm, so that there was a way between dry land. He adds its mystery, that in the waters of baptism he reduced to nothing the heads of unclean spirits.
73.14: 73.14 Food. Augustine: Christ is food, etc., up to: or they bite him himself by reproaching and accusing. Cassiodorus: Or while he tempts, he is food, because one makes progress from that. Or, to the peoples of the Ethiopians. Jerome: To those unwilling to be converted you have given him as food, in whom they may take delight.
73.15: 73.15 Fountains and torrents. Augustine: In others the word becomes, etc., up to: and it marks the abundance of preaching. Cassiodorus: Or the whole concerns the wicked. Fountains, whose evils flowed in continually; torrents, who sin suddenly and violently: God breaks these apart and dries them up. The rivers of Ethan. The floods and counsels of the devil. The day is yours and the night is yours. Augustine: He illuminates the day, but that of unchangeable wisdom. The moon consoles the night, that is, the manifestation of the flesh: The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (John 1). And likewise: Night to night declares knowledge (Ps. 28). The dawn and the sun. Augustine: Or the moon, that is, the carnal man, who changes like the moon, yet is not to be abandoned. Or the dawn and the sun, that is, the beginning and the progress of wisdom, the foolish and the perfect.
73.17: 73.17 You have made all. Cassiodorus: Or everything from this place is to be taken historically: The day is yours. The bounds of the earth, etc. Cassiodorus: As boundaries mark off territories, so the Apostles and Prophets distinguish them, and these guard the rights of faith; or all is to be taken historically.
73.18: 73.18 Remember. Cassiodorus: Now, as is happening everywhere, he prays for the Jews, and by counting up benefits he moves the merciful judge. As if to say: Remember this creature of yours. This. Augustine: Of your creature, of which creature of yours? The enemy has reproached the Lord, and the foolish people has provoked your name, etc. Augustine: Asaph, with understanding, grieves over his former blindness, and so prays for the Jews that they may confess their errors. He prays for what he knows will be; for there were among the Jews vessels of mercy.
73.20: 73.20 Look to your covenant. The same: Let the remnant be saved, because many who tend toward the earth have been darkened and filled with earth. Cassiodorus: Look. Fulfill what you promised, that you may establish the New Testament, which concerns eternal things. He recalls the promise because merits fail. Likewise because they are filled with iniquities, hence follows darkness, because those filled with iniquities lose the light of wisdom, because the dark places of the earth are houses by an earthly dwelling, that is, blind through love of earthly things.
73.21: 73.21 Let not the humble turn away confounded. Cassiodorus: The pleasing is put for the hateful, so that the love of the devout may temper the hatred of the stubborn. Confounded. The same: To be confounded is not for the humble but for the proud, who attribute not to God but to themselves.
73.22: 73.22 Arise, O God. Cassiodorus: Now Asaph, with understanding, shakes off the earthly promises of the Old Testament. Your cause. For they say: Where is your God? He is despised by the Jews as he walked on earth, and by false Christians as he sits in heaven. Judge therefore, let not my hope be deceived, I who have believed what I have not seen. Your cause. After all things, he makes it the cause of the judge, to whom the nature of his business is declared. Your cause, against those who murmur, that by manifest truth they may preach what they foolishly denied. All the day. Augustine: He says this so that the very continuance might stir the gentleness of the patient judge.
73.23: 73.23 The pride of those who hate you. Cassiodorus: At the end he sets the accursed evil, which is pride.
74.1: 74.1 Unto the end, destroy not, etc. Augustine: This psalm admonishes, etc., up to: that the Jews may believe and not corrupt the faith.
74.2: 74.2 We will give praise to you, O God. Augustine: Certain, then, of what has gone before, he begins: We will give praise. The repetition is an affirmation, that you may not regret having confessed; hence the Lord also doubles: Amen, amen. Let it be, let it be. And Joseph on Pharaoh's dream, who saw seven ears of grain and as many barren ones, and seven fat cattle and as many lean ones. Cassiodorus: Repetition is a confirmation to signify truth. One would suffice to signify firmness; the other was added. To confess sins even once to an earthly judge brings death, but to God frequent confession brings life. Hence invocation, then narration; hence follows: We will declare. We will call upon your name. The same: After confession God can be invoked, upon a man thus cleansed; and as by confession he is emptied of evils, so by invocation he is filled with goods. We will tell of your wonders, etc. Cassiodorus: The proud man is terrified by judgment, etc., up to: in whose person it is added:
74.3: 74.3 When I shall take a time. He takes according to the man what God himself gives, that is, the power of making judgment. Justices. Let those about to judge therefore first pray to be absolved.
74.4: 74.4 The earth is melted. Cassiodorus: He shows that all are without excuse in judgment, by the fact that he sent ahead the Apostles and Prophets. The earth and all. Augustine: Formerly firm, it flows away into diverse desires. Or, the earth, formerly bound by vices, by the breath of the Holy Spirit has been melted, that it might send forth the shoots of virtues.
74.5: 74.5 To act unjustly. Augustine: It is evil to sin; it is worse to persevere, and most ruinous, in defending oneself, to pour the blame back on God. Lift not up the horn. Cassiodorus: The greatest vice is that of excuse; he lifts up a horn, as it were, who strives to excuse his sins through others, as by the persuasions of devils, or by the necessity of the stars.
74.6: 74.6 To speak. Like those who say they have sinned not by their own fault but by the necessity of the stars, that it may be imputed to God and not to themselves. Or those who know their sins but promise themselves impunity.
74.7: 74.7 For neither from the east. Cassiodorus: Why this? Because the judge is such that he cannot be avoided, because he is everywhere; for he is God. Augustine: He judges from no one place apart, who is present everywhere as God. Cassiodorus: Mystically. The east, those on whom the sun of justice rises, etc., up to: because God is present and the knower.
74.9: 74.9 For in the hand of the Lord there is a cup. Augustine: The cup is the law and all Scripture, etc., up to: what was before, and this he exalts. Cassiodorus: The cup, the law; the unmixed wine, the heavenly mystery, etc., up to: not only the Jews.
74.10: 74.10 But I will declare it for ever: I will sing to the God of Jacob. Cassiodorus: All will drink, but separately: I, that is Christ, with the body, will declare for ever, as long as the age shall be.
74.11: 74.11 The horns of the just, that is, the gifts of Christ, which are the exaltation of the just.
75.1: 75.1 A canticle. Because it treats of the goods of Christ, namely that he is known, that he dwells, that he enlightens, that he saves. He breaks the glory of the Jews. For the Assyrians. Cassiodorus: Against the Jews, who are not directing but erring. Or, because they exalt themselves, since they seek salvation without grace and persecute the Church, as formerly the Assyrians the Jews. They are refuted here, the names of glory taken away, and are proved to be able to do nothing without grace.
75.2: 75.2 In Judea God is known. Augustine: The Jew boasts that God is known to the Jew, and it is true; but to the Jew inwardly, not in the flesh. Augustine: The Prophet says: if you are Jews, then God is known in you; but if he is not, then you are not Jews. In Judea. The same: With the two sons of Joseph taken in, together with the remaining eleven sons of Jacob there are twelve tribes, excepting the tribe of Levi, which was priestly and lived on tithes. The land was divided among the twelve tribes. Among these one is Judah, from whom come the kings, and from the kingdom all are called Jews. They confessed Caesar, not Christ; those of Judah are now no longer Jews.
83.5: 83.5 Blessed are they that dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they will praise you. Augustine: The good already have this, namely that they dwell in your house. There follows: For ever and ever they will praise you. This is the whole business of the saints there: there is no necessity there, which is the mother of all human actions, for for whom would they do anything there, where none are in need? They have therefore and they do that by which they are blessed. And everyone who is blessed is called blessed by having or by doing.
83.6: 83.6 Blessed is the man whose help is from you: he has disposed ascents in his heart. Cassiodorus: By what help one comes to the house.
83.7: 83.7 In the valley of tears. Cassiodorus: The valley of tears is the humility of the penitent. Augustine: But whence the weeping? Because he afflicted us by the law, through which we learned that sin fights against the spirit, and we groan, how, namely, we may come to the place which he has appointed, by his aid and help of course. In the place which he has set. For the lawgiver will give a blessing. Which cannot be expounded, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, that is, the future kingdom, which God disposed and ordained so that one comes to it by steps.
83.9: 83.9 O Lord God of hosts. Cassiodorus: He prays and humbles himself to obtain this help. God of Jacob. Augustine: As you made Jacob Israel by appearing to him, so make me Israel.
83.10: 83.10 Look upon the face, etc. For he himself speaks in us, hence the Apostle: Do you seek a proof of him who speaks in me, Christ? And in us he is received, as he says, He who receives you receives me. Look. The Father always looks upon Christ. Cassiodorus: But cause him to be looked upon by the Gentiles through the presence of the incarnation; or, so through the face we are made known to others. Augustine: Look therefore upon the face, that is, make Christ known to all, that we may go from virtue to virtue.
83.11: 83.11 One day. Unchangeable, namely without rising and setting, to which yesterday does not yield, which tomorrow does not press. Above thousands, above the infinite present days, which have an end. For which I have chosen, though I could reign, to be an outcast in the opinion of men, in the house, in the Church. Behold how sweet it is to be pressed by the burden of the winepress.
83.12: 83.12 For mercy. Cassiodorus: Therefore I prefer to be in the house of God than elsewhere, because in it he gives mercy, by which he justifies, after the truth of the promised reward. But to whom? To those who walk in innocence.
83.13: 83.13 O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes, etc. You who do such great things as cannot be told.
84.2: 84.2 You have blessed, O Lord. Augustine: A psalm of the new blessing, etc., up to: of the turning away of iniquity.
84.3: 84.3 You have forgiven. The same: He speaks of future things as past.
84.4: 84.4 You have appeased. Cassiodorus: Pause, on the turning away of wrath, that is, of punishment.
84.5: 84.5 Convert us. He asks for what he knew was still to come. As if: What I said as past, I pray that it may be done. Augustine: Convert us. Prophetically he spoke of future things as past, but here he prays that they may truly come to be, saying, Convert and turn away, as if to say, I spoke of them as done. And because I see the future, and because they are not yet, I pray that they may be.
84.6: 84.6 Will you be angry for ever? He foresees that this punishment will pass: For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive. Are you angry. Augustine: The wrath of God is every punishment which one suffers. As was said to Adam when he sinned: Cursed is the earth in your work, and in labor and the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread. From wrath, therefore, we are mortal and subject to suffering, but renewed in Christ. From generation. The first generation was mortal from wrath, the other will be immortal from mercy: but we do not merit this mercy by being converted to God by ourselves, for he himself converts us. And hence he adds: O God, converting, as if, as the quickening is from you, so also the conversion.
84.7: 84.7 O God, you being turned. Cassiodorus: Not extending, but God converting. First he gives the desire of conversion, afterward leads to life. Or, O God, you turned from wrath at the coming of the Son. You will quicken us. So long before it is had. And then, your people shall rejoice in you, who before rejoiced wrongly in themselves.
84.8: 84.8 Show us, O Lord. Augustine: The Prophet foretold this by praying, etc., up to: Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God (Matt. 5). Cassiodorus: Show. Or he asks for himself that Christ be shown spiritually only; he knew indeed that he would come, but asks that we behold with a pure heart, not with bodily eyes like the unbelieving: for the Jews saw and crucified. And for the future: Give us your salvation, that is, Christ to be embraced and possessed, that he be not taken from us, and so it is read partly of the present, and partly of the future. Mercy. Augustine: Christ is called mercy, because he showed us mercy, teaching that whatever good man has is from God, and so man is not proud. But thus clinging to God and enjoying him, he rejoices in him.
84.9: 84.9 I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me. Cassiodorus: Whence he knows and through whom it is done, and what he himself bestows when he comes. Peace. Augustine: Christ. Peace toward God and neighbor, and through Christ.
84.10: 84.10 Near to those who fear him. The same: Everywhere demons were worshiped, etc., up to: immortal in our mortal body.
84.11: 84.11 Mercy, etc. The same: After he said, etc., up to: how truth is sprung out of the earth (Luke 8).
84.12: 84.12 Truth is sprung out of the earth. The same: Confession from man, that he accuse himself, etc., up to: the justification of the one confessing is given.
84.14: 84.14 Justice shall go before him. The same: The first justice of man is, etc., up to: and visiting, will set his steps in the way. He will walk. It will increase, or run before, preparing the way for him; and the Lord in the prepared way will set his steps.
85.1: 85.1 A prayer of David. Augustine: This psalm is the second of those that are entitled by the name of prayer, in which Christ, Son of God and of man, one God with the Father, one man with men, prays in the form of a servant, who is prayed to by us in the form of God. He prays for us as our priest; he prays in us as our head; he is prayed to by us as our God. Cassiodorus: The prayer of Christ of the faithful, etc., up to: that it might restrain the boldness of foolish and heedless rashness. Augustine: Christ says these things in us, and we in him. Cassiodorus: He prays in ascending, hence he concludes: All nations worshiping.
85.2: 85.2 For I am holy. Augustine: Christ is properly the holy one who sanctifies, etc., up to: have mercy on him who cries, gladden the one lifted up.
85.5: 85.5 Mild. The same: Bearing man until he perfects him, etc., up to: when he is not yet perfect.
85.6: 85.6 Give ear. Cassiodorus: See the order of the prayer, etc., up to: hearing my supplication.
85.7: 85.7 Of tribulation. Augustine, Cassiodorus: When one cries out more earnestly, etc., up to: for there is none like you among the gods, O Lord.
85.9: 85.9 All the nations whom you have made shall come and adore before you, etc. Augustine: If there is a nation which God has not made, that one will not adore. He announces the Church spread everywhere, which has now been fulfilled: And note that, as Scripture says: In a multitude of people is the glory of the king, and in the diminishing of the people the destruction of the prince. There follows: And they shall glorify your name.
85.10: 85.10 You are God alone. The same: Or you alone are great against those to come, who call themselves great and gods.
85.11: 85.11 Lead me, O Lord, in your way. Cassiodorus: He prays for all those now adoring, and speaks in the members. O Lord, lead, etc. It is one thing to be led to the way, and another to be led in the way, lest one fall in it: men everywhere need to be helped, whether they are in the way or outside it. But the way is Christ, who says: I am the way, the truth, and the life. Let my heart rejoice. Augustine: In worldly fear the cause comes first, etc., up to: but he who fears and does not hope is cast down.
85.13: 85.13 From the lower hell. The same: By this we understand, etc., up to: these are opinions, not assertions.
85.14: 85.14 O God, the wicked have risen up against me, and the synagogue of the mighty, etc. Cassiodorus: Again he prays for himself, having made mention of his passion and glory, whence those for whom he prayed have great mercy and are rescued from hell.
85.16: 85.16 Give your command. Augustine: As if to say: Let the time of patience pass, let the time of judgment come, whence not only Christ but also the saints will sit as judges, who are the sons of the handmaid, that is, of the Church.
86.1: 86.1 A psalm. Cassiodorus: Because it treats of the Church according to power, where it does its works. Of a canticle. That from the earthly Jerusalem you may be raised to the understanding of the heavenly, namely from action to contemplation. The Prophet proclaims the heavenly Jerusalem to the sons of Core, which he commends through its foundations, and gates, and fame, so that their affection may be increased. Its foundations. A psalm of the heavenly Jerusalem: the Prophet, full of the Spirit, turning over many things within himself about this city, of which he had said nothing yet, bursts forth in this: Its foundations, etc. The first praise is from the foundations; let the solidity of the whole city be noted. Its, does not refer to anything previously set down, but to the meditation of the Prophet's heart, because he had never been silent about her in his heart, though he had with his mouth.
86.3: 86.3 Things said. Augustine: These are those things which the Lord foretold of her through the prophets.
86.4: 86.4 I will be mindful. The same: Pause. The Lord speaks of the same Jerusalem. I will be mindful of Rahab. He shows what those glorious things are; as if to say: These are they: in that city, says the Prophet in the person of God, I will be mindful of Rahab and of Babylon, who do not belong to the people of the Jews. Glorious things of you, where not the Jew alone is, but all nations. Rahab. She sent out the scarlet cord by the window, that is, the Church of the Gentiles has on her forehead the sign of the blood of Christ. Hence: The publicans and harlots shall go before you into the kingdom of heaven. Rahab means breadth or impetuosity, the Gentiles, who wander widely and impetuously through vices. To Babylon belong all the wicked, as to Jerusalem all the saints. Behold the foreigners. I will be mindful. Why did you say this? Behold the foreigners, that is, the nations, Tyre, the narrowness of vices, or of penance.
86.5: 86.5 Shall not Sion say. According to another reading: Mother Sion shall say, a man. Augustine, Cassiodorus: As if to say: Whence will strangers come to Jerusalem? Hear whence. There is a certain man, that is, Christ, who says, mother Sion, that is the Synagogue my mother according to the flesh; and through him they come; who is that man? He is the one who was born in her and founded her; he himself says, mother, to that city. Cassiodorus: Or, he commends Sion spiritually, etc., up to: of which princes? Augustine: Of these, according to another reading, who have been made, namely princes, in her, that is, who were made princes; before they were in her, they were not princes, but the outcasts of the world: for God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong.
86.7: 86.7 As of those rejoicing. Cassiodorus: Pause. He concludes in few words, touching on the future blessedness. Augustine: As of those rejoicing, having gathered all things together he concludes: As of those rejoicing. As, because such will be the joy as we do not know here, and therefore, since it could not be expressed, he says, as he could, as of those rejoicing.
87.1: 87.1 Mahalath. Augustine: A choir, that the choir may answer the singer by singing in harmony, etc., up to: for he is said to have been a certain man of the east.
87.2: 87.2 O Lord God. Cassiodorus: He admonishes us to imitate the death of Christ. First he prays for help, relating the contempt shown by enemies: hence, praying in the form of a servant to the Father, he says: O Lord.
87.3: 87.3 Let my prayer come in before you. The same: The power of pure prayer, which like a person enters before God and accomplishes the commission: where the flesh cannot arrive.
87.4: 87.4 For my soul is filled. Augustine: These feelings of human weakness, etc., up to: but signs of human weakness.
87.5: 87.5 I am counted. Because I bore not only heavy but also insulting things.
87.6: 87.6 Like the wounded sleeping. Cassiodorus: Because he himself was wounded by the lance and shut in the tomb, but he differs in what follows, whom you remember no more. In the sepulchre. That is, lulled to sleep in carnal pleasure, hence God does not rouse them. And they are cast off from your hand. Augustine: For this does not refer to the sleepers among whom are the just, of whom, although God does not yet remember them that they rise, it was nevertheless said: The souls of the just are in the hand of God (Wisd. 3). Or, they have set me as guilty by the truth. In the lower pit, that is, in the waters of hell, namely in darkness and in the shadow of death.
87.7: 87.7 In the lower pit. Cassiodorus: Or of hell: because by so abject a death he was taken away into the darkness of oblivion, whom no one will seek. And the shadow of death, the place of the wicked, in which they are punished.
87.8: 87.8 Your wrath is strong upon me. The same: They thought that the wrath of God had destroyed him and that God had brought all indignations upon him, when he allowed him to be crucified.
87.9: 87.9 You have put far away. The same: What his friends did in the passion. Acquaintances. Not those whom he knew, for then he knew all as God, but those to whom he is known.
87.10: 87.10 All the day. Augustine: By the outstretched hands is understood the continuance of good works, from which he never ceased. For on the cross that stretching was not even for a whole day, nor can the whole be taken for a part when he adds whole; but because these works did not profit all, he adds.
87.11: 87.11 Will you work wonders for the dead? He means the dead in heart, for whom the miracles of Christ are indeed done, but do not profit them: for wonders were done for the bodily dead, when some came back to life. And when the Lord entered hell and ascended from there victor over death, a great miracle was done for the dead. Will you work wonders for the dead? Cassiodorus: He shows that their works do not profit them. Or shall physicians raise up, etc. Augustine: In the Hebrew not physicians, etc., up to: No man can come to me, unless the Father draw him.
87.12: 87.12 In the sepulchre. Hence in the Gospel of such men: You are like whitened sepulchres, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but within are full of dead men's bones, as if, so also you with hypocrisy and iniquity. Your mercy and truth. Augustine: Scripture loves to join mercy and truth, especially in the psalms.
87.13: 87.13 In darkness. The dead placed in the sepulchre, and the darkness, and the land of oblivion are the same.
87.14: 87.14 But I, O Lord, have cried to you. Cassiodorus: What he endures in his own; behold the choir answering the precentor. The same: And I, as it were, with those with whom I am one. Augustine: And I. To these dead their works do not profit, etc., up to: Why, O Lord, do you cast off.
87.15: 87.15 Why. Cassiodorus: Behold how much he desires. Why, O Lord. He proposes that the cause is to be sought: which is, that by the delay of good, and by adversities multiplied, prayer, as if repelled, may be kindled more ardently.
87.16: 87.16 Exalted. The same: First with a swollen heart, afterward, Humbled. Through confession. Troubled, that is, confounded over sins, by condemning them.
87.17: 87.17 They have passed over. Cassiodorus: They did not come about gently. Augustine: Because it was said not of the faithful but of the unfaithful: The wrath of God abides upon him (John 3). For he scourges the sons whom he receives, hence: Whom I love, I rebuke and chastise (Apoc. 3). And elsewhere: I will strike and I will heal: I will kill and I will make to live (Deut. 32). The same: They passed over and troubled me. Because we suffer one thing now from condemnation, and fear another from eternal vengeance. Your terrors. Cassiodorus: Which I suffer: because it pleased you, not by my merit. Augustine: The terrors of the future judgment, which all flesh fears. They have troubled me. According to the weakness of the flesh. Augustine: Terrors sometimes trouble me, so that, with evils hanging round, they trouble the mind of the one thinking, as though waters seemed to flow about and surround on every side, whence friends and acquaintances desert through fear, hence the Apostle: All have forsaken me (2 Tim. 4).
87.18: 87.18 They have surrounded me. Cassiodorus: Sins shut one in on every side with copious flood. All the day. Augustine: Because at no time are evils absent from the Church until the world ends. But all these things happen so that the prayer of the Church may go before God until that salvation comes where there is nothing of evils.
87.19: 87.19 Friend. Cassiodorus: Also those who are joined by pious and faithful love. Neighbor and acquaintances, etc. Kinship. Often the human duties of the just are withdrawn through fear.
88.2: 88.2 The mercies. Cassiodorus: This psalm, on the hope of Christians and the magnificence of the Lord, says many things by which no one is led astray who prays worthily, which the true Israel so understands. First the Prophet promises to sing of mercy and truth. For ever. Cassiodorus, Remigius: How does he sing mercies for ever, and give thanks, who does not remember misery? And how is blessedness full if the memory of guilt touches the mind? But often, joyful, we remember sad things, and, healthy, pains without pain, and are the more joyful and grateful for it; so also the recollection of misery takes nothing from blessedness. Truth. The promise. In my mouth: it does not slip from the mouth, but in the mouth it is long turned over as something sweet.
88.3: 88.3 For you have said. Here he says: How does he know? And what are the mercies of God through Christ? Augustine: What mercies, and what truth shall I sing? Behold. For you have said. As if to say: I, a man, say with assurance what you, God, have said, made manifest through the Spirit. Mercy shall be built up. Augustine: He repeats both what he foretold. Because all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. Truth is not displayed in the fulfillment of promises unless mercy first goes before in the remission of sins. Finally, truth belongs to the Jews, to whom the promises were made, mercy to the Gentiles: as the Apostle says: For I say that Jesus Christ was minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers: and that the Gentiles are to glorify God for his mercy (Rom. 15). In the heavens. Those who declare the glory of God, through whom mercy is built up.
88.4: 88.4 I have sworn to David my servant. This man is secure because God has said it: more secure because he swore. The oath of God is the confirmation of a promise; from both the man becomes Ethan, that is, strong.
88.5: 88.5 For ever. Cassiodorus: The building of mercy is not temporal, as the ruin of iniquity is temporal: for temporal iniquity is destroyed in some, that in them eternal mercy may be built up, hence the Lord says to Jeremiah: Behold, I have set you over the nations and over kingdoms, to root up and to pull down, and to waste and to destroy, and to build and to plant. To generation. Augustine: For a generation cannot, etc., up to: he will sit, and then in the saints.
88.6: 88.6 The heavens shall confess. Cassiodorus: Pause. Second, in diverse ways he describes the praises and power of God, as if, as you have said, so it shall be. They shall confess, they shall praise. The heavens shall confess your wonders. For in all the mercy shown to the lost, in the justification of the ungodly, what do we praise but the wonders of God? You praise that the dead have risen; praise more that the lost have been redeemed. For you see a man who yesterday was a whirlpool of drunkenness, today an ornament of sobriety. You see a man who yesterday was the mire of lust, today the honor of temperance: yesterday a blasphemer of God, today a praiser of God. You see a man who yesterday was a slave of the creature, today a worshiper of the Creator: these are the wonders which the heavens confess. For your truth. Cassiodorus: Or without for. Wonders, how he does and administers all things everywhere. The truth in the Church where it is believed: the Word made flesh, and the Trinity, God first.
88.7: 88.7 For who. Augustine: It is to be noted that the heavens and the clouds are the same, namely the preachers. But heavens, the preachers, on account of the brightness of truth. Clouds, which are misty because of the mortality of the flesh, and because they pass away, where also things are hidden which afterward will shine in the judgment. Among the sons. Either of the heavenly ones, or of men. Lest he therefore be thought merely man: for he is by nature, we by adoption; he begotten, we created; he begotten from eternity, we made in time; he only, we many.
88.8: 88.8 Above all. The same: Angels, or men, who are his attendants unequal to him, who draw near to him by his gift.
88.9: 88.9 To you. The same: Who have made all things, etc., up to: to be tempted above what man is able.
88.11: 88.11 Wounded. He was humbled in losing those he held; wounded, his heart struck, where he was proud. The proud one. Augustine: Namely the dragon, who was made in the sea to mock him, who through the humble Christ, in whom others are humble, are humbled; Christ humbled himself that he might humble the proud one. For the proud held the proud: the devil is wounded when Christ is wounded, he is not yet wholly dead. The enemies. The aerial powers or the Jews scattered through the world, or from among men he took some who are the spoils of the devil, others you left, whom you allowed to go away after him.
88.12: 88.12 The heavens are yours and the earth is yours; the world, etc. The same: Therefore he triumphed in heaven over the devil, because heaven is his; on earth over Judea, because the earth is his. Why then did they exalt themselves in what is another's? You have founded. Why then do they raise themselves against him whose is the circuit of the world, and all the creatures that are in it?
88.13: 88.13 The north. The devil. The sea you have created. The world. Foolishly then they raise themselves against him by whom they were created. Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name. Augustine: Mountains of Syria, and through them the Gentiles are understood, the whole from the part, by synecdoche. They shall rejoice. At the coming of Christ, allegorically. Tabor, the Jews, to whom the light first came. Hermon, the Gentiles, who were first anathematized. They shall rejoice in your name, the two walls joined in the cornerstone. Augustine: Tabor. The light coming from the highest light, at whose coming his anathema is made, that is, of the devil, who held us in his error. Which is: it has been given by you that we be enlightened, that we give anathema to the devil.
88.15: 88.15 Justice and judgment are the preparation of your throne. Cassiodorus: The throne of God is eternal, but in the judgment it will appear prepared, when he shall be seen to judge justly. Or now men, by discerning and holding just things, prepare themselves a seat for the Lord. Mercy and truth shall go before your face. By likeness to the forerunner preparing lodging for the Lord.
88.16: 88.16 Blessed is the people that knows, etc. Cassiodorus: He knows who places his joy not in his own but in the Lord's power, or who understands in his heart what he sings with his mouth: hence follows this reward, in the light, that is, in the contemplation of the Trinity they will persevere. Jubilation. Jubilation is a joy which cannot be explained in words, and yet cannot be wholly kept silent. O Lord, in the light of your countenance they shall walk, and in your name they shall rejoice. Cassiodorus: He commends the grace of which the jubilation is. Augustine: Or in your good pleasure, that is in Christ, therefore in him, because he took on our flesh, in whom is all hope.
88.20: 88.20 Then you spoke in a vision. Cassiodorus: Pause. Third, the promises of the Father concerning Christ. The preceding praise is not doubtful, which the paternal authority confirms. Cassiodorus, Augustine: Then. When you appointed the covenant, or when you said these things to me, then you spoke to the saints, the remaining prophets, in a vision, for they did not speak ignorantly, as Montanus and certain other heretics said.
88.21: 88.21 I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him. Augustine: Strong in hand, an obedient servant, therefore I have placed help in him.
88.23: 88.23 The enemy shall have no advantage over him. The same: The devil, hence: The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me (John 14). The son of iniquity shall not hurt him. Judas shall not add; he will not add effect to his will.
88.24: 88.24 His enemies from before his face. Augustine: When his face looks upon sinners, they are separated from crimes, which have no place in his presence.
88.25: 88.25 And my truth and my mercy shall be with him, and in my name shall his horn be exalted. The same: Often mercy and truth are commended to us, etc., up to: where these meet each other.
88.31: 88.31 But if they forsake. I promise this not only of those who persist, but also of those who fall.
88.33: 88.33 With a rod. For who is a son? etc., up to: And with stripes, etc. I will not scatter. Augustine: He himself does not take away mercy from one who is indeed a Christian: but if a man is so wicked that he flees as his father approaches, he alienates himself; the father does not cast him out.
88.35: 88.35 Neither will I profane. The promise would be profaned if it were unfulfilled. Because of the bad fish, is nothing from that net put into the vessels? The good fish will certainly be put in, that is, those whom he predestined.
88.36: 88.36 Once I have sworn. Cassiodorus: Man swears frequently, God once, who does not change. In the holy place. In the man Christ, in whom was to be fulfilled what I swore; or David, that is Christ, through holiness. Seed, the Christians.
88.38: 88.38 As the sun in my sight. Augustine: According to the soul, etc., up to: in heaven, that is Christ. But you have cast off. Cassiodorus: Pause. Fourth, he sets down things adverse to the aforesaid promises, lest they be thought to be fulfilled in anyone other than in Christ in the future. But you have cast off. As if: these goods are for Christians, but not for the Jews, who deprived themselves of the promise, and this is: But you have cast off your Christ, that is, the anointed David, from the kingdom for the sin which he committed against Uriah over Bathsheba; And you have despised, or scorned, because he suffered many unworthy things; you have put off, long in tribulation; the covenant, the promises made to the Jews, were carried to the Gentiles. Augustine: But you. Or, all these things concerning Christ and the Church: you cast off your Christ to the gibbet, and gave him over to contempt. Or you put off from glory, for a time, or according to the members.
88.40: 88.40 The covenant. The promise seems overturned, and the saints are reckoned profane. The hedges, the prelates, you have destroyed, while they are slain. And you have made his stronghold a terror. Those who strengthened others by teaching are now a fear, while they are afflicted, and some have been plundered by those passing by on the way, which is Christ.
88.44: 88.44 You have turned away the help of his sword. That is, the preaching. You did not help him in battle, but gave him to sufferings. You have destroyed him from cleansing, etc., that is, some of the world have failed and been brought down to the earth. You have lessened, as is thought, while they are quickly taken from life. Augustine: Why did God promise those things, etc., up to: that this promise might be awaited in others.
88.45: 88.45 You have destroyed him. All these things came upon the Jews, though Christ and the eternal kingdom were not taken from them, but deferred. His throne you have dashed to the ground. That is, their kingdom has been destroyed everywhere on earth, because now there is no prince from them.
88.46: 88.46 You have shortened. Because their kingdom would have stood long if under God. You have covered him with confusion. Because he bears the reproach of unbelief. You have shortened. Augustine: They thought they would reign for ever, but you shortened the days of their kingdom, so that it did not stand, according to their opinion.
88.47: 88.47 How long, O Lord? Cassiodorus: Pause. Fifth. Behold in what the promises were fulfilled, namely in the substance of David, which lives and delivers the soul, that is, in Christ. Augustine: But how long do you not raise up Christ? What substance? That which is nothing except through him. Who is the man that lives and shall not see death? No one. In these he now asks help for man, or specially for the Jews.
88.48: 88.48 Remember what my substance is. The same: David says this, set in the flesh among the Jews, in hope in Christ. What is my substance? Even if the Jews fail, my substance does not fail, the root does not wholly perish, whence Mary will come: and from her will come the seed to whom the promise was made. For from that people came the Virgin Mary, from the Virgin Mary the flesh of Christ, and that flesh is not sinful, but the cleanser of sinners. Have you made all the children of men in vain? All the sons of men have gone into vanity, yet you did not establish them in vain: whence then do you cleanse them from vanity? Through the seed, in which is my substance; of which he adds: Who is the man?
88.49: 88.49 Who is the man? The same: This fits none but Christ: for even if he finds some rising again, and they shall see death no more, yet they themselves will not deliver their souls from the hand of the lower world, but he who can lay down his soul and take it up again, from whom no one takes it. Cassiodorus: Or thus, no one will live, or deliver his soul: and since this is so, where are the mercies? Now he asks that the promises be fulfilled which he made to David.
88.50: 88.50 Where are your ancient mercies? The same: Pause. Sixth, the promises are fulfilled in the members also, not temporally but spiritually. And he speaks in the person of the Church.
88.51: 88.51 Be mindful, O Lord. Augustine: To reward, he seems to have forgotten, while he delays. Of the reproach of your servants. Cassiodorus: Brought upon the servants by many nations. Augustine: Which I, the Church, have held in, that is, borne. In my bosom, in the secret of the mind, because openly she did not dare to speak.
88.53: 88.53 Blessed. Cassiodorus: Against the curses of the nations. Augustine: Blessed. An exclamation from the sight of the brightness of Christ.
89.1: 89.1 A prayer of Moses. Augustine: Since the old life and the new, etc., up to: and sees wonders out of the law of God. Cassiodorus, Remigius: This psalm treats of the failing of the human race, which will be taken away through Christ. Lord, a refuge. Cassiodorus: First, he sets forth the eternal refuge for man in time.
89.2: 89.2 Before the mountains. Lest it seem that he was not a refuge to us before we existed, he adds before. Mountains, the earth. Augustine: Behold, every rational creature is distinguished by this difference, that by the name of mountains is meant the loftiness of the angels, and by the name of earth the lowliness of men: and so he not unfittingly distinguished the words so as to say that the mountains, that is the angels, are made, and the earth, that is men, formed. Made or formed. To be formed or fashioned is usually said of bodies: to be made, from nothing. From age. More aptly he would say, etc., up to: but here age is put for eternal. From age. Behold what eternity is a refuge for us, etc., up to: Turn not away, for a thousand years. You are. He says excellently, because he is unchangeable. He does not say you will be, or you were, since the unchangeable essence of God knows neither past nor future; hence it was said: I am who am. And, He who is has sent me to you. And: But you are the selfsame, and your years shall not fail.
89.3: 89.3 Turn not away. Cassiodorus: Second, he sets out the infirmity of man, for whom he asks help. Into lowliness. That is, earthly concupiscence, etc., up to: who taught us to seek heavenly things.
89.4: 89.4 Yesterday. Augustine: He does not say, at least like tomorrow, etc., up to: in anxiety and trembling, and it is as nothing.
89.6: 89.6 In the morning like grass. Augustine, Cassiodorus: Let it be changed from the quality of the night. In the evening let it fall. In the extremities cut or broken. Cassiodorus: In the morning like grass. I have said that the years are held, etc., up to: youth, which flowers and passes. The evening: old age, when the vigor of man grows cold. Or, in the morning like grass. An apt comparison, as grass is changed from the quality it has in the night to a worse when the sun has risen: so man is changed for the worse.
89.7: 89.7 We have fainted in your wrath, and in your fury we are troubled. Augustine: Made mortal and subject to suffering, which we nevertheless fear to end by death, hence follows: And in your fury we are troubled. Age. Our perverse life. Or age, the posterity. In the light of your countenance. Cassiodorus: Those things are covered which have pardon: those are illumined which are punished.
89.9: 89.9 For all our days. Augustine: Our knowledge has failed, reason darkened by sin; or the time of life is shortened and has almost failed, because the days of our life have been reduced to fewness. Our years like. Cassiodorus, Augustine: The misery and brevity of this life is expressed here by the likeness of the spider, which weaves empty webs to catch flies by guile: hence like the spider, that is, we labored in corruptible things, we wove empty things. Cassiodorus: Life was shortened through the wrath of God, because they sinned through presumption of a longer life. And we ourselves have failed in your wrath. Augustine: That is, our being has failed through hardships. Our years shall meditate, they shall not work, because they pass without profit. Or, shall meditate passively, that is, our years shall be reckoned like the spider, that is, like empty and useless.
89.10: 89.10 Seventy. The same: The appetite for earthly things, which are done in seven days: if in virtues, eighty, that is, eternity is sought. Years. Or the years, another reading. In which space of time they are called long-lived, who even up to eighty years seem to have some strength. Eighty. Because even short of eighty years there are some infirm, etc., up to: awaiting the redemption of the body. Meekness. It is clemency, if God's; taming, if ours. For he himself through clemency is meek, and by taming makes us meek, and so we shall be corrected.
89.11: 89.11 Who knows. The same: The power of man's wrath is to kill the body, afterward to do nothing. God punishes both here and afterward sends into Gehenna: and by few is his wrath rightly understood.
89.12: 89.12 Make your right hand so known. Cassiodorus: Third, he prays and affirms deliverance. Augustine: Your right hand. He has so made Christ known, etc., up to: that he may set at the right hand. And the learned in heart in wisdom. Or the fettered in heart. Which is the same, because those who are instructed in wisdom put the foot of the mind into the fetters of God, that they may not stray from his way. Whom God has so made known in the New Testament that for the sake of faith they despise all that is held great in the Old, and seek for eternal death: considering this he says, for those who suffer much from the world for eternal things.
89.13: 89.13 Return. As though his face were turned away from the afflicted. How long. Another reading: for a little while. Cassiodorus: Not wholly, which profits more, if some tribulation always admonishes us.
89.14: 89.14 In the morning we were filled with your mercy, and we have rejoiced and are delighted. Augustine, Cassiodorus: Now it is night, in which we hunger: but then we shall be satisfied by the sight, hence: I shall be satisfied when your glory shall appear. And elsewhere: In the morning I will stand before you, and will see. But now for this we have rejoiced, and in the evil days in which we say: Look upon your servants.
89.16: 89.16 Look upon your servants. What God does in himself, the Prophet prays to be done for his people: he prays, namely, that he spare the sinning Jews, if not for their merits, at least for the works he has done in them. And direct their children. As if, though they themselves are dispersed through iniquities, or the children, in the end they may be set right by faith, who by themselves are perverse and unconvertible.
89.17: 89.17 And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us, and direct the works. Jerome, Cassiodorus: Let the image of God recreating be impressed on the mind. Or the brightness of God is upon us, when we are adorned by the impression of the cross, and carry the banner of triumph on the forehead. Cassiodorus: For the image is threefold, etc., up to: that I may remember you, understand you, love you.
90.1: 90.1 The praise of a canticle. Praise, and it is human: but this is of a canticle, because it is nothing but divine. For this psalm is a hymn against demons.
