The Prophet therefore says of any saint: He who dwells in the help, etc. Cassiodorus: It shows the temptations of the devil overcome through humility by Christ, and by his own, remaining in the help of God, that we also may learn through him to overcome temptations, because he is the door through which, if any man enter, he shall go in and go out, and shall find pastures. Augustine: The door is Christ; to enter through him is to imitate him, not in divinity, and power, and miracles, but in that in which he was made for us, that is, in the humility to which he calls, saying: Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart. The devil tempted Christ with this psalm. But the temptation of Christ is our teaching, following whom we conquer from him. He who dwells. Cassiodorus: He first describes the one trusting in God alone, wholly hedged round by the protection of God. He who dwells, that is, who always places all his hope not in himself but in God, will be protected in every way by God. Note the correspondence of the words: for as he always dwells, so also he will always abide. The one affirms, namely that he dwells; the other promises, namely that he will be protected. He shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven. That is, that he not turn aside to the right or to the left, as in the Old Testament it was commanded the children of Israel to go by the king's highway, not turning aside to the right hand or to the left. The king's highway is the way of Christ our king, who so ran the way of the world that he was neither enticed by prosperity nor broken by adversity.
90.2: 90.2 My God. Cassiodorus: Lest you think that after the taking up and refuge nothing more is to be asked, he adds: I will hope in him, so that he never presume on himself; if Adam had done this, he would have stood well.
90.3: 90.3 From the snare. The same: Temptation, either by deeds, which is here called the snare; or by words, which here is from the harsh word; as if, though it seem light, yet it is grave to be tempted by a word. The snare, the cunning of spiritual or carnal enemies; the harsh word, every saying which moves away from the divine rules. Augustine: From the snare of the hunters, the demons, who set snares not in the way, Christ, but around it, to the right or to the left. Into which some fall also through the harsh word, such as those who do not wish to be Christ's because of those who insult the Christian name, and those who fear the detractions of men, so that they cease from the way of God.
90.4: 90.4 With his shoulders. Augustine, Cassiodorus: He promises the benefits of God to the one who hopes. The shoulders are the working of wonders, by which as by shoulders the power of God is shown. The wings, the admonitions of the Prophets, which carry to the heavens. He will overshadow. So that neither the sun of divinity nor the moon of humanity may burn you. In the wings, protection. With his shoulders. Another reading: Between the shoulders. Augustine: That is, he places you before his breast, etc., up to: that we may hope under his wings.
90.5: 90.5 His truth. The same: It is of God, who does not respect persons, nor mixes those who hope in themselves with those who hope in God, but distinguishes the humble and the proud. Cassiodorus: Or truth, the incarnation of Christ, hence: Truth is sprung out of the earth (Ps. 84), which both overshadows with the shoulders and defends with a shield. As he has noted the kinds of defense, he notes also the kinds of dangers, that the deliverance may be more welcome. From the fear of the night. From the likeness of danger, whence there is so much fear. From the fear of the night. Augustine: He who sins in ignorance, etc., up to: A thousand shall fall at your side.
90.7: 90.7 A thousand shall fall at your side. Cassiodorus: Second, he says that the head of the one trusting in God, that is Christ, lifted up in heaven, can be touched by no one, who also protects his offspring on earth: but the presumptuous fall from him. Behold the certainty of the protection of the one trusting in God through Christ. At your side. The side of God is the crown of the just, who will judge with him, hence it is said: Send from your side, that is, those who have counsel with you. The side of Christ, then, is the Apostles and their imitators, to whom he promised: You shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19). The twelve seats are the perfection of the tribunal, on which shall sit all who have left all things and followed Christ.
90.8: 90.8 Nevertheless. Cassiodorus, Augustine: Although you permit the impious to persecute your own, yet not with impunity: with your eyes you will consider the evil they willed; the good that is done through them unknowing will be repaid to them, and the saint, who has the eyes of faith, sees them now exalted and thundering, and in the end struck with lightning: he said this lest the weak be moved. Cassiodorus: Nevertheless with your eyes. Though those who fall tempt you with harsh things, nevertheless. Or, though the demon not approach, which is through the wicked: yet you will consider not what they do, but what they intend.
90.9: 90.9 For you are. Augustine: Christ is one, head and body, of whom he speaks now as of the head, now as of the body, the person not changed. And therefore note carefully where he speaks of Christ according to the head, and where according to the members. The Most High. The refuge of God is on high, deeply hidden, that one may flee from the coming wrath. For many so make for themselves the refuge of God, to which they flee from temporal evils. You have made the Most High your refuge, that is, by rising, by ascending, you made the refuge high, that I may now hope to follow where you have gone before.
90.10: 90.10 The same: The tabernacle of God is the flesh, etc., up to: this is rightly understood of Christ.
90.11: 90.11 For to his angels. The tempter said this to the Lord when he tempted him: he cast this at him, doubting of his Godhead. But Christ was tempted for our sake, that in him we also may learn to overcome the tempter. Augustine: So also he wished to be baptized by a servant, not for his own need, but for the profit of man, that we may not disdain to be baptized by fellow servants.
90.12: 90.12 In their hands they shall bear you up. The same: Christ was lifted into heaven by the hands of angels, etc., up to: who cannot be overcome.
90.13: 90.13 Upon the asp. After human weakness, divine power is shown, which commands such things. And he speaks of Christ according to the members. And you shall trample. Augustine: The Church treads the serpent, which is wary of its cunning. The lion. He openly rages against the martyrs. The dragon lies in wait through heretics, to corrupt the virgin of Christ, hence the Apostle: I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Cor. 11).
90.14: 90.14 Because he has hoped in me. Augustine: Third, the words of God, with which he consoles the Church, to which he promises defense here and rewards in the future. Cassiodorus: He commands the angels concerning you, saying: Because in me. The certainty of the promise through the promise of God.
90.15: 90.15 He shall cry to me. Augustine: We are not to fear in tribulation, etc., up to: at that time let us labor the more to resist.
91.1: 91.1 A psalm of a canticle. Augustine: Because of the weariness of minds, etc., up to: seeking the glory of God, not your own.
91.2: 91.2 It is good to give praise. Cassiodorus: First, he treats how the good man, undisturbed, keeps the sabbath of the mind, perceiving that all things are done well by God, which the fool does not know. Augustine: Good things present, given to us by God, are consolation: when they are lacking, it is justice. For God consoles us and corrects us: in both let us be grateful to him, saying: It is good to give praise, etc.
91.4: 91.4 Upon the ten-stringed instrument. The same: He sings the psalm who does well with cheerfulness. He who does it with sadness does not do it himself: he carries the psaltery, he does not sing on it. Upon the ten-stringed instrument. If you only speak well, it is a song without the lyre; if you work and do not speak, it is a lyre without song; and therefore speak well and do well.
91.5: 91.5 For you have delighted me. The same: Hence the Apostle: We are his workmanship, etc., up to: How magnified. In the work of your hands. Cassiodorus, Jerome: Both in the beauty of this world's fabric itself, and in its obedience, and arrangement, and in the causes, and in the effects, and in the works of hands, which I use or which I admire.
91.6: 91.6 How magnified. Cassiodorus, Jerome: In substance, and in form, and in power, and in the rest. Your thoughts are exceedingly deep, by which you made such things and rule them.
91.7: 91.7 The senseless man, etc. Cassiodorus: You have delighted me in your works, but the senseless man shall not know, and the fool, who if he knows does not guard himself, will not understand these things which he has said, or will say after. The highest kind of knowledge is to know that God bestows such things as the human mind cannot reach. The senseless man is he who, empty of heavenly wisdom, is full of human cunning; who does not know the works of God, because he thinks everything happens by chance; the fool is brutish, who knows not even worldly things.
91.8: 91.8 When they have sprung up. Cassiodorus: He asserts that the wicked will perish, etc., up to: the Jews thought that you would die by the common lot.
91.9: 91.9 But you are the Most High. Augustine: You look down from above from eternity, etc., up to: not long-suffering, eternal by the Word.
91.11: 91.11 And my horn shall be exalted. The same: Although they themselves will perish, etc., up to: all heresies will perish.
91.12: 91.12 And my eye has looked down. The same: And therefore even now he has looked down, and will hear from the truth within. And of the rising up. Cassiodorus: Or, those rising up against me, he will hear the malignant at the last: when they will rebuke themselves, saying, What has pride profited us, and riches? (Wisd. 5). My ear. Augustine: Of him standing at the right hand, it will hear in the future this, namely, Depart, you cursed, into everlasting fire. From which evil hearing the just man shall not fear. Behold this for those: What of the just? (Matt. 25).
91.13: 91.13 The just man shall flourish like the palm tree. They like grass. The just man like the palm, for its height, and because the root is rough, with beautiful foliage at the top and end, and it bears fruit slowly; so the labor roughens the just man here, which in the heights the beauty of immortality will crown, and, as it were slowly, after long labors, he will receive the reward of his works. The just man like the palm. Cassiodorus: The third part. That the just flourish, so that they may rejoice devoutly in this promise. The cedar. Augustine: The palm and the cedar, these trees do not wither in summer, like grass.
91.14: 91.14 In the courts of the house. Cassiodorus: The court is the beginning of the dwelling; the house is the inner part. In the courts, then, they shall flourish, that is, at the very beginning of the resurrection, when they shall hear: Come, blessed of my Father (Matt. 25).
91.15: 91.15 They shall still increase. The same: The Church will begin to be more fruitful when she has been brought to the end of the age: for then, through the sufferings of the elect, the number of the blessed will quickly be filled. And old age is understood here otherwise than above.
91.16: 91.16 That they may declare. The same: Here, or, when they receive the reward they will declare that he is just, who fulfills his promises to his own. And there is no iniquity in him. Augustine: That he permits those to suffer for him here, whom he will not adorn there. And right, who rewards, not unjust so as to defraud of the reward, but kind so as to heap it up.
92.1: 92.1 For the day, etc. Augustine: On the day before the sabbath, etc., up to: which the sixth day signifies. The Lord has reigned, etc. Cassiodorus: The praise of Christ is sung here, etc., up to: from the praise of the house, there, Your house. Clothed with beauty. Augustine: Christ beautiful in these, etc., up to: the world which shall not be moved. He is clothed with beauty. Cassiodorus: That is, with comeliness, etc., up to: from the incarnation, when he taught men. He girded himself. He does not say, girded, or girded up, or girded about, but girded beforehand. For we are girded to work, girded about to fight, girded up to go, girded beforehand to minister. Augustine: Girding then signifies works, etc., up to: because he who conquers anger is better than he who takes a city. He girded himself. Cassiodorus: Ascending with the company of angels, or by vigor of working. For he has established. Augustine: He put on beauty and strength to found the earth, hence he adds: For he has established.
92.2: 92.2 From then. The same: Or from that, it designates the time of grace, perhaps he understands this from the day before the sabbath, that is, the sixth age of this world, in which the Lord came: but lest you think he began then, when he came born, he adds, from eternity you are.
92.3: 92.3 The floods have lifted up their voice. Augustine: Because the disciples hearing, etc., up to: of the world, which began to be angry, or to persecute. The floods have lifted up their waves, etc. Cassiodorus: This is lacking in others, etc., up to: who does all good things, he adds: Wonderful is the Lord on high.
92.5: 92.5 Your testimonies. Augustine: Because the elevation of the sea is wonderful, etc., up to: and crowns from the prediction. Cassiodorus: Testimonies. Or thus, etc., up to: though in brief words, contains.
93.1: 93.1 A psalm of David. Augustine: For the weak, who also murmur in heart, etc., up to: wholly teaching patience. On the fourth day of the week, the day on which God made the lights, etc., up to: hence he admonishes to patience.
93.2: 93.2 The Lord is the God of vengeances. Do not hasten to punish another, if he has hurt you; as you would not wish to be punished at the request of another whom you have hurt: and if he sins against you, do not sin worse by blaspheming God, nor desire vengeance; which, if it come, perhaps will find you first. He has dealt freely. Augustine: In the time of weakness, as when he taught in the temple, as one having power, because neither his truth nor his power can be opposed. And because so then, now Be exalted, because, how long the sinners.
93.4: 93.4 They shall utter. Cassiodorus: He sets out their sins, etc., up to: proceeds by exaggerating. All who work shall speak, etc. They shall utter, they answer others, Augustine: that is, they have something to answer, etc., up to: the wicked speak saying that God does not care for these things.
93.6: 93.6 The widow and the stranger. Cassiodorus: God protects these, etc., up to: without a father, the devil, and a mother, concupiscence.
93.7: 93.7 Nor will he understand. Augustine: As if, he will not attend to these things, he neglects them, nor does he attend to see, God does not care for me, what I do?
93.8: 93.8 Understand. Cassiodorus: The second part; against blasphemers, etc., up to: that his counsel, unknown to the wicked, he opens to his friends. You fools. Those who openly blaspheme, saying God does not see. Or thus: You senseless, that is, ignorant, understand, you who now by living well are among the people, that is, in the number of the good. And you fools, that is, improvident, even if you know, at some time be wise.
93.10: 93.10 He who rebukes the nations. Augustine: Does he not daily rebuke for original sin, and for the things above mentioned? Or, He who teaches. For the sake of which teaching God sent his Son, etc., up to: hence the Apostle: We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, that every one may receive, Rom. 14, etc.
93.11: 93.11 The Lord knows. The same: But you do not know the thoughts of God, because they are just; but by deeds God discloses his counsel to his friends, why he spares the wicked. That they are vain. The thoughts of such men are vain, which they themselves cannot know, but the Lord knows them to be vain.
93.12: 93.12 Blessed is the man. Cassiodorus: These are the vain, etc., up to: all will know God, the heavens will be rolled up like a book. And out of your law, etc. Augustine: Learn patience from the law, until the pit is dug; it is not for you to know how, and why it is dug for him.
93.13: 93.13 Until, etc. Augustine: The happiness of the wicked is a pit; the labor of the good is the scourge of the father; happiness is a pit, because when God spares through impunity, the man becomes puffed up, and when he thinks himself high, he falls. Until the pit be dug. Behold the counsel of God: he spares the wicked so that a pit may be dug for them. It is still being dug, and you already want to bury him: you hasten too much. For the sinner a pit, etc. Not for everyone, but for the proud, etc., up to: give thanks to him from whom you have it, and do not despise another.
93.16: 93.16 Who will rise up. Cassiodorus: The third part, where he says that there is fluctuation for the just, and the waves of the world, that is, evils through the wicked, that, pricked, they may cry to God, and nothing else may please them, and then the deliverance becomes more welcome. Augustine: Who will rise up, as if to say, etc., up to: but whence shall I conquer? Only because the Lord. He will stand with me, etc. Cassiodorus: Enduring in the battle line; but because he conquers who sustains the force, he loses who strikes.
93.17: 93.17 Unless the Lord. Cassiodorus: He could have been deceived by vain persuasions, unless the Lord had delivered him.
93.18: 93.18 Was my helper. As the Lord delivered Peter walking on the water, lest he sink, who said to the Lord: Lord, if it be you, bid me come to you (Matt. 26). Augustine: As Christ by his own power, etc., up to: hence he adds, your consolations have given joy to my soul.
93.19: 93.19 In my heart. The same: He signifies wholesome thoughts, namely that when he thought on the eternal recompenses, he despised temporal evils.
93.20: 93.20 Does the seat of iniquity cleave to you? The same: No wicked man sits with you; and since they have nothing to do with you, why then are they made? That you may prick through them, and, pricked, they may cry to you, and at last these perish; which is shown in the three verses that follow. The seat of iniquity. Cassiodorus: It is the possession of the world with love, which does not cleave to God, who commands his own to flee these things. You who frame. Augustine: From this I understand that the wicked man does not cleave to you, etc., up to: and that sorrow is a precept; but the other is shapeless. Sorrow, that is, from sorrow or labor the precept, etc., up to: and then the wave rises, in which he is aroused.
93.22: 93.22 And the Lord is become my refuge, and my God the help of my hope. The same: Why? Because if you were not in danger, you would not seek a refuge: you are pricked by sorrow, that you may seek a remedy; the hope of the world departs and the hope of God comes.
94.1: 94.1 Praise. Cassiodorus: Devotion. Song signifies cheerfulness. Come, let us rejoice. Theodoret: King Josiah was very devout, etc., up to: but the psalm is composed in the person of Josiah, and of the priests of God. Cassiodorus: Of the time of grace, in which one enters into rest, the prophet describing the praises of God first invites the Jews, whom he foresaw able to resist Christ.
94.2: 94.2 His face, etc. Augustine, Cassiodorus: The sight of the judge to come, that nothing then may be left in us to be examined. In confession. Augustine: Praising him, accusing ourselves, etc., up to: of which praise the psalm treats. Let us make a joyful noise in psalms. What we say in psalms, or do, let us feel in jubilation.
94.3: 94.3 Above all gods. Or rather he calls men gods, over whom he is king, not over demons.
94.4: 94.4 For in his hand, etc. Cassiodorus: After the aforesaid greatness of the Lord, he comes to his clemency.
94.5: 94.5 The sea. Augustine: The world, whose waves God confines to a limit, not allowing us to be tempted above what we are able (1 Cor. 10); which waves even bring us advancement, God effecting it, nor do scandals hurt you, which receive their measure from God.
94.6: 94.6 Come, let us adore. Cassiodorus: First he called the unlearned to rejoicing: now, the glory of God having been shown, he calls to penance, which is harder. Let us weep. Augustine: If perhaps you are anxious over the sins which have made you far off, weep: a tear extinguishes the flame of sin which burns in the conscience. Who made us. Behold the great confidence: you can fail yourself, you cannot restore yourself, he restores who made you.
94.7: 94.7 And we are his people, etc. Augustine: The order of words is elegantly changed: He did not say sheep of the pasture and people of his hand, that you may understand those themselves to be sheep who are the people, sheep of the hand, not those at a distance, because there are also sheep which we did not make, but he himself by his grace made us sheep.
94.8: 94.8 Today if you shall hear his voice, etc. Cassiodorus: But we are the people and the sheep. But to all these a condition is proposed, if you hear his voice, which voice he adds, Today. Harden not. The same: Christ himself now admonishes that they not be hardened, lest it befall them as their fathers.
94.9: 94.9 As in the provocation. The same: The majesty of Christ speaking, etc., up to: the fault of the parents is repeated, that vengeance may be feared.
94.10: 94.10 Forty years. Augustine: By forty years he signifies all the ages, etc., up to: as he himself says: I am with you even to the consummation of the world.
95.1: 95.1 A psalm of David. Cassiodorus: In the Old Testament it is read, etc., up to: this psalm does not treat of that actual event. Sing to the Lord. The same: In the preceding psalm he forewarned the Jews that, hardness laid aside, they should believe Christ; but because it would remain, now he admonishes all nations. The second psalm on both comings. First he speaks to the prelates, that they themselves sing and announce. A new canticle. Augustine: Covetousness sings the old, etc., up to: whoever has entered, is outside.
95.2: 95.2 To the Lord and bless. Jerome, Cassiodorus: Three times to the Lord, to distinguish the Trinity of persons; because the praise of Christ is the honor of the Trinity. And it is the figure epimone, that is, frequent repetition of a sentence, which heightens it for praise or blame.
95.3: 95.3 Declare. He speaks to the prelates, declare, because so the building of the house grows. From day to day. Cassiodorus: The Old and New Testament are days, which shine with the eternal sun, the one foretells, the other shows the thing done. Jerome: He declares therefore from day to day, etc., up to: by which the feet of our affections are protected from the thorns of vices.
95.4: 95.4 Great is the Lord. Augustine: Made little, because you are little, understand the great one, and you will be great in him.
95.5: 95.5 He made the heavens. The same: The Apostles and angels, whence if he made the heavens and angels, then also the Apostles, who command demons.
95.6: 95.6 In his sight. For such, namely the confessing and the just, behold him and are beheld by him. Holiness and magnificence. Augustine: As if to say: He who wishes to be magnificent and powerful, as the angels are, let him first be holy, which comes from him who sanctifies: for you cannot be holy by yourself. By his sanctifying, then, a man becomes holy, and so magnificent.
95.7: 95.7 Bring to the Lord, you kindreds of the Gentiles. Cassiodorus: The second part, where he speaks to subjects, etc., up to: that none be excepted, native or stranger. Glory. The same: Because the man in whom God is glorified lives well. Honor. When thanks are rendered for good things, whence, There was not found any to give honor to God, but this stranger. Into the courts. The same: The courts are the prophets or apostles, through whom one goes to the Lord; from the courts, the prophets or apostles, one comes into the court of the Catholic Church, where majesty is adored. Augustine: Or, Enter into the court, that is, into the teaching of the prophets and apostles.
95.9: 95.9 Adore the Lord in his holy court, etc. That is, in the Catholic Church, or through the courts, prophecy; through the court, the Gospel. Let the earth be moved. He wishes all those admonished to be moved. As if to say, enter and adore, you good. But the earth, etc. The whole earth. Cassiodorus: Not some part; let no one therefore say: Behold, here is Christ, behold, there; he adds, For he has corrected the world, etc.
95.10: 95.10 Say among the Gentiles. The same: That he has reigned and corrected and judged. Has reigned. Another reading: Has reigned from the wood (Matt. 13). Augustine: Of the cross, by which man crosses the sea, and becomes a world that shall not be moved. The peoples with equity, etc. Others add, And the nations in your wrath. Cassiodorus: The peoples, then, that is the good, he will judge in equity, but the nations, that is the wicked, in his wrath.
95.12: 95.12 Then shall all the trees of the woods rejoice. Cassiodorus, Jerome: Then, when he shall correct, etc., up to: because he is come, that is, will come to judge the earth. Because he is come. Augustine: First he came in the Church, in the clouds, that is, the apostles, and filled the whole world; hence: Henceforth you shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds (Matt. 26): whoever believes in this coming will rejoice at the last coming.
95.13: 95.13 He shall judge the world. Cassiodorus: He includes every man generally, to be judged according to the equity of God. But how he will be judged he explains by saying, the peoples with truth, because in the separation there will be two peoples, to whom he will give the sentence of truth, that some go to life, others to punishments. Augustine: By the world he means all the sons of Adam, etc., up to: the south.
96.1: 96.1 A psalm for David himself. Literally it touches here on this, that when Absalom, the wicked son of David, who in his lifetime persecuted his father, was dead, the land was restored to David, and he reigned in peace, of which it is not treated here, but rather of what is signified. Augustine: David signifies Christ, whom wicked sons, that is the Jews, crucified, and renounced the kingdom to him. But the land was restored to him, when Judea, which had crucified him, believed: and the apostles, who had wavered, were confirmed: but other sheep also from the Gentiles were brought in. Or, the land was restored, when his flesh rose again, after the resurrection all these things which are sung here were done. Augustine: The prophets, foreseeing these things in the Spirit, rejoiced, etc., up to: for to the palate of faith the honey of the divine promise tastes sweet. Cassiodorus: The fourth psalm on the first coming, by which the world was freed. First he describes the powers of the Lord, shows that all things have been restored to him, and rebukes idolaters. The Lord has reigned. Cassiodorus: The prophet, seeing the superstitions of the world abound before the resurrection of Christ, sets against them: The Lord has reigned. Augustine: Who else then is to be worshiped? As if, no one; hence: Let the earth rejoice. What remains for idols? As if, nothing. The islands. The Churches of the whole world. Many. Not all, because of the assemblies of heretics. Cassiodorus: Then he says what the Lord is at the first coming.
96.2: 96.2 Clouds and darkness. To the impious, who are blind, he is cloudy and dark, to whom he shines with no brightness; but to the good, Justice and judgment. Those who are corrected are his throne. Before his coming fire shall go before, because the impious, inflamed with wrath at the preaching of the prophets, planned their death, and were inflamed to indignation all around, because many, though the preachers were few.
96.3: 96.3 A fire shall go before him, etc. Augustine: As if the corrected are the seat of God, etc., up to: if they are wicked, to consumption; if good, to restoration.
96.4: 96.4 His lightnings have shone. The same: The clouds were cheap in human form, but a wonderful brightness appeared in their words or deeds, and from this the earth was moved.
96.5: 96.5 They melted. The same: Even if the pagan does not now believe, yet he has been conquered.
96.7: 96.7 Let them be confounded. This has already been done. Augustine: For idolatry now ceases. And let them be ashamed who adore stones, because dead.
96.8: 96.8 Adore. The same: The adoration of angels therefore ceases, but they adore. The evil angels themselves wish to be adored; the good adore, and do not permit themselves to be adored. Or at least by this example let idolatry cease. Sion heard and was glad. Cassiodorus: Second, after the restoration of the earth, every kind of rejoicing, etc., up to: as the brethren rejoiced over Cornelius, whom Peter baptized. And they rejoiced. Augustine: The apostles who were in Judea heard, the brethren, that the Gentiles had received the word of God, and they were glad and glorified God.
96.9: 96.9 The earth ... gods. The same: By the earth and gods understand sinners and the just. Or, he signifies that he rules over earthly and heavenly things.
96.10: 96.10 The Lord keeps. Augustine: If, when you have begun to hate the wicked one, persecutions follow, do not fear, because the Lord keeps the souls of his saints, from whom the last kind of persecution is to be removed.
97.1: 97.1 A psalm of David. Cassiodorus: The third psalm of those that treat of both comings: in which there is cause of hope through the mercy of the first coming, and of fear through the judgment of the second: these things, though often repeated, are always new by the varied description of words and sentences. Sing to the Lord. Cassiodorus: First he speaks of the showing of the saving right hand. He has saved. Augustine: It is greater that he raised the whole world from eternal death than that he raised the dead. For himself. Many are saved bodily, but for themselves, not for him: who, having received bodily health, grow wanton, but those who are healed within through faith, are healed for him, or save themselves.
97.2: 97.2 Salvation ... justice. Augustine: Who saves and justifies. He has revealed. The prophets foretold future things under a veil: but the veil is taken away, when truth is sprung out of the earth.
97.3: 97.3 Of mercy and truth. Augustine: Mercy is that he promised, truth follows this, because he fulfilled it. But to whom? To Israel, that is, to him who now through faith sees the truth, and afterward in vision.
97.4: 97.4 All. The same: Because Christ was not given to some only.
97.5: 97.5 Sing joyfully. Cassiodorus: Second, he says that he is to be praised and announced in every way, because the judge has come.
97.6: 97.6 With trumpets of beaten metal and the sound of the horn trumpet. Augustine: Of bronze, which are drawn out by hammering, etc., up to: as the horn adheres to the flesh and overcomes it. Jerome: With beaten trumpets, of silver, in the manner of the Jews. Mystically, drawn out under the hammer of the whole earth, that is, the devil. Augustine: Tribulation is the hammering; progress, the drawing out: such a trumpet was Job, hence he sounded like a trumpet, saying: The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away.
97.7: 97.7 Let it be moved. The same: That is, let the sea of the law be sweetened, the wood of the cross being placed in it. And the fullness thereof. All the sacraments of the law, etc., up to: but the rivers, etc. The earth. Cassiodorus: That is, every sinner.
97.9: 97.9 The world. All earthly men. In justice. Augustine: Because they have not merited mercy. The peoples. Cassiodorus: The faithful of the Jews and Gentiles, who will receive what is equal to their merits.
98.1: 98.1 A psalm of David. Augustine: The prophet describes Christ as a king giving good things, etc., up to: but the veil is taken away, when truth is sprung out of the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven (Ps. 48). The Lord has reigned. Cassiodorus: Of the power and kingdom of Christ, that he be adored in the man. He shows Christ reigning, and whoever resists, high above all, hence he admonishes them to yield to him. Let the peoples be angry. Cassiodorus: Mockery. They may be allowed in security to be angry, because they will do no more harm: he says it by permitting, not by commanding. He sits upon the cherubim. The same: The earth can do nothing against him, even though he himself was on earth where he suffered the anger of the people. Cherubim. Augustine: It is interpreted as fullness of knowledge, which is charity. The fullness of the knowledge of the law, which is the seat of God, will be also in you, if you have charity, against which the angry can do nothing. For what is earth against heaven?
98.2: 98.2 The Lord is great in Sion. The same: If you do not understand what is above the Cherubim, see this, that he is great in Sion. Sion is the soul which contemplates God. In Sion great. Cassiodorus: He explains who the Lord is: born in Sion. Great, lest he be lowered by the passion. Or, nevertheless the Lord is great in the Sion of the Jews, and above the peoples of the Gentiles.
98.3: 98.3 Great. Augustine: It was small when they were angry, that is, spoken of by few, but now spread through all the earth. Terrible. The same: Because even if he is preached as crucified, he is the judge to come, and will not err in judgment. And the honor of the king. Cassiodorus: He explains how they ought to confess. The honor of the king is the glorious preaching, judgment demands discernment; he is to be worshiped not by light will, but by fixed deliberation, which is from himself; hence he adds: You have prepared directions. Or the honor of the king is the condemnation of the guilty, whence the glory of the king is increased.
98.4: 98.4 In Jacob. Augustine: Not only to the patriarch, but to the people, whom he signifies. You have done. These things which another could not.
98.5: 98.5 Exalt. Cassiodorus: The second part admonishes to adore him, because he was theirs by fathers. As if, because he does these things for us, therefore Exalt. Footstool. Augustine: Scripture calls the earth his footstool, etc., up to: in whose honor he adores the footstool. Of his feet. Cassiodorus: The feet are the unfailing stability of the Godhead. Holy. That you may distinguish the body from the Godhead, though one person.
98.6: 98.6 Moses. Cassiodorus: A priest, because if he did not offer victims, he offered the vows of the people, and made supplication for the people.
98.7: 98.7 The pillar. Cassiodorus: The strength and beauty of the house. In this form he spoke, which announced the Church, or the flesh, but then in the cloud, now openly through the Son: The cloud spoke to them. The same: To them, then, in the cloud, who now speaks to us in the footstool, that is, in the assumed flesh, openly. His testimonies and precepts. The same: A testimony is a signification of a preceding thing placed by some signs: hence it is often said in the law: This shall be for a testimony to you. The precepts are like the precepts of the law given through Moses.
98.8: 98.8 You were propitious to them. Augustine: It is said only of sins, propitious in pardoning, propitious also in avenging; behold, even if these were so great, they still had something of sin; hence he adds, for all their devices. Avenging. Lest human exaltation steal in; hence: There was given me a sting of my flesh (2 Cor. 12). Devices. Another reading: affections. Augustine: Which God alone knew in their hearts; hence it was a punishment to them to suffer those with whom they were, for whose sins they grieved through charity as if for their own. For it was not, as is thought by many, a punishment to Moses not to enter the promised land, into which even wretched men entered; but a figure that those who were under the law and did not wish to be under grace would not enter into rest.
99.1: 99.1 A psalm of confession. Confession is twofold; one is of praise, the other of sins. Confession of praise suits the perfect, confession of sins beginners; hence in this psalm the prophet admonishes to confession. Cassiodorus: This psalm teaches both to praise God unceasingly and to lament our sins unceasingly: because neither is one to despair in evils, nor ought the mind to be lifted up in good things. First he enjoins on the perfect the chief kind of confession, that is, praise. Rejoice. Augustine: If the voice rejoices outwardly, etc., up to: and in what order and how wondrously he made. All the earth. Admonishing to praise. He does not urge one corner of the earth: but as he knows the blessing sown everywhere, so he requires jubilation from every side. Serve in gladness. Augustine: This service is not of bitterness, nor of indignation, but of happiness and freedom. Let charity then make you a servant, because truth has made you free. Hence the Lord: If you continue in my word, you shall be my disciples indeed: and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free (John 8). In gladness. Because freed; not murmuring, as in the desert: hence he adds the reward.
99.2: 99.2 Come in before his presence. It is a great thing to rejoice in the sight of so great a one. Come in. Cassiodorus: Second, the second kind of confession for those about to enter; and let it not be doubted, for mercy is with him.
100.1: 100.1 A psalm for David himself. Cassiodorus: This psalm contains the form of perfect holiness, as the hundredth number is perfect. For David himself. That all that is taught here may be applied to the virtues of Christ, nothing to an earthly king. Here we are taught to seek good things, to refuse evil, which is the perfect conduct of life. Mercy and judgment I will sing. Cassiodorus: Christ sings here, and we in him. First he proposes concerning mercy and judgment. Mercy and judgment I will sing. These two are joined in mutual fellowship: in them he briefly includes all the works of God. And here is the cause set forth why he is as he afterward adds. Augustine: Let no one presume on mercy for impunity, because there is judgment with it; let no one changed for the better fear judgment, because mercy goes before. These are always together in him: but in times they are distinguished by their effects, mercy now, judgment in the future.
100.2: 100.2 I will sing and understand. The same: He gives this to sing, that I may understand in mind what is not plain to the eyes, that is, I may believe that the Lord will come, whom this one so desires, who will come in the unspotted way. Cassiodorus: Because he passed through the world without sin; or, I will sing and understand, being in the unspotted way, when, etc. Or, I will sing, I will work cheerfully, and by this I will understand. When will you come to me. In the second coming, or at the death of each. Or, when will you come to me, through the flesh in the first coming, because in the unspotted way. I walked. Cassiodorus: Second, he explains what the unspotted way is. Augustine: I walked. What is the unspotted way? It begins from innocence, and is completed in it; and there is no need of many words: Be innocent, and you have perfected justice. But man harms in two ways, namely if he makes another wretched, and if he abandons the wretched. The innocent is he who harms neither himself nor another. Cassiodorus: I walked. As if to say: I did not seek transitory things, but ran the way of the world, being in the midst of your house. Innocence can do this, to make one dwell in the midst of the house of God, as an honorable example to others.
100.3: 100.3 I did not set before. Cassiodorus: He sets out innocence by parts. First, because he has nothing to do with the wicked, he says: I did not set before, up to, my eyes. After which, he has a portion with the just, and drives the wiles of the devil from his heart, there, in the mornings. Augustine: I did not set before. As if: I walked in innocence: by this the whole Christ says that I did not set before, that is, I did not love an unjust thing.
100.4: 100.4 It has not cleaved. Cassiodorus: He sets out transgressions. A perverse heart: one who transgresses in heart; the one turning aside, the heretic who dissents from the Catholics: and the one who strays from the right paths I did not acknowledge, because even if sealed with us by the sacraments, they are not true.
100.5: 100.5 The proud. Augustine: And Jesus feasted, etc., up to: hence: Blessed are they who hunger and thirst after justice (Matt. 8).
100.6: 100.6 My eyes. Here he follows out the other part of innocence, namely, that he has part with the just. As if to say: With such you did not eat, from what then were you fed? Of the earth. Augustine: Those living on the earth, where there are so many allurements, hence the greater crown. Or Cassiodorus: who are throughout the whole world. That they may sit with me. Augustine: Let them remain with me in the truth of faith, or share with me the eternal kingdom, or judge with me.
100.7: 100.7 He shall not dwell in the midst of my house. Cassiodorus: That is, of the Church. Though the grace of correction be tolerated for a while, it is not preeminent in merits, it can do nothing; there is not grain in my people, but chaff. He shall not dwell, this especially suits priests, not to dwell with the wicked.
100.8: 100.8 In the morning. Cassiodorus: The third part, where he shows what the end of the wicked is. And Christ speaks here. In the morning. After avoiding the wicked, the just man, returned to himself, adds that he expelled the suggestions of the demons from his heart in the morning, that is, when at the beginning of temptation, as in twilight, they begin to appear. I put to death. By prayer, by which they ought to be cast out, that they not grow. The sinners. The demons, who make all flesh sin. From the city of the Lord. The soul of the just, whence the devil is scattered and removed. All that work iniquity. That is, the submissions or suggestions of the devil. Augustine: He has already enumerated that only the good cleaved to him, etc., up to: this also suits the just man, who foresees that this will be, and therefore conducts himself so.
101.1: 101.1 The prayer of the poor man. Augustine: According to the form of a servant, etc., up to: the bridegroom for the head, the bride for the body. Christ, poor in us, and with us, and for us, prays here in the person of the penitent, recognizing his lowliness and the cause of the lowliness, and asking to be freed from sins and restored to his former state. He admonishes therefore to take note of one's own misery and to ask the mercy of God.
101.2: 101.2 O Lord, hear my prayer. Cassiodorus: The fifth psalm of penance; the fourth which is called prayer. The first part, a prayerful beginning. And my cry. The prayer grew into a cry. Let it come; let not the clouds, which are for the wicked, hinder. The same: Epimone through three verses, that is, frequent repetition of a sentence.
101.4: 101.4 For they have vanished. Cassiodorus: The second part, in which there is a tearful prayer; in which is set out what the poverty is, what the tribulation. Whence he cries, he now opens. For they have vanished. My days have vanished like smoke. Augustine: For to the exalted Adam the days fail, the strength of the mind is contracted. Misery can move a merciful judge. My bones are dried up like fuel. The strong, whose frying pan they are, who are scandalized, etc., up to: for now man is fried, while he fears he will burn.
101.5: 101.5 I am smitten as grass, and my heart is withered. The same: Made mortal. Grass is green, but when struck easily feels injury: so the flesh of man, flourishing in the law of God, is cut off by the same and withers.
101.6: 101.6 From the voice of my groaning. Cassiodorus: The nature of sinners is shown, because while sin is sought, the contemplation of God is not had. My. Augustine: Not of those who groan over earthly things and not over spiritual, etc., up to: to bear the weak.
101.7: 101.7 To the pelican, etc. Augustine: He sets three birds, three places, etc., up to: who, if not among men, is outside on high, saying to those who sleep in the night. Or, the wise sparrow flies to the heights of virtues, where it is safe from snares. Who is solitary or unique, on account of charity which makes him one out of many, is on the housetop, or the building, on account of the height of faith, that he not come down to take anything out of the house, that is, the flesh. Dwelling. The same: Or in the ruined walls, which are commonly called ruins, where walls stand without roof, where dwells the night raven, a bird that loves the night.
101.9: 101.9 All the day. Cassiodorus: Or, the whole can be taken in the person of the just man. As if to say, etc., up to: or, in my dejection I was refreshed, so much did it please me.
101.10: 101.10 Ashes. Augustine: By ashes and weeping penitents are signified. For ashes and sackcloth are the arms of penitents. Drink. Cassiodorus: Temporal pleasantness. Or the longing for the fatherland I mixed with tears because of the delay; or the drink of the Scriptures, which recall ancient things.
101.11: 101.11 From the face of your wrath. Cassiodorus: Wrath, vengeance; indignation, a motion of the mind by which we are indignant even at sons. Wrath is called an impulse to punish, which does not fall upon God. But it is anthropopathic. Of wrath. Hence the Lord also says: The wrath of God abides upon those who believe not (John 3). He does not say, will come; but abides, because it is not taken away, in which one is born.
101.12: 101.12 My days have declined like a shadow. Because I turned aside from the true day, my days that turn aside are like me.
101.13: 101.13 But you, etc. Cassiodorus: The third part, where the certainty of obtaining pardon is shown. Now the fallen man rises to prophesy, now the penitent lifts his head. Augustine: A promised memorial, memorable, from you our restoration, because you are mindful of us, or we mindful of you.
101.14: 101.14 The time is come. Augustine: Because God willed all things to be done in order, and appointed time for this, where the opportunity is fittingly ordered.
101.15: 101.15 Her stones. Augustine: There are stones in Sion, etc., up to: hence it is that, the Holy Spirit being sent, many of those who crucified the Lord believed.
101.17: 101.17 In glory. Augustine: Who was first seen in weakness in that Sion; hence: We saw him, and there was no sightliness, nor beauty (Isa. 53).
101.18: 101.18 The prayer. This is done in the building of Sion: they pray, the builders groan, who are one poor man, and many poor; hence in the title in the singular, here in the plural. But one is said on account of the truth of the peace of the Church, many on account of its breadth.
101.19: 101.19 Let these things be written. Cassiodorus: He who above was squalid in penance, now adorned with the honor of a prophet, commands that what he has said be confirmed by the testimony of Scripture, that the future age may learn. In generation. Augustine: When these things were written, they did not so profit the generation of the Old Testament; they profit another, that is, the new.
101.20: 101.20 For he has looked down, etc. Augustine: After the groanings of the sorrowing, now there are words of consolation, now the poor man rejoices. And because above he said: The Lord has built up Sion; and again: Let these things be written; now he declares both; as if this is what he said was to be written, that he has looked down. He has looked down. He speaks as of the past what was to be future.
101.21: 101.21 Of the fettered. Augustine: The fear of God, the fetters are, etc., up to: and when loosed are turned into glory. Cassiodorus: The fettered, the saints, etc., up to: hence their discourse runs together into the Church in general. To release the children. Augustine: But we are the children of those put to death, who are released from the knots of sins and the bonds of desires.
101.23: 101.23 He answered him in the way of his strength. Cassiodorus: The fourth part, where, after the certainty of pardon, he says that he passes from his brevity to eternity. Augustine: He answered. Because: I say, that I may announce the name of the Lord and his praise in Jerusalem, etc., up to: he does not despise, but renders fruit. He answered him. That is, he believes that Christ has risen. But because he foresees that some will say, there was indeed once a Church gathering all into one, but now it ceases. The fewness, he says, of my days: not the eternity of those where I shall be, but the temporal days, as long as I shall be in this age. Tell me. Because of those who say there is no longer a Church. This voice is not idle, this petition is not empty. For the way itself, that is Christ, has so announced: I am with you even to the consummation of the world (Matt. 28). The whole time until the end is that fewness of days: because all that is finished is small, that from it we may pass into eternity. Tell me and:
101.24: 101.24 Call me not back in the midst of my days. Let it not be, as the heretics say, etc., up to: but they are only half, if the eternal are not added.
101.25: 101.25 In the way of strength. Augustine: In the faith by which he believes that Christ has risen. Christ was the way of strength after the resurrection, when, no longer weak but strong, he calls the Church in heaven. The praise of faith is not that it believes him dead, which the pagan also believes, but glorified. Or, the Christian religion is briefly defined when it is called the way of strength. Or, in generation of generations. There is a generation of generations which does not pass, gathered out of all, that is the saints. In it shall be the years of the Lord, which do not pass, that is the eternity of God, which is the very substance of God, having nothing changeable.
101.26: 101.26 In the beginning, O Lord. As if: Call me not back, because I tend to eternity, which he explains, saying: In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth.
101.27: 101.27 They shall perish. Augustine: That the heavens themselves shall perish, this is clear of those nearest the earth; hence Peter also: But the heavens and the earth which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire (2 Pet. 3). Of the higher ones it is not certain, but if they remain, they remain not in themselves, but in God.
101.28: 101.28 And as a vesture you shall change them. Understand the heavens, which cover all things, which also shall be changed. And your years shall not fail. Augustine: Which shall be in the generation of generations. But shall we be able to be there? Certainly, because the children of your servants shall dwell there.
101.29: 101.29 The children of your servants. Augustine: As children entered the land of promise, etc., up to: with all the newness of children. Children. A joyful conclusion. The children of the prophets and apostles, much more they themselves. Seed. Works, whence eternal fruit. Shall be directed. Because nothing crooked enters.
102.2: 102.2 Bless the Lord, O my soul. Augustine: After the prayers of the poor man, the heralding of one rejoicing. All who are in Christ as one man, who rouses and exhorts his soul to bless the Lord, wishing to define why he is to be blessed, lest anyone be found slothful in this. Cry with the voice, if there is a man to hear; without voice, if there is no man to hear, because God hears. Cassiodorus: By his benefits he urges to bless God. Augustine: The Prophet, speaking in the person of the just in general, according to the higher power of the soul, that is reason, exhorts the soul to bless, saying: Forget not. Let not the delight of sin be before your eyes, but the condemnation and the remission of God: think on all your evils, for as many as they are, so many are the good recompenses of God. Recompenses. Not gifts. Man gives evils for goods, and God recompenses him with goods for evils. He gave, when he made me; he recompenses when he justifies.
75.3: 75.3 In Sion. Augustine: Note the fitting order of the words: Judea is confession; then Israel, that is, seeing God, and so there is a place at peace with God; hence follows: In peace, then in Sion, that is, in contemplation, when he will see God face to face, there will be his dwelling.
75.4: 75.4 There he broke the powers. Cassiodorus: In Judea, in Israel, in Salem, in Sion, where God the author of peace came, all these things, which are also the names of their glory, flee.
75.5: 75.5 You give wondrous light from the eternal hills; they were troubled, etc. Pause. Christ enlightens, the Jew sleeps; Christ judges, that man perishes. Augustine: You enlighten, but through the mountains, which first receive the light, namely through the Prophets and Apostles. But at the enlightenment all the foolish of heart were troubled. He puts forward from this why he will be terrible in the future, etc. They have slept. Cassiodorus: Growing cold toward eternal goods, they rested in the flesh, not seeing what would profit. Their sleep, which is far from the rest of the good, because this one is deceptive; seeing in a dream that they have treasures, when they awake they find nothing; hence he says: And all the men of riches have found nothing. A definition of the covetous. They found nothing. Because they placed nothing in the hands of Christ, who says: I was hungry, etc. Remigius: For in the poor he hungers, who is rich in heaven. Men of riches. Who place their only hope in the uncertainty of riches. Hence he does not say, those having riches: for many have them who do not love them. In their hands, etc. Cassiodorus: As if they were still seeking in their hands, when they already recognize that they have held nothing.
75.7: 75.7 At your rebuke, etc. Augustine: The noise of a rebuke usually rouses, but so great is the weight of God rebuking that they slumber, that is, they have a hardened heart. Who have mounted. The same: Whose pride has grown, not humbled by the humble Christ. Horses. Cassiodorus: Any worldly exaltations whatever; hence in the Law the children of Israel were commanded not to multiply horses for themselves. Solomon also had no horses from Judea, but bought them from Egypt.
75.9: 75.9 From heaven you have made judgment to be heard. Augustine: Hence the Apostle: At the revelation of our Lord Jesus from heaven, with his angels, they will come to execute judgment (1 Thess. 1).
75.10: 75.10 When he arose, that is, when he who is here humble will appear mighty. Or, when he arose from death, afterward to come to judgment. Augustine: When coming from heaven you will make it heard, that is, known to all. The power of the judgment is set forth, whence earthly men are terrified, and with power lost they are still; it was still when he arose. The meek of the earth. The same: Those who have peace of mind, not rejecting the yoke of God.
75.11: 75.11 For the thought. Cassiodorus: Pause. He now admonishes the devout to offer vows. As if to say, deservedly he saves the meek. For the thought, that is, they will praise you in thought and in deed, that is, the remnants of the thought, etc. The thought of man. The same: The conception of the vow. The remnants, the fulfillment of the vow, the working, what remains after the thought. The remnants of thought. Augustine: For the first thought, etc., up to: which is to celebrate solemnities. Cassiodorus: Because the Lord alone is the one to whom festival is owed: they will pay their vows to God. The first thought condemns evils. The remnant. Because afterward a man must always remember past evils, that he may mourn; although the world here keeps holiday when it feels itself free of sin, so that after amendment the Jews are commanded to offer a festive gift to God.
75.12: 75.12 Vow and pay. Augustine: Some vows are common, concerning those things without which there is no salvation; others are particular, such as to vow chastity and the like. Cassiodorus: Vow. There are certain things which we ought to fulfill even without promising: such as, You shall not kill, and the like, etc., up to: those who are round about, that as servants they will offer, or let them offer, etc. Augustine: There are, as it were, those in the middle, etc., up to: having the Spirit of God, not of princes, that is, the proud. Gifts. The same: Which are offered on the altars. To the terrible one, and to him who takes away. Whom the good fear, but the wicked do not fear. The spirit of princes. Cassiodorus: He takes away the spirit of pride or of fear, and makes his own reins, those who govern their body.
76.1: 76.1 Unto the end, for Idithun. Augustine: The congregation speaks, passing over, that it may arrive at the end, which is Christ. He teaches therefore to trample on the desires and allurements of the world, and to put nothing before oneself except him from whom are all things. Cassiodorus: Transcending all things, it seeks God and finds him.
76.2: 76.2 I cried to the Lord with my voice. Augustine: With the intention of devotion to the Lord, asking nothing else from him, because he is Lord and because he is God. My voice to him. The voice is for the sake of that for which it is uttered; he adds this lest it be thought he cries to God for anything other than for himself, above whom there is nothing. Cassiodorus: He does not say what he asks, because it need not be told to him who knows what is expedient. He gave heed to me. Cassiodorus: For God to give heed is to give all that is asked, and more than is asked.
76.3: 76.3 In the day of my trouble I sought. Augustine: How did you seek? etc., up to: who does not do justice before men that he may be seen. He refused to be comforted. The same: He sets out the tribulation, etc., up to: who finds or fears a scandal in all men is secure in no one.
76.4: 76.4 And I was exercised. Augustine: Or, I chattered, that is, I exulted, speaking like a chatterer who for joy neither would nor could be silent; and again in chattering my spirit failed, which before had wasted away with weariness of evils.
76.5: 76.5 They anticipated the watches. Cassiodorus: Pause. Having found God, who alone is good, he deliberates whether he will lead him back. Augustine: They anticipated the watches of others. My eyes, like one who rises before the time for business. Or, my eyes, my affections. They anticipated the diligence of others. Or, by watches he means the night vigils, which we keep and customarily so call in the praises of God, and therefore: I was troubled. Cassiodorus: Because I could not attain what I seek. I did not speak. I did not murmur against God. Or, I was troubled, because while in the secrecy of night the mind searches, it sees the human race rushing into sins, and with holy sorrow is tormented for others, having already leapt over vices. He is silent, because at night he has not the solace of human conversation, a time when he thinks more cautiously; therefore he adds: I thought of the days, etc. My eyes. Another reading: my enemies anticipated the watches. Augustine: That is, they kept watch over me, etc., up to: yet it does not cease, he wishes to transcend this also, hence he adds:
76.6: 76.6 I thought upon the days of old, etc. Therefore troubled: because I thought of the days of old of Adam, in which man fell. But against the days of old he sets eternal years: therefore troubled, because man desires the former and neglects the eternal. I had in mind the days of old, and the eternal years. Cassiodorus: What happened to Adam for his disobedience? From that I knew that this was the failing of man. And the eternal years, which he would have had by persevering, I kept in mind, which the foolish do not. And I meditated also in the night, that is, in this failing. With my heart, that is, with reason, if in any way I might return to the eternal years. He speaks silently with reason who is exercised calmly in it.
76.7: 76.7 And I was exercised. In the very meditation: I swept my spirit; I purged my mind. Others read: I winnowed my spirit, thus discussing with myself:
76.8: 76.8 Will he cast off forever the human race? That he may be more pleased. As one who was already pleased by his grace in the Old Testament, will he not add that there be more in the New through the coming of the Son? He who treats of piety feels this. I was exercised and I swept. Augustine: Or, I chattered, no longer outwardly, etc., up to: where he found this, that God will not cast off forever. That he may be more pleased, that is, that he himself, who was angry in rejecting and inflicting evils, may be gentler in freeing and calling back.
76.10: 76.10 Or will God forget to show mercy? Augustine: In another way, there is no mercy unless God gives it: and he himself would be without it. The stream runs, the fountain is dried up.
76.11: 76.11 And I said: Now I have begun. Cassiodorus: What he found by deliberating, namely that Christ changes men and redeems them. The same: And I said. To this meditation, etc., up to: when passing over myself I came to God, here there is no danger. I have begun. Augustine: Something where I am safe, where enemies do not anticipate; now the Most High has begun to change me. This change of the right hand, etc. Cassiodorus: From anger to mercy, so that servants become sons. The same: Of this change, etc., up to: these are the things that soothe the holy.
102.3: 102.3 Who forgives. Augustine: He does this in the sacrament of baptism. Who heals all your infirmities. He does this in the life of the faithful man, while the flesh lusts against the spirit, so that we do things we would not; the languors of oldness are healed from day to day by growing newness, from faith, which works by love.
102.4: 102.4 Who redeems your life from corruption. This is done in the last resurrection of the dead. Who crowns, etc. This is done in the judgment, where when the king shall sit on the throne, to render to every man according to his works, who shall boast that he has a glorious heart and clean from sin? Therefore it was necessary to commemorate there mercy and compassion, where it might seem that debts would be so paid that there would be no place for mercy.
102.5: 102.5 Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's. Augustine: So great a likeness is given, etc., up to: whom age has closed the mouth, forgetting to eat our bread.
102.6: 102.6 Doing. Augustine: The second part, where he admonishes to bless through the things done for the ancients and done for those after. Mercies. Which those obtain who love their enemies, etc., up to: for after mercy he adds concerning judgment, saying, And judgment.
102.7: 102.7 To Moses. Augustine: Through Moses all the saints, etc., up to: through whom he gave the law, that sin might abound.
102.11: 102.11 For. The same: Heaven is all around the earth, whence even to sinners come light, air, breath, rain, whence fruit: without heaven the earth ceases to be; so is the protection of God over those who fear.
102.12: 102.12 As far as, etc. The same: When sin is forgiven, sins set, grace rises, sins are in the west; turn away therefore from the west of sins, and tend to the rising of grace, and you rise.
102.14: 102.14 He remembered, etc. The same: Or according to another reading: Remember that we are dust. As if to say: He knew our frame, that is our weakness: which frame, turned to God, says: Remember that we are dust, that is, let your mercy persevere toward us, lest we forget your grace. Or, Man is like grass, etc. For man goes forth like a flower, etc., up to: The mercy of the Lord. He shall flower out. Cassiodorus: That is, at most he will so flower or flower out, that is, be deflowered. And so out is either intensive or privative.
102.16: 102.16 For the spirit has passed in him. And he shall not continue.
102.17: 102.17 And his justice. Augustine: Mercy and justice is recompense. He says, upon children's children; many just have no children, much less children's children, but works are children; children's children the reward of works.
102.19: 102.19 The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven. Cassiodorus: He proclaims the future judgment, lest sinners grow insolent; as if, you also ought to be mindful to do, because the Lord is in heaven.
102.21: 102.21 Bless the Lord, all you his angels, mighty. The same: Third, he admonishes the heavenly beings and all other creatures to bless. Bless the Lord, etc. He says it congratulating, not commanding, or admonishing. His ministers. Augustine: Bless you, etc., up to: that what he has in his mouth he may show in his work.
103.1: 103.1 A psalm of David. Cassiodorus: Again he admonishes to bless God, first through heaven and earth and their ornament. Augustine: Even if all things here can truly be taken literally and religiously, etc., up to: in all things a spiritual sense is to be sought. Bless the Lord, O my soul, etc., you are magnified. In knowledge, you who are always great by nature, who cannot grow or diminish, because you are perfect; Confession, that is, you have creatures on every side, which confess you, and which are comely and luminous. Or, beauty in the essence of God, and light on every side. Cassiodorus: Or he signifies the incarnation, through which the confession and beauty of the supernal majesty was made known, and men confessed him, who are light in knowledge. Augustine: You have put on confession, that is the Church, etc., up to: and a garment without spot or wrinkle.
103.2: 103.2 Stretching out the heaven like. Cassiodorus: What things confess? Heaven, earth, sea, with all their ornament, of which singly in order what follows. Augustine: Stretching out the heaven like. Literally, heaven, as a roof, etc., up to: afterward at the end Scripture will be rolled up like a book.
103.3: 103.3 Who cover. The same: Literally these are waters, etc., up to: whose upper parts are the two precepts of charity. Or you who cover with waters, that is, with the spiritual sense, the surface of Scripture, or with spiritual gifts you fortify the charity of those, so that nothing can separate them. Upon the wings of the winds, etc. Wind is a motion of the air, etc., up to: but the charity of Christ surpasses the charity of all.
103.4: 103.4 A burning fire. Cassiodorus: That is the seraphim, who are the higher order, you make your ministers, hence in Isaiah: One of the seraphim flew to me, who are the higher order.
103.5: 103.5 Who have founded the earth upon its own stability. The same: Therefore the Holy Spirit in this psalm says hard things according to the letter, that we may seek spiritual things.
103.7: 103.7 At the voice of your thunder. The same: By terrible winds the waters will be dried up; the wicked will fear at the threat of judgment.
103.8: 103.8 They ascend. Augustine: The wicked, as mountains, etc., up to: that the Church may be allowed to preach freely. Cassiodorus: God permits the proud, etc., up to: that they may no longer occupy the world.
103.10: 103.10 In the valleys. Augustine: Of the humble subject to grace, and even if they are mountains in spiritual height, the fountains of the Holy Spirit flow, who rests upon the humble. Between the midst. The same: That is, between the midst, etc., up to: and such a mountain is not to be listened to.
103.11: 103.11 All shall drink. The same: All were in the dish of Peter let down three times, etc., up to: that the Church may be gathered. The wild asses. The same: Great untamed wild asses, etc., up to: or the proud Jews will put off drinking until the last time.
103.12: 103.12 Over them the birds of the air. The same: Not all birds remain, etc., up to: others on the left are condemned.
103.13: 103.13 Of the fruit of your works. The same: Let no one therefore glory in his works, but let him who glories glory in the Lord, for the earth is filled by the grace of God. Thus therefore grace is given freely. If it is rendered to the works of men, it is called a wage.
103.14: 103.14 For the service of men. The same: Hence, when I was free of all men, I made myself the servant of all, etc., up to: to whom he gave an example of taking necessary things from subjects. In oil. To each is given the Spirit for manifestation: grace therefore and a certain shining, etc., up to: that the face may be cheerful in oil. And bread. Bread and wine are therefore the same. For this bread and wine are justice, truth is Christ: both this and that gladden and strengthen the heart.
103.16: 103.16 Which he has planted. The same: Why does he leave the whiteness of the world for those planted by himself? Because there the coot, a bird which lives in the waters; these are they who remain in the grace of baptism. Or, the herodius, a most rapacious bird, and Christ does not reject such either.
103.17: 103.17 There the sparrows. The same: Tiny birds, etc., up to: that they may nest in the cedars of Lebanon. The house of the herodius. Augustine: It is the leader of those sparrows, or cedars, which however cannot be said in Latin, because cedars are of feminine gender, and this in no way literally, for the house, that is, the nest of the coot, which is a sea bird or a marsh bird, how is it the leader of sparrows? But by this he intimates that spiritual things are to be sought. And if the sparrows nest in the rich of the world, etc., up to: but they will not perish, because the rock is their leader. Cassiodorus: Or the coot, a bird which lives in the waters, these are those who remain in the grace of baptism, whose house is baptism. And it is as if he said: Who are the sparrows? Those who are baptized. And this is, the house of the coot, that is, baptism, which is the house of the regenerated, is the leader of those sparrows, that is, of Christians. Jerome, Cassiodorus: The herodius, a most rapacious bird, etc., up to: because he himself converted converted many others to the faith. For the harts, the rock. Augustine: The harts are the great spiritual men, etc., up to: this is that rock of which, as was said above, the birds of the air give voices.
103.19: 103.19 He made the moon. Cassiodorus: After earthly things he passes to heavenly, which nevertheless do things for the earth, that is, serve. After so many kinds of Christians, which he signified by animals, and the aforesaid ordering, ascending he adds concerning Christ and the Church, namely how this temporal Church waxes and wanes, as though the setting and rising of the true sun made it.
103.20: 103.20 You have appointed, etc. And it was made night in them, that is the dark obstinacy of the mind. And they shall pass away. Augustine: Not, as above, the converted, the Gentiles, but demons, who at the time of the passion found the hearts of the apostles wavering; but when Christ rose, because they cannot be in all, they remain in the dens, that is the hearts of the obstinate: so when Christ sets in anyone, evils flourish; when he rises, they flee. The setting. The sun sets so that it may rise: so he who sleeps, that is Christ, will he not add to rise again? He set because he willed, no one takes away his soul; when he set, darkness fell on the apostles, their hope failed.
103.21: 103.21 The young lions, etc. Augustine: There are also princes of demons, and like young lions the contemptible demons, who in darkness seek to seduce souls; the greater lion always goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5), but they are fed by the errors of men.
103.22: 103.22 The sun is risen, etc. Cassiodorus: After he has said what the setting of the true sun did, he adds of its rising.
103.24: 103.24 In possession. Augustine: Another reading: creature. The same: Through Christ the Father, etc., up to: yet wood was given in which we may sail across.
103.25: 103.25 This great sea, etc. Cassiodorus: The second part where he says: How he leads the Church across the sea of the world to the shore of the fatherland. Creeping things, etc. Augustine: The evil spirits, whose snares creep.
103.26: 103.26 That dragon which you have formed. The same: Besides these animals, etc., up to: became greater in malice. To play with him. The same: It is said in Job (Job 40) that Satan is mocked by the angels of God, who are set over the aerial powers, that they may not harm us.
103.27: 103.27 Food. The same: The food of the dragon is earth, because it was said to him: You shall eat earth all the days of your life (Gen. 3). Because those who love earthly things are the food of the devil. But the food of the just is the word of God, hence: Not in bread alone does man live, but in every word that proceeds from the mouth of God (Deut. 8).
103.28: 103.28 Your hand, all shall be filled with goodness. Cassiodorus: Or the hand is the power which abundantly fills all things.
103.29: 103.29 But when you turn away. Augustine: Many filled with goodness attributed it to themselves; but God, wishing to prove to them that they do not have it from themselves but from God, so that with goodness they may have humility, sometimes troubles them, turns away his face, and they fall into temptation.
103.30: 103.30 Send forth your spirit. Cassiodorus: Their dust is called their own, because from themselves they have that they are dust. But the Spirit of the Lord: behold the medicine for those returned to dust.
103.32: 103.32 To tremble. Augustine: The trembling of humility is better than the confidence of pride. Hence the Apostle: With fear and trembling work out your salvation (Phil. 2). Mountains. The same: Who were proud, boasting everything of themselves. As happened on Mount Sinai.
103.33: 103.33 I will sing. Cassiodorus: The third part, where he promises that he will sing always. As if to say: The Lord has done these aforesaid things, and having considered these. In my life. Augustine: Present and future; of hope and of sight. Now hope is our life, afterward the eternal will be. The life of mortal life is the hope of immortal life. As long as I am. The same: Because in him I am without end, I will sing as long as I am, lest another act of that life be thought than to sing: because he who is praised cannot come to weariness, he who praises does not come to weariness; but he is always loved, always praised.
103.34: 103.34 Let my speech be pleasing. Another reading: Let my disputation be sweet to him. Augustine: For man's disputation with God is the confession of sins. Hence Isaiah (Isa. 1): Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes, learn to do well, judge for the fatherless, and come and let us reason together, says the Lord. Your disputation therefore is the sacrifice of your humility, which is sweet to God.
103.35: 103.35 Bless the Lord, O my soul. The same: He repeats what was at the beginning of the psalm: Bless the Lord, O my soul, by this hinting that the end of good things is like the beginning.
104.1: 104.1 Alleluia. Cassiodorus: Here for the first time alleluia, nor before was it placed by anyone, which no tongue has presumed to change. Alleluia, praise. Ia is the name of the invisible God, which suits him alone. Through twenty psalms which bear this title, the great deeds of God are told, and great is the exultation in them. Cassiodorus: Here the prophet commends the good in that people Israel, who with other faithful are the true seed of Abraham, children of the promise. Give praise to the Lord. Augustine: The first psalm to which alleluia is prefixed, etc., up to: which temporal things the mercy of God gave them, he adds.
104.2: 104.2 All. Cassiodorus: All; nothing is to be passed over in silence from shame. Or all, which they shall tell, are wonders, for no one can tell all.
104.3: 104.3 Be praised in his name, that is, rejoice, Christians, to be named from Christ. Augustine: Be praised, he does not forbid being praised, if good; if not, only in the Lord, who makes men good. Be praised in his name. As elsewhere, In the Lord shall my soul be praised: what he adds there, let the meek hear and rejoice; here too in a way, let the heart rejoice, as if to say,
104.4: 104.4 The face, etc. The same: That is the presence, etc., up to: the wicked can fear the presence which the good loves. Jerome: By the martyr Hippolytus, etc., up to: there about to take the Church from the Gentiles.
104.5: 104.5 Remember, etc. Augustine: Seek him himself, etc., up to: if that which God is, it is great to seek, or see what he has done. Wonders, etc. The same: Little by little he ascends from visible wonders to judgments: thence to the eternal covenant, where there is both precept and promise.
104.7: 104.7 In all the earth. The same: Do not think the sons of Abraham are in one nation according to the flesh, because in all the earth are Jacob and Israel, to whom he makes his judgments manifest, but not to another nation.
104.8: 104.8 For ever. The same: That is, to eternity, hence afterward, an eternal covenant. Which covenant, if the Old is understood because of the land of Canaan, of which follows. How is it eternal, when that earthly inheritance cannot be eternal? Of the covenant. For that which is promised is called a covenant, and the teaching in which the promise is declared, and for which, when kept, it is rendered. The same: What we ought to receive is the promise: what we ought to do, the commandment. This is faith, that the just may live by faith, and to this faith the inheritance is promised. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Behold three patriarchs, whose God he specially says he is: I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob. Behold threefold authority.
104.10: 104.10 For an everlasting covenant. The same: That is, which from the very word fulfilled, etc., up to: and the son abides in the house for ever.
104.11: 104.11 The land of Canaan. Cassiodorus: That is, what is signified by it: for he gave even this land as a figure of the eternal inheritance (1 John 4). Augustine: Fittingly the eternal inheritance is called the land of Canaan, because from it the servants are cast out and the sons received.
104.12: 104.12 When they were few in number. Cassiodorus: What supports of temporal life he furnished to the fathers and their children both in flesh and in faith, not that they cling to these, but refer them to eternal good, that, drawn by these, they may seek the justifications and law of God.
104.13: 104.13 From the kingdom. Augustine: Not that it was then, but that the kingdom of Israel would be.
76.13: 76.13 In your devices. Augustine: That is, in the precepts which you have devised, or by which you are found. Cassiodorus: Or in observances, that is, the precepts which are to be observed, I will be exercised; for it is not enough to read the Scriptures, but one must show the fruit of works: instructed in these, he bursts forth into praises. Augustine: In your devices or affections, not in mine; or the affection is in earthly things: so in the works and meditation of God there is a certain inner affection, when the world is looked upon, and in creatures the Creator is sought, and he is found nowhere displeasing, but everywhere pleasing.
76.14: 76.14 O God, your way is in the holy place. Augustine: By what has been said I am certain that I shall come, and with him as leader. The same: God in the holy place, that is, in Christ, the way of returning to you. And since this is so, what God is great? etc. Your way. The same: Of worshiping you and coming to you; hence he joyfully sets the power of God before the idols, which were falsely worshiped.
