76.15: 76.15 Wonders. Augustine: The deaf, blind, feeble, dead and paralytic were healed. These things were done in bodies. In the soul, some are sober who a little before were drunkards, unbelievers, worshipers of idols. Among the peoples your power. The same: To unbelievers, that they may know Christ only in the body; to believers, in reality and Godhead; he adds: What you have bestowed, you have redeemed.
76.16: 76.16 The sons of Joseph. Augustine: That is, the Gentile people. Or, by Joseph Christ is understood: for as Joseph, sold into Egypt, reigned, so Christ among the Gentiles, first humbled in the martyrs. The same: Joseph, who came to the Gentiles, is interpreted as increase: and it signifies the Gentiles, from whom the people of God has been increased. Or, Joseph, Christ sold by the Jews and driven out to the Gentiles; his sons, whom he chose from the Gentiles.
76.17: 76.17 They saw you. Cassiodorus: Pause. He sets out what Christ works in the world. Augustine: As if to say: Since you made your power known, either through him they saw you, O God the Father, or, they saw you, O Christ, who are the power and the arm, etc.
76.18: 76.18 A multitude. Cassiodorus: Not a few, but a multitude. The sound, in the groaning over faults, in the giving of thanks: for the diverse vows of the peoples sound like a rough sea. The sound of waters. Augustine: Whence these sounds of waters, this disturbance of the deeps? Because the clouds gave a voice, of whom it is said: I will command my clouds not to rain upon it.
76.19: 76.19 The voice of your thunder. Cassiodorus: The voice of thunder rolls back, so that a rumbling and winding sound is perceived. Allegory: in the wheel of the whole world. The wheel. Jerome, Augustine: It is what expounds the circuit of the earth, which the clouds went around, thundering with precepts and flashing with miracles. The earth shook. Cassiodorus: Those who dwell on the earth. The earth itself is called sea by likeness, because human life is bitter, subject to storms, where the larger fish devours the smaller.
76.20: 76.20 In the sea. Augustine: Literally, when Christ walked upon the waters. Or, in the hearts of men, whom he subjects to himself. Or, by the earth the Jews, by the sea the Gentiles are understood. And your footsteps shall not be known. A silent rebuke of the Jews; as if to say: Although he came openly and showed himself by miracles, he was not recognized by the unbelieving Jews, whom he led by the hand of Moses and Aaron, that is, by the working of the miracles which they did. Your footsteps, etc. He touched some, that is, the Jews, who say, Christ has not yet come, and do not see him walking on the sea.
76.21: 76.21 Like sheep. Because they are not truly sheep, but goats. Of Moses and Aaron. Cassiodorus: Moses is interpreted as taken from the river; Aaron, mountain of strength: by these names the powers which they wrought are expressed. Moses, among other things, made a way in the sea, signifying that the people are freed by baptism. Aaron held the image of the Church, which is compared to a most strong mountain.
77.1: 77.1 Understanding. Augustine: Because these things narrated, etc., up to: what seem plain are parables and riddles. Attend. Cassiodorus: First the Lord himself speaks, that reverence may grow. My people, who obey me. The mouth of God is Asaph, who below has spoken these things: How great things we have heard from the beginning. Of the Old Testament: or, the faithful Synagogue reproaches the wicked.
77.2: 77.2 In parables. Augustine: Parables, likenesses of things. Propositions. Which in Greek are problems, questions having something to be solved.
77.3: 77.3 How great. Cassiodorus: He says in summary what God did for the Jews: yet to the ungrateful, and so, if it does not profit them, it nevertheless profits their children, lest they become like the fathers. Augustine: First God spoke in man, now man himself: How great things we have heard. God said that beforehand from himself, that his speech might not be despised.
77.5: 77.5 And he raised up, etc. Augustine: This testimony. The beginning, whence above: I will utter propositions from the beginning. The beginning is the Old Testament, the end the New. There fear, which is the beginning; but here Christ, the end of the law unto justice for everyone who believes (Rom. 10), who gives the Spirit, hence: Charity, which casts out fear (1 John 4). The old law is called the testimony of this New Testament, because it has testimony from the Law and the Prophets: hence the tabernacle of testimony was so called, which figured so many mysteries. The Old Testament is therefore called testimony insofar as it proves and attests, law insofar as it commands. Cassiodorus, Remigius: He raised up the testimony, as though dead in Adam, that is, the law; or, while it is described, it is raised up, previously lulled to sleep by ignorance. The testimony in Jacob, this is perhaps that Jacob, having wrestled with the angel, limped when his thigh was touched: which signifies that the Jews stand partly by faith, partly depart from salvation: and so the testimony of this matter was what happened to Jacob. Behold a parable. To his children. And these same children are another generation, namely the people of grace.
77.6: 77.6 Another generation. The commandments of God were handed down through generations, lest anyone think they were given to one.
77.7: 77.7 That they may put. This is the usefulness of fatherly preaching. Let them seek out. Augustine: Those who were said above to have known, let them now seek out, that, hoping in God, they may be helped to fulfill by him.
77.8: 77.8 Perverse. Cassiodorus: That which does not receive the truth, and is therefore twisted, embittering above all bitternesses, so that they were armed against the Savior. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: Go and say to the embittering house (Ezek. 2). It did not direct its heart. The same: He has a twisted heart who does not correct what has been wrongly understood, and does not perfect what nature teaches: His spirit was not believed with God (John 1), that is, even if reason persuaded well, he did not assent to it. Was not believed. Augustine: When the spirit of man cooperates with the working Spirit of God, what God commands is done: and this is nothing but by believing in him who justifies the ungodly, which faith the perverse and embittering generation does not have. The same: He says much more expressly, etc., up to: but that generation, even if it believed God, did not believe in God.
77.9: 77.9 Sending forth the bow. Augustine: He speaks figuratively, etc., up to: David to his brothers, so the Christian people to the people of the Jews. Or, The sons of Ephraim. The same: Bending and sending the bow, that is, sending something with the bow. Or, bending the bow and sending arrows, that is, promising to keep the law, openly saying: All that the Lord shall say to us we will do, and we will hear (Exod. 24). They turned back and failed in the day of battle, that is, of temptation; hence the prophet Hosea says: Ephraim has become like a silly dove, having no heart (Hos. 7), because it is not hearing but temptation that proves a promise of obedience. Of benefits. Euthymius: Of the benefits which he conferred on the people of Israel, such as that he led them through the Red Sea unwetted. He speaks of wonders because he had changed the rivers of the Egyptians into blood. In saying that God showed them these things, he does not mean that they saw them with their own eyes, but that they so received them from their forefathers.
77.12: 77.12 Before their fathers, etc. Cassiodorus: He now begins to narrate what he did for them from the exodus out of Egypt; and yet they did not cease from murmuring and from tempting. Augustine: Before their fathers. Who are the fathers, etc., up to: with the wood of the cross approaching like the rod of Moses. In the land of Egypt. The same: To remove all doubt, he names both the region and the place of the deeds. So Christ, placed on earth, knew before the fathers, and taught the humble commandment: Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart (John 7).
77.14: 77.14 In a cloud. Jerome and Cassiodorus: They judged this to be future. The day is Christ, yet he is hidden from the faithless by the cloud of the flesh; and as the cloud was for them against the heat of the sun, so for us Christ through the incarnation gives refreshment against the heat of vices. All the night, the whole time of life. In the illumination of fire. The fire of the Holy Spirit guards Christians in this age by the brightness of his name.
77.15: 77.15 The rock. Cassiodorus: In the desert. First the water of the sea like a rock, now the rock a fountain. In the desert, where it is necessary that the gift be the more welcome. He gave them drink. Like cattle, not men, because they gave no thanks.
77.16: 77.16 As. Cassiodorus: The water that proceeds from Christ fails by no diminution, but becomes a fountain of water springing up to life everlasting.
77.17: 77.17 They sinned still more. Cassiodorus: They added, so that amid so many benefits they did not believe; and that this might be understood as the greatest sin, when the Lord said in the Gospel: The Spirit will convict the world of sin, he added in explanation: Of sin indeed, because they do not believe in me (John 4, 16). As therefore he says there that to sin is not to believe, so here he says to sin is not to believe. Unto wrath. The same: Not believing that God can do difficult things for them, which is most grievous before God; so also we, washed by baptism, provoke God to wrath. In the waterless place. Augustine: Or, in another desert, literally, or rather in themselves, because although the skins were full of water from the rock, their minds were nevertheless dry.
77.19: 77.19 A table. Cassiodorus: Mystically, the refreshment of wisdom, or the body of Christ.
77.21: 77.21 Therefore he heard. Cassiodorus: Because vengeance was delayed, he first gave what they asked, lest he seem unable. He put off. Augustine: The punishment; giving first what, though by tempting, he asked, lest he seem unable; and after he gave it, fire, that is, wrath, went up against Israel. And this is what he said before: A fire was kindled in Jacob.
77.23: 77.23 And he commanded. Both are set down briefly, namely that he heard, and that wrath went up; here he plainly begins to narrate. And first he follows out how he heard, afterward in the next part how he took vengeance. And the doors of heaven. Cassiodorus: The doors, the preachers themselves, by whom heaven is entered; or the Scriptures. He opened. Because he gave his own the Spirit that they might understand the Scriptures.
77.24: 77.24 Manna to eat. Augustine: It signifies the bread that came down from heaven, which is the food of angels; that man might eat it, the Word was made flesh (John 1), which is rained through the evangelical clouds on the whole world, and, their hearts opened as if heavenly doors, is preached to the believing Church, not to the tempting Synagogue. Cassiodorus: Manna, what is this? because this food is sought with wonder, and is known to be the body of Christ. The bread of heaven. The same: None other than Christ, by whom the heavenly ones, that is, the angels, are refreshed by contemplating him; and this bread, that is the Word, by which the angels are fed as with great food, being made milk through the flesh, man eats.
77.26: 77.26 The south-west wind. Because the quails are there.
77.27: 77.27 And he rained upon them, etc. Augustine: So also a little faith, etc., up to: hence: If I have spoken to you of earthly things and you do not believe me, how if I tell you heavenly things? etc. (John 3). Like dust. Cassiodorus: This dust signifies the subtlety of understanding, which ascends to the heights. The sand, the countless abundance of prudence seasoned with the taste of salt. Feathered fowls. Heavenly desires, on which the soul, fed, grows fat; we can take these as within the enclosure of the Church, hence he adds:
77.28: 77.28 And they fell in the midst of their camp. Augustine: Signifying by this that the winds come of their own accord to men, and carry to them words sent from God, that they may hear them in their dwellings and around their tents: for their sound has gone out into all the earth.
77.29: 77.29 And they ate. Those were convinced who thought this impossible for God.
77.30: 77.30 Their food was still in their mouths, and the wrath of God, etc. Cassiodorus: Of the vengeances, and their feigned turnings back, from fear of punishments; and yet the sentence of God tempered by mercy. Food. The same: Manna, quails. He hindered the elect of Israel. Augustine: That is, he hindered them from benefiting those whom he desired to counsel with a father's affection. Or rather, he fettered them, that the elect might bear troubles with them as an example, not of justice alone, but also of patience. He hindered. The same: By their murmuring, as Moses, who said: Can we bring forth water for you out of this rock? (Num. 20).
77.32: 77.32 In all these they sinned still, and did not believe in his wonders. After all these corrections the sins are graver, and always increase.
77.33: 77.33 And they failed, etc. Augustine: When by believing they could have had days in truth without failing. Their days and years in vanity. Cassiodorus: By likeness to one who dies at birth, born in vain. With haste. Augustine: Even a life that seems long passes quickly.
77.34: 77.34 They sought him. Cassiodorus and Augustine: Not the slain, but those left. But he speaks so because they are one people, as of one body. They came early in the morning to him, etc. Cassiodorus: Diligently, or before light; hence: It is vain for you to rise before light. The devout man prays in the light, the impious before light. They sought. They returned, they came. Augustine: All this to acquire temporal goods and avoid evils; and so not God but those things were worshiped.
77.37: 77.37 Neither were they counted faithful in his covenant, etc. Cassiodorus: He who truly believes does works; hence faith is so called because what is said is done (fiat); hence he says: Nor faithful in his precepts.
77.38: 77.38 But he is merciful and will be propitious. Augustine: Here the wicked promise themselves impunity, but mercy is shown even to the wicked, before the judgment, since he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil. So also he spared that nation, lest he root it out entirely, but it remains in the succession of descendants, as Cain, having received a sign, that no one should kill him. To their sins, etc. Augustine: Of the people, who are the same in the succession of sons; as afterward he took them out of Egypt and brought them into the mountain of his sanctification (Gen. 4), though not them but in succession. So here also when it is said: he will be propitious to their sins, we understand that what the Apostle says is also fulfilled: The remnant shall be saved (Rom. 9), who will believe in Christ, which he foresaw here when he adds: And he did not scatter them. And he abounded to turn away, etc., because: He did not kindle all his wrath, etc. That is, he did not punish them as much as they deserved, because he even forgave that they killed the Son.
77.39: 77.39 A spirit that goes and does not return, etc. Therefore he calls back by grace, because they cannot return by themselves; hence in Proverbs it is said of the way of iniquity: All that walk in it shall not return (Prov. 2), namely by themselves, but they will be called back by grace. This is the wandering sheep, which was brought back to the flock on the shoulders of the loving shepherd.
77.40: 77.40 How often. Cassiodorus: About to tell of the plagues of Egypt, made on their account, comparing their evils with the benefits of God, he says they forgot, and tempted God. Augustine: Because flesh or a spirit that goes, how often therefore? as if to say, many times they embittered him.
77.41: 77.41 And they turned back, etc. Augustine: He repeats their unfaithfulness, in order to recall what plagues God inflicted on the Egyptians for their sake, for which reason they ought not to have been ungrateful.
77.42: 77.42 From the hand of the afflicter. Cassiodorus: Tribulation is usually in memory, but not for them. He beautifully sets the hand of God against the hand of Pharaoh, saying: His hand and from the hand of tribulation; which differ greatly. Augustine and Cassiodorus: Mystical senses from this place.
77.44: 77.44 And he turned, etc. He sent upon them wrath, etc. Here he begins to set out the plagues wrought in Egypt for the liberation of the Jews, and he lists ten plagues, as there are ten in Exodus. Some are listed here, however, which are not in Exodus, which we cannot interpret except figuratively, where also what happened are called parables, as often it does not follow the order of the history, but adds other things, or changes certain things for the sake of signification. Water into blood, therefore, signifies thinking carnally about the causes of things. The dog-fly. They are the habits of dogs. The frog. Talkative vanity.
77.46: 77.46 Blight. What others interpret as mildew harms secretly; it is compared to a vice that hardly appears, such as trusting much in oneself. For a noxious air works this secretly in the fruits: so in morals hidden pride, when one who is nothing thinks himself to be something. The locust. Malice wounding by the mouth, namely by unfaithful testimony. Hail. It is iniquity carrying off the goods of others; hence thefts, robberies, plunder. But the plunderer himself is laid waste the more by his own vice. Frost. The vice by which the charity of neighbor is frozen, as by night cold, in the darkness of folly.
77.48: 77.48 Fire. Which in Exodus is taken only with the hail in the lightnings, to harm the fruits; yet it is not read to have burned possessions, it signifies the savagery of anger, by which homicide is also committed. By the death of cattle, the loss of chastity is signified. Concupiscence, by which offspring arises, is common to us with cattle: to have it tamed and ordered is the virtue of chastity. The death of the firstborn. It is the loss of the justice by which each person is bound to the human race. The Egyptians were struck with ten plagues against the ten precepts written on the tables. And here are ten plagues, although they are not set in that order, but in place of three that are in Exodus, namely the gnats, the boils, the darkness, which are not here. Three others are here which are not there: mildew, frost, and fire. For such things are frequently varied for fitting understanding. Signs. Cassiodorus: These are, for hard hearts, like footprints impressed with a mark. Wonders, which signified certain future things. Tanis, a city; the humble commandment, which is necessary for us here, that we may be raised up in the future. And he gave to the blight. These are not read in Exodus, so let them be explained only by a mystical interpretation. The locust. Augustine: Eating one another, it signifies detractors, who enviously gnaw the fruits of others. Their mulberry trees in the frost. Augustine: The mulberry is of a warm nature, by which charity is understood, which is killed in the frost. To hail. The same: What the hail could not harm, that is the soft things, Exodus says afterward were eaten by the locusts. He delivered. Cassiodorus: By the death of cattle, the fall of the foolish is shown. The same: To fire. Fire is covetousness, which lays waste possession, that is, the state of the mind.
77.49: 77.49 The wrath of his indignation, etc. Cassiodorus: The order of vengeance: first God is angry at sins when they are not repented of, then he leaves the malice of man to his own indignation, wrath and tribulation, that those who do not obey God may be afflicted by their own adversities, as is said there: Therefore he delivered them up to a reprobate sense (Rom. 1). Indignation of man belongs to swollen pride; wrath to unspeakable boldness; tribulation to confused despair: then through the devil they are hurled into unlawful assaults, stripped of the defense of God. By evil angels. Augustine: These things were done by the judgment of God, etc., up to: by evil angels, then, God punishes both good and evil men, but the good only with bodily punishments, the evil with bodily and spiritual punishments.
77.50: 77.50 For his wrath. Augustine: There was a path of the wrath of God, by which with hidden equity he would punish the Egyptians; for which God made a way, to bring them out, as it were from hiding, through evil angels into open crimes, and so to punish them openly.
77.51: 77.51 The firstborn in Egypt. Augustine: The firstborn are the highest commandments, such as: You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart; when these are not kept we are bereaved of the offspring of reason.
77.52: 77.52 And he took away his own people like sheep, and led them like a flock in the desert. Augustine, mystically: This also happens within us, where, instructed, we are transferred in mind from the power of darkness into the kingdom of God, sheep in spiritual pastures. Cassiodorus: And he took away. Because he led those brought out of slavery into the promised land; and again they offend.
77.54: 77.54 And he brought them into the mountain of his sanctification. Augustine: Not the same whom he took away, but them by name and nation; yet it signifies that many were converted to the Church, which he prefers to be understood; she is the mountain which Christ acquired. And he cast out the nations from before their face, etc. Augustine: Or the wicked spirits. All of which Christ cast out from before the face of the faithful; and by lot divided the land to them. By this it is signified that one and the same Spirit works all things in us, dividing to each as he wills.
77.55: 77.55 In their tents. Cassiodorus: In which sins reigned, he made the virtues reign.
77.57: 77.57 Even as their fathers turned back, etc. Augustine: Throughout he speaks as if of the same people; yet now of those in the promised land, whose fathers were those who embittered him in the desert. A perverse bow, etc. The same: The perverse intention of the mind, as against God, who had said: You shall have no strange gods (Exod. 20), which he opens more fully. Stirred up to wrath, or, into a perverse bow, which is hard to release, and they themselves easily went back. Or, a perverse bow, which does not shoot straight but turns its arrows upon itself, that is, the malice of the deceitful.
77.58: 77.58 To jealousy. Or they were jealous; another reading, when they give the honor of God to others.
77.59: 77.59 God heard. Cassiodorus: Of the vengeance in the promised land, which was also turned back upon those by whom he punished.
77.60: 77.60 And he rejected the tabernacle. Augustine: At this time of Eli the priest, when they were defeated by the Philistines and the ark of the Lord was taken, and they themselves were devastated with great slaughter. For it is read in the book of Kings that then thirty thousand footmen of the people fell. He rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh. Bede: Which was in Shiloh, etc., up to: but because they did not attend to that, nor made a tabernacle for God, therefore the Lord deservedly rejected it. Where he dwelt among men. Augustine: When therefore it was not worthy that he should dwell in it, he rejected what he had established not for his own sake but for theirs. Cassiodorus: So he leaves our bodies, which the Holy Spirit inhabits while they are well treated.
77.61: 77.61 And he delivered. Cassiodorus: For if with sinners the good also are delivered to captivity, it is a trial; they are not captives in mind. Or, delivered to the enemy, but free and joined to God. Their strength. Augustine: He diminished freedom of choice, and took away powers in the wicked, which is not so in the good, although they are sometimes taken captive bodily with the wicked.
77.65: 77.65 And the Lord was awakened. Cassiodorus and Augustine: He ascribes human ways to the Lord, for the sake of explaining the matters. As one asleep. This is said from the person of the senseless, who think thus, when he does not help those in peril, that he is drunk with wine, when he does not help so quickly. And in truth he sleeps and is a stranger to those who so senselessly think, and to the negligent and faithless, who rouse him by no voice of praise or deed. But he is aroused to vengeance by evil acts, as here by the sins of those who placed the ark among idols. As one mighty, because then men are quick to anger, and mighty in strength, when they rise from sleep after drunkenness. Augustine: And he was awakened. Christ, drunk with the wine of the passion, sleeping in the tomb, was awakened from death, as one mighty in the resurrection. The same: As one asleep. He seemed to sleep when he gave his people into the hands of those whom he hates, when it is said to them: Where is your God?
77.66: 77.66 And he struck iniquity. Augustine: With this punishment it will be tormented, etc., up to: for he gave them everlasting reproach.
77.67: 77.67 And he rejected. Cassiodorus: Of king David, and the place of the kingdom. Augustine: He did not say, etc., up to: so from the beginning of the election of the Hebrew nation it proceeds to Christ.
77.69: 77.69 As, etc. Augustine: Unicorns are those whose firm hope is lifted up to that One of whom it is said: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek. A holy thing. It is the holy people, the royal priesthood.
77.70: 77.70 David his servant. Augustine: Who is of Judah, etc., up to: the teeth of the Church are those through whom he speaks, or through whom he passes the rest into his body as by eating. The flock is called shorn, because it has laid aside the burdens of the world like fleeces, and laid at the feet of the Apostles the prices of their things sold; coming up from the washing of baptism, it brings forth twins, namely the works of twofold charity; hence: none was barren among them; Christ was transferred from these, but he feeds flocks among the Gentiles, who are Jacob and Israel.
77.71: 77.71 Jacob. Israel his inheritance. Augustine: He repeats: unless it is said, now according to this state Jacob is a servant: when the inheritance will see face to face. Hence also he received the name: for Israel is so called from the contemplation of God. He transferred him to this, that he should feed, and so he did.
77.72: 77.72 And he fed them, etc. Augustine: It seems perhaps, etc., up to: and he taught this which he did. PSALM 78
78.2: 78.2 Carcasses. Cassiodorus: Corpses, as though they rage not only against the living. To bury is of piety, to cast out is of cruelty. They have poured out. The same: He exaggerates, to move the judge.
78.4: 78.4 We are become. Cassiodorus: The glory of Jerusalem, wonderful in the whole world, has been turned into a reproach to the neighbors, which is graver than if to distant ones, because these are constant. Or, neighbors, affections, to near ones now willing to believe, so that martyrs say this.
78.5: 78.5 How long, O Lord? Cassiodorus: A prayer on his own part against the enemies and the insulting neighbors; as though they rage so: But, O Lord, how long? Augustine: He asks that he not be angry to the end, that is, that that devastation not persevere, but that he temper the correction. By the name of wrath, the vengeance of iniquity is understood; by the name of zeal, the exacting of chastity, that the soul not fornicate away from God. Note that this befalls men for sins, even the just, as the three young men and the Prophets in captivity bear witness. Like fire. The same: Burn until the gold of the virtues is perfectly purified, the wood, that is the vices, reduced to ashes.
78.7: 78.7 They have devoured. Augustine: By delivering to the teeth of wild beasts. They have laid waste, by the overthrow of the city, which was stripped of its citizens, or, because they killed those substituted in place of the slain citizens; Jacob for a man, a man, namely for the nation, which offended. The patriarch is pleasing, that his memory may soften the sins of the people. Jacob. Augustine: This is the inheritance spoken of above. His place. Cassiodorus: The city, where the temple was, where they gathered for the feasts.
78.8: 78.8 Of our iniquities. Bede: That is, those we have drawn from our fathers, to which now correction is not due but damnation, unless the mercy of your grace be present. For it is written: The soul that sins, the same shall die. And, I will visit the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation (Ezek. 18). Of old. Cassiodorus: He does not speak only of the past, since even at this time some Jews were following idols; but of sins like the old ones, which they committed for countless years. Let them prevent. The same: Before the judgment which every man fears, because unless indulgence comes first in the judgment, the guilty is not absolved. Exceedingly. Let no one presume on his deeds.
78.9: 78.9 Help. Cassiodorus: In the battle of the defense of the laws, because they trust not in their own but in the powers of God. For the glory. Not for merit, that being rescued we may give honor to your name. For the glory of your name. Let it be attributed to the goodness of the holy name, not to us, since it cannot be had by our deeds. Help us, O God. By this he is neither ungrateful to grace nor takes away free will. For he who is helped also does something by himself. Deliver us. Augustine: He delivers, that is, snatches from evils, when he both helps us to do justice and is merciful to sins, without which one does not live here.
78.10: 78.10 Lest perhaps. Augustine: That common taunt of the faithless: Where is he? Either he is not, or he cannot; an insult not to be borne. Let him be made known. Or here in the converted iniquity is destroyed, which he had wished before, or, they perish in the end, which he says here not by wishing but by prophesying. Augustine: Because the just man does not delight in the punishment of his enemy, because he does not hate him, but in the divine justice, because he loves God; the unjust man does the opposite.
78.11: 78.11 Of the fettered. Augustine: By the corruptibility of the flesh, which weighs down the soul, through which the persecutor sometimes prevails: only those feel these fetters who groan under the burden; the Apostle desired to be released from them and be with Christ. Or, the fetters are the precepts of God, by which the saints are bound, which, patiently borne, are turned into ornaments, hence: Put your foot into her fetters (Ecclus. 6). Cassiodorus: Of the fettered, he speaks literally of those whom the Gentiles bound: who pray with groaning that the Church not fail in the brethren, and so punishment consumes them. According to the greatness. Augustine: For so great a thing followed among Christians as the enemies would never have believed. The children, because they were kindled by the example, not frightened. Possess the children of the slain. The same: This the holy martyrs always prayed, that their blood not be fruitless to those after them, that the harvest might grow from where it was thought to perish. Cassiodorus: A holy prayer that he not cast away the children of those who were punished for him. Possess them, lest they be stained by any error.
78.12: 78.12 And render. Cassiodorus: Even if he repays bodily, it is nevertheless the salvation of their souls. Sevenfold signifies the perfection of the heavenly gift, when we are filled with the Holy Spirit. Into their bosom. In the secret of their minds, where conversion takes place. Reproach: for injuries let them render praises; a glorious vindication, when God is praised by the mouth of enemies. Or sevenfold. The sevenfold retribution signifies the perfection of punishment, as also of good things, when it is said he will receive sevenfold in this age: which is set for all goods, as having nothing and possessing all things; because in this number fullness is signified. Or sevenfold for infinite. Reproach. Augustine: Render this, that is, for this reproach give them over to a reprobate sense. For a man, when he is given over to a reprobate sense, that is, in the interior sense, receives the desert of future punishments.
78.13: 78.13 But we. Cassiodorus: An exultant conclusion, not of conquerors but of sufferers. And a sweet conclusion of the lamentation. Augustine: But we. These are the remnant gathered by Mattathias. Or, it is to be taken generally of every kind of the devout and true Christians, so that the Christian people also are mixed in there; this is the flock for which he prayed that he not be angry longer. The same: Or, in generation, that is, in the age to come, we will declare, not for the instruction of others, but for the honor due.
79.1: 79.1 Understanding, for those who shall be changed. Augustine: For the better, etc., up to: the testimony of faithlessness. Asaph. Enlightened, he treats of the coming of Christ and of his vineyard, a good testimony concerning the head himself and his body, the king and the people, the shepherd and the flock.
79.2: 79.2 You who rule, etc. Augustine: Here Asaph, enlightened, speaks of the coming of Christ, who converts man, and strengthens the vineyard brought out of Egypt: this is the testimony for those who are changed. Cassiodorus: Above, fearful, he prayed for the sins of the Synagogue: now he presumes, and gives testimony to those changed for the better. This psalm is a testimony of the Synagogue concerning the head himself and his body. The same: A prayer for the first coming, through which the restoration of the human race is made. The same: When completed, he ends. O God, son. You who rule, spiritually, Israel, seeing you; Give ear, that is, pour the light of your goodness upon us, that we may be bright from you, who by ourselves are dark. Joseph. The same: You lead the faithful people into the folds of God, as sheep to pastures, of which: Other sheep I have that are not of this fold, and them I must bring, that there may be one fold and one shepherd (John 10). Proper words for each: Israel is ruled, Joseph is led, that is, the devout people. Appear. The same: He asks that he who was in the secret of majesty may appear through the incarnation before the Jews as was promised, working in them these virtues which are signified by these names, Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. Augustine: Appear before. Known to angels, be known to men.
79.3: 79.3 Before Ephraim. Augustine: That is, the nation of the Jews, where these tribes are, namely before fruitfulness, and the son of the right hand, that we also may be the fullness of knowledge through charity, which is God; and before Manasseh, that is, forgetful, that you may now come into his mind, according to that: All the ends of the earth shall remember and be converted. The same: Stir up. He repeats, etc., up to: crucified from weakness, rise from power. Cassiodorus: Stir up the power of miracles, etc., up to: hence: God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able, etc. (1 Cor. 10).
79.4: 79.4 Your face. Augustine: This face was veiled to Asaph in the time of Christ's weakness, and then Asaph fell sick, unable to behold what was veiled by a cloud; of which it is said: God will ascend upon a light cloud, and will enter or go into Egypt, that is, flesh free from sin; and he enlightened it when he rose and ascended, and so we are saved.
79.5: 79.5 How long will you be angry? Augustine: Wrath passes from the servant, not that he scourge, as is evident, but that he not condemn: for even in the converted wrath remains, but correcting. For he scourges every son whom he receives (Isa. 9, Heb. 12).
79.6: 79.6 You will feed us. Augustine: He sets out here the sufferings which the saints are to endure at the time of the coming. As if to say: Even if I wish for the coming of Christ, yet in that time we shall suffer much, because he has fed, etc. In measure, etc. Augustine: According to your strength, that you may be instructed, not crushed; hence: God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above, etc. (1 Cor. 10). Or, according to the measure of the faults.
79.7: 79.7 You have made us a contradiction. Cassiodorus: While the neighbors, who are of us, are against us. Our enemies laugh, from all of whom, that we may be saved, O God of hosts, etc.
79.8: 79.8 O God of hosts. Augustine: It is the way of one who desires to repeat frequently what he asks with such prayers.
79.9: 79.9 A vineyard. Cassiodorus: Of the vineyard, how begun and perfected. Augustine and Cassiodorus: A vineyard out of Egypt, as if: we shall be saved, but the Jews, for whom you did so much, you will destroy: not for a light fault, but because they did not recognize the coming of Christ. Or, we shall be saved because you have so foretold. A vineyard out of Egypt. But why will you destroy? This is said of the unbelievers. Out of Egypt. As he cast those out of Egypt, so he cast the Church out of the darkness of vices: he plants the Gentiles in virtues, and leads through this desert of the world. The roots: he makes martyrs and others firm, and fills the world. Cassiodorus: A vineyard out of Egypt, by mystical figures, etc., up to: which was thus spread throughout the world. Leader, while he leads it on a spiritual journey. The roots: prophets, Apostles, martyrs and others, from whom, stretching out its shoots, it occupies and covers the world. Leader of the journey. Augustine: Or another reading, etc., up to: and it is not another, but the same vineyard: thence the Apostles, thence also other just men, though some branches were broken.
79.11: 79.11 It covered. Cassiodorus: The height and breadth of the vineyard is set out here. The vineyard is heavenly, which overshadows even the loftier mountains by life and doctrine, and makes them grow to greatness. Vines which climb trees are called shrubs, by which the lesser in the Church are understood. The cedars, not the proud but those who are God's, are the martyrs, who are high in the Church; these also the Church protects in her bosom. The branches, the sons of regeneration, who flowed forth from the river Jordan, because there the rule of baptism began. Mountains. Augustine: The Prophets, etc., up to: in like manner they cover the cedars of God, that is, the teachers. The cedars of God. The same: Because there are cedars to be overthrown, namely the proud, who are the cedars of the world, but not of God.
79.13: 79.13 Why. He wonders why the defense of the Lord was withdrawn from such a vineyard. Augustine: Why. Because it was proud against the planter, and killed the servants sent to it, and finally the son and heir, the hedge was destroyed, and the Gentiles found it destroyed, and wasted it. Asaph first laments this, but not without hope: for he is now speaking of those who direct their heart.
79.14: 79.14 The boar. Augustine and Cassiodorus: Vespasian, strong and savage, and hostile to the Jews, who count this animal among the others as unclean. The singular wild beast. Titus, who consumed the remnants with terrible devouring, who is called singular, that is, proud. Or the boar and the wild beast are taken for the same, namely the Roman army. And see by what sins man toils and perishes. Singular. Augustine: Every proud man says: I am, I am, and there is no other. The boar. Cassiodorus: The devil, strong and fierce, from the forest, because his thoughts are wild and pathless. But you, O Lord God of hosts. Or connect thus: So the vineyard has been laid waste, but that a remnant may be saved, O God of hosts, turn back, look serenely at the end of the last age; he prays for this remedy for those changed for the better.
79.16: 79.16 And perfect that which your right hand has planted. Augustine: Do not establish another, but perfect this one. For in this is the seed of Abraham; there is the root which bears the wild olive. Perfect, because blindness has happened in part in Israel, that the fullness of the Gentiles might come in, and so all Israel be saved (Rom. 12). Upon the son. Cassiodorus: Upon you the founded, etc., up to: but of the fire of good love it is said: I am come to cast fire upon the earth, and what will I, but that it be kindled? (Luke 12).
79.18: 79.18 Let your hand be. Cassiodorus: A great sacrament, and a gift to God, because for so long the salvation of Israel could be doubted, until Christ came: but then the promise was fulfilled, and the Church, joined to the Bridegroom, departs from him no more. He says therefore: Let your hand be; he prays for the working of the holy incarnation.
79.19: 79.19 We depart not. Cassiodorus: Any further, when you shall quicken the son of man: this is the usefulness from him.
79.20: 79.20 O Lord God of hosts, convert us, and show your face, and we shall be saved. Cassiodorus: Great is the sweetness of this verse, in which he sets out the rule of the whole religion. For first God converts us, and then shows us his face, that is, looks upon us with the light of his goodness: after which he finally saves us. The prophet repeats this therefore, because through it each one briefly implores what is expedient.
80.1: 80.1 For the winepresses. Augustine: In which three, etc., up to: the psalm of Asaph is sung, that is, to the Lord's congregation. Asaph, etc. Cassiodorus: Because according to history it speaks to the Jews, spiritually to Christians. Augustine: First he says what is to be done by the elect, who are the oil, the wine, the birds.
80.2: 80.2 Rejoice to God. Asaph, having set before himself the image of a certain solemnity, stirs the elect to the celebration.
80.3: 80.3 Take a psalm. Augustine: The words of God, that human acts may come together into one society: for this is the peace of Jerusalem, this is the reckoning of giving and receiving; hence the Apostle: If we have sown spiritual things to you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things? (1 Cor. 9).
80.4: 80.4 Sound the trumpet. Augustine: Up to the division, or literally, it is to be understood simply of the Jews, or allegorically of Christians. Augustine: Sound the trumpet, and announce, etc., up to: hence Isaiah: Cry, cease not, lift up your voice like a trumpet, etc. On the new moon, the trumpet. Cassiodorus: At the beginning of the month the Jews were commanded to sound the trumpet, that is, at the beginning of the new moon, which is also called the feast of trumpets, which they celebrated in memory of this fact, that the Lord showed Abraham a ram caught among the briers, which he sacrificed in place of Isaac.
80.5: 80.5 For it is a precept in Israel, and a judgment, etc. The same: The trumpet is to be sounded because the law was given to the Jews through Moses, and because he is to be judge.
80.6: 80.6 In Joseph. Augustine: The Gentiles are Joseph, etc., up to: where he ought to have had a heart.
80.7: 80.7 From the burdens. Augustine: What burdens? His hands served in the basket, that is, in servile work. Sins are servile works, according to that: Whoever commits sin is the servant of sin (John 8). They served in the basket. The same: In the uncleannesses of sins, in earthly and muddy works.
80.8: 80.8 In tribulation, etc. Cassiodorus: So the Prophet: The Lord turns aside, saying, In tribulation; the benefits of God are charged against them, that the offense may be reckoned the graver. I heard you in the secret place. Augustine: That with the heart you may believe unto justice. I proved you, that with the mouth confession may be made unto salvation. Of the tempest, etc. Not in a tempest of the sea, but of the heart: where one heard must be tested, at the water of contradiction: for one already walking the way of God has opponents in many ways. This is the water of contradiction, which the ancients felt, but it is now almost dried up: for then the waters of the peoples were troubled and resisted fiercely. Then, as Samson, the strong man, that is Christ, was going to take a wife from the foreigners, that is the Church from the Gentiles, a roaring lion met him, that is the people of the Gentiles, but he tore it apart like a kid of the goats: and because this roaring people was nothing but a feeble sinner. But with that ferocity slain in it, it no longer roars so; rather we now find in it the laws for the Church, like a honeycomb in the mouth of the lion. The water of contradiction. Christ was so also in himself, as it was said of him at his birth: This child is set for the fall and for the resurrection of many, and for a sign which shall be contradicted (Luke 2), as the Jews contradicted the title of the cross.
80.9: 80.9 Hear, my people. Cassiodorus: Pause. Thus far of the oil of the winepresses, now of the dregs, which is said to be guarded against; here the reprobate are rebuked. I will testify to you. The Lord of judgment himself makes himself a witness of the truth, both here and in the future, that no one may doubt. Then he adds what he wishes him to understand: Israel, if you will hear me; by calling him Israel he signifies him as familiar to himself, and invites him to the commands. In you, in your heart, where there ought to be truth, not falsehood. Lest the Word of the Father be thought recent, in time. A strange god, one by name, not in essence. Strange: it is almost an equal crime to think God recent, and to serve idols.
80.10: 80.10 There shall be no new god in you, nor, etc. Augustine: Some make for themselves new gods, either idols, or a Christ unequal to the Father, and devise other such things in the heart: and so earthly thought in all is the temple of idols; opinion is diverse, vanity one. Therefore Samson tied the tails of foxes together to burn the harvests of the Philistines. Samson is interpreted as their sun, namely of those for whom he himself shines, not of all: of whom the wicked will say: We have erred from the way of truth, and the sun of justice has not shone on us (Wisd. 5). And elsewhere: The sun of justice is risen, and health in his wings (Mal. 4). The foxes are the insidious, especially heretics, hiding in winding caves, deceiving, foul in odor: who, although they seem to disagree with one another, yet agree in evil, that is, in their hinder parts, are held by a similar vanity, and burn the harvests, not of our people, for God knows who are his, but of the foreigners, who are vessels of dishonor.
80.11: 80.11 Who brought you out. God is made known by his own deeds.
80.13: 80.13 And he let them go. Although I filled the mouths of the Prophets, yet they were not heard because of the dregs, hence the vengeance is worthy: for I also let them go, etc.
80.15: 80.15 For nothing perhaps. Cassiodorus: If we resist God, he does not oppose our enemies, nor lay the hand of defense upon them.
80.16: 80.16 The enemies of the Lord, etc. Augustine: The Prophet likewise. Have lied. Not by those who fulfill promises: this is not the pagans, because they promised nothing.
80.17: 80.17 With the fat of wheat, etc. Augustine: Literally, either manna, or the body of Christ, or spiritual understanding.
81.1: 81.1 A psalm of Asaph. Cassiodorus: A psalm of the two natures in Christ, in which Christ, or the Prophet speaking, reproaches Asaph himself, that is, the Synagogue, which saw the Lord bodily and yet did not know him. First he announces that God stood, and rebukes the opponents; man stands, God discerns. God stood. To whom it does not belong to stand, who fills heaven and earth, who is within all things not enclosed, outside all things not shut out, but briefly he indicates God as man. He stood. Augustine: The Son, who was sent to the sheep of the house of Israel, but the spiritual presence of the Godhead, which is everywhere and does not properly belong to the Synagogue, nor varies with time. Why he stood there: Behold he judges the gods, that is, according as he is God, that is, not by merits but by grace he distinguishes the vessels, some unto honor, others unto dishonor. But he does this standing in the midst, hence: In the midst of you there stands one whom you know not, hence also here: They have not known nor understood, but the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears, and rejoices with joy. Of the gods. Whom he afterward calls sons of the Most High, there: I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High. Hence also: I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me. They are called sons not only by the grace of the New Testament, but by the grace of the Old, which freed them from Egypt.
81.2: 81.2 How long. Augustine: This is the voice of the one discerning: he sent the law and the Prophets, and you resisted, but how long? Did I send the Prophets up to the coming, and you afflicted them with injuries, or killed them, or consented to those who did it? But since it is not even worthy to speak with those who did this, you who were silent and wished to imitate them, how long will you judge iniquity and accept the persons of sinners? Is the heir also to be killed, who came for you, who for you wished to be without a father like an orphan? who for you hungered and thirsted, as a needy man, who for you was made poor, though he was rich?
81.3: 81.3 Judge for the needy and the orphan, do justice to the poor and the humble. Cassiodorus: Pause; he admonishes them to understand that Christ is God, even if he was needy and poor, which he says they did not do.
81.4: 81.4 Rescue the poor. Augustine: He shows that not even those were free of blame who yielded Christ to the princes, when they were feared on account of the multitude, and could have freed those men from the deed and themselves from consent. Cassiodorus: For he who stops opposing when he can, consents.
81.5: 81.5 They shall be moved. Cassiodorus: From here it is plain of whom he had spoken: this sign happened at the crucifixion. Or spiritually, earthly men were moved at that time, having seen so great a miracle; like the centurion who said: Truly this was the Son of God. Augustine: All the foundations shall be moved. As if to say: through this blindness of Israel, all the foundations of the earth shall be moved to faith, that is, the fullness of the Gentiles shall enter in. Or, in the death and passion of the Lord the earth was moved. Or foundations, that is, the abundance of happy earthly things shall be moved. Or by wondering that a dead poor man is worshiped. Or by following him with earthly things despised. He adds all, because there is no one who does not marvel or is not converted. The kingdom of earthly happiness is pride, against which the humble Christ came, reproaching those whom he wishes to make high through humility, with these words: I said: You are gods, you good; but you evil, you shall die like men. Or he says to all: You are gods, that is, to all I promised heavenly things; but you like the first men, who sinned by persuasion, and you greater, like the devil, who sinned by pride.
81.6: 81.6 I have said. Cassiodorus: What was set before them? But they perished. I have said: They have not known nor understood; yet I have said. All receive these promises if they keep the commandments, that they may be sons and of God: this to the just; but you, this to the wicked.
81.7: 81.7 Like men. Augustine: As if: Since you are soon to die like men, you are not corrected by it; but like the devil, who does not die in the flesh, you are puffed up, that you may fall: for through diabolical pride they envied the glory of Christ, and the humility of the cross became cheap to them. But that this vice may be healed, it is added from the person of the Prophet: Arise, O God, etc., like one. The crowd that fell is called one, because alike in pride: You shall fall, but:
81.8: 81.8 Arise, O God. Augustine: That is, condemn these, because when they are rejected, you shall inherit. Or judge the world, because it is yours, and this is, you shall inherit.
82.1: 82.1 A canticle of a psalm. Cassiodorus: Because in active matters divine contemplation must be maintained. It deters the wicked from persecution of the people of God, and admonishes the good to patience. A psalm of the coming of Christ to judgment, where the good, who suffer here, will be crowned, and the wicked, who persecute them, will be tormented.
82.2: 82.2 O God, who is like to you? Cassiodorus: Having set forth the fear of the future judge, he describes the malice of the enemies. Augustine: O God, who is like to you? Even if a man like others; even if judged, you are reckoned with the wicked: who is like when you shall judge in brightness? Therefore then be not silent, you who were first silent and restrained your power, that you might be held and killed. O God, who is like to you? This is not referred to the divinity, to which he thought no man to be compared. Therefore he does not say: Who is like to you? which would certainly refer to the divinity; but he says, Who will be like to you? referring this to the form of a servant, in which he will be unlike other men when the judge shall appear in glory; or this can be referred to the divinity according to what he says: O God, who is like to you? in the power of the Godhead: for Christ, whom the wicked saw outwardly, this man sees within, namely the Almighty.
82.3: 82.3 For behold, etc. Augustine: He designates the last times of Antichrist, when what is now pressed by fear will break out into free voice: which voice, because it was irrational, is called a noise rather than speech. Who hate you. Cassiodorus: Many, but one head, Antichrist: who is exalted so as to be called God.
82.4: 82.4 Against your people. They have lifted up their head, but have not pressed down your people. Augustine: Against your people. He says this derisively: for they cannot harm the people of God, for whom God is; hence the Apostle: If God is for us, who is against us? (Rom. 8).
82.5: 82.5 They said, Come. Augustine: Behold the counsel in which they meditated vain things. This is that sound which is not speech, but makes a vain din. From the nation. Cassiodorus: In the singular, because all Christians are one nation, born from one font of baptism; or all the good, whom that Antichrist calls one nation: behold the persecution of Antichrist, who intends to take away the Christian name utterly as if it were evil.
82.6: 82.6 They have made a covenant. Augustine: A testament, in the Scriptures, is called not only that which has no force unless the testator is dead, but every pact and agreement that is valid among the living is called a testament, as Laban and Jacob made a testament. So also the wicked made a kind of pact among themselves, to persecute the good with one accord.
82.7: 82.7 The tents of the Edomites. He has set out with what zeal they acted maliciously; he then shows who the malicious ones are, saying: The tents of the Edomites, etc. Of the Edomites, and the Ishmaelites. Cassiodorus: By these names he declares the enemies of Christ, who in the times of Antichrist are likened to so many evils: because as those fought against Israel, so these will then fight against Christians. The Moabites. Augustine, Jerome: Hence the Moabites, whom Lot, drunk, begot of his elder daughter. The Hagarenes. From Hagar, who are also interpreted as proselytes.
82.8: 82.8 Gebal. Augustine, Jerome: Vain valley. For Ge is valley, Bal is vain. Ammon. Hence the Ammonites, whom Lot, drunk, begot of his younger daughter. Amalek. Son of Eliphaz, the firstborn of Esau, from whom the Amalekites.
82.9: 82.9 Assur. Augustine, Jerome: Literally Nebuchadnezzar, who was king of the Assyrians. The Edomites: earthly or bloody. The Ishmaelites: obeying themselves, not God, because they follow their own perverse thoughts. Moab, from the father, which is in an evil sense. The father indeed is good, whom the daughter used unlawfully, as the law also is good, if one uses it lawfully, not incestuously. The Hagarenes: proselytes, that is, strangers, who are not citizens, but enter in secretly with a foreign mind, and when they find an occasion to harm, show themselves. Gebal: vain valley, that is, deceitfully humble. Ammon: a troubled people, or of sorrow. Amalek: a people licking the earth. The foreigners: although in the Latin name they indicate themselves as strangers, and on this account enemies, yet in Hebrew they are called Philistines, that is, falling by drink, like the drunk with worldly luxury. Tyre: in Hebrew sor, tribulation or distress, according to that: Tribulation and distress upon every soul of man that works evil (Rom. 2). Assur: bringing low, or lifted up. Lot: turning aside, the apostate angels, sons of turning aside, because by turning aside from the truth they departed into the retinue of the devil, hence in the Apocalypse: The dragon fell and drew with him a third part of the stars; of whom the Apostle says: Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers (Eph. 6).
82.10: 82.10 Madian: turning aside from judgment. Sisera: exclusion of joy. Jabin: wise, of whom: Where is the wise? where is the scribe? Cison, where they were defeated, is interpreted as hardness. Endor, where they perished, fountain of generation. And it is understood as carnal generation, not the water of baptism of the regenerate. Oreb: dryness; Zeb: wolf; Zebee: victim of the wolf, not of God. Salmana: shadow of commotion. All these fit the wicked, whom the people of God overcame in a good cause. Do to them as to Madian and Sisera, as to Jabin at the brook. Cassiodorus: Of the vengeance on the wicked; as all those were defeated in figure by the people of God, so he prays that these be overcome in truth. As Madian. Augustine: As those who turn aside from judgment, thinking they will not be judged: and who exclude the future judgment, and all these perished at Cison, and at the fountain of Endor.
82.12: 82.12 Make their princes like, etc. This is for all in common. But specially, make their princes: he desires this for the soldiers of Antichrist, who are not to be converted.
82.13: 82.13 Let us possess the sanctuary of God for an inheritance. Augustine: Of God; they invade it as their own.
82.14: 82.14 Make them like a wheel, and as stubble before the face of the wind. Cassiodorus: By this comparison he predicts many calamities of theirs. Of the wind. The lightness of sinners is compared to wind, because it flits hither and thither.
82.15: 82.15 Fire and flame burning the mountains. Augustine: They are fittingly said to be in the judgment, when both the thick forests of sinners and the mountains of pride shall be burned.
82.17: 82.17 Fill their faces. Cassiodorus: Having prophesied the punishments of the stubborn, he prays for those who are going to believe, who have not praisers of their crimes but blamers, whom reproach often corrects. Augustine: It is better to fall that one may repent than to be proud under the hope of religion: hence the Prophet says: And you, O daughter of Sion, shall come even to Babylon, and there you shall be delivered (Mic. 4). Fill their faces. This good and desirable thing would not be prophesied for them unless among those enemies there were such to whom it will be granted before the judgment: for now also the same body heals, and washes the head, but in part, not universally as at the end: and yet some will be converted from it, for whom he prays here.
82.18: 82.18 Let them be ashamed and troubled, etc. Augustine: Here of the wicked who will not be converted. Let them be ashamed, in the future, of the evils they did. And let them be troubled, at the punishments they will suffer. And this for ever and ever, that is, to eternity. And let them be troubled. Again he returns to those who are now confounded that they may not be confounded for ever; as if to say: Let those be troubled for ever; but let those who seek the name of the Lord now be confounded for their sins salutarily, and perish insofar as they are wicked. And so let them know; or, then let the wicked be confounded, in soul and body, and perish utterly beyond repair. And now let them know what they now refuse. Cassiodorus: It is to be noted that in the eleven preceding psalms Asaph has been introduced, that the hardness of the Jews might be softened by the frequent voice of the Synagogue itself, or that they might believe the very name to which they seemed devoted. He has treated in the aforesaid psalms of the incarnation of the Lord, and the faith of the Gentiles, and the judgment, by which the transgression of the Jews is rebuked. Hence eleven is fitting: for the number eleven is that of transgression, because it passes ten and does not reach twelve, hence there were also eleven hair-cloth curtains in the tabernacle of the Lord, and the Apostles were eleven, the most wretched Judas rejected, at the time of the passion, when they fell away from the faith, hence: You have appointed darkness, and it was made night (Ps. 103).
83.1: 83.1 Unto the end. Augustine: Nothing is said here of visible winepresses, hence it is clear they are spiritual. The grape on the vine, the olive hanging on the tree, enjoy the free air, and neither is wine nor the other oil before the pressing: so those whom God foreknew before the ages to be made conformed to the image of his Son, before they approach the service of God, enjoy a delightful liberty in the world. But when they approach the service of God, it is said to them: Son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation (Eccles. 2). Behold the winepress; they are crushed, stripped of the coverings of carnal desires, as of grape-skins they are stripped of the old man, and flow down into the storehouse of God: therefore the winepresses are called those of the Church of the present time. But who in these are the sons of Core, that is, of the bald, namely of Christ? For the bald Elisha mocked by the boys was a figure of Christ, who was crucified at Calvary. Therefore the Christian is pressed here, that he may seek the rest which is not here, and God becomes his refuge. For he who leans on earthly things leans on a staff of reed. For the winepresses. Augustine: In the winepress the fruit of the grape or the olive flows out: so in pressures the merits of the saints are manifest, which lay hidden in peace. Cassiodorus: The second psalm on charity. First on the inestimable desire of the eternal house.
83.2: 83.2 How lovely. Behold how great a warfare. For even the sparrow, how secure.
83.4: 83.4 For even the sparrow, etc. Augustine: He gives two things to two: the heart is like the sparrow; the flesh like the turtledove, to which he also gives young: with the heart we think of God, as if the sparrow would fly to the house; with the flesh we do works. Cassiodorus: As the sparrow leaves the woods and, having found a house, rejoices where it fears no snares, so the soul rejoices when it knows a house is prepared for it in heaven. The spirit, which is as a sparrow flying on high, tending to God himself. The nest, etc. Augustine: The nest is for a time, the house for eternity. By nest he means faith, and the conformity of the sacraments of the Church, the nest which the turtledove seeks to lay her young. For she does not cast them anywhere, but in the nest of the Church does good works salutarily, for which she is saved: in this she differs from others who do works but not in the nest of faith. For pagans also do works, clothe the naked, etc., and heretics do many things: but not in the nest of the Church, and therefore they are trodden upon, not saved. This flesh is the woman by whom the sparrow is seduced, but it will be saved by the generation of works, if in the nest, that is, if it shall persevere in faith. And God provides the means from which the nest is made, for he clothed himself with the hay of flesh that he might come to you. Your altars, O Lord. Cassiodorus: Where souls feast at the heavenly banquet, where the soul may rejoice as in its house. Augustine: And the flesh lays up its works, hence: Blessed are they, etc., where he shows to what blessedness the warfare leads.
104.15: 104.15 Do not touch. The same. Although these words are not in the history, God nevertheless spoke them, either secretly in the hearts of men or through an angel. Christs, the same: because even then there were Christians, if hidden ones; hence Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad (John 8). For apart from this faith, no one, either before or after, has been reconciled to God, for there is one mediator, Christ (1 Tim. 2).
104.16: 104.16 And he called. Augustine: The fourth part, where he begins to narrate, etc., up to: he ordered to be what already was in his plan. So he called, and he broke all the support of bread (Gen. 37).
104.17: 104.17 A man. The same: Joseph, sold by his brothers, was afterwards exalted in Egypt for his righteousness. Joseph. The same: If Joseph was both humbled and exalted, etc., up to: but seek first the kingdom of God, and all things shall be added.
104.18: 104.18 In fetters. The same: We do not read of Joseph's fetters in Genesis, but we must believe that what was passed over there is told by the Spirit in the psalm. Cassiodorus: Even if he found favor with the keeper of the prison, he was nevertheless first in distress. It continues: The iron passed through, etc. As though, besides the sufferings of the body, the iron, that is, the tribulation of hard necessity, which was in his troubled and anxious soul, passed through, etc. Or, according to another reading, his soul passed through the iron, that is, through the tribulation of hard necessity. The sense is the same as the former.
104.23: 104.23 In the land of Ham, etc. Augustine: Ham was the father of Canaan, from whom the Egyptians trace their origin.
104.24: 104.24 And he increased his people, etc. The same: The fifth part. Here he briefly sets forth what was done in Egypt, which he afterwards relates fully. He also tells how he strengthened his people over their enemies. And he strengthened it: namely through the signs of Moses; for before, the male offspring of the children of Israel were being killed, and they themselves were worn down making bricks. But afterwards, by a mighty hand and through the signs and wonders of the Lord, they became fearsome and honored.
104.25: 104.25 He turned. The same: He begins to narrate how this came about. He turned, not that God is the author of evil, but he makes good use of the wicked: when he increased the prosperity of Israel, they were turned to envy it, because they were already evil. That they might hate. Envy is hatred of another's happiness.
104.26: 104.26 He sent. He who could do all things by himself, that he might teach with what moderation he had done these things. Whom he chose, even him. The same: It would have been enough to say, whom he chose; but nothing is to be sought in what he added, even him; it is the custom of divine speech, for the sake of explanation.
104.27: 104.27 The words of his signs. The same: By which he was proclaimed by them, etc., up to: therefore, by them he performed words not of voices but of signs, or of prodigies.
104.28: 104.28 The same: Or: They provoked his words, which is plain. Or, Moses and Aaron did not provoke his words, because they bore with them, that is, with the Egyptians, even the hardest, patiently, on account of the Lord's command, until all things that the Lord had ordained were accomplished in them. Darkness, etc. Cassiodorus: They suffered it among the plagues. But here he says their hearts were darkened, who despised the commandments of God. Blindness is a fitting beginning of the plagues, without which they would not have incurred the rest.
104.29: 104.29 He turned their waters. Augustine: The second plague, which in Exodus is the first, which signified that he would turn the waters of the Red Sea, and for them into death.
104.30: 104.30 The land brought forth. Augustine: He turned their land into frogs, for they were so many that it is fittingly said by hyperbole.
104.31: 104.31 He spoke, and the dog-fly came, etc. The same: For in his Word they existed without time, before they came to be in time through that same Word; or he spoke through angels, or in a way through Moses, that it should happen then, when it was to be done.
104.32: 104.32 He gave them rains, etc. The same: It is like that other: and their land gave forth frogs.
104.34: 104.34 The locust and the caterpillar. The same: The locust and the caterpillar are one plague, because the one is the parent, the other the offspring.
104.36: 104.36 And he struck. The same: Since there are ten plagues, etc., up to: who could not despise the reward of their labors, though temporal.
104.37: 104.37 And he brought them out, etc. The sixth part, according to Cassiodorus and Augustine. Above he told what evils the justice of God brought upon the enemies of the Israelites; now he sets forth what temporal goods the mercy of God gave them, that, helped by these, they might seek the law of God. Augustine: And he brought out: God said to Abraham, etc., up to: then follows the second benefit: And there was not one infirm, etc.
104.38: 104.38 For the fear of them had fallen upon them. Israel feared lest it should consume the remnants of them. Augustine: Here is fulfilled what he said above: and he strengthened it over its enemy.
104.39: 104.39 He spread out a cloud for their protection. And this is the second part, according to Augustine, where he sets forth what temporal goods the mercy of God gave them, the evils having been told above which the justice of God brought upon their enemies. Augustine: Now he begins the benefits which were done for them as they journeyed in the wilderness.
104.40: 104.40 They asked. Augustine: the good, for the sustenance of the weak. The quail: and he filled them with the bread of heaven, which is also flesh, because here he speaks not of the bitterness of the wicked but of the faith of the elect: these are to be understood as having asked, so that the murmurs of the bitter might be suppressed.
104.42: 104.42 For he remembered his holy word. The same: By all these benefits God commends the merit of faith in Abraham; hence he adds: for he remembered.
104.44: 104.44 And he gave them. Augustine: Not that they should worship him on account of these things, but that they should refer them to the eternal good, that is, that they should keep his statutes. They possessed, etc., not that these are to be held as the highest good, but that they might have leisure for them, whereby the highest and eternal good could be acquired, not that they should dissolve in luxury or grow sluggish in them.
104.45: 104.45 Statutes, etc. Cassiodorus: There are cases where the precept is evident and absolute, as, You shall love God and neighbor, which must be kept. The law concerns those matters which are not bodily but spiritual: and therefore it must be sought out, because it is a shadow of things to come. The law. As concerning its circumcision and other matters, which must be diligently investigated, because they are spoken of mystically.
105.1: 105.1 Alleluia. Alleluia. Some say that one alleluia belongs to the end of the preceding psalm, the other to the following. Jerome reports that this rule is to be held. Cassiodorus also agrees with his assertion. But most, wherever there is alleluia, give it to the following psalm: and sometimes once, sometimes twice; as the Lord in the Gospel now said amen, now amen amen, for the greater certainty of the matter. Augustine agrees with these, especially since no Greek codices have alleluia at the end of the psalm. Give thanks to the Lord. Augustine: This psalm is joined to the preceding one, etc., up to: it therefore admonishes to a twofold confession, of praise and of sins. Cassiodorus: The Hebrew, having left behind the unfaithfulness of the fathers and turned to the mercy of God, persuades others to be turned to the same mercy, praying that they may be joined to the well-pleasing people, which was to be gathered at the coming of Christ.
105.2: 105.2 Who shall speak. Cassiodorus: This man, who asks for mercy, is filled with the contemplation of the divine works, and in wonder says: Who shall speak?
105.3: 105.3 Blessed are they who keep. Augustine: Or because it follows, etc., up to: judgment and justice, for blessed are they who, etc.
105.5: 105.5 To see, etc. Augustine: that we may see you in that goodness which you provide for the elect, that is, that by your grace we may see, lest we remain blind. That you may be praised: it is remarkable that in very many codices, etc., up to: because it is not praised except on account of you.
105.6: 105.6 We have sinned. The second part, where he enumerates the sins of the fathers which they committed in Egypt, and yet says they were freed by God. Iniquity. Cassiodorus: He says the same a third time, that the confession may appear pure; it is loosed the more quickly, the more keenly a man condemns himself.
105.7: 105.7 They did not understand. Augustine: That is, what you willed to give them through those things, namely not a temporal but an eternal good, which is awaited through patience; and therefore they, being impatient, murmured, and wished to be blessed with temporal things. Cassiodorus: There are two things that commend benefits, understanding and memory, both of which he reproves in them. And first understanding, when he says: they did not understand the wonders. They provoked, going up. Augustine: Fearing God and despairing, etc., up to: whence he deserved to obtain, among others, the privilege or the principate of the kingdom.
105.9: 105.9 As in the desert. The same: Because where the depths were, it was made dry, like a desert where there are no waters.
105.10: 105.10 He redeemed them from the hand. The same: At what price? As if to say: at none; but it was done in a figure of baptism, in which we are redeemed from the hand of the devil by the blood of Christ; hence he also said the Red Sea, because blood was prefigured by its color.
105.12: 105.12 And they believed in. Augustine: Behold the hard hearts of the Jews, who believe not before, but after the miracles: it would have been better to believe the one who promised.
105.13: 105.13 They quickly did, forgetting. The third part, where he sets out the sins which they committed after the exodus: yet the mercy of God did not fail them, appeased through Moses. Or the rebuke, through the justice of God, of one who avenges against certain ones through Moses. Cassiodorus: They quickly did. They were changed with the greatest speed, etc., up to: for God delayed giving, that he might test them.
105.14: 105.14 They lusted with desire in the desert. Augustine: Such a manner of speech is like they praised, etc. Cassiodorus: The excess of desire is shown by the doubling of the word.
105.15: 105.15 Fullness. This is not the fullness of which it is said: Blessed are they who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be filled (Matt. 5). Into their souls. Augustine: Their animal nature, which is sustained by food: whence also in the Gospel: Is not the soul more than food? Or, souls, so that the will, which had asked in despair, might be overcome by abundance; after fullness follows sedition, whence he adds.
105.16: 105.16 And they provoked. Cassiodorus: Aiming at honor through envy, Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord: this provocation was over the priesthood, which Aaron and his sons had.
105.17: 105.17 The earth was opened. The same: The praise of God, who avenged his own; the kind of punishment inflicted shows it: those are swallowed by the earth who savored earthly things.
105.18: 105.18 In the synagogue. The same: For Korah and two hundred and fifty with him, wishing to have the priesthood of Aaron, took censers to burn incense, and therefore were consumed by divine fire. Sinners. Augustine: He does not say sinning, which the good also do: but sinners, greatly wicked and burdened with the heavy loads of sins.
105.19: 105.19 And they made. Cassiodorus: Not bearing the absence of Moses, while he tarried on the summit of Mount Sinai to receive the law, they made a calf. Horeb. Interpreted Calvary, where the crucifixion took place, etc., up to: the impatience of the light-minded did this, as all evils are born from it.
105.20: 105.20 In the likeness. Augustine: He does not say into a likeness, but in the likeness. And it is a manner of speech like that above: and they believed in his words.
105.21: 105.21 They forgot. Cassiodorus: A great forgetfulness indeed in memory, if not of the deliverance. Terrible things. Because they afflicted their adversaries, and showed these whom they ought to fear.
105.23: 105.23 Had stood in the breach. Augustine: Saying: If you do not forgive them, blot me out of your book. How much the intercession of the saints avails! Moses, secure about the justice of God, by which he could not be blotted out, obtained mercy for those who would justly perish. To turn away his wrath. Concerning the water of contradiction and the immolation of sons, whence God was more vehemently angered, and yet afterwards took pity. And for nothing. The fourth part, where he likewise enumerates other sins, and says God was appeased through Phinehas. They did not believe his word. Augustine: They despised what was signified through it, etc., up to: they did not wait for his counsel. In their tents. Cassiodorus: They murmured, because this befalls not the laboring but the idle, whence the greater envy of the crime grows.
105.26: 105.26 And he lifted up his hand over them, etc. Cassiodorus: This justice of God is put first, so that the piety that follows may be the more glorified, which piety is shown in what follows, where God is said to be appeased by the intervention of Phinehas.
105.28: 105.28 And they were initiated to Baal-peor. The same: Or, they were consecrated, as though worshipping only for a time: a graver excess and more vehement anger; they devoted their sons to demons. Augustine: And they were initiated, before it said, etc., up to: he delivered him whose destruction was to be greater.
105.30: 105.30 And Phinehas stood. Cassiodorus: With a firm mind, etc., up to: because he who does well, prays.
105.31: 105.31 And it was reckoned, etc. Augustine: God, who knew with how great a love for the people this was done, reckoned it to his priest for righteousness, not only as long as there is a generation, but even to eternity.
105.32: 105.32 And they provoked, etc. Cassiodorus: The fifth part, where he deals with the water of contradiction, and the immolation of sons, whence God was more vehemently angered, and yet afterwards took pity. As if they provoked by their inventions, as was said above; now they provoked again.
105.33: 105.33 And he distinguished with his lips, etc. Cassiodorus: This miracle, etc., up to: he did not hold the confidence he ought. Augustine: And he distinguished. As if God could not do this, etc., up to: yet he was not estranged from the kingdom of God's grace.
105.35: 105.35 The nations. Those seven peoples who possessed the land of promise.
105.36: 105.36 And it became a stumbling block to them. Cassiodorus: The land of promise, given as a reward, was turned into ruin for those who transgressed, because through conformity with the nations they became idolaters.
105.37: 105.37 And they sacrificed. Augustine: Although the history does not narrate these things, yet the prophet here cannot lie. Cassiodorus: If not in the first age, it was done in the following age, what David narrates.
