105.38: 105.38 And were slain. Augustine: A figurative expression, the container for the contained, that is, men; for they themselves were killing their souls by sacrificing their sons, and were defiled in their works.
105.39: 105.39 By their inventions. The same: Not that they were the first to invent, but because they imitated others. This is clearer in the Greek, both here and above; whence others translate: pursuits, or affections, or pleasures.
105.40: 105.40 He abhorred. Cassiodorus: That is, he turned away from them: to be turned away from is the last of all evils, whence ruin follows, and he delivered.
105.41: 105.41 And he delivered them, etc. The same: Behold, those who gloried in idols are subject to the disgrace of servitude, because they serve enemies, which is hard. Who hated. It is grievous to serve one who has been offended, who is appeased by no obedience.
105.43: 105.43 Often he delivered, etc. Cassiodorus: A twofold mercy: for he set forth above the benefits of God, and yet their iniquity did not cease; he brought vengeance, and again has pity on the afflicted. In their counsel. Augustine: The counsel of man is evil for the man himself, who seeks what is his own, not what is God's.
105.45: 105.45 Of the covenant. Cassiodorus: The reason is that Israel not perish as a matter of debt: the New Testament, where is the coming of the Lord, who was promised to Abraham. He repented. Augustine: Because he changed what seemed likely to destroy them. Cassiodorus: He repents then when he sees us repent, and is to us such as we are to him. Augustine: God does nothing as though by sudden counsel, but what he foreknew from eternity. But he is said to change what would seem to follow according to the causes of things, when other causes intervene to the contrary. Yet he foresaw both the causes and what would happen, unchangeably.
105.46: 105.46 Into mercies. Cassiodorus: On account of diverse gifts: the prophets, apostles, martyrs and confessors were from the Jews, whom he gave into mercies: and this in the sight of all, they had begun them, that is, of the nations, so that the nations who had formerly despised them might marvel at them. Or, made free in the presence of the demons, under whom they had been captives.
105.47: 105.47 Save us. Cassiodorus: The sixth part. Now, filled with abundance of the praise of God, he prays for what he saw would be: that the Church be gathered from all nations, and sing eternal praises. Augustine: Save us, as if: You have given mercies in the sight of all, etc., up to: it follows: And gather us from the nations.
105.48: 105.48 Blessed be the Lord. Cassiodorus: This is the praise which he desires the gathered to sing; this the Church now sings, glad for so great a good. From age, up to, etc., that is, from eternity to eternity, because he will be praised without end: this is the third consummation of the body of Christ in immortality, which was prayed for at the beginning of the psalm: Remember us, O Lord, in the good pleasure of your people, to see, to rejoice, that you may be praised with your inheritance.
106.1: 106.1 Alleluia, alleluia. Augustine: This psalm commends the mercy of God, etc., up to: which the Apostle set down, although signifying the same things. Give thanks to the Lord. The same: This psalm teaches what we are by ourselves, etc., up to: first it admonishes the redeemed to give thanks. Give thanks. Cassiodorus, Augustine: Its seven divisions, etc., up to: seventh, it treats of the heretics, there: And they were made few.
128.1: 128.1 A song of degrees. The same: The eleventh degree, etc., up to: a joyful conclusion is put with certainty of pardon, there: Let Israel hope in the Lord. Out of the depths. Augustine: He who feels himself in the depths, etc., up to: as Scripture says: The sinner, when he has come into the depth of vices, despises.
128.3: 128.3 Who shall endure. The same: Because almost every human life is barked at by sins, and every conscience is accused by its own thoughts. The heart that presumes on its own righteousness is not chaste. Let it presume, then, on the mercy of God, for with him is propitiation, whence he adds:
128.4: 128.4 For with you is propitiation. As if: With what hope do you cry out? Because there is mercy in you, which is why he says so: Or join it thus. Augustine: No one can endure, etc., up to: there is therefore one hope: For with you is propitiation, etc. For your law's sake, the same: I have endured the law of mercy, etc., up to: and you gave this law in that very necessity.
128.6: 128.6 The morning watch. The same: Let him hope from the morning watch who hopes for nothing else from God than immortality. From the morning watch, etc., up to: hence in the law the head and tail of the victim were offered to the Lord. Let Israel hope in the Lord. Cassiodorus: The second part, where is the joyful conclusion: Secure about himself, he proclaims that they should always hope in the Lord. As if, just as the soul hoped, so let Israel hope likewise.
128.8: 128.8 And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities. The same: Here he has now said what he will do, whom he called merciful and plenteous.
130.1: 130.1 A song of degrees. Cassiodorus: The twelfth degree is humility, which he shows himself to have inwardly and outwardly. He therefore admonishes to humility. Lord, my heart is not. The same: First, setting himself forth as humble, he brings punishment on the one who is not humble; second, by his own example he admonishes to hope. Showing himself humble within and without, he says. Neither have I walked. Augustine: I was not proud, I did not wish, as in marvelous things, etc., up to: The greater you are, humble yourself in all things.
130.2: 130.2 If I was not humble in mind. The same: Nourished on milk, which is the Word made flesh, that so I might grow to the bread of angels, to the Word who is with God, but not. I exalted, like the heretics. Who, if they have somehow begun to grasp something, or have seemed to, grow proud from it; and while they are still tender on their mother and are carried in hands that they may grow, who were carried in the womb that they might be born: they are separated from milk before time, whence they are extinguished. So the retribution. The same: He binds himself with a curse, etc., up to: thus God will reveal to him who thinks otherwise, for he resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. As one weaned. For as five stages are told, etc., up to: because God was man; but not changed into man.
130.3: 130.3 Let Israel hope. Cassiodorus: The second part, where he concludes, admonishing the others by his own example.
131.1: 131.1 A song of degrees. The same: In the thirteenth degree, now humble and meek, etc., up to: whence in Isaiah: Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, but upon the humble and quiet, and him that trembles at my words? Remember, O Lord, David and all. The same: First, showing the vow of building a house, he prays that he fulfill it. Second, he shows the house built, there: Behold, hear. Third, he tells the promises of God made to the built Zion, there: The Lord has sworn. Wishing therefore to build a house for the Lord, he says in the person of the whole Christ the head: O Lord, etc. David. Augustine: Literally, meek, that he did not repay Saul evil for evil. As he swore and vowed a vow. That is, that he may fulfill what he promised: let no one presume to pay what he vowed by his own strength. The Church vowed in meekness to be the house of God, than which nothing more pleasing can be offered to God. It is a house if it seeks not its own things but rejoices in the common: evils arise from private things, whence he says: If I shall enter. He knew he was hindered by what was his own from becoming God's place.
131.3: 131.3 If I shall enter, until I find a place for the Lord. The text is left in suspense, and it is an aposiopesis, as if he said: If I do this or that, let me never be believed hereafter. As if David swore to the Lord: If I shall enter into the tabernacle of my house, etc. Cassiodorus: Or from the person of Christ from that place: If I shall enter into the tabernacle of my house, namely of the heavenly dwelling. The tabernacle is the heavenly dwelling. If I shall go up, etc., to the right hand of the Father, where is the bed, that is, rest and the end of labors.
131.4: 131.4 Sleep, the rest of the three-day death. Then in other words he repeats the same. And slumber to my eyelids. And rest to my temples until the holy Church be founded by preaching. It is an aposiopesis, as though: let me be believed no more. And to my eyelids. Augustine: There is one who does not sleep but dozes: now he is drawn away from earthly things, now he turns back to them, often nods his head.
131.5: 131.5 And rest. From the rest of the temples sleep comes to the eyes, because for those about to sleep the temples begin. When, therefore, something temporal begins to delight one toward sin, the temples are weighed down; but do not give yourself to that delight, and sleep does not come to the eyes, by this thought, if, as if rubbing the forehead, you shake off sleep. I find: the same: he says it because he sought long. A place for the Lord: he sought it in himself, who rests upon the humble and quiet. The place of God is, if one forsakes his own things; or at least if he loves not himself but God. Tabernacle. The same: We still groan. In the house we shall praise, because groaning belongs to pilgrims; praise to those already dwelling in the homeland. To the God of Jacob. He says he has paid, as above he said he promised.
131.6: 131.6 Behold, we have heard. Cassiodorus: The second part, where the built house is shown, and where he also prays that those be exalted, and that the Jews not be altogether estranged. It in Ephrathah, Augustine: or it, etc., up to: where were the thorns of idolatry. Cassiodorus: Behold, hear, namely that the Lord would be born in Ephrathah, Bethlehem, where the Lord was born: it was heard that he is born in Bethlehem, but on account of the faith of the nations he was found in the fields of the wood.
131.7: 131.7 We will go in. Augustine: We too, persevering in our service, have entered or will enter into his tabernacle, the God of Jacob: he belongs to this house who is joined by charity to others as to living stones. He enters, then, who loves, and he who enters becomes the house of God. In the place. The house of God is where he ought to be adored: apart from which God does not hear unto eternal life. He belongs to the house who is joined together by charity with others. Or the place where the feet of the house of the Lord stand is Christ, in whom they persevere.
131.8: 131.8 Arise. The same: And it is said by him who says, I slept troubled: Arise from death into your rest, that you may be troubled no more, because death shall no longer have dominion.
131.9: 131.9 Priests. The same: He takes the same as priests and saints, namely all the faithful. Or, by priests he signifies the prelates of the Church; by saints, the faithful subjects. The ark, therefore, which he had prayed to arise, he distinguishes by the parts of the Church. Priests: as in the Old Testament the priests were adorned with various ornaments, so evangelical priests are adorned with various virtues: these are the ornaments God requires. For what the priests of the law bore on their garments, evangelical priests ought to have in their hearts.
131.10: 131.10 For the sake of David your servant. Cassiodorus: Remember: And well I say for the sake of David, because the Lord swore to David. For the sake of: then from the person of David himself asking God the Father. Augustine: For because Christ turned his face from the Jews to the nations, the Father is asked on account of the remnant, that they may be saved, which was fulfilled in the apostles and in many others. And he says: for the sake of David, as though saying: Remember me also, that for my sake you not utterly cast off the Jews.
131.11: 131.11 He swore. Cassiodorus: The third part, where he tells the promises of God made to the built Zion, that is, the Church. And David speaks in his own person or in that of the whole Christ. And he will not be frustrated, otherwise: he will not repent. Augustine: God is said to repent, etc., up to: for you do it because you had erred: he does it, and sets free. Of the fruit of your womb. He could have said of the fruit of your loins, etc., up to: because those whom David ruled temporally, Christ rules spiritually.
131.12: 131.12 If they keep. The same: They seem to make merit, etc., up to: this is not changed. And their sons. Cassiodorus: If they keep the covenant. They will sit upon your throne, that is, they will be partakers of your blessedness: that as you are of royal power, so they too, in their measure, and this, Forever and ever, that is, to eternity.
131.14: 131.14 This is my rest. The same: So God loves us that he says he rests if we rest in him.
131.15: 131.15 The widow. The same: The widow is the soul that understands itself deserted of all help except God's alone. With bread. God is the bread, who in the flesh made himself milk.
131.16: 131.16 Her priests. Or a distinction is to be made between priests and saints, as above. And it is, Her priests, that is, the prelates, I will clothe with salvation, that is, Christ, that is, that they may be honorable for teaching. And her saints, that is, the subjects. They shall rejoice with joy in Christ. They shall rejoice with joy. The same: Because they are clothed with salvation, etc., up to: who dwells in him, therefore, he has exalted securely.
131.17: 131.17 The horn of David, I have prepared a lamp for my Christ. The same: The spiritual height of the Church, etc., up to: before the death and resurrection of Christ.
131.18: 131.18 I will clothe with confusion, etc. Cassiodorus: The Son will do this, to whom all judgment has been given. But note that the Father, who speaks here, does what the Son does.
132.1: 132.1 A song of degrees. The same: The fourteenth degree: Charity, which makes brothers dwell as one, whence blessing and life. Behold how good. And this psalm is an atom, etc., up to: here therefore the just man, exulting in the dwelling together of brothers, says: Behold how. Behold how. Augustine: This verse, most famous in the whole world, like a trumpet of the Holy Spirit has gathered the divided: it has given birth to very many monasteries. Cassiodorus: Behold. As though it is explained more by showing than by the tongue. To dwell as one. Augustine: This applies to all Christians, but properly befits monasteries, from which, however, the blessing descends to the rest, as even to those brothers from Judea, of whom it is said: They had one heart and one soul.
132.2: 132.2 Like the ointment. Theodoret: The priestly oil, etc., up to: it perfects the fragrance of perfect virtue. The beard. Augustine: Behold the specification, that is, on the apostles and the other primitive saints, who first contended in faith, but could not be conquered, because they followed the head that had already suffered. Aaron. The priest, who offered himself, etc., up to: but could not be conquered. By them. To the hem. Cassiodorus: Or by the hem, which is the end of the garment, etc., up to: the usefulness of concord reaches even to the subjects.
132.3: 132.3 Like the dew. The same: Dew is a fine water from which the earth sprouts, and it signifies the grace by which sinners are converted. Hermon. Augustine: literally a mountain beyond the Jordan, etc., up to: the rest are taken up who are of one heart.
133.1: 133.1 A song of degrees. Cassiodorus: The fifteenth degree: the charity of the age. And this is the third psalm on charity, of the charity of God, with which he deals here, as above of the charity of neighbor. Not that there is one grace by which God is loved and another by which the neighbor is, but because grace has different acts, and different things are loved by it. He therefore admonishes to love God. First, he invites in the plural to bless God; second, he desires him to be blessed, there: May he bless. Behold is the word of one pointing. And to whom he makes this demonstration he specifies, you servants of the Lord. You stand. It is for servants not to sit in the house of the master. Or, it is understood of the same: And by the house the Church is understood, by the courts the breadth of charity. For in charity, which extends even to enemies, there is breadth; in hatred, narrowness. As if he said, bless, you who stand, that is, persevere, In the house of the Lord, that is, in the Churches; and who stand, In the courts of the house of our God, that is, in the breadth of charity, where no one is cramped.
133.2: 133.2 Lift up your hands. As Moses lifted up his hands while the people of Israel fought against Amalek, Lift up, I say, to holy things: that with intention you may work the eternal good, for otherwise it does not avail. May the Lord bless you. The second part, where he wishes the faithful to be blessed. As if to say, bless, and that you may be able to, May the Lord bless you, with the blessing which is out of Zion. He can, because it is he who made heaven and earth. Cassiodorus: May he bless. Above he exhorts many to bless God, but he himself blesses only one, because, though they are many, they are yet one, and blessing befits unity. Whence the one who first went down was healed in the pool. Be, then, in one, and the blessing will come to you.
134.1: 134.1 Alleluia. Cassiodorus: After the degrees which lead to eternity, alleluia is composed, that the Church may enjoy the praises of God, for whom such a gift is prepared. Praise. First by a demonstrative address he admonishes, etc., up to: who and why they ought to praise he adds: Praise, you servants.
134.3: 134.3 Praise the Lord, etc. Augustine: If all things are praised because good, etc., up to: in whom the whole seed of Israel is understood, the whole Church is thought of. Sing to his name, that is, praise him, because he did what the thing of his name requires, when he gave himself incarnate to be tasted by men.
134.4: 134.4 Jacob. The same: Interpreted wrestler, and it signifies those who wrestle against spiritual wickedness. Israel for his possession. Literally. The other nations the Lord placed under angels to be kept: Jacob he chose for himself, to till as a field, to sow, to possess, to keep.
134.6: 134.6 All things whatsoever. The same: As if to say: He is great in essence, great in works, etc., up to: but the spirit of man is unknown, whence behold it is said.
134.7: 134.7 Who brings forth the winds out of his treasuries. Who struck the firstborn. The same: Faith, from which we begin, by which, living, a man advances to the better; Egypt is affliction: whoever therefore afflicts the Church and causes scandals, even if called a Christian, loses faith. From the end. Either from the bottom of the earth, or from the encircling of the ends of the earth. Lightnings and rain. Lightning causes terror, rain joy. He who terrified by lightning, therefore, refreshes with rain.
134.8: 134.8 Who struck. The same: This he did among men for the sake of his cup. If he said what you love, hear also what you should fear. From man even to beast. Cassiodorus: This he often repeats, etc., up to: which he destroys in the prudent and the unlearned.
134.10: 134.10 Strong kings. The same: The spirits of the world: who are slain while they cannot do in us what they wish.
134.11: 134.11 Sihon king of the Amorites, etc. This was done under Moses: of this it is read in the book of Numbers, that when they forbade the children of Israel to pass through their borders, they were struck by him, and the people of Israel possessed their land. Canaan. The same: Humiliation, evil, namely, when the holy fall from honor.
134.12: 134.12 And he gave their land for an inheritance. The same: That is, heavenly blessedness, which the demons abandoned through pride, he gave to the faithful. This is the true land of promise, which is more truly called an inheritance, which is in peace, than that actual one, which the children of Israel often lost. The inheritance of Israel. Augustine: The inheritance is the nations of Israel, namely of the faithful people, whom they feed with tribulation, teaching patience, or those whom Israel cultivates by conforming them to itself.
134.13: 134.13 To generation and generation. The same: One generation is that by which we are reborn through baptism, the other that by which we shall rise: God has not forgotten to call in this one, to crown in that.
134.14: 134.14 For the Lord will judge. Cassiodorus: The cause of praise, because the Lord saw the people for whom he did so much, sent prophets, afterward also his Son. But because they were hard, he will judge them in the future, and will be comforted in his servants, that is, the faithful, when he restores eternal rewards. Behold the gradation of praise is led on to judgment. Augustine: Or, thus. Therefore from the present, etc., up to: that they may see, and those who see may become blind.
134.15: 134.15 The idols. Cassiodorus: The second part: after he has filled himself with the praises of God, he reproves the worshipers of idols by mocking them, because it is perfect praise of the truth to destroy falsehood; the same things were said above, but repeated they increase the shame.
134.16: 134.16 They have mouths and shall not speak. Augustine: The craftsman could make those outward parts; but he could not give breath, nor hearing to the ears, nor light to the eyes, nor voice to the mouth.
134.18: 134.18 Let those who make them become like them. The same: Knowing these things, they mock the idols, etc., up to: nor do they perceive the good fragrance of Christ.
134.19: 134.19 House of Israel, bless the Lord. Cassiodorus: This is the third part, where, after the idols have been mocked, he admonishes all ranks to celebrate the praises of God: as if to say: Let the worshipers of idols become like them. But you, who are the house of Israel. House of Aaron, bless. Augustine: The leaders are the house of Aaron: the ministers, the house of Levi, all the peoples who fear; all generally are the house of Israel; let us all say with one voice: Blessed.
134.21: 134.21 Blessed be the Lord. The same: Or according to the interpretation of the names, etc., up to: where we shall see him in eternal peace.
135.1: 135.1 Alleluia. Augustine: This psalm contains the praise of God, where although many things are said in the praise of God, yet especially the mercy of God is commended here. Cassiodorus: The different beginnings of the verses, etc., up to: so near is the divine presence if it is sung purely. Give thanks to the Lord. The same: First, he sets forth the magnificence of God and the establishment of the whole world. Second, he tells what he did in Egypt and for the people of the Jews as a figure of us, there: Who struck. Third, he deals with the Christians, there: and gave their land for an inheritance. Give thanks to the Lord. Augustine: Let us now praise, etc., up to: through mercy is eternal blessedness.
135.2: 135.2 Give thanks to the God of gods. He calls men gods, to whom the word of God came, in another psalm, where he says, I said, You are gods and sons of the Most High, etc. And they are not called gods because all are good: for if all were good, he would not say in the same psalm: but in the midst he judges gods, that is, discerns, concerning whom he also adds: Give thanks to the Lord of lords.
135.3: 135.3 Who does great wonders. The same: As is placed everywhere at the end, etc., up to: therefore give thanks, for his mercy endures forever.
135.4: 135.4 Great wonders alone. The same: Because some things he does through men or angels, and some great things he himself alone, which he also first carries out.
135.5: 135.5 Who made the heavens. The same: He made therefore the whole creation by himself, etc., up to: whence, You have made all things in wisdom, O God. Or typically, the heavens in understanding, that is, the spiritual saints, to whom he gave not only to believe but to understand divine things. But the simple who hold only firm faith are called, as below the heavens, earth, and because in the baptism they received they stand, as upon the waters, by firm faith, he has established the earth, as it were, upon the waters.
135.6: 135.6 The earth upon the waters. The same: But by which the heavier earth is borne by the lighter waters, etc., up to: so the Lord sat upon the well, that is, beside it.
135.7: 135.7 Who made the great lights. The same: that is, he conferred the gifts of graces on his faithful.
135.9: 135.9 The moon and the stars for the power of the night. Cassiodorus: It can also be said otherwise mystically, etc., up to: that through these the lesser ones may shine.
135.10: 135.10 Who struck Egypt. The same: The second part, where he tells what he did in Egypt and for the people of the Jews, under a figure of us. Now he begins what he did through men or through angels. With their firstborn. He struck the firstborn of Egypt, etc., up to: but God excludes from himself.
135.12: 135.12 With a mighty hand. The same: The hand of God is invincible action, which comes from the arm, that is, from all singular power.
135.13: 135.13 He divided the Red Sea into parts. The same: Literally, into twelve parts for the number of the tribes, so that each tribe had its own ways of going; typically, thus by various ways one passes from the world to God. By the Red Sea the age is understood.
135.15: 135.15 And shook off Pharaoh. The same: He shook off the devil with his ministers, like dust, which is quickly shaken off. In this quickness both the power of God is shown and those earthly filths are indicated which we are wont to shake off. Pharaoh. The same: Fittingly the devil is understood by Pharaoh: Pharaoh kills the males, saves the females; so the devil smothers virtues, nourishes concupiscence.
135.21: 135.21 And gave their land for an inheritance. Cassiodorus: The third part, where he comes down to the Christians, setting out the benefits given them, that you may know thus one author of all.
135.22: 135.22 To Israel his servant. He takes by Israel the servant, Christ, etc., up to: he gave no price to the Egyptians.
135.25: 135.25 Who gives food. Theodoret: From the singular Providence, etc., up to: in the Gospels he says: Behold the birds of the air, which neither sow nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. To all flesh. Augustine: To every kind of men, Israel and the nations, not as manna to the Jew alone.
136.1: 136.1 A psalm of David. Cassiodorus: The third psalm on the lamentation of Jerusalem, etc., up to: but this on the captivity made by Nebuchadnezzar. Augustine: There are two cities mixed in body, etc., up to: who in mind and desire are citizens of Jerusalem. By the rivers. Cassiodorus: First, those to be captured long afterward, etc., up to: he begins with longing for the homeland, saying: By the rivers, etc. When we remembered, Augustine: In a hostile land the remembrance of the homeland is sweet, etc., up to: both are of Babylon.
136.2: 136.2 On the willows. The same: Which are watered by the rivers of Babylon, etc., up to: but by delaying we hang up. Cassiodorus: The force of grief is heightened when the delight by which they were wont to console themselves is suspended. For there they asked us. Basil: And from this they began to gain no little advantage, etc., up to: that they wished even to hear our songs.
136.3: 136.3 The words of songs. Augustine: Or, of canticles, as, what does Christ profit? or, what is the other life? But here, where they are full of evils, we ought not to strike the instrument to sound, but to hang it up. The same: The devil craftily seeks to mock, etc., up to: and he bound himself with an oath, saying: If I forget, etc.
136.4: 136.4 How shall we sing. The same: One must beware lest anyone, fearing to displease such people, seek their friendships and begin to delight in Babylon.
136.5: 136.5 My right hand. The same: Whatever you do for eternal things, the right hand works; if you aim also at something else, the left has mixed itself in; and delighting in it as though in the right, you lose eternal things.
136.6: 136.6 Let it cleave. Cassiodorus: Let me become mute in the praises of God, which is the consolation of weeping and miseries. My tongue. Augustine: The song of Jerusalem is our tongue, the song of the age a barbarous tongue. He is mute to God who has forgotten Jerusalem.
136.7: 136.7 Remember. Cassiodorus: The second part, where a turning to God is made against the enemies. Remember, in the day of separation, that they be punished. The sons of Edom. Augustine: The sons of Edom, that is, the Idumeans, were a hindrance to those rebuilding Jerusalem; or, they were allied in the destruction of Babylon, whence he says, O miserable daughter of Babylon. Edom morally is carnality, which seduces us to illicit movements. Edom. The same: Esau stands for all the carnal; Jacob for the spiritual; the elder, the carnal man; the younger, the spiritual, because first that which is animal, afterward that which is spiritual. All the carnal are enemies of the spiritual, whence he says: Remember, deliver us from them. Empty. Cassiodorus: By likeness of a cistern, from which if water is drawn, one comes to the foundation. But what does it profit to take away life from such, for whom in the foundation, which is Christ, there is eternal life? While the wicked think to harm, they give crowns.
136.8: 136.8 Daughter. Augustine: By succession the city of the wicked was made the daughter of Babylon, as the Church; Jerusalem, namely the city of the good, by succession the daughter of Zion. Cassiodorus: The daughter of Babylon morally. It is the flesh, which confusion, etc., up to: they dash against the rock Christ, that being broken they may perish.
136.9: 136.9 Blessed is he who shall hold. Augustine: What retribution? As Babylon smothers those born in the world, while they are small, with the errors of parents and of the age: so those who are now young, having been given knowledge of God, dash the little ones of Babylon, that is, the cupidities as they are born, before they gain strength; thus they are more easily conquered, but even the larger ones must be killed at the rock.
137.1: 137.1 A psalm of David himself. Cassiodorus: The captive, who had wept, as though Jerusalem and the temple were rebuilt, and as a fellow citizen of that part of Jerusalem which was not captive, that is, of the angels, exults and first praises the benefits given to him. In the person, therefore, of the Church, which is in the higher places in hope, expecting to be there in reality, he says, I will confess. I will confess to you, O Lord. First, he commends the benefits given to him: second, he tells how these are extended to all, there: Let them confess to you, O Lord, etc. In the sight. Augustine: In praising, I set before me the angels, to whom I expect to be made equal in dignity, as now, so afterward. These set nothing else before them in the praise of God than himself. In the sight, therefore, of the angels, in that purity with which the angels behold you, so that they rest in you alone, I will sing to you.
137.2: 137.2 Above mercy. The same: All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth: there are no other ways by which he comes to us, there are no others by which we come to him: let us render these to God, mercy in coming to aid, truth in judging. Above every name your holy name. Cassiodorus: Or above your holy name, when your worship became known to us.
137.3: 137.3 In my soul. And because in the soul carnal multiplication can occur, he adds, strength, as though I ask nothing else in the soul but strength.
137.4: 137.4 Let them confess. The same: The second part, where he tells how these goods are to be spread to all. As if by my example: Let them confess, etc. All the words of your mouth. Augustine: Which are now everywhere revealed and sent to all nations, etc., up to: and so, the fleece being dried, they have heard all the words, etc.
137.5: 137.5 Great is the glory. The same: If they are humble, they love and sing this; for if they exalt themselves, let them fear what follows. For the Lord is high. He looks on the lowly. Cassiodorus: This is not the human condition, where the humble is despised and the proud regarded; but the Lord regards the humble. And the high he knows from afar. Augustine: The proud does not do this, etc., up to: those mourning this sojourn, whence he adds.
137.7: 137.7 If I walk in the midst of tribulation. He does not otherwise give life except in the midst of tribulation, whence, Blessed are they who mourn, woe to those who laugh. Upon the wrath. The same: This very thing, that they are angry with me, is your punishing of them, that is, their punishment. For to be angry is for them a penalty, not only a fault. While you permit this, then, you stretch out the hand of vengeance over all. Your right hand. God has no right or left, but the right hand of God is called eternal happiness, the left temporal happiness. At times, then, he does not save his saints on the left, but he always saves them on the right.
137.8: 137.8 The Lord will repay. Augustine: What I cannot, etc., up to: in whom the prince of the world found no sin, why he should kill him.
138.1: 138.1 Unto the end, a psalm of David. Cassiodorus: A psalm full of the depth of mysteries, etc., up to: veiled in the prophets, manifest in the Gospel. Augustine: The whole Christ speaks, as one and entire man, etc., up to: as two in one flesh. Lord, you have proved me. Cassiodorus: First, of the knowledge of God, etc., up to: fourth, how the wicked do not harm him, there: If you slay, O God, etc. Lord, you have proved. Augustine: Now restored in Jerusalem, etc., up to: this is the person of the whole human nature returning.
138.3: 138.3 You have understood. Cassiodorus: The foreknowledge of the Godhead is shown here, etc., up to: because the assumed man cannot be equaled to the divine substance. From afar. Augustine: When I am still in pilgrimage, before I come to the homeland, as the father meets the younger son returning, because he understood his thoughts from afar, because he had said within himself, worn out with need: I will arise and go to my father. My path, namely the evil one, by which I went, forsaking my father. And my line. Another reading, my boundary, to which I have come: I had gone far indeed, but you were there. He speaks as a fugitive caught, with the vengeance of God following him.
138.4: 138.4 And all my ways: before I went them, and you permitted me to go in toil, that I might return if I would not labor, this I confess. For there is no guile in my tongue: now justified in your grace.
138.5: 138.5 My last things, when I fed swine; the old, when I asked a part of the substance, this according to the parable. But mystically, the old, when we fell through the ancient sin: the last, punishment, when we came into this mortality, which is the last, if we wish to return; otherwise the eternal remains. You formed me, for the labors for which we are all born. You laid. Another reading, You made heavy your hand, the avenger, healthfully weighing down the proud, that it may raise the humble, in the heavy hand.
138.6: 138.6 Wonderful, and incomprehensible to me. Knowledge has been made. It is not easy for me to contemplate you, whom I proudly left, as it was before when I was with you, when I said, give me the part of the substance. From me, that is, from my sin. It is strengthened, another reading, it has grown strong. And I shall not be able to attain from myself. Augustine: In Exodus it is read that the Lord, etc., up to: I am not hidden from you, whose boundary you see.
138.7: 138.7 Where shall I go from your Spirit? Cassiodorus: The second part, where he now deliberates that he must not flee from him, but to him, from the angry to the appeased, which will be through the very one with whom the world is full: for the Spirit of the Lord fills all things. Where shall I flee from your face? He turns this way and that, as though seeking a place to flee.
138.8: 138.8 If I ascend into heaven, you are there, etc. Augustine: If I lift myself up, I find a restrainer; if I grow proud of my righteousness, You are there, whose truly is the righteousness. If I descend, I shall have come by sinning, To hell, or into the deep, and unwilling to confess, I shall say: who sees me? You are present to avenge. He finds a plan, but thus I shall be able to flee the angry one.
138.9: 138.9 If I take wings, the two wings of charity, which I had lost. Wings. Cassiodorus: Those of my power, that is, the efficacy of the Godhead, by which he raised the body from the tomb. He took them at daybreak, before light, that is, at the time of the resurrection: and dwelt in the uttermost parts of the sea, that is, above the widest end of the age. And I shall dwell in the uttermost parts. Augustine: In mind, at the end of the age, that I may love not the age but its end, in which there is rest for me. But he himself leads there, whence he adds:
138.10: 138.10 For even there your hand. But considering the length of the way, he adds:
138.11: 138.11 And I said, perhaps darkness will trample, etc. The iniquity of the age abounds, by which the wings of charity can grow cold. And because in the night I despaired of crossing the sea, the night became light for me: The woman came, the wisdom of God, who had lost the drachma, on which is the image of the king, that is, man: she lit from herself a lamp, which is of clay, that is, flesh, and the night being illuminated, found the drachma. And I said. Augustine: I deliberated. Perhaps you. He calls darkness that lower part of the rational creation, standing opposed, namely the wicked men or the flesh, whence he fears: And it is, Darkness, that is, the lower rational creature holding the left-hand way. They have trampled me. The same: So I feared, but the night became light in my delights, that is, those who were formerly night will be enlightened in delights. Because you. Sinners.
138.12: 138.12 They shall not be darkened, etc., and the night, by the sinners living. As the day, that is, the saints from the Jews. As his darkness, so also his light, because to the extent you acknowledge, to that extent he forgives. But whence is this to me? because you have possessed my reins. For darkness. Augustine: He who does not confess his sins darkens his own darkness; but if he confesses, God enlightens. As his darkness. Of our night, that is, the miseries of human life, etc., up to: whom the light does not lift up.
138.13: 138.13 For you have possessed my reins. The same: Whence this difference for you? because the inward possessor holds not only the heart, that is the thoughts, but also the reins, that is the delights: so that the light of night may not delight, but the light of his wisdom.
138.14: 138.14 I will confess to you. Cassiodorus: The third part, where he says, to one flying back to God, God illuminating and possessing the reins, how great is the exultation and multiplication. My soul knows exceedingly. Augustine: Now my soul knows greatly: before, your knowledge was wonderful from me, and I could not attain it; but now I can, because you have lit the night, possessed the reins, taken me from the womb, that is, because your grace has come to me and enlightened me.
138.15: 138.15 My bone is not hidden from you, which you made in secret. The same: Bone from bone, not from mouth, etc., up to: whence the Apostle: As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. Basil: Again he speaks of the foreknowledge of God, either he says all its secrets are his, or something else that he says, namely the handiwork and formation. My substance in the lower parts of the earth. Augustine: In the flesh, and yet the bone does not yield to the evils of this lower place, etc., up to: let them not despair, then.
138.16: 138.16 Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and in your book all, etc. The same: He who until now spoke from the person of the body, here now speaks from the person of the head. Days shall be formed. Another reading, By day they shall go astray. This day, still abiding, was Christ, etc., up to: because the apostles were made leaders and shepherds of the Church. As if by merit I strengthened them, etc., up to: in the promise it was said to Abraham: I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven and as the sand of the sea.
138.18: 138.18 I am still with you, etc. As before death, which the Jews thought they had taken away. Or, still, that is, in death itself, which does not seem of a dead man. Or, even if the resurrection is a sign of divinity, yet I am still hidden from many, with you, that is, as you. Augustine: I am still with you. Not yet with them by knowledge, because they do not yet recognize, because they did not recognize Christ soon after the resurrection. Or, all this time I am with you in secret at the right hand of the Father, before he is revealed in that brightness in which he is to come.
138.19: 138.19 If you slay the sinners, O God, etc. Cassiodorus: The fourth part, how he is not harmed by the wicked. Augustine: If you slay. He adds what he meanwhile suffers, etc., up to: in judgment he will say openly: Amen I say to you, I do not know you, depart from me.
138.21: 138.21 Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord? As if, If you slay, Did I not hate those who hated you? Them also I will kill. Augustine: As heretics not understanding, etc., up to: how then am I contaminated by their mixture? Prove me, O Lord. The same: Up to now concerning heretics and others following them, separated from the Church, now he also treats of the wicked or feigned ones joined to it, whom the Church endures, and groans. As heretics separate themselves and others, etc., up to: but you, God, prove me and know.
139.1: 139.1 Unto the end, a psalm of David. The same: The complaint, groaning, prayer of the body of Christ set among the wicked, not yet having the good in fact but in hope, where is full exultation. He admonishes us to pray to God against the evils of the age.
139.2: 139.2 Deliver me, O Lord, from the man. Cassiodorus: First he sets forth who the enemies are, what evils they stir up, opposing prayers to them. Second, he says what help he has against evils, there: I said to the Lord. Third, he opens what the evils of the enemies are, there: The head. The Church therefore, laboring among the wicked, cries out. From the unjust man. Augustine: The unjust is he who harms, whence when he had said, From the evil man, as though explaining, he added, From the unjust man.
139.3: 139.3 Who have devised. Cassiodorus: He follows how the wicked persecute: for they attack the good in three ways, namely by tongue, hand and heart: and he puts the heart first, saying, Who have devised, as if to say, Deliver me from the people of the wicked. Augustine: Who, although on their lips they often put forward good things, yet have devised iniquity in the heart.
139.4: 139.4 They have sharpened. He shows how they persecute by the tongue. Like a serpent's. The same: In the serpent is cunning and guile to harm: therefore it also creeps, having no feet, so that it is not heard when it comes; its track is smooth, but not straight: so the wicked creep to harm, having hidden poison under a smooth track, whence he adds, The poison of asps is under their lips.
139.5: 139.5 Keep me, O Lord. Cassiodorus: Of the persecution made by hand, that is, by deed, he adds. Keep me, because he deceives in many ways, which one cannot guard against.
139.6: 139.6 The proud. Augustine: By this name he briefly set out the whole body of the devil: hence it is that they both call themselves just and refuse to confess; every proud man is also envious, like the devil, who envied man what he had lost. And they stretched out cords for a snare, etc. Whence Isaiah: Woe to those who draw sin as a long garment, because they add sins to sins, etc., up to: and let him be cast into the outer darkness.
139.7: 139.7 I said to the Lord. The same: Interlude. The second part, what help against evils, as if to say, the wicked attack in so many ways, and what is the remedy amid so many and such great evils? I said to the Lord: You are my God. A great confidence, for though he is God of all, yet he is properly of those who enjoy him. Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication. The same: The voice of men and their soul, etc., up to: not as men of the master, who buy with a purse; you with blood.
139.8: 139.8 The strength of my salvation, you have overshadowed my head. The same: You who give the strength of my salvation, etc., up to: however much the enemy rages.
139.9: 139.9 Do not deliver me, O Lord, from my desire. The same: The devil sets forth gain, etc., up to: except from your desire.
139.10: 139.10 The head of their circuit. Cassiodorus: Interlude. The third part, where he says what the evils of the enemies are. Augustine: As if he says, Your shadow covers me, etc., up to: or are overcome by their assertion. The labor of their own lips shall cover them. Cassiodorus: That is, their false and lying assertion shall cover them, because they are overcome by their own false assertion.
139.11: 139.11 They shall fall upon them. Augustine: Or coals of fire upon the earth, etc., up to: whence the Apostle: To some we are the odor of life unto life, to others the odor of death unto death (2 Cor. 2).
139.12: 139.12 The talkative man. The same: Whoever wishes to be directed, etc., up to: of outward things it is necessity, not will. The unjust, etc., to destruction. Which is not done to the needy, who, if he is caught by evils, yet not to destruction; God scourges every son whom he receives. And though the good are now afflicted, yet they will confess amid grievous things, which is more praiseworthy: And they shall dwell, therefore nothing is feared in the world.
139.14: 139.14 But yet. Cassiodorus: The conclusion of the psalm, where he says that if the good are delivered and avenged of their enemies, they do not give it to themselves but to God, whence, and they shall dwell with him. They shall dwell with your countenance. Because they will see God as he is.
140.2: 140.2 Let my prayer be directed. Cassiodorus: Let prayer be incense, etc., up to: who repents at the end. The lifting up of my hands, etc. Augustine: Let all understand this of the head, etc., up to: he adds from the voice of the body.
140.3: 140.3 Set, O Lord, a guard. Note that he asks a guard to be placed on both the heart and the mouth: a double fortification is needed, so that neither an unjust thought may be savored, nor a perverse will burst out into foolish words. The door. Augustine: By likeness of one who stands around a door, so that one may not enter or leave who is not permitted.
140.4: 140.4 Incline not. Cassiodorus: As if: For this set the door, that there be no making excuses: for this greatest vice rules over men, whence they repent more slowly; hence in the book of Kings: To resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to submit is like the crime of idolatry (1 Kings 15). To make excuses for excuses. The same: It is the habit of the shameless that, when caught, they first excuse themselves by some falsehoods, and then, convicted, seek others, imputing their vices to time or necessity, lest ever they yield to the truth. I will not communicate. The same: Or, I will not be combined. They are said to be combined when two are bound together, so that one hinders the other, so that there is no free flight. I will not be combined, by likeness of the flesh. With their chosen. Augustine: The chosen are those who justify themselves, despise the rest, like the Pharisee (Luke 18); and defend sins in every way. With such this man does not wish to be combined, that is, joined, lest he be hindered by them.
140.5: 140.5 The just man shall correct me. Cassiodorus: The second part, where this faithful man, now on the contrary corrected by the just, spurns the false flatterers, about to be of profit to the wicked by word and conduct, in which he also asks to be guarded. But the oil of the sinner, etc. The same: Feigned love, which softens minds from the rigor of truth to harmful things.
140.6: 140.6 Judges. Augustine: The powerful, the learned, who judge of conduct, etc., up to: whom all worship.
140.7: 140.7 They shall hear. The same: With the ear of obedience, not like Adam, etc., up to: near to cursing. The fatness of the earth. The same: There are certain despised things from which nevertheless the earth receives richness, etc., up to: who are the bones and the firmament of the faithful or of faith.
140.8: 140.8 Beside hell. The same: He says beside hell, not in hell: because although they die by the common lot, yet they do not descend into hell like the wicked, but eternal life is given them. For to you, O Lord. Cassiodorus: The frailty of man having been told, he takes refuge in divine remedies. Take not away from your good things, but let my hope be always in you: and let my eyes always look to you. For he does not ask against what the saints wish, namely to be taken from the world and to be with Christ.
140.9: 140.9 Keep me from the snare. By snares and scandals he briefly notes the evils of the whole world. Snares are the flattering bonds, the desires of the flesh; but when the devil does not succeed through these, he strives with scandals, which he stirs up through the restless. Or otherwise. And he says, those setting a snare are the open persecutors: but the workers of iniquity he says are those who consent to them, who fail through fear of persecution. And it is: Take not away my soul, but rather, Keep me from the snare of persecution, which they have set for me. Augustine: This is what the persecutors do, who place the bait of this life as in a trap. If the bird loves this bait, it falls into the trap: because from fear of death it succumbs to persecution. Keep me. From the scandals of those who work iniquity. That is, from the scandal of those who, by consenting to them, slip, and so work iniquity. As if he says: Keep me from the persecutors who terrify, and from the lapsed.
140.10: 140.10 The wicked shall fall into his net. Words fit for comparison, since he does not wish to be combined with those. They shall fall from vice to vice, but I am alone until I pass. Alone, that is because he does not walk with the worst. Alone. Augustine: The same as he says, etc., up to: so also the other ancients. Until I pass. As a traveler of this world, who is captured by no pleasure.
141.1: 141.1 Understanding of David. Cassiodorus: This psalm is the fifth of those which are titled with the name of prayer, where nothing else is said than what has been said in other psalms, but the same. Augustine: But since by repetition of this kind the common weakness is looked after, they are not repeated superfluously, so that, repeated, they may be better committed to memory; whence it is written in Proverbs: A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise (Prov. 12), because the wise man thinks over what he has heard; by going over it he ruminates; but the foolish man swallows it, that is, does not think, gives it to oblivion; and these are those clean animals in the law that ruminate; the others are unclean. David, fleeing Saul, hid in a cave, but this is not what is treated here, but what it signifies. For David signifies Christ. The cave, however, the flesh, or the world, or the sepulcher. David, therefore, Christ, with his members in the world, or Christ in the flesh, or in the sepulcher.
141.2: 141.2 With my voice I cried to the Lord. First prayer against evils is set down, second he treats of the end of evils, there: I cried to you, O Lord. He admonishes us therefore to pray. And in the person of the whole Christ, as of one crying to God from a cave, he says: I made supplication. Augustine: What he says, I cried, he explains: I made supplication. As if to say: My cry is supplication, not murmur, not blasphemy.
141.3: 141.3 In his sight. Augustine: The Lord will repay: pray in secret; whence in the Gospel: But when you pray, enter into your chamber, and having shut the door, pray to your Father, who sees in secret, etc. (Matt. 6).
141.4: 141.4 And you knew. The same: He adds this, lest hearing, my spirit failed, they should think him cast down. As if to say: If they think me cast down, because my spirit failed, you see me standing, whose Spirit gives me life. Paths. Of justice, which they do not see. In the way. Many ways, because many precepts: one way, because all are reduced to one, that is, charity. Augustine: In the way, according to their wish; beside the way, according to the truth. For Christ is the way, who does not allow them to set a snare in the way so that there is nowhere for us to go; yet he allows them to set it beside the way, lest we turn aside from the way.
141.5: 141.5 I looked to the right. Augustine: Which the wicked did not see; and this is, and there was none who would know. Cassiodorus: For when you suffer all things, who knows what you are attending to? Augustine: He who looks to the right sees; he who to the left is blinded. Or, the apostles did not stand at the right, because by carnal fear they were scattered, but I stood firm. Flight has failed me. Both of the body and of the mind. And there is none who seeks. Cassiodorus: Because there is no consolation, but he alone was left for the passion. Flight has failed. Augustine: He says he was shut in. Flight failed, because he did not flee in mind, though in body at times. The shut-in does not flee in body, because he cannot. The strong does not flee in mind, because he does not wish to. Flight fails the shut-in or the strong; flight indeed, of which it is said in the Gospel: He sees the wolf coming and flees (John 10), where the Lord blames the hireling. But another is the flight of the body, which the Lord permits, saying: If they persecute you in one city, flee to another (Matt. 10). And there is none who seeks my soul. The soul is sought either by persecutors or by lovers. Thus flight fails in two ways, in the captured and in the strong.
141.6: 141.6 I cried. Cassiodorus: The second part, where he treats of the end of evils. My hope. Because I choose you from among all. My portion. Humbly and commonly he says the portion is his in the land of the living, when the whole is his. This is evident from what he said to the thief: Today you will be with me in paradise: which is the land of the living eternally.
141.7: 141.7 From those who persecute me. For the devil through his vessels, that is, through the sons of distrust, carries out the persecution of the body, that within the ruin of the heart may be made.
141.8: 141.8 Bring my soul out of prison, etc. Augustine: Speaking from the person of the Church, he explains from what she is to be freed. Another reading, out of the prison. Because she is straitened in the corruption which is the penalty of the body: after these straits, in the house of God all life will be confession, that is, the praise of God; now the prison hinders confessing. This prison or cave can be called the world, where all is vain: whence he asks the soul to be brought out, which suffers much from it, etc., up to: but its corruption and temptation is the prison.
142.1: 142.1 A psalm of David. This psalm is the seventh of the penitential, which are therefore seven, that by the same number by which we sinned, we may wash away sins. Cassiodorus: For as we sin in the week of this world, so by this number of psalms the remedy of penance is set against sins. In which psalms there is such a form, that it begins with tears and the end is in joy, lest anyone despair of pardon. Augustine: As Absalom David, so Judas Christ, false brothers his body; or illicit movements and activity. Lord, hear, etc. Cassiodorus: First he seeks an exordium; second he narrates his evils, and what he did against them, there: for the enemy has persecuted; third, a supplication confirmed by reasons is set, there: hear me quickly; fourth, a joyful conclusion is set, there: your good Spirit. He admonishes to penance, and to prayer, to pray. In the person of the whole Christ he says: O Lord, etc. In your truth. Cassiodorus: This is not against the humility which asked to be heard: but it is the truth and justice of God that he not dispute with one who asks, not judge him who condemns himself; whence it is added: and enter not, he did not ask for the justice of judgment. Augustine, Cassiodorus: In your truth, in your justice. Or he speaks of the justice and truth which spares the penitent, and absolves those who condemn themselves, and takes truth and justice for the same. And it is, in your truth, and your justice, that is, according to the justice and truth by which you pardon the penitent and those who accuse themselves.
142.2: 142.2 And enter not into judgment. Augustine: They enter into judgment with the Lord who establish their own justice, which this humble man does not; whence the prophet: Why will you contend with me in judgment? You have all forsaken me, says the Lord. With your servant. It is unworthy with a servant, let alone with a friend: and if you say friend, I say servant, a fugitive I return, I seek peace, I am not worthy to be called your son.
142.3: 142.3 For he has persecuted. Cassiodorus: The second part, where is the narration of the evils he suffers, and what he did against them.
142.6: 142.6 I remembered. Augustine: The members say this, etc., up to: but you had not begun to be. I meditated. Because indeed all things are good, in which he perceives, because whatever good is in himself is from God. On the works of your hands. As if he says: I sought the craftsman in the work, and in all created things the Creator: your creature became a spectacle to me. I remembered the days. Cassiodorus: This man, recalling that he made heaven and earth, and that he did good to the ancients, forgets the miseries of the world. And from these things which God made he consoles himself.
142.7: 142.7 Quickly. Cassiodorus: The third part, where a supplication confirmed by reasons is set. My spirit has failed. Augustine: Let your Spirit fill me, because mine has failed: now I am poor in spirit. For he in whom his own spirit lives is proud in his own spirit, and is lifted up against God. Whence elsewhere: You will take away their spirit, and they shall fail (Psalm 103). Into the pit. He descends into the depth, because he also loses confession, as one who sets before himself license to sin without hope of pardon, the reins of iniquity let loose. Such a one does not hear God saying: Turn to me, and I will turn to you (Zech. 1).
142.8: 142.8 In the morning. Cassiodorus: After the night of sins. Augustine: It is morning when sins are loosened. Make known to me the way. God has done this, etc., up to: we shall come to pure light, to the Word in the beginning with God. My soul. Cassiodorus: Like a vessel I have brought to the fountain: fill it, therefore.
142.10: 142.10 Your good Spirit. Cassiodorus: The fourth part, where is the joyful conclusion. For your name's sake, O Lord, you will quicken me in your equity. The grace of God is commended here: because he says he is quickened not by merits but by the name, which is Jesus, but with this the grace of equity has mercy, for although God does all things freely, it is nevertheless of his justice to justify suppliants whom he sees assailed by demons.
143.1: 143.1 A psalm of David against Goliath. Cassiodorus: David, the whole Christ, etc., up to: and so his head is cut off by his own sword.
143.3: 143.3 Or the son of man, that you think of him? Augustine: It is a great thing that God values, and makes so much of, that for him he gave his Son, and for him is even made bread, which is the bread of angels: for God does not value man as man does, who buys a horse at a higher price than a man.
143.4: 143.4 Man is like to vanity: his days pass away like a shadow. The same: When man was created, he was made like to truth, to vanity by sinning. Vain are all transitory things, in comparison with the ever-abiding truth. Cassiodorus: It is vain, which falling from its substance vanishes: like smoke, like a shadow. So man himself wastes away, whence he adds, His days, that is, his life known, that is, passing, thus passes as a shadow.
143.5: 143.5 Lord, bow down. Augustine: The humble David, from the person of the Church, full of grace, presuming on God, fighting here, calls upon the help of God. As if, we are in the struggle, but lest we fail. Lord, bow down. Cassiodorus: Lord. The same opens, etc., up to: and in the form of God took the form of a servant.
143.7: 143.7 Send forth your hand. Cassiodorus: He turns his words to the Father: Send forth your hand, that is, Christ; from on high where he is with the Father, that he may put on flesh. Augustine: Or he treats of the second coming in the person of the Church. As if he says: Do so now. Send forth your hand from on high, that is, Christ from heaven for judgment. For the Lord will come in the voice of an angel, and in the trumpet of God he will descend from heaven. Then from the person of the Church he adds: Rescue me, namely, by that hand. And deliver, etc., as in the text.
143.9: 143.9 O God, I will sing a new song to you. Cassiodorus: The second part, where, as though he whom he was praying to had come as victor and deliverer, he promises to sing to him in the New Testament and the Old: and prays to be delivered by him from those who think blessedness is in earthly things. Song. Augustine: By another name this signifies the law, which he signified by the five stones.
143.10: 143.10 From the sword. Augustine: What he called above waters, he here calls the sword; whence here he adds what he did there: And rescue me from the hand of strange children. Evil. Of which: Their tongue is a sharp sword (Psalm 56). There is also a kindly sword, of which the Lord says: I came not to send peace, but the sword (Matt. 10). This is the two-edged sword (Apoc. 19), mighty with both edges, namely of the Old and New Testament, by which all corruption is cut away from the members of Christ.
143.12: 143.12 Whose sons. Here he explains who the strangers are, and what is their right hand of iniquity, and how they have spoken vanity. Augustine: He enumerates their happiness; this is their right hand, this is the vanity which they speak, when they call these things blessedness. Cassiodorus: Whose sons. Or, mystically these can be understood from that place, etc., up to: but have sprouted with new errors. Daughters. Cassiodorus: Which have no strength of constancy. Adorned. Not beautiful by nature, but adorned by men. These daughters are the thoughts or preachings of those who do not have the true Church but a likeness.
143.13: 143.13 Storehouses. Hearts made of diverse things: whence they breathe forth the worst belchings, which stink. From this to that. Unstable, because they have no root of truth.
143.14: 143.14 Their sheep fruitful. Literally, because he wishes to show them clinging to perishable things. As if he says: Their wealth is fruitful, while they themselves are barren in faith; whence mystically their disciples are these fruitful sheep, because they themselves beget many others in error. In their goings out. Not in their comings in, because all the good they seem to have goes out from them, soon to perish. Oxen. Not lean with labor, but fat with ease, as for those who abound in riches, while they themselves are fasting from the truth. Or mystically, oxen, teachers abounding in earthly things. Walls. Which are made of stones alone in gardens or vineyards; nor does that itself fall for them, therefore they are prosperous. Cassiodorus: Neither passing, nor outcry, disturbs their quiet, etc., up to: which leads to death.
143.15: 143.15 Blessed. He does not blame them for abounding in these things, but because they take them for the right hand, that is, for blessedness: and this is the vanity which they have spoken. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob also abounded in these. Happiness is the left hand, that is, temporal, mortal.
144.1: 144.1 A praise of David himself. Cassiodorus: This psalm briefly contains what is widely spread out in the divine Scriptures, etc., up to: lest anyone could err in his praise: Augustine: God fills the saints with the Holy Spirit, etc., up to: and therefore his spirit in his servants praises him, because he causes himself to be praised. Cassiodorus: As the seven psalms of penance, so also the seven spirits, according to that sacrament which the Lord commanded Moses, to put seven lamps in the tabernacle, shining with perpetual light. I will exalt you. Cassiodorus: First the prophet promises infinite praise; second, he says that all will carry out the praise of God in nine ways, there: Generation and generation; third, he explains the same more broadly, there: merciful. Forever and ever. Cassiodorus: He who does not begin here will be mute in the future.
144.2: 144.2 Every day, etc. The same: He who here every day, will in the eternal day deserve to praise with continual exultation. Augustine: He says well now every day, that when the one day without end has come, he may go from praise to praise, as from virtue to virtue. Forever and ever and ever. Cassiodorus: Of which praise elsewhere: They shall praise you forever and ever (Psalm 38), because they will always love him whom they will always see, than which vision nothing is more delightful.
144.3: 144.3 Greatly. Cassiodorus: By one word he gave to think what cannot be fully grasped: and therefore never cease from praises.
144.4: 144.4 Generation and generation. Cassiodorus: Second, he promises that all will carry out the praise of God in nine ways. Your works. Augustine: If we fail in greatness, let us praise the worker even from the works, from the created the Creator, from the creatures the creator. Cassiodorus: There are nine works: power, magnificence, holiness, wonders, strength, greatness of terrible things, memory, justice, which will be explained afterward: from these as from places and seeds all praise is drawn, in the manner in which all arguments are taken from the few places. And your power. Augustine: For they do not praise the works except to announce the virtue of the worker. But some eloquent men praise the creature, forgetful of the creator. The holy praisers, however, if they love the works, praise the worker more: and on account of these they love him. If in the things made some beauty, usefulness, virtue is perceived, it is praised the more in him who made it. If you praise the works, you also praise yourself, who are a work of God. And that comes to mind: Let not your own mouth praise you, lest you seem arrogant (Prov. 27). But it is not arrogance, because you praise God in you, not yourself.
144.6: 144.6 And the strength. If he did not threaten, there would be no correction; if he did not caress, there would be no exhortation. He is therefore lovable and terrible. They will therefore speak of the strength of the one who disciplines and punishes, if, preaching the eternal kingdom, they do not keep silent about the eternal fire.
144.7: 144.7 They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness. Augustine: He himself, through his abundant sweetness, is first mindful of us, calling us, going before us by his grace, and thence we are mindful of him. He says they shall pour forth, not they shall eat. Augustine: He eats who learns, he pours forth who teaches: yet he pours forth what he eats. This memory, because it is exceedingly sweet, must be eaten and poured forth. So eat, then, that you may pour forth.
144.8: 144.8 Merciful and compassionate. Cassiodorus: Third, he explains more broadly what he briefly set out in the second. As if: Deservedly they will praise in these, because merciful, etc. The parts of praise are put here which were above, but they cannot be explained one by one: for who could fully explain his works or power? Augustine: Merciful and compassionate. To those to whom he has given pardon. Patient. To those to whom he has not yet given, but waits to give.
144.9: 144.9 Cassiodorus: Mercies. He begins from works, so that he is called merciful when he restores the fallen. Compassionate, by nature, even when he creates. Patient, he takes this from the second place of praise, namely from power, which he praises, not that he hung the earth, restrained the seas, adorned the heavens with stars, etc., but because he tolerates sinners that they may be converted. And his mercies. Augustine: For if you take away your evil works, and none remain in you but his works, his mercy will not leave you: but if you do not leave your works, his severity will be on your works, when he shall say: Go, you cursed, into everlasting fire (Matt. 25).
144.10: 144.10 Let all your works confess to you, O Lord. Augustine: Let them praise as those do who have no sense of praising, who are the matter of praise: because when you inquire, you find great force in them, which is from God. And your saints. Cassiodorus: Everything that is confesses either by itself or through rational creatures. Or saints, that is, angels and men. This from holiness: for it is the holiness of God that the saints owe him confession.
144.11: 144.11 The glory of your kingdom. The same: It is therefore taken from the wonders. As if: How wonderful is he who made heaven and earth, and filled them with diverse goods.
144.12: 144.12 To make known. The same: This is taken from the strength of terrible things, etc., up to: to whom, the magnificent, nothing is compared.
144.13: 144.13 Your kingdom, etc. The same: He praises from the perpetuity and effect of dominion. And this is taken from greatness: if it is great to rule for a time, it is greater to have no end of dominion. The Lord is faithful in all. The same: This is taken from abundant sweetness; whence above: The memory of the abundance of your sweetness. Faithful, because he fulfilled the gifts of the advent. It belongs also to abundance that he lifts the falling, raises the crushed; whence the remembrance of sweetness is had, and is poured forth in his praises.
144.14: 144.14 Those who fall. Cassiodorus: From their evils, whom God lifts up, all of them. Or, from these temporal things, as the saints, like Job, who lose something in the world and become cast down, are the falling: but all these he confirms, because the just man falls seven times and rises; but the wicked are weakened in evils (Prov. 24). And he lifts up all who are crushed. Augustine: Those belonging to himself, because he resists the proud.
144.15: 144.15 The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord. The same: He treats more broadly of justice, so that he who hears the merciful one may fear the just: and it is of justice to satisfy those who hope, bodily or spiritually. For food is not always to be given, but in due season: for to many asking it is wholesomely deferred. And you give them food in due season. The same: The physician therefore gives to the sick what is fitting, etc., up to: blessing God at all times.
144.16: 144.16 You open your hand. The same: Even if at times you do not give, you give nevertheless opportunely: you defer indeed, you do not take away.
144.17: 144.17 Just. Cassiodorus: By the very name he opens justice, so that it may be plainly shown that this is praise from justice. Ways are the dispositions and wills, which are all just, even if he scourges. In his ways, and holy in all his works. It should be known that Ways pertain to disposition, works to effect: these are divided according to us. But with him, to will is to do: because by his will things have being.
144.18: 144.18 The Lord is near to all who call upon him. Cassiodorus: Propitious, who is everywhere, and this from justice.
144.19: 144.19 He will do the will of those who fear him. The same: He concludes about justice: for it is fair both to guard those who love and to destroy sinners.
144.21: 144.21 The praise. Cassiodorus: All having been set out, a brief conclusion follows, by which he concludes that which cannot be explained.
145.1: 145.1 Alleluia. Cassiodorus: This voice, like a saving music, like a heavenly harmony, which delights not only men but also angels, expresses the praise of God. It is fittingly prefixed to this psalm, where the just man exhorts the soul to the praise of God: because in adversities the soul is sometimes, willing or unwilling, disturbed. Whence above: Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you disturb me? But to take away its disturbance, he suggests joy from hope, if not in reality: Hope in God, etc. Augustine: Raised by this hope the soul praises God here. Cassiodorus: First, he counsels himself, as all, to praise, lest he pray in vain things; and as though acquiescing in the counsel, he asserts that he will praise there where he can fully. Second, he admonishes others not to hope in man, there: Put not your trust. Third, he teaches that all hope is to be placed in the Almighty, there: Blessed, etc.
145.2: 145.2 Praise the Lord, O my soul. But it is asked, by whom, to whom is this counsel given? If it is said that the flesh counsels the soul, this does not seem true, since counsel is usually given by the better and worthier to the inferior: but the flesh is inferior to the soul. For the soul, though blamed because sinful, is nevertheless said to be better by nature than the body praised in its own kind, because the spiritual nature surpasses the body, which it moves, rules, gives sense to, holds: and it itself, infinite, is near to the substance of God. So gold, blamed because filthy, is above lead praised for purity: so also a bad man above the best horse. Counsel is not therefore given to the soul by the flesh, however tamed and pacified: which, nevertheless, is dead because of sin. Nor does mortal flesh counsel the immortal soul, because it is always beneath the soul; but the higher part of the soul, namely the mind, which thinks on divine wisdom, clinging to it and sighing for it, sees certain parts of itself disturbed by the movements of the world, carried off to outward things by the desire of earthly things: whence it calls it back to the inward and higher. Exhorting itself, then, according to sensuality, it says: Praise the Lord, my soul. For what pleases you in this world? Divided by so many loves of worldly things, gather yourself to the author: here for you is peace and security. Then the soul answers the mind, as though weighed down here and unable to desist as is fitting. I will praise in my life. Here in death I will praise feebly, because the body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks on many things (Wisdom 9); here hope feeds, life in the future. In my life. Cassiodorus: When I shall have perfectly clung to him, from whom to be separated, as now happens, is death: but hope consoles, in which in a way living it praises. As long as. Not that at some time it will not be, because it will be forever, and therefore truly long.
145.3: 145.3 Put not your trust, etc. Cassiodorus: The second part. Counsel having been given and affirmed, where he will be able to praise fully, as though far removed, and meanwhile while there are evils by which the soul is disturbed, he admonishes not to hope in man, but in God. Augustine: Or as one placed in mind at the end of the age: he teaches not to love for eternal things what is soon to end; as if also by my example, put not your trust, etc. In the sons of men. The same: In one son of man is salvation, and hope in him. Not because he is the son of man, but because he is the Son of God. Not on account of that which he took from you, but on account of that which he preserved in himself.
145.4: 145.4 His spirit shall go forth, etc. Cassiodorus: First he cleanses hearts by forbidding harmful things, that afterward he may attend, by admonishing, to wholesome things.
145.5: 145.5 Blessed is he whose God is the God of Jacob. Cassiodorus: The third part, where he teaches that all hope is to be placed in the Almighty, whom he describes from his deeds, that the Gentile world, so often convicted, may rest. Augustine: Harmful things being removed, he teaches what is of salvation, namely in whom one must hope. His helper is his hope. Cassiodorus: He was thus the helper of Jacob himself, etc., up to: that is, of this true Jacob, as of that one.
145.6: 145.6 Who made heaven and earth. The same: Because even the worshipers of demons have hope in their god, he specifies in whom hope ought to be, that is, in Christ, and this he shows to the end of the psalm, describing him through all things. All that are in them. Lest you think another is creator, or that the creator of the tiniest things exists.
145.7: 145.7 Who keeps truth forever. Cassiodorus: Christ, who is the truth, every man a liar. He executes judgment. These two pertain to justice. Christ the judge avenges those who suffer for his name, and gives food to those who love him. To those who suffer wrong. Augustine: Not every trouble is a wrong. What you suffer by right is not a wrong, as what a robber and other criminals suffer. It is one thing, then, to suffer wrong, another punishment. For one suffers punishment by right, but wrong is contrary to right.
145.8: 145.8 The Lord looses the fettered. Cassiodorus: This for the abundance of sweetness. The Lord lifts up the crushed. Those whom the devil crushes, the Lord lifts up. The Lord loves the just. Cassiodorus: Whom he places in eternal blessedness.
145.9: 145.9 He will receive the fatherless and the widow. Augustine: The whole Church of the nations is an incomer to the fathers, a daughter not by flesh but by imitation. The fatherless are all those in pilgrimage, whose father is absent; and every faithful soul is a widow, the bridegroom being absent: whence they desire the more the father and the bridegroom, and these God protects, not seen but desired.
145.10: 145.10 The Lord shall reign forever. Cassiodorus: This is from magnificence. He will reign in us, when our hearts will be firm in him, which is not yet the case.
146.1: 146.1 Alleluia. Augustine: Here again he speaks of the praise of God, where the prophet admonishes to praise him who gathers Israel. Praise the Lord. Cassiodorus: First he shows whom he gathers and how. Second, after what was said, he rebukes those as yet hesitating and doubting, showing whence they can praise God, namely if they are humble, there: Sing before.
146.2: 146.2 The Lord building up Jerusalem. Augustine: Or he took Jerusalem as the general Church, etc., up to: whom the Father sent to redeem our captivity with the price of blood.
146.3: 146.3 And binds up. By likeness of a physician, etc., up to: and the Lord binds up their bruises. Jerome: As that Samaritan who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 10), when he saw the wounded man lying on the road, bound up his wounds. But of those who have not bruised their heart it is said through Isaiah: There is no plaster to apply, nor oil, nor bandages (Isa. 1, according to the Seventy). The bindings of God are the temporal sacraments, by which meanwhile we have consolation; which will be taken away when perfect health comes.
146.4: 146.4 Who numbers the multitude of the stars, and calls them all by names. Cassiodorus: Not foreign ones, like the astrologers who name Jupiter and Venus. Or, typically, concerning the saints, because he gives each his own gift; or, all are in familiarity, by the likeness of the Lord, who knows the names of his servants.
