146.5: 146.5 Of his wisdom, etc. Augustine: The very measure, and number and weight, etc., up to: see what follows, but humbling sinners.
146.6: 146.6 But humbling sinners. Augustine: For those who reprove intelligible things, therefore savor earthly things, thinking of the incorporeal God in bodily terms. He does this to those who wish to mock the law before they know it. Since, therefore, it is a great thing to advance to intelligible and spiritual things, let us be meek, let us knock and do what follows.
146.7: 146.7 Sing before. Thus one will come to understanding, thus the image will be reformed in God. Sing before. Cassiodorus: Second, from what was said, he rebukes and urges those as yet hesitating, showing whence they can understand, if humble and not proud. As if: And that you may be able to understand, sing before, etc.
146.8: 146.8 Who covers the heaven. Cassiodorus: He recalls the works through which power is shown. For to this end he wished certain things in the Scriptures to be obscure, that the servants of God might have something by interpreting to pour upon the ears and hearts of men, who receive from the clouds of God the richness of spiritual joy. For the service of men. The preachers, who serve men. Whence the Apostle says: And ourselves your servants through Jesus Christ (2 Cor. 4). These sow spiritual things and receive from the high ones of the age hay and grass, that is, temporal things.
146.9: 146.9 And to the young ravens. Augustine: For all that is given to the Church by the rich is hay. The same: The Jews, who called themselves alone just, and all the nations sinners. And truly our fathers were ravens, but we do not remain so: yet rightly we are called and are the young of ravens. The raven does not call, but we, being sent away, call. Cassiodorus: The young ravens are said to feed on dew and the kindness of the weather, and are ignorant of the paternal foods, that is, the stench of carcasses: so the innocent sons of the pagans, who call.
146.10: 146.10 In the legs of a man. In the composed bearing of the presumptuous and bold. For by the man he notes the bold presumer. In the legs is noted an uncomposed gait, in the legs of a man. Or, according to another reading, in the tents of a man, that is, in the conventicles of heretics, it will be well pleasing to him. Note that he does not say in the tents of God, but of a man, designating by this the boldness of the heretics.
146.11: 146.11 Upon those who fear, etc. Augustine: He joined hope to fear, because fear is of no avail without hope of pardon: for Judas, fearing but despairing, hanged himself by a noose. He who fears God, then, let him hope also in him. You will appease him if you hope in his mercy, and for the future so beware of sinning that you pray concerning the past that it be forgiven you.
147.1: 147.1 Alleluia. This psalm creates love for the future Jerusalem. It is attributed to Haggai and Zechariah, who in the captivity prophesied the restoration of Jerusalem, which, as Jeremiah foretold, took place after seventy years, that is, after the revolution of the whole of time, which is accomplished in seven days. Praise, O Jerusalem. Cassiodorus: This whole psalm proclaims the power of God. First, he tells the goods of the future Jerusalem, second, he tells what goods are given here to the saints, there: Who sends forth. Augustine: The prophet, still set in captivity, etc., up to: we who have heard one thus pouring forth.
147.2: 147.2 He has strengthened the bars of your gates. Augustine: Note that the door is closed, the prudent having been admitted and the foolish virgins shut out, so that no one now goes out or comes in. And fittingly after the admonition to praise he adds about the shut doors: for with the door of Jerusalem shut it praises securely, because no one has gone out at whom to grieve; no one enters whom to fear, whence scandals would be. scandals.
147.3: 147.3 With the fat of wheat. The same: With the bread that came down from heaven: in the world he is shut in flesh, known by faith alone, then he will be seen as he is.
147.4: 147.4 Who sends forth his word. The second part adds what gifts are given here to the elect, through which the truth of the future can be recognized. To the earth. Augustine: That he may be known on the earth. For unless he sent his word to the earth, by which we are weighed down and hindered from returning, we would not be lifted to the fat of wheat that satisfies. For on the earth, where we labor weary, languid, slothful, cold, namely in the desert, he does not forsake, but manna, he who sends forth his word, etc. It runs swiftly. Augustine, Cassiodorus: Or up to swiftness, that is, from God, so that swiftness itself is that than which nothing could be said more choicely or expressly. He does not say a swift word, swift with a swiftness in which it shares more or less: but by the swiftness itself, by which the rest are called swift, nothing is swifter. And again, what is swift, as a horse is to someone, is not everywhere: but swiftness itself is everywhere, is not in a part. It belongs to the Word of God not to be in a part, to be everywhere by himself. This is the wisdom which reaches from end to end mightily, yet not by local motion but by immobility. But also of the spirit of wisdom it is said, active, mobile, certain, undefiled; this swiftness does, that it be both always everywhere and nowhere be held shut in. But who is sufficient to think on these things? There is, however, hope for grasping the Word, because he has predestined us.
147.5: 147.5 Who gives snow, etc. Augustine: To the earth. For as charity grows cold, etc., up to: and these, while he calls them to penance, he scatters mist like ashes. The same: He scatters mist like ashes, etc. Ashes pertain to penance, etc., up to: and he who predestined and called to penance. Literally: God scatters snow like wool, mist like ashes, makes crystal like morsels of white bread. For crystal is a kind of stone like glass, but white: and snow is said to be ice hardened over many years, so that it cannot be dissolved. His crystal, etc. That is, the obstinate, who are not easily dissolved like snow.
147.6: 147.6 He sends his crystal like morsels, etc. Another reading, like pieces of bread, that they may feed others, that they may preach the truth which they attack. All together, one bread; individually, pieces; whence: We, many, are one bread in Christ (1 Cor. 10). Paul was a crystal, hard and bright: hard, because he persecuted the Church; bright, because skilled in the law. But God dissolved him, and he became bread, who taught the truth. But unless he dissolve, Who shall stand before the face of God? Another reading, shall subsist. Augustine: It is the cold, who forsakes, does not call, does not pour in grace: and who else will dissolve? No one. Whence the Apostle: Who will deliver me from the body of this death? (Rom. 7). As if he says: I grow cold, no one dissolves, unless the grace of God sends forth his word.
147.7: 147.7 He shall send forth his word, and shall melt them. Cassiodorus: For when the Word of God comes, neither cold, nor obscurity, nor hardness can despair. For they are wholesomely melted, and pour forth streams of spiritual benefit for others to drink from, according to that: All you who thirst, come to the waters (Isa. 55).
147.8: 147.8 Jacob... Israel. Augustine: Or the same is signified by Israel, etc., up to: because he was not sent but to the sheep that were lost of the house of Israel (Matt. 15). His judgments. The same: Judgment begins from the house of God, etc., up to: adding three other psalms of praise, that in this work the grace of the Trinity may shine forth.
148.1: 148.1 Praise the Lord from the heavens. Cassiodorus: By the mention of a few things he exhorts the whole creation to praise God. There are some that have the spirit of praising God in that affection with which God pleases them: some have no understanding, but because they themselves are good in their order, and are referred to the beauty of the whole, they do not praise by themselves, but God is praised by those who attend to them: and so in a way they praise, because from them praise of God is born in us, to which the prophet here admonishes us.
148.5: 148.5 For he spoke, and they were made. Cassiodorus: This against those who say the world is coeternal with God; it follows: He commanded. By his word, and they were created. First he said, made, afterward created. For we too can make, but not create. He alone, therefore, creates, which is proper to the Godhead. Praise from the works.
148.6: 148.6 He established. From power he is omnipotent, whose works are not changed. Forever and ever. Cassiodorus: And even if heaven is new, yet those things are said to be well established by God which are renewed through Christ and abide improved. And this is praise from power.
148.7: 148.7 Praise the Lord. The second part, where, having enumerated the heavenly things, he descends to the earthly. Turned, then, to those, as exhorting us to praise God by considering those things which, when considered, open the praise of God, he says: O you who are of the earth. All depths. Augustine: The depths of the waters, etc., up to: he exhorts them, that is, us, to praise by the consideration of them.
148.8: 148.8 Which do his word. This because it seemed to some that God ruled the higher things but despised these lower, and these were ruled by chance; but God does these things too, and is praised in these least things, and alleluia is sung.
148.13: 148.13 Confession. Cassiodorus: Above he spoke first of heaven, afterward of earth; here of all together. And he takes by heaven all higher things, and by earth all lower things. Augustine: His confession is above heaven and earth. All things confess him in themselves or in others; the beauty of all is the voice of those who confess, in those who attend to them, that is, let those who attend praise him, both for earthly and heavenly things, than whom there is nothing better.
148.14: 148.14 He has exalted the horn of his people. The same: Behold what Haggai and Zechariah prophesied. Now the horn of his people is humble in tribulations, but when the Lord comes it shall be exalted.
149.1: 149.1 Alleluia. Cassiodorus: After all the creatures whom in the preceding psalm he admonished to praise God, because they were created by him, here more properly and specially he invites Israel to a new song for the newness made for it, which is the more wonderful work of God: this is the sanctification of Israel, by which from old it was made new. Sing to the Lord, etc. Cassiodorus: First he admonishes in many ways to praise the king who is benevolent and beneficent to them. Second, he treats of the joys of the saints, there: They shall rejoice. Augustine: Whoever wishes to sing this song, let him love eternal things, that he may be made new. For the old man sings an old song about earthly things. The new man sings a new one about spiritual things; a song namely of peace, a song of charity and gladness. For whoever follows the old animosity, not the new charity, does not sing the new song. His praise in the Church. Cassiodorus: Here he specifies where and by whom this song ought to be sung.
149.2: 149.2 In their king. The same: That is, in Christ, who is king and priest. Augustine: As king he fought for us from the cross, conquering the devil: as priest he offered himself for us, finding nothing in men to offer for them.
149.3: 149.3 In choir. The same: Because there is no dispersion, but dearest unity; then the exultation will be of the timbrel and the psaltery, not the act of the thing itself.
149.4: 149.4 Because the Lord is well pleased. The same: In the first creation of things we read that all pleased God, etc., up to: or when he will make him equal to the angels.
149.5: 149.5 The saints shall exult. The same: The second part, where he treats of the joys and power of the saints. Glory. It is the frequent praise of good acts, over which the just rejoice in their beds, that is, in conscience, because they have so good a Lord, who gives grace to sinners and eternal life in merits. The fool outside rejoices in the fables of men; for the saints this is the manner of joy, that good things be referred to him who gave them.
149.6: 149.6 Exultations. The same: The power and might of God is proclaimed in the glory of the saints. In beds, in diverse mansions is the glory of the saints. Of which the Lord: In my Father's house are many mansions (John 14). In their throat. Those who in heart and tongue do not cease to praise him, from whom they have eternal things. Swords. Receiving the power of the word of God, they will judge with the Lord, sitting upon twelve seats; and then truly vengeance and rebuke will be made upon the peoples, then the kings of the earth will be bound: so that it is not free to go out. And the nobles shall bear iron chains, as heavy to carry and which cannot be broken: and so the written judgment will be made, that is, approved by the angels. Of which the Apostle: Do you not know that we shall judge angels? (1 Cor. 6). And lest you think the apostles alone judge, he adds, this glory, namely the power of judgment, is for all his saints, that is, the perfect, who for Christ left all earthly things. Augustine: The exultations of God in the throat. For they so rejoice in their beds and throats, that is, in heart and tongue, that they do not ascribe to themselves that they are good, but to God, from whom they have received what they are, and they hope for that which they are not yet.
149.8: 149.8 To bind. By these bonds of the commandments and precepts of God the kings of the nations, the nobles of the age, are bound by the weak and contemptible of this world, whom the Lord chose to confound the strong; and he filled them with the Holy Spirit, and gave them two-edged swords, that they might turn the hearts of the nobles to the fear of Christ, and, secular nobility being despised, choose poverty and nobility in Christ. For he wished to profit the emperor through the fisherman, not the fisherman through the emperor. Augustine: Through these he binds kings and nobles in iron chains, lest they proceed to unlawful things.
106.3: 106.3 And from the sea. Cassiodorus: For the south he puts the sea, understanding the ocean of that region; this can be taken for any part of the world.
106.4: 106.4 They wandered. The same: The second part, where the first temptation, etc., up to: fourth, for being heard, the confession, that is, the praise.
106.5: 106.5 Hungry. Augustine: It signifies the curious of the world, who sought the truth by diverse opinions, and did not find it. Their soul, etc. God commends himself, as is expedient for us; we faint that we may ask, and love the one who comes to our aid.
106.6: 106.6 And he led. Augustine: As if: he rescued from ignorance; showing the way, Christ. Behold, he freed them from error; but how he delivered them from the hunger and thirst with which they burned, he will tell afterward; but he puts confession first.
106.8: 106.8 Wonders. Jerome: As if mercies were given in a wonderful manner of redemption.
106.9: 106.9 The hungry. Cassiodorus: Either knowing his desire, or not knowing his desire but failing from excessive fasting, as usually happens to one worn out by too great hunger or sickness, so that he has no desire to eat but fails from extreme want of food. Sitting. Augustine: The third part, where the second temptation is set, etc., up to: and let us consider that we also can do this.
106.11: 106.11 Because they provoked. The same: This is another, again attempting, etc., up to: whence he was angry with them. The counsel of the Most High. That those who were proud might be humbled in straits, which was a wholesome counsel, that the disease of the world might be cured by the contrary remedy.
106.12: 106.12 And there was none who. The same: For when God withdraws his help, you can labor against vices, but not conquer; and when you are pressed by your perverse habit, the heart will be humbled, that you may learn to cry out, whence he adds: And they cried out.
106.13: 106.13 And they cried out. Cassiodorus: For a similar cause, the same sentence as above.
106.16: 106.16 Gates of brass. The same: The gates of brass are the vicious habits of men, which do not allow those shut in to go out. Bars. The unclean spirits, which bolt the gates. Of brass, of iron, he puts for strength, but the power of God breaks them.
106.18: 106.18 All food. Augustine: The fourth part, where the third temptation is set, which is weariness. Those who above languished with hunger are likewise endangered by disgust; so do not think that those who are full are safe, for they also die of disgust. And this is all food, etc. Augustine: After one has come from ignorance to truth, from error to the way, from hunger of wisdom to the word of faith, and after he has overcome the difficulties of evils so as to live without complaint, weariness remains, so that at times he delights neither in reading nor in prayer; he has escaped inexperience and desire, but dies of weariness.
106.23: 106.23 They who go down to the sea. The fifth part, etc., up to: if the whole ship is in danger.
106.24: 106.24 They saw the works of the Lord. Augustine: Or they saw, etc., up to: he explains their storms, adding: he spoke and it stood. In the deep. He spoke and the spirit of the storm stood, etc. The same: The deep is the heart of men, from which the winds burst forth, and storms of sedition and dissension arise.
106.27: 106.27 Like a drunken man. The same: They stagger, because their prosperity or adversity is greater than their strength. And all their wisdom was swallowed up. They appear restlessly wise when they speak, when they read; but when the storm comes, all human counsels fail; what is to be done is not seen. It remains, then, to cry out, that God may make their heart firm, lest it be tossed by temptations.
106.32: 106.32 In the Church. Augustine: Behold from what he has said all these things, and where all the aforesaid things are done.
106.33: 106.33 He made rivers. Cassiodorus: The sixth part up to here, how he makes even the evils of enemies profitable. Augustine: He made rivers. Consequently the Church is commended, etc., up to: whence the benefits toward the Church of God are plainly shown.
106.34: 106.34 Into saltiness. Cassiodorus: Salt moisture, where it prevails, takes away fruitfulness. For the wickedness of those who dwell in it. Augustine: On account of the wickedness of those who inhabited that land, that is, the tabernacle of the Lord, with deceitful minds.
106.37: 106.37 And they sowed. Cassiodorus: They sow fields and plant vineyards who purify their bodies by heavenly discipline, so as to bear the fruit of good works.
106.38: 106.38 Greatly: Cassiodorus: for exceedingly, or because many are called, but few are chosen.
106.39: 106.39 And they were made few. Augustine: The seventh part, where something is also said about heretics, etc., up to: but they were not of the fewness of the elect. Vexed. Cassiodorus: Either persisting through heretics, or heretics by the snares of the devil. Grief and tribulation for those who forsake the author of salvation.
106.40: 106.40 Contempt was poured out. Augustine: Or, contempt was poured out, etc., up to: and what did he do even about those seduced ones? Behold.
106.41: 106.41 He helped the poor man. God could have always endured them within, but we would not have profited from them. But when they are separated, and disturb us by questions, there arises in us a zeal for inquiry and an example of fear, that he who stands may take heed lest he fall. And what happens to those seduced ones in the poor man's being helped? And he set them like sheep. You thought it was one poor man; but this poor man is of a great household, of many churches: yet there is also one Church, one sheep. These great mysteries, long hidden, and therefore sweetly found.
106.42: 106.42 The upright shall see and rejoice. Augustine: Behold to what the Psalmist tends: namely to show that the good are exalted by the mercy of God, as the wicked are ground down by pride.
106.43: 106.43 Who is wise and will keep these things? The same: A conclusion, as if to say: since the Lord helps the poor man, therefore: Who is wise? Mercies. That he frees from error, etc., up to: and the wicked shall stop his mouth.
107.1: 107.1 A song of a psalm. Augustine: From the last parts of two, etc., up to: that the sayings of the prophets might be fulfilled. Cassiodorus: Here many of the same things as above, etc., up to: and they are well joined, for they in no way conflict. The same: In the first, David's flight is dealt with, etc., up to: A song for divine things, a psalm for active works.
107.2: 107.2 Ready. Cassiodorus: The sixth psalm on the two natures in Christ. My heart is ready. First Christ gives thanks, because, undertaking the passion, he rose into glory. Second, what salvation was brought to all the earth, there: That they may be delivered.
107.7: 107.7 That they may be delivered. The same: The second part, what salvation was brought to all the earth over which is glory; here also the humility of humanity and the power of majesty are shown. Save. That they may be delivered in the future, here save them lest they fall. Or, he asks to be saved in the resurrection, that the faithful may be delivered, who by such a sign sensed his divinity. As if: that I may sing and make psalms, Save me in the resurrection by your right hand, that is, through the Word, who is the arm of the Father, that so your beloved may be delivered. The order of the words is reversed. For he says: Save me and hear me, and save me.
107.8: 107.8 I will rejoice. Augustine: Or I shall be exalted; above, I shall be glad; here, however, I shall be exalted, which is quite fitting, because gladness comes from exaltation. And Christ speaks here in the person of the Church.
107.9: 107.9 And Ephraim. The same: Ephraim is mine, that is, mine is the fruitfulness, which is the support of my head. This fruitfulness comes from the fact that the head received me, or I the head. Cassiodorus: Or Ephraim, that is, fruitfulness, is the support of my head, because when my head received the crown of thorns, it bore fruit beyond all: for Christ has gained the whole world.
107.11: 107.11 Who will lead me into the fortified city. The same: As a man, Christ asks, that he may answer; he denies that this can be done by man. The city is hell, which no one could open. The nations of Edom, to whom he became known after the resurrection: these things could be done by the Godhead alone.
107.12: 107.12 Have you not rejected us, and will you not go forth. The same: He says us in the plural, because here Christ suffers with his members, above, saying in the singular, he will lead me. Seek the expositions of all these in the ninth psalm.
108.1: 108.1 Unto the end, a psalm. Augustine: A prophecy about Christ, etc., up to: and the things expressed about Judas, as that: And let another take his bishopric. Cassiodorus: The fifth of those which treat more broadly of the passion.
108.2: 108.2 O God, my praise. Cassiodorus: He admonishes to turn aside from the wickedness of Judas, etc., up to: so Christ, as man praying to the Father, says: For the mouth of the sinner. The same: A fitting contrast, because the wicked do not keep silent their reproach.
150.1: 150.1 Praise the Lord. Cassiodorus: Of the praise of God in his saints, who glorified praise without end. The city of God, namely the unity of all the saints, is admonished to sing with mouth and mind. To this summit all psalmody is brought, which is sung with a nuptial sweetness. Praise him in the firmament. Augustine: There is strength in the firmament, etc., up to: who, honoring one another in turn, give praise to God. Cassiodorus: To whom the prophet at the beginning showed the form of conduct, now, those received into that Jerusalem, he says God is to be praised in them, who gave all things. In the firmament, because by his death he conquered the devil and led believers to heaven. In his mighty acts, or powers, because all things are subject under his feet.
150.2: 150.2 According to the multitude of his greatness. How is this, since there is no end of his greatness? But it is said to the spiritual and holy. And though there is no end of his greatness, God is praised according to it, since he is praised without end. But how he ought to be praised, he says by mystical similitudes to the end of the psalm: Let the trumpet sound for the king, the psaltery sing to God: the harp with the rest for the bridegroom. For the terrible trumpet is either taken up in war, or is prepared at the coming of kings; the psaltery sounds from above, the harp from below: all these, compared to human acts, are said figuratively to sound the praises of God there.
150.4: 150.4 With strings and organ. Cassiodorus: He puts strings for every musical instrument which sounds by the tension of strings. The organ is like a tower built of diverse pipes, sounding by the breath of bellows; and that you might take all these of men, it comes to the mouth of man: and explaining what it is to praise with strings and organ, he adds. Praise him with cymbals, etc. The well-sounding cymbals are our lips, which, harmonious with the heart, sound well in the praises of God, in which there is a likeness of cymbals, and they render harmony, and therefore they are rightly among the musical instruments. Cassiodorus: The well-sounding cymbals are, of mixed metals, very small bowls, which give a sharp sound. But because he wishes all things understood spiritually, he concludes with a fitting end:
150.6: 150.6 Let every spirit, angelic and human, praise the Lord. Not flesh and blood, not the habit of the age: but what is more sublime in the nature of things, which savors heavenly things, grasps eternal things. A brief and perfect knowledge, that all things praise God spiritually; in these is the perfection of all music. For there is breath in the trumpet, striking in the harp and in the cymbals, voice in the choir. By these musical instruments is signified a spiritual harmony, which is perceived not by the ears but by a pure mind. Augustine: There are three kinds, etc., up to: it is the voice of eternal life: Let every spirit praise the Lord.
108.3: 108.3 Without cause. Augustine: As righteousness pleases the pious for its own sake, so iniquity pleases the wicked.
108.4: 108.4 Instead of loving me. The same: Those who speak against Christ in his members do more harm, because they kill the souls of those who would believe, than those who killed his flesh, which was soon to rise again.
108.5: 108.5 And they set against me. Augustine: There are six differences, etc., up to: which is good for evil, which God as judge also does. Cassiodorus: Every sin is contracted in three ways, etc., up to: which Christ did, praying for the Jews.
108.6: 108.6 Set over. Augustine: The second part, where he begins to prophesy what they shall receive for their impiety. Above, concerning many, etc., up to: whose person Judas bore. Set a sinner over him. As of Judas, so of them.
108.7: 108.7 When he is judged, let him go out condemned. Because those who remain in wickedness store up wrath for themselves. Let his prayer become sin: because it is not made through the mediator.
108.8: 108.8 Let his days be few. According to the kingdom, which did not stand long afterward. Bishopric, that is, Christ, whom the people of the nations received when he was sent to them.
108.9: 108.9 Let his children be orphans: the kingdom having been lost, as though a father; or God the Father. Wife, that is, the people. Widows, the kingdom being lost.
108.10: 108.10 Let them be carried away, as was done in the captivity. Let them beg, under the kings of the nations.
108.11: 108.11 All his substance, that is, his life, punishing each point of sin; their debts are not forgiven, because they are forgiven only in Christ. And strangers, that is, the devil and his angels. Let them plunder his labor, because they do not lay up treasure in heaven.
108.12: 108.12 And let there be none to him, etc. That is, there is no helper for him who lacks Christ. Nor let there be any to pity. I do not say for having temporal things, but eternal.
108.13: 108.13 Let his children come to everlasting destruction. Therefore because they remained in one generation, that is, because they were not regenerated. And let his name be blotted out. That is, of earthly Jerusalem, which is in bondage with her children, which killed the prophets.
108.15: 108.15 And let it perish from the land of the living, that is, the Church. Their memory, because though they were natural branches, they were made.
108.16: 108.16 Because he did not remember. By repenting. To show mercy. Toward the members of Christ.
108.18: 108.18 Cursing, and it shall come to him: and he would not have blessing. Augustine: Sins now delight, but they are called a curse, because they prepare torments.
108.19: 108.19 With which he is covered. He seems to say here, etc., up to: let him always be ready, whence here he says he is always girded.
108.20: 108.20 With the Lord. The same: They speak against Christ in particular who say he is not from the Father, or is less than the Father. Evil against my soul. Saying that he could not have risen, though he wished.
108.21: 108.21 And you, Lord. Cassiodorus: The third part, where he prays, etc., up to: help me, according to the man. For your name's sake. For by no works, etc., up to: because your mercy is sweet.
108.22: 108.22 For I am needy and poor. The same: The need and poverty of Christ is the weakness from which he was crucified.
108.23: 108.23 Like a shadow when it declines I am taken away. Cassiodorus: As night comes from a declining shadow, so death comes from mortal flesh.
108.24: 108.24 Changed. Augustine: The flesh of Christ was therefore changed, etc., up to: because Jesus was not yet glorified. For oil, that is, spiritual grace, from which Christ is named.
108.25: 108.25 They shook their heads. Cassiodorus: The raging threaten by shaking the head. Augustine: They shook their heads, because they saw him hanging on the cross, but not yet when the flesh was changed.
108.26: 108.26 Help me, Lord. Cassiodorus: He asks as man, he grants as God.
108.27: 108.27 This is your hand. Augustine: Christ is this hand, and is the Word with God and made it, when the Word was made flesh. For he was without time according to the divinity, and was made in time according to the flesh.
108.28: 108.28 They will curse, and you will bless. The curse of the wicked is one: God, when he blesses, does what he says.
108.29: 108.29 As with a double cloak, etc. Others interpret instead of diploid, a double mantle, that is, let them be confounded within and without, that is, before God and before men.
108.30: 108.30 Greatly with my mouth. Greatly is usually put for more than ought to be, but also for very. In the midst. Augustine: That is, in common, or in the heart.
108.31: 108.31 Because he stood at the right hand of the poor man. The devil at the right hand of Judas, etc., up to: but to save his soul from those who persecute.
109.1: 109.1 A psalm of David. Cassiodorus: This psalm is the seventh, etc., up to: whatever is contained in either Testament. Cassiodorus: The prophet exhorts to submission to Christ. First the prophet relates the words of the Father about the Son, etc., up to: this of humanity. The Lord said. Cassiodorus: In our manner, that man may be instructed. To my Lord. Distinguish the persons, and understand one nature and power. Sit. Rest after labor, and reign together, according to the man. At my right hand. In my better and hidden goods, until you reign openly. And this is, until I make your enemies, etc. Augustine: Sit, not only on high, that you may rule over the lofty, but also in secret, etc., up to: if he does not see what he believes. The footstool of your feet: by comparison, where full subjection is also marked. Through the feet, eternal stability: this daily happens in the converted.
109.2: 109.2 The rod of power. The kingdom of Christ begins from Zion, that is, from the Jews, whence he adds, The rod of power, etc. From Zion. The prophet is not speaking of that kingdom of Christ, etc., up to: and the remission of sins among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.
109.3: 109.3 With you is the principality. Cassiodorus: Second, the Father indicates the nature of the Divinity, etc., up to: when in the resurrection they will be radiant, like the angels of God. Augustine: Now he rules, now there is power; but on the day of special power, etc., up to: how the Father has the principality with him. This then, but now. From the womb, that is, as from my secret and hidden substance, etc., up to: who offers himself, whence follows, He swore, etc. Cassiodorus: Or With you is the principality: this the Father says; as if: this I grant you more than to another, because you are Son by nature. Augustine: Or it can be taken as from the person of the prophet speaking, etc., up to: with the Holy Spirit, who makes the saints radiant.
109.4: 109.4 The Lord has sworn. Cassiodorus: Third, the prophet deals with the humanity of Christ, etc., up to: hence it is established that the victims pass away according to the order of Aaron. He will not repent: you are a priest forever. Augustine: No repentance befalls God: for he knows what he does, and does not change his counsel, but by the word repentance is signified a change of things happening otherwise than one hoped. For it is as when you repent of having done something, you grieve over the deed you did.
109.5: 109.5 Kings. Augustine: Those who wish, or wished, to blot out the name of Christ.
109.6: 109.6 He will crush, that is, he has made weak, etc., up to: and now he will judge among the nations, so that he fills ruins, not those lifted up. He will judge among the nations. Cassiodorus: He breaks kings, as it were, for pride: he judges peoples for common sins: both, that they may be humbled to conversion. Or,
109.7: 109.7 Of the torrent. Cassiodorus: Of the passing and turbulent passion. In the way, by which one goes to another dwelling. He will lift up the head. Whence: For this reason God has exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.
110.1: 110.1 Alleluia. Cassiodorus: The first psalm through all the letters of the alphabet, etc., up to: third, he asserts that these same were redeemed, and that the New Testament will remain, there: Redemption. I will confess. Augustine: This is not a confession of sins, but of praise: that one mourns, this rejoices: that one shows the wound to the physician, this gives thanks for health. In the council. Not rashly, but from reason, namely for eternal things, like all the just. Cassiodorus: In the council of the just. Here never among all the just, where the wicked are mixed in, but they are now seen to sing in the future fellowship, carried away in hope to the heights. In the council, that is, when they judge with the Lord. In the congregation, when gathered from the whole.
110.2: 110.2 Great works. This is the matter and cause of the confession. Great are the works of the Lord, in that he makes the wicked man godly. Sought out. Augustine, Cassiodorus: Like which there is nothing, when he permits the devil to rage, etc., up to: not so: for his justice endures forever and ever. For all his wills. Augustine: Nothing overcomes the will of God, who, even if he wills that you not sin, does not however prevent it. If he wills to spare the penitent, he also wills to punish the unrepentant; thus concerning man God always fulfills his will, because man does nothing from which God does not work what he wills.
110.3: 110.3 His work is confession and magnificence. Cassiodorus: As if: I will confess, because great are the works of the Lord. Any works are also great, if in them are seen the intention and will, which is the confession of sins, and the magnificence of good works: and justice, that is, the reward, which is justly given.
110.4: 110.4 He has made a memorial. The same: Second, he says the faithful are filled with an abundant gift, promising the coming of the Lord, that the inheritance may be eagerly sought. Augustine: He has made a memorial of his wonders. Humbling this one and exalting that one, etc., up to: what will he receive when glorified in the future?
110.5: 110.5 He gave food. Cassiodorus: He makes confession and magnificence, etc., up to: that all things may be fulfilled. He will be mindful, etc. Augustine: He who gave a pledge has not given the whole, etc., up to: they enter through the piercing straits of the passion.
110.6: 110.6 The power of his works. Cassiodorus: The power of his works is that the blind see, etc. What he did is known to the Christian people. That he may give them the inheritance, this was the intention of the miracles, that they might believe.
110.7: 110.7 That he may give them the inheritance of the nations. The same: As if, although he gives them the inheritance, they will nevertheless suffer much. The works of his hands. The same: That is, of his power. Truth, when he restores to the converted what was promised: Judgment, which he threatens to the wicked. Augustine: Truth, which the holy martyrs hold, for which they are also judged here; and judgment, by which in the future they will judge those by whom they are judged here. The same: The works of his hands are truth and judgment. Let truth be held by those who are judged, etc., up to: this is the inheritance of the New Testament.
110.8: 110.8 All his commandments are faithful. Cassiodorus: Because they preserve those who keep them, they are not lies. Confirmed. Not sent in vain, like human words: Done, not merely said, in truth, because all things are fulfilled. In equity. Augustine: Because all things are with the balance of justice.
110.9: 110.9 He has sent redemption. Cassiodorus: Third, he asserts the redeemed, and the New Testament consecrated by eternal grace; or. His name: the beginning of wisdom. The same: That is, the Son, who in humanity is holy, in the power of divinity terrible. Let the advocate be loved, the judge feared, that you be not negligent, that you not despair. The fear of the Lord. The same: The dread of judgment is the gate of conversion, if the discretion of love is added. His praise endures. The intention of the psalm, whence alleluia is prefixed, began with praise and ends in praise; the faithful people, freed from the devil and giving thanks, expressed what is to be done here by the devout, and what is to be performed in heaven: here because he frees, there because he crowns.
111.1: 111.1 Alleluia of the return. Augustine: Haggai and Zechariah were long after David, etc., up to: that it may be established eternally. Cassiodorus: The perfection of this building, etc., up to: as those freed from captivity and cheerful over the goods they have. Blessed is the man. Cassiodorus: Here the Psalmist shows, after the deliverance, etc., up to: third, he asserts that adversities come upon the wicked. He who fears the Lord. The fear of the world makes men wretched, but the fear of God makes them desire those things through which man is blessed. In his commandments. This is the fear of God, that he wills. And he does not say he will do, etc., up to: and earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that thinks on many things.
111.2: 111.2 Mighty. Augustine, Cassiodorus: Behold the rewards of that blessed man. His seed. That is, the reward of good work; will be mighty on earth, not this one, where it is derided, but the heavenly. Or even here in this time, where it is less seen. Seed, works of mercy, whence an eternal harvest. Mighty, because by a very small thing, as if great, the kingdom of heaven is bought. Generation. Not of the flesh but of imitation. Or the works of the upright. The upright are those who do not resist the Father correcting them, and believe him who promises, and do not believe their works have perished when they are not repaid temporally. For there are those who do those good things hoping for a reward here from God, or wishing to please men, which is not the blessed man: and yet,
111.3: 111.3 Glory and riches are in his house. That is, in the secret of the heart, where he dwells with the hope of eternal life, where holy riches and eternal glory are stored. Justice. This is his glory, these his riches, which however he has from God. It endures forever. As if he is not blessed temporally.
111.4: 111.4 There has risen. Cassiodorus: Second, he deals with the coming of the Lord, etc., up to: that he may fortify it in judgment with firm pleadings and assertions. Or,
111.5: 111.5 He has mercy. The same: He who gives to the needy lends; he who lends a loan is to receive as much back afterward.
111.7: 111.7 His heart is ready to hope in the Lord, his heart is strengthened, it endures, etc. Augustine: It is therefore plain that he here seeks not his own things but those of Christ, patiently bears labors, confidently awaits the promises. Cassiodorus: Or, if anyone threatens evils, he does not fear, but is ready.
111.9: 111.9 He has distributed. He hopes not to fear, because he has distributed. He has given to the poor. Augustine: Behold, this man was buying what he did not see, but he was keeping a treasure in heaven who deigns to hunger and thirst in the poor on earth. His justice endures forever and ever. Cassiodorus: He gave his own, and lived justly and piously; or, he who gives his own works justice. His horn shall be exalted in glory. Because he is humble here, there he will have power.
111.10: 111.10 The sinner shall see. The same: Third, he asserts that the contrary comes upon the wicked. He exhorts with the goods of the blessed, he terrifies with the evils of enemies, and this psalm is instructive for the faithful. He shall be angry, gnash with his teeth and waste away, the desire of sinners shall perish, saying: What has pride profited us, and the boasting of riches? (Wisdom 5).
112.1: 112.1 Alleluia. Cassiodorus: Because he is rightly to be praised who by the merit of humility takes the nations to himself, he explains the title of the psalm. For Alleluia, as we have said, is interpreted praise the Lord, just as the psalm begins. Praise. The same: First the Prophet admonishes the devout to praise continually and proclaim everywhere. Second, he himself does what he admonishes others, that is, he praises God there: Who is like the Lord? (1 Cor. 14). So, admonishing to praise, he shows who, and whom, and how long, and where, and why they should praise. He says: Children. Not in understanding, but in malice, especially pride, that is, the humble, whence: Do not become children in understanding, but in malice be infants, that in mind you may be perfect. Augustine, Cassiodorus: Praise the Lord, children, the simple and pure, who ought to praise.
112.2: 112.2 Blessed be the name. Cassiodorus: Behold, he has said who, and whom they ought to praise; then he adds: how long he is to be praised, namely always. Blessed be the name of the Lord: do not think I command praise for an hour, etc., up to: through the nations the carnal, through the heavens the spiritual.
112.3: 112.3 From the rising of the sun. Augustine: Here he says that he ought to be praised everywhere.
112.4: 112.4 Above the heavens. The same: The apostles, through whom he reigns among the nations, and so it is; therefore I invite to praises, because he is to reign over all.
112.5: 112.5 Who is like. Cassiodorus: Second, he himself does what he admonishes others, that by deed he may teach others. Who? No one who can by himself. In the high places, etc. Angels and saints: and though high, he does not despise the humble.
112.6: 112.6 The lowly. These are they who by his gift become high, and he sits in them. He looks on, each of the humble. On earth, the saints whom he regards just as, conversely, he hates the proud.
112.7: 112.7 Raising up from the earth: from the labor of the body. From the dunghill, he is lifted up whom the vices of the flesh do not rule.
112.9: 112.9 Who makes to dwell. Cassiodorus, Augustine: He explains where he raises and lifts up, etc., up to: from the mammon of iniquity through works of mercy. The barren. Augustine: Namely Sarah, that is, the Gentile Church, which was formerly barren, whence it is signified by Sarah. Her, I say, he makes to dwell in the house, that is, in the Church of the Jews, among the Jews themselves, that in the cornerstone the two walls may be joined, and there be one sheepfold. Of children. The same: In whose person these things are said, etc., up to: when I know that I am without children, and a widow.
113.1: 113.1 Alleluia. Cassiodorus: Likewise here alleluia is placed for another reason, etc., up to: as becomes clear in the exposition of the psalm. When Israel went out. Augustine: Here past events are not narrated; rather future things are foretold, because in those deeds future things were signified: and therefore not all things are said here that were done there, but some things differently, lest he be thought to recall past events. Cassiodorus: First the Prophet tells what wonders God gave to the Hebrews in figure, and to Christians in spirit. Second he asks why these things were done, there: What ails you, O sea? Third he rejects the empty idols of the nations and commends the worship of God, there: The idols of the nations. When Israel went out. As when Israel, that is, the house of Jacob, went out of Egypt, that is, from a barbarous people. Barbarous. Augustine: A barbarous tongue is one that does not praise God.
113.2: 113.2 It was made. Cassiodorus: As that people, when it went out of Egypt, etc., up to: they can resist vices, and this.
113.3: 113.3 The sea saw it, that is, the sinners of the world. The Jordan, those who with various desires carry men off into the great sea, that is, the bitter malice of this world; but these cease at the coming of the Lord, as though turned backward. The sea saw. Augustine: This is said here differently from how it was done. There it is read that it stood on the side where the waters flowed from above, nor is anything said there of the mountains leaping, but both what was done there and what is said here are figures.
113.4: 113.4 Rams. The same: Those who with the horns of both, etc., up to: every knowledge raising itself against Christ. Hills. Cassiodorus: From colendo (cultivating), of middling size: for these things are not to be taken literally; so do not doubt that by the sea, and the Jordan, that is, by ancient deeds, are signified these things which are done today spiritually.
113.5: 113.5 What ails you. The same: Second he asks why these things, to arouse wonder. And he resolves it: At the presence of the Lord.
113.7: 113.7 At the presence. The same: One answer to both, because there is one author, who made both the ages marvel, and his own, that is, the mountains and hills, rejoice: for when Christ appeared, men were moved from their superstition to the worship of God. At the presence of the God of Jacob. And as though asking, who is the Lord? The God of Jacob, not new; who makes them wrestle.
113.8: 113.8 Who turned the rock. The same: The hard hearts of the Jews, into the water of baptism. The cliff. The Gentiles, that they too may pour forth watered fountains of preaching. Augustine: That is, himself, hard at first when he was unknown, etc., up to: he would flood over all who believe, saying: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.
113.9: 113.9 Not to us. Cassiodorus: When he said that God gives good things, etc., up to: truth, when he restores rewards, or punishes the wicked. Therefore, Give.
113.10: 113.10 Lest at any time: the wicked often charge this against the good who are afflicted. Mercy. Augustine: that is, restoration. Truth, that is, the promise fulfilled. Where is God. The same: The nations, who have visible gods, are accustomed to say this: because we worship an invisible God.
113.11: 113.11 In heaven. The same: that is, in Christ the man, according to that: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. Or, in heaven, Cassiodorus: that is, mighty over all creatures. All things whatsoever he willed he has done. Whereby he is shown omnipotent.
113.12: 113.12 The idols of the nations. The same: Third, he proves the idols empty, and shows how useful is the worship of God. And here is a perfect demonstration in reproach and in praise. Augustine: Having shown the power of the true God from his works, he passes to the visible gods of the nations. Silver. The same: But because God made this, he says, The works of the hands of men, they venerate what they made from it, for God created the material; but the folly of men added the form.
113.13: 113.13 They have mouths. The same: They are shaped by the hand, etc., up to: and served the creature rather than the Creator.
113.15: 113.15 They will not cry out. The same: After speaking, which is proper to man, he adds this common thing, etc., up to: an idol lacking life and sense.
113.16: 113.16 Like to them. The same: See the shameful worship, when he says, like to them, which they truly are; or let them understand themselves to be like them.
113.17: 113.17 The house of Israel. Cassiodorus: Here he shows the usefulness of the Christian religion.
113.18: 113.18 The house of Aaron. Augustine: But lest what is hope for the lesser seem already a reality for the greater, he adds, The house of Aaron.
113.20: 113.20 Mindful. Cassiodorus: That he might convert, and blessed the converted through the same.
113.22: 113.22 Upon you. Augustine: Because the number of teachers has grown. Upon your children. Because the number of followers has also grown. So you both, fathers and sons, are blessed by the Lord, who made you heaven in the elders and earth in the lesser; or made every creature.
113.23: 113.23 Blessed are you of the Lord. Cassiodorus: He who above wished them blessed, now confident says, Blessed, which pertains to God, that you serve him. Truly the Lord's, because even the heaven of heaven, that is, Christ, is for the honor of the Lord; or,
113.24: 113.24 The heaven of heaven, that is, the empyrean, he gave to the Lord Christ, according to the man. But the earth. This lower one he gave. To the children of men. That in it they may purify themselves, or the people to the preachers; whence: As the Father has sent me, so I also send you (John 6). The heaven of heaven. Augustine: He speaks of those whose minds, etc., up to: whom the weak, without support, cannot yet see.
113.25: 113.25 Nor all who go down. Cassiodorus: Or not all who go down; for the saints too went down, but not into the lower place.
114.1: 114.1 Alleluia. This title is often repeated, because the praise of God is both the dignity of works and the price of labors, that is, it is merit and reward. Augustine: The Prophet, freed from the pit of sinners and set upon the rock, first gives thanks because he was heard, and says he called upon him against all dangers. This psalm is a consolation for the faithful against the sorrows of the world. I have loved. The same: The sheep that had strayed says this, the returned son, the pilgrim of this world. Cassiodorus: I have loved. Not on account of the temporal goods given to me, as unbelievers do, but because, etc. God is loved even by unbelievers because he gives good things; whence: I will confess to you when you have done well to him (Psalm 48). He is loved perfectly when the mind is not moved by adversities, but is kindled by hope: which manner he afterwards explains, I have loved. Not because he made me a king, gave prosperity, but because he hears prayer in distress.
114.2: 114.2 And in my days. Augustine: Namely of my misery, which I made for myself by sinning, which are full of labor and sorrow, that is, of old corruption. I will call upon. Which is not without faith; whence the Apostle: How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? (Rom. 10). So when he says, they will call upon, he notes that the lover is not idle. In which, They have surrounded me, etc. Or, in the days of salvation, that is, the time of fullness; whence: Behold, now is the acceptable time, etc. (2 Cor. 6).
114.3: 114.3 Sorrows. Cassiodorus: Sins, whence the sorrow and death of the soul; or, eternal, this will be in hell. The perils of hell. Augustine: For, suffused with carnal pleasure, I did not notice the evils surrounding me.
114.4: 114.4 Tribulation and sorrow. The same: As if: those first surrounded me, but afterwards I found tribulation and sorrow, that is, that outward affliction is useful.
114.5: 114.5 O Lord, deliver. Cassiodorus: Second, he likewise cries out, that being freed he may come to rest. Merciful is the Lord. Augustine: Because first he inclined his ear to me and called me. Just. Because again he scourges. He has pity. Because he receives to blessedness. What he scourges ought not to be so bitter as what he receives is sweet, because the Lord keeps the little ones, whom he seeks as grown heirs.
114.7: 114.7 Return. The same: Not by your merits or strength, but because the Lord has done well to you.
114.8: 114.8 From death my eyes. The same: Death is unbelief; whence: Let the dead bury their dead; and again: The dead shall not praise you, O Lord (Psalm 103).
114.9: 114.9 I will please. The same: He said, etc., up to: and this in the land of the living, who live eternally.
115.1: 115.1 Alleluia. This psalm is fittingly titled with the voice of praise, because in this psalm are the words of the martyrs, who flourished in confession and obtained the rewards of God. I believed, etc. Cassiodorus: First the benefits of God are recalled, and since they doubt what worthy thing to render for them, the cup of the passion, which is given by God, comes to mind. Second, they call themselves servants, and sons of the handmaid, that is, of the Church, there: O Lord, for I, etc. A true and fitting order, first to believe, afterward to speak: lest one not yet believing dare to speak, but let confession follow faith. But lest confession be given to the strength of man, he says it is man's own to be a liar: which he would not readily know unless he had been carried to the heights by an excess of mind. For it is a great thing if anyone sees himself as imprudent. And since man has nothing good of his own, what is to be rendered? I believed. Augustine: He does not say: I believed and I spoke, because he did not only believe the other things that faith requires, but along with them also believed both what reward he ought to hope for by speaking, and what penalty he ought to fear by keeping silent; so the love of speaking is instilled by the reward, and the necessity is imposed by the penalty. Wherefore. For he does not believe perfectly who does not speak what he believes; that servant is slothful, or timid, but faithful: what he received, he spends, and gains, and therefore enters into the joy of his Lord, who says: Well done, good and faithful servant, enter into the joy of your Lord (Matt. 25). In my excess. Or, in my ecstasy. Augustine: And here it is called ecstasy, etc., up to: that is, every man is a liar.
115.2: 115.2 What shall I render to the Lord? The same: This man, terrified, looks at his own weakness and sees that he is not to presume about himself. For of himself man is a liar, and Peter too, when he presumed, was found a liar: but it is the power of God if he does not believe. Seeing this done in himself by the grace of God, he adds, that he has repaid me. He does not say, for all that he has given. What good things, then, preceded in man, that of all the gifts of God it could be called not a giving but a repaying? What had preceded but sins? So God repays men good for evil, having suffered for them, when men repay evil for good.
115.3: 115.3 I will take the cup of salvation. The same: The passion, by comparison, etc., up to: what is said afterward. Cassiodorus: The cup, because it is drunk under measure. Whence, God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able (1 Cor. 10). Of salvation, because it is propitiated for eternal salvation.
115.5: 115.5 Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints. Augustine: He who first suffered grants that his sufferings be imitated; and therefore: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints. He bought it with the blood he shed for them, that they might not hesitate to die for him. Purchased, then, at this price, he confesses his condition: O Lord, for I, etc.
115.6: 115.6 O Lord, for, etc. Cassiodorus: Second, they call themselves servants and sons of the Church, because there is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church, lest any of the heretics think his martyrdom pleases God. O Lord. He wonders that he has received such things as the Lord did for the redemption of the world. And to increase the wonder he repeats: I am your servant. The son of your handmaid. Augustine: The heavenly Jerusalem, free from sins, handmaid of justice. But those who are outside the Church are not sons of the handmaid, even if they call themselves servants because they have the name of Christ and martyrs, as the heretics do. The son of your handmaid, not a schismatic. Or as the handmaid, not for herself but for the Lord; so I too in my death will bring forth some for you, as in life.
115.7: 115.7 You have broken my bonds. Cassiodorus: By the power of martyrdom the bonds of sins are broken, because all things are washed away in blood. This verse is believed by some to be of such power that sins are forgiven a man if it is said at the end of life with a threefold confession. The same: Who precious. O Lord, I will sacrifice to you; speaking to God, he affirms what he had said above. I will sacrifice. Augustine, Cassiodorus: And because you have broken, I will sacrifice to you, as one grateful, a sacrifice of praise. So what:
115.8: 115.8 I will pay my vows. Not everywhere, but in the courts, that is, in the Catholic Church, not of the heretics. The house of the Lord. He shows what it is. In the sight of all his people. Cassiodorus: He ought to be praised publicly who wished to suffer for all, that more might be built up. I will pay my vows. Myself, who am the image of God which must be rendered to God, etc., up to: and more plainly here he names Jerusalem. Augustine: But lest anyone think that by Jerusalem only the Jews are signified, who boast of this name, let him hear the following Psalm: Praise the Lord, all nations. These are the courts of the Lord, for that people.
116.1: 116.1 Alleluia. Cassiodorus: A short psalm, the first of all an atom, that is, without division: for by reason of its brevity it admits no division, but surpasses all by the compendium of its speech, and is like a point of the psalms, from which diverse forms are shaped. A wonderful variation against weariness, to speak wholesome things, now briefly, now at length. Praise the Lord, all nations. Cassiodorus: That none be passed over of the whole world. Augustine: And these are those courts of the house of the Lord, and that whole people, of which he treated in the preceding psalm. Not the Jews alone, who try to claim that for themselves, I say praise him. And praise him together. Cassiodorus: that the praise of all may be brought into one, which is that of the Catholic Church.
116.2: 116.2 Confirmed. Cassiodorus: Because what he promised through the prophets he fulfilled by the coming of Christ; and he has strengthened mercy, that it may never be moved, for he who gave, keeps. It endures forever. Augustine: Whether in what he promised to the pious, or in what he threatens to the wicked.
117.1: 117.1 Alleluia. Cassiodorus: The fifth psalm of the first coming, adorned with many figures, has verses with the same endings, some with the same beginning, some refrains and ornaments of this kind. The faithful people, freed from sin, etc., up to: Blessed is he who.
117.2: 117.2 Let Israel now say. The same: As I do to you, so admonish one another; or, let him say, that is, confess. For his mercy is forever. Behold four verses with the same endings.
117.5: 117.5 Out of tribulation. The same: He puts forth an example from himself, to invite others to mercy.
117.6: 117.6 The Lord is my helper. The same: The same beginning in two verses.
117.7: 117.7 I will look down on. Another reading, I will see. The same: Here, that I may become safer and more cautious. My enemies. Those to be condemned.
117.8: 117.8 It is good. The same: Second, he says that confidence is to be placed in God alone, through whom he escapes the enmities of the nations and comes to true life.
117.9: 117.9 In princes. Augustine: Angels, etc., up to: who makes them good according to their measure.
117.10: 117.10 All nations. Cassiodorus: Behold from what he frees, from hidden or open tribulation, either by not permitting to fall, or by raising up from a fall.
117.11: 117.11 Surrounding me, etc. Augustine: As though giving the reason why he can overcome so many, he says what he first suffered in the head.
117.12: 117.12 They surrounded me, etc. The same: What was done by the ignorant the Holy Spirit foretells by mystical subtlety. The Jews, not knowing, did the thing that is sweeter to us than all things, the passion of God, as bees, while they think they are storing for themselves, make honey for others. And they burned. Or this is better taken of the Church. For after the Lord's passion the Jews also burned against the Church of the nations like fire in thorns of sins. For they, that is, the sins, in the faithful people they burned with the fire of persecution; wishing to harm it, they made it advance. Because I avenged. When they were converted, malice being extinguished in them, they were joined to the Christian people; or, being judged at the end, they will feel the judgment of truth without mercy.
117.13: 117.13 Pushed, etc. Cassiodorus: As when the good are given to punishments that they may fall from faith, and the Lord took hold. Augustine: Because he to whom the Lord is strength and praise falls no more than the Lord falls: but they fall who wish to be strength and praise for themselves. Pushed, I was overthrown, etc. After showing that he delivers by not permitting to fall, he shows also that he delivers by raising up from a fall.
117.14: 117.14 He has become my salvation. The same: It does not happen that he becomes what he was not to himself; but he is salvation to them when converted, which he was not to them when turned away.
117.17: 117.17 I shall not die. The same: The Church says this, as the persecutor thinks he can blot out the Christian name by the slaughter of funerals, when he rather increases it.
117.18: 117.18 Chastising. Cassiodorus: Why he endured so much he indicates: Chastising; whatever they do is the chastisement of the Lord. Let them claim nothing for themselves; he is not given to death whose vices are purged. Augustine: Often the father corrects his sons through wicked servants, preparing punishment for the latter, inheritance for the former. What the inheritance is can be known from this: Open the gates. What is within? Entering, I will confess.
117.19: 117.19 Open. Cassiodorus: Third, he desires the gates of Jerusalem to be opened to him, where he speaks also of the cornerstone. Open, O prophets, who bear the keys of the kingdom of heaven. The gates. Cassiodorus, Jerome: Those who have entered through these gates of doctrine truly praise; outside the Catholic Church there is no praise of God. Cassiodorus: All these gates lead to one, which is Christ, through whom the just enter heaven; whence: I am the door; if anyone enters by me, he shall be saved (John 10). And elsewhere: No one comes to the Father but by me (John 14). Augustine: Behold he has made mention of both ages: and because this gate, Christ, has appeared, I will confess to you, glad, giving thanks, because you heard at the coming of the Son; for the earlier just ones asked for his coming. The gates of justice. That is, the gates of death, etc., up to: that is, through it to life.
117.22: 117.22 The builders. The same: The Jews alone, worshiping God, were building, the others being destroyed by idolatry; but they did not finish, because they despised Christ.
117.23: 117.23 This was done by the Lord. Or, This was done to him by the Lord, according to another reading. The same: That is, to the honor of the Father.
117.24: 117.24 This is the day. This is the jubilee year, observed figuratively under the law, which is called remitting, or beginning, because then slaves were set free and possessions were restored to their owners: and on this day we have been redeemed from the slavery of sin, and an eternal inheritance has been restored to us. Cassiodorus: This is the day. Though he made all days, this one in particular, on which the Lord came, on which it is fitting to rejoice, because the devil lost his right and man lived again; and because this is,
117.25: 117.25 O Lord, save, etc. Behold the desire of a great petition. Save, from the ruin of the world. Prosper, that these sorrows may be turned into eternal joys.
117.26: 117.26 Blessed, etc. Cassiodorus: Fourth, he persuades that the courts of God be frequented, rejoicing at the coming of Christ. Augustine: Accursed, therefore, is he who comes in his own name, etc., up to: who will be accursed. Cassiodorus: Blessed. Praise for the coming, and, O rest of the Christians, we the elders, as priests, have blessed you, which profits much, because we have blessed you out of the house of the Lord. Out of the house. The same: That is, the Catholic Church, etc., up to: because the confession after benefits is joyful.
117.27: 117.27 Appoint a day. Augustine: The great, who go beyond, who with the mind touch the Word, God with God, etc., up to: that is, that he may reach eternal joys. A solemn day. In the old law (Deut. 10): Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles, the three principal solemnities, on which it was commanded that no one appear empty in the sight of the Lord. He is empty who has not Christ in himself, who is the foundation, which no one can change. Hence on those three solemnities the faithful people offer a coin as a hand offering, signifying the inward. For on a coin are the name and image of the king. Let each, then, offer a coin spiritually, that he may have in himself the name of the king, that is, of Christ, being called Christian from Christ; and may present to God the image, that is, the soul, stamped with the light of his countenance. The horn of the altar. Cassiodorus: Or by the altar is understood the sacrament of the body and blood, etc., up to: he will not have eternal life. Or, the altar is understood as the mind of man; whence in the law it was commanded (Exod. 27) that the altar be made four-cornered and hollow: four-cornered, because the human mind ought to be fortified by four virtues, prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance; and it ought to be hollow to receive the word of God and the fire of love. For swelling rejects what is poured in; whence in Leviticus (Lev. 1) it was commanded that the crop of the throat and the feathers be cast away when a turtledove or dove is offered. The crop signifies the swelling of pride; the feathers, empty inquiries into lofty things; cast these away, then, that you may be a hollow altar.
117.28: 117.28 You are my God. And to say it more plainly, the sense of these words here is this: Let this festal day, on which the lamb was slain, not suffice on earth, but let it be established in frequent observances until, with minds uplifted, we arrive at his inner divinity, where we shall sing praises thus: You are my God, etc. Thus, as he began praise, so he ends it.
117.29: 117.29 Give thanks to the Lord. From the beginning which we abandoned, to the end to which we return, there is nothing more wholesome to delight us than the praise of God.
118.1: 118.1 The exposition of this psalm, as very long, we omit. See the Commentaries on the Psalms of Ambrose, Cassiodorus, and Augustine, from which the ordinary gloss on this place is taken word for word.
119.1: 119.1 A song of degrees. Cassiodorus: The blessedness which the preceding psalm sang in united variety, etc., up to: by these degrees, therefore, one ascends and descends with unstumbling foot of the mind. Augustine: A song of degrees. The name of degrees is ambiguous among us, etc., up to: and the height of his divinity itself. The first degree is to go out from the evils of the world and renounce all vanity. Cassiodorus: The beginning of progress is to leave carnal vices and to supplicate the Lord; hence in the old law, when a Gentile slave was bought, his nails were scraped and his hair shorn (Deut. 12). Because one must strip off all vanity, to be bound to the service of God. Here from the renunciation of the world, by certain degrees of merits, one comes to perfect and eternal charity, which is placed at the summit. To the Lord when I was in distress. Cassiodorus: First, beginning to ascend, because he finds many besieging, he asks to be delivered from their tongues: second, he complains of the mixing with the wicked: Woe is me.
119.2: 119.2 Lord, deliver, etc. When a man begins to ascend, that is, when he thinks to make progress, having despised the world and clinging to God alone, he begins to suffer the tongues of adversaries, that is, of detractors, and, what is graver, of those who as if giving counsel turn him away from salvation: he who does not suffer these is not yet attempting to progress. Therefore, about to ascend, he first prays against them: Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips.
119.3: 119.3 What shall be given to you, etc. Cassiodorus: In the manner of one thinking deeply he hesitates, and seeks a remedy. What shall be given to you, or what added? He has put two words, to be given and to be added; arrows are given for arms, coals are added as if for consolation.
119.4: 119.4 Arrows. Augustine: The heart is pierced with arrows by the words of God, etc., up to: that the place may be pure for the building of God.
119.5: 119.5 Woe is me. Cassiodorus: Second, he complains of his sojourning and of the mixing with the wicked. Having received the arrows and coals, made wheat, he is not yet in the barn, but on the threshing floor where much chaff presses upon him; seeing therefore many evils which he had not seen before, he cries out: Woe is me. To no man do the wicked appear unless he has become good; for when the herb grew and bore fruit, the tares appeared. Prolonged. Though the time is short, to desire it seems too long. Kedar. The same: A son of Ishmael, from whom the Saracens descended, who would more truly be called Hagarenes from Hagar; but from Sarah, the nobler and free woman, they claimed the name for themselves, and both are read to have dwelt in tents. The tents of Ishmael are rightly called Kedar: Kedar belongs to Ishmael. Augustine: Isaac therefore, etc., up to: if now the wicked cannot be separated from the good, they must be borne with.
120.1: 120.1 A song of degrees. Cassiodorus: The second degree is to ask divine defense, to which nothing is shown able to stand in the way. Augustine: For he to whom dangers meet as he goes out of the world ought to implore divine help, etc., up to: Such is he who lifts his eyes to God. Cassiodorus: First he lifts his eyes and prays: second he affirms what he prayed, showing the power of the help obtained. I have lifted up my eyes. The same: He who as though bowed down cried out, now breathing again, lifts his eyes to the holy intercessors.
120.3: 120.3 Nor let him slumber. Augustine: If faith sleeps in you, Christ sleeps in you. Cassiodorus: This is said in the human manner; as when a weary guard dozes, theft is suffered.
120.4: 120.4 Augustine: Behold, he will not slumber. Christ slumbers, etc., up to: but lest you still think this of some man, he adds, The Lord keeps. He who keeps Israel. Augustine: He who cannot see the face, etc., up to: and for him Christ does not sleep.
120.5: 120.5 The Lord keeps you. Cassiodorus: The second part, where he affirms what he had prayed. And as if someone were to ask, Who is that keeper? he adds, The Lord keeps, etc. Augustine: It is not without cause, etc., up to: namely the love of God and of neighbor.
120.6: 120.6 By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night, etc. The same: God is the sun, etc., up to: or the moon, that is the Church, will not permit to be burned in the night of tribulation. Jerome: Or by day are understood prosperous things, etc., up to: so now he preserves us in prosperity and in adversity.
120.7: 120.7 May the Lord keep your going in. Cassiodorus: He concludes all things: may he join good endings to good beginnings. Augustine: May the Lord keep your going in. He keeps those entering, etc., up to: now nothing will harm forever.
121.1: 121.1 A song of degrees. Cassiodorus: The third degree. A great joy: to dwell in the Church with a pure mind, and worthily to serve God in this pilgrimage: hence we sigh for the heavenly Jerusalem, to which we are lifted by the two wings of love. I rejoiced in these things, etc. First he rejoices that he is admonished to go to Jerusalem, where the saints, secure, will judge with the Lord. Second, about to ascend, he desires an abundance of peace: Pray for the things that are for peace, etc.
121.4: 121.4 The testimony of Israel. Augustine: That is, in whom it is recognized that they are truly Israel. For when the grains are with the chaff, the whole is thought to be chaff; but when they are separated, then there will be the testimony of Israel.
121.5: 121.5 Seats. The same: That is, the just, in whom God sits, etc., up to: let all who are to be questioned, then, beware.
121.6: 121.6 Pray. Cassiodorus: The second part, where he speaks to the judges, wishing them an abundance of peace, which he proclaimed by the love of the brothers. For those who love. Augustine: He who loves in another a good which he himself cannot have, it is reckoned to him as if he had it; whence: If charity has nothing to give, let it give a cup of water; and it is reckoned to him as much as many things to Zacchaeus (Matt. 10). The means are unequal, but the charity is not unequal.
121.7: 121.7 Let peace be. The same: Charity is a virtue strong as death, etc., up to: he adds: For the sake of my brothers. In your towers. The same: That is, in your heights. The judges are few, but many will belong to each of them, whom they will receive into the eternal tabernacles, and then there will be abundance in the towers; and God is the whole abundance of them, both of those who receive and of those received.
121.9: 121.9 For the sake of the house of the Lord our God. Or read it so that this verse is the explanation of the preceding. As if: I spoke peace concerning you, for the sake of neighbors and brothers, namely: I have sought good things for you for the sake of the house of the Lord our God. The meaning of these words is not changed. For you. O you, heavenly Jerusalem, because you are the house of God, and so in that I love you, I love God.
122.1: 122.1 A song of degrees. Cassiodorus: The fourth degree: amid whatever straits, one must constantly presume on the Lord, until he has mercy and hears. He who above lifted his eyes to the mountains now lifts them to God. To you I have lifted up. The same: First the voice of the afflicted looking to God, not to other patronages; second, he prays for mercy against those who mock. Augustine: To you I have lifted up. Where would he lift them, except to where he was heading as he ascended? This man does not look to himself, like the proud who pleases himself: for he who displeases himself, such a one pleases God; and he to whom God is pleasing displeases himself. I have lifted up. The ascent, then, is in the affection, etc., up to: but one who is a pilgrim and desires his homeland.
122.2: 122.2 Behold, as the eyes, etc. Cassiodorus: The servant lifts his eyes to the hands of the master, when he is in need or when he is beaten, because both are in the master's power. As the eyes of the handmaid. Augustine: The servant is the people; the master, Christ; the handmaid, the Church; the mistress, the power of God and the wisdom of God. And though we are already sons and friends by grace, we are nevertheless servants by creation, because every creature serves God. Cassiodorus: He gives a comparison of servant and handmaid, master and mistress, lest the female and weaker sex think itself excepted.
122.3: 122.3 Have mercy. The same: The second part, where he prays for mercy against those who mock. The servant who is beaten, having lifted his eyes to God, bursts out in the needed cry: Have mercy. We are filled. As when it is said: What do you believe, madman? Do you see what you believe? Has someone returned from the dead and reported to you what is done there? Behold, what I love, I see and enjoy.
123.1: 123.1 Unless it had been. Cassiodorus: First the holy martyrs, mindful of how great things they have escaped, ascribe it to mercy alone; second, they give thanks that they were delivered.
123.2: 123.2 Mountains round about, that is, angels, prophets, apostles are its wall: whence Isaiah: And a wall and bulwark shall be set in it (Isa. 26); but lest you remain in the mountains, he adds, and the Lord round about. Let there be no hope, then, in the mountains, but in the top of the mountains: whence Isaiah: In the last days there shall be a mountain on the top (Isa. 21), etc. Those who trust. Cassiodorus: First he asserts, etc., up to: because they are many, and they are one. Mount Zion. Jerome: Christ, on whom the Church is founded: that mountain literally will be moved at the end of the age.
123.3: 123.3 Perhaps they would have swallowed us up alive. They live who know that an idol is nothing. They are dead who think it is something. Therefore the dead are swallowed up who think that what they do is an evil to be done; but the living are those who do know that what they do is evil, but, overcome by persecution, pass into the company of the wicked, and prefer the sweetness of this life to God, as some who out of fear of death sacrificed to idols. Augustine: Note also that Peter, that is, the Church, swallows up many, but not living ones. To whom it is said: Kill and eat (Acts 10). For he eats no one, that is, incorporates into his members, unless he is killed, that is, renounces the devil. He who is eaten by Peter is therefore killed in evil but made alive in good. The opposite happens to him whom the devil swallows. The rod of sinners. Augustine: For they sometimes rule for the discipline of the good, but this will not always be, as the prophet here plainly says: and therefore the just do not fail, because they know the time to come, when Christ, appearing in his brightness, will gather all nations before him, and divide them as a shepherd divides the goats from the sheep, and will place the sheep on the right, the goats on the left. The lot. Cassiodorus: That is, the just chosen by lot, or those who are the lot and inheritance of God.
123.4: 123.4 Water. Augustine: The sinful people, and it is by likeness of the Egyptians: which water flows as a torrent with force, but soon passes; whence he adds: a torrent. Do good, O Lord. The same: The second part, where, the people having been strengthened, he prays for what he knows will be, that prosperity come to the good and vengeance to the wicked.
