123.5: 123.5 Unbearable water. Augustine: Without substance, as are vices and sins and the sweetness of this life, etc., up to: and might bring back the prodigal son, worn down by long need, to the father. But those who turn aside. The same: By a like sentence they also perish who turn aside from the commands of the ruler, and who strive to will evil works; failing, together with those compelling them to fail. Peace upon Israel. Augustine: By one name the paternal inheritance is called, which is Christ. For he himself is our peace, who made both one, who will give us peace upon peace.
123.6: 123.6 Blessed be the Lord. Cassiodorus: The second part, where the saints give thanks that they were delivered and that the snare was broken.
123.7: 123.7 Our soul. Augustine: Or, as when someone makes a great noise, etc., up to: which is like a snare. Of the hunters. The same: The hunters are the persecutors, the bait in the trap is the sweetness of this life. The snare broken. Cassiodorus: With the martyrs slain, there remains no sweetness of life by which they could be caught again: but they themselves were not broken together with it, rather delivered. Broken. The same: As if to say: because it was of iron; not torn, like tow, so great the strength of the passion, so great the power of him who delivers. PSALM 124
124.1: 124.1 A song of degrees. Cassiodorus: The seventh degree, in the figure of the Old Testament, prophesies through the coming Christ the return from captivity, as if from Babylon: whence now consolation, and sowing that more may be reaped. Augustine: Redeemed by the blood of Christ and converted from captivity, they sing these things, while pilgrims, groaning on the way. Zion is Jerusalem, eternal in the angels, captive in men. When he turned. Cassiodorus: First the greatness of the deed is shown, with the greatness of the joy: second, he prays for conversion from the captivity still to come, there: Turn, O Lord. When he turned. Augustine: Or, when he has turned, etc., up to: turn, O Lord, our captivity. As. The same: It is not always put for likeness, but for property, as here; whence it is also said: He did it as a just man, which truly he is, so these are made as the consoled, that is, they rejoiced, receiving consolation in the resurrection of Christ, who went before that we may follow.
124.2: 124.2 Our mouth. Cassiodorus: The secret of the heart, where joys are first, which afterward burst out through the office of the tongue. Augustine: Our mouth. Of the heart; from there proceeds the evil or good that cleanses or defiles us; whence not: What proceeds from the mouth defiles (Mark 7). Not from the mouth of the flesh, but of the heart. For it is not if you name thefts and other evils that you are unclean, but while you think them, even if you are silent. Among the nations. The same: Not the nations, because not all believe. He has magnified, because they see them even working miracles; a firm testimony from the adversary. Cassiodorus: And truly he has magnified, lest you doubt the words of the nations.
124.4: 124.4 Turn, O Lord. The same: The second part. He prays for the conversion that is to come, in which there will be sowing in the hope of joy. The same: The coming of the Lord and the redemption having been foretold, they pray again that their sins be forgiven. In the general remission they rejoice, and pray pardon for themselves. Turn, O Lord, our captivity. The same: None literally in the days of David, but the world was captive under the devil, etc., up to: we must not therefore desist, because he who sows in tears. Theodoret: He calls the south Jerusalem, etc., up to: that they may be compelled and make their way like a torrent.
124.5: 124.5 In tears. Augustine: Spiritual sowing is always in tears, whence: Blessed are they who mourn. But those who sow in the flesh sow with gladness: but after weeping: because grief seizes the end of joy. The same: Zacchaeus, Behold, half, etc., up to: Whoever gives a cup of cold water shall not lose his reward (Matt. 10). Going. Cassiodorus: By progress in a better life. Sending, sending ahead of themselves into that age. Their own, not from plunder but from their own labor; coming, to judgment. This is common to all, but only the good come to joy. And they wept. Augustine: Because they were wretched, etc., up to: he desires many to be sick.
125.1: 125.1 A song of degrees of Solomon. Cassiodorus: The eighth degree, etc., up to: and in himself, the cornerstone, built the Church of the two walls of Jews and Gentiles. Augustine: Here of Solomon is added, because he built the temple, in a figure of the peaceable Christ, who built the Church out of two walls. Lest you take it of that Solomon, he says, Unless the Lord build. In this hope is to be placed, but in no man: because that Solomon too fell who built the temple. Cassiodorus: First, he admonishes how those who ascend ought to conduct themselves, namely, that they learn that building and keeping are only from God. And exaltation in the future is only after humiliation. Second, he tells what the inheritance is, and how gathered, there: Behold the inheritance. Unless the Lord. The same: As if to say: Jesus has now come, has led back from captivity: now the city Jerusalem is being built; but let those who ascend learn that building and keeping are only from God, and exaltation only after humiliation in the future; for though glad over the grace of the New Testament, yet in so great a gift no one is to presume. The house. Augustine: To this every one who advances ascends: from this every one who fails falls; by loving God you ascend, by loving the world you fall. For these are songs of lovers, and of those burning with a certain holy desire. They have labored. The same: All labor in this building who preach the word of God in the Church. The city. Cassiodorus: He passes from the house to the city, that there be no presumption either in individuals or in a small gathering. And although house and city, according to the metaphor drawn from different things, are different, yet the Church which both signify is one.
125.2: 125.2 Before light. Augustine: If you rise before the light rises; the light is Christ, after whom one must rise, not before; as he does who puts himself before him: wishing to be exalted here where he was humble: as the sons of Zebedee did: but the resurrection, that is, the exaltation, follows the sitting, that is, the humiliation, as Christ our light rose exalted after death. You sit. Sitting sometimes signifies the honor of judging, but here humiliation. You eat the bread of sorrow. Augustine: He eats the bread of sorrow who groans in this pilgrimage, that is, in the valley of weeping refreshes himself with affliction, saying: My tears have been my bread day and night (Psalm 41). Sleep. Cassiodorus: Temporal death, in which there is secure rest.
125.3: 125.3 Behold the inheritance. The same: Second, what the inheritance is and how gathered. As if to say, the beloved after sleep will rise. The fruit of the womb. Augustine: The womb of the Church, etc., up to: because he acquired all through the obedience of the passion, whence: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance (Psalm 2).
125.4: 125.4 As arrows. The same: But whence was so great an inheritance made? Because the Lord is mighty, who, as he strongly shot the arrows, the apostles, from the bow of sacred Scripture, those shot out reached to the ends of the earth; and the sons of the shot-out are such as those who were shot. Sons of the shot-out. The same: The sons of the apostles; to whom it was said, Shake off the dust from your feet (Matt. 18). But thus they seem, etc., up to: who were sent by the hand of God to the ends of the earth.
126.1: 126.1 A song of degrees. Cassiodorus: The ninth degree is that the peaceable one be feared with chaste fear, who alone exalts, keeps, builds. First he enumerates the goods of the one who fears; second he wishes the goods for the one who fears. Blessed are all who fear the Lord. It should be known that there are four fears, etc., up to: of which the Prophet here says: Blessed are all who fear the Lord.
126.2: 126.2 The labors of your hands. The same: And note that he began with many, saying: Blessed: but because all are one in Christ, it follows in the singular, The labors of your hands. Augustine: He says the labors of fruits, when he should say: the fruit of labors; but because labors too are taken with joy on account of hope, and themselves give delight, and are now food; but the fruit of them will be more delightful, when the saints shall come with exultation carrying their sheaves.
126.3: 126.3 Your wife. Cassiodorus: Though this could be taken literally, etc., up to: it pertains to the New Testament. Augustine: Or by the wife is understood the Church, and the discourse is directed to Christ, when it says your and you; yet the voice or person is not changed on account of the unity of head and body. For Christ is one man, head and body, and in the head each of the faithful has this.
126.4: 126.4 He shall be blessed. Cassiodorus: Where there is blessing, all good things flow together for the joy of sweetness. He shall be blessed. The same: The second part, where from piety he asks that those who fear be blessed; here he wishes good things for the one who fears, namely such as are not common to the wicked.
126.5: 126.5 Or, The Lord. Augustine: Of the Jews, Out of Zion, etc., up to: because they cannot be so.
127.1: 127.1 A song of degrees. Cassiodorus: The tenth degree, that he who fears chastely bear all things for him, which now benefits the Church among the wicked. Often they have fought against me. Augustine: The wicked, even if they hear the word of God, etc., up to: that they bear so many wicked. Cassiodorus: Showing first what he has borne, he consoles the weak. Second, he treats of the reprobation of the persecutors, there: The Lord is just. Often they have fought against me. As if: O sons, do not marvel at these things, etc., up to: because the Church grows in adversities.
127.2: 127.2 For they could not prevail against me. Augustine: Namely to prevail, so as to draw me into consent to sin.
127.3: 127.3 Upon my back. Cassiodorus: What the wicked cannot do publicly to all, they try secretly to persuade individuals, so that those who, coming from the front, would be seen are not noticed from behind. They prolonged their iniquity. Another reading, they made their injustice far from me. Augustine: Even if the wicked are with the good in the world, even if they are also in the Church: lest anyone think iniquity is next to justice, even if I bear them, yet their iniquity is far from me; so let no one fear the wicked mixed among them, who are far away. The Lord is just. Cassiodorus: The second part, where he treats of the reprobation of the persecutors.
127.4: 127.4 Who hate Zion. The same: Which not only open persecutors hate, but also those who enter feignedly. For those who do not wish to observe the word of God hate the Church. Let them be like the grass of the housetops. Cassiodorus: The wicked are compared to the grass of the housetops, etc., up to: but in neither is there fruit for the wicked. Gregory: The rush is said to wither before all herbs, etc., up to: as though it loses the appearance of greenness, etc.
127.6: 127.6 Which before it is plucked up. Augustine: They are not yet finished in the judgment of God, and already they have no sap of greenness. And they have not said. Cassiodorus: There was a custom among the Hebrews that a traveler would bless those who were working: whence here the opposite is said, because to those who work in vain no blessing is given. And they have not said. Whom the angels will not gather, to whom the apostles did not preach. And this is what he says: Augustine: And they have not said, etc. Especially among the Jews, it was a custom to say to anyone working: The blessing of the Lord be upon you. We have blessed you in the name, etc. Cassiodorus: They bless the good not in their own name but in the name of the Lord: from whom are all things, not from them.
38.3: 38.3 From good things, and my sorrow, etc. The same. To the announcing, etc., down to that is, of those who leap over, I have spoken. Augustine. That is: unwillingly I kept silent among the wicked, etc., down to even if the acts of one who leaps over are anything.
38.4: 38.4 My heart grew hot within me. Augustine. If the slothful man will be condemned, etc., down to he becomes a greedy steward.
38.5: 38.5 I have spoken. The same. Not to instruct a hearer, but to God who hears, by whom I am heard within. And the number of my days. Jerome. The number of the days that now are does not truly belong to one who passes over; but to one who clings, it seems to.
38.6: 38.6 Behold, measurable. Cassian. As though, the end being known, and the days that are, he looks to the things he has left behind, and compares them with one another. And my substance, etc. Augustine. He who sees that this substance is nothing, etc., down to which will be before you.
38.7: 38.7 Nevertheless. Cassian. Seeing the coming of Christ, he returns to the weakness which he has amid his virtues. Augustine. Great are the things we have said and believe; yet this is not eternal, but all is vanity. And, desiring the eternal in place of the changeable, he reproaches human life, to which that which he says is subject, lest anyone think the saints are strangers to temptations. Or, although the days are measurable, although the substance is nothing, yet all is vanity in the rational creature, which, according to different desires, longs for the whole creation. Nevertheless. Although I gape after eternal things, etc., down to whose conversation is in heaven. Every man. Augustine. If he is wicked, he is vain in worldly things; if good, to one who wishes to be with Christ, life is vain. Nevertheless. Augustine. Diapsalma. How all are under vanity and chance; and from this he sets himself to wait for the Lord, and asks to be set free. In an image he passes. The same. Although he so devotes himself to vanity, etc., down to because he seeks earthly things with misery and toil. He stores up. The same. Of the other vices the Prophet chose avarice, to show what he intends: for it is the root of all evils.
38.8: 38.8 The expectation. The same. Of the first coming, or the second, etc., down to not in our purses.
38.9: 38.9 Deliver me from all my iniquities. Cassian. Not only from those, lest he fall back into the things I have passed over, but from all altogether. For man is imperfect because he has not received what he desires; he is perfect who knows this very thing that he lacks.
38.10: 38.10 I was dumb. The same. Held in reproach, etc., down to and it is necessary, because I have failed. Take away your scourges from me. Augustine. Since you made me, do not destroy me; only yield, that I may be drawn forth, not crushed.
38.11: 38.11 With rebukes for iniquity. With which you rebuked the human race: yet you rebuked it by our deserving, on account of our iniquities, and these rebukes are for correction; otherwise iniquity would remain uncorrected. You have corrected man. Augustine. There is a shapeless sorrow which does not amend; and a formed one, which gives form by instruction. And such sorrow is a precept, that is, it has the place and image of a precept.
38.12: 38.12 And you made my soul to waste away like a spider. The same. Dried up from the love of virtues and of knowledge. As a spider weaves an empty web in the gathering of temporal things. Or, while he draws iniquity out of himself like a spider, he dies by the emptying of his entrails. Cassian. Or, a spider has a slender body, and stands not on the ground but on high, and weaves its webs by the emptying of its entrails: so the soul of one converted and afflicted forsakes earthly things, and, wasted by the fear of God, accomplishes subtle works. Nevertheless. Augustine, Cassian. Although he is rebuked, although they waste away, yet through human weakness one is confounded by various things, except the man who contemplates God with a pure mind.
38.14: 38.14 Hear my prayer. Cassian. Diapsalma. On the journey he asks that the evils of the world be present to him and his sins forgiven, that he may depart with a prosperous end. The same. But because I do not ask these things, etc., down to to move mercy. Be not silent, for I am a stranger. Augustine. Already with you, but still a lodger: because from here I shall pass over to eternal things, where I shall not be a lodger. A stranger with you. Cassian. Not in the city of the devil, but received into yours, transferred from Babylon to Jerusalem. As all my fathers. Lest anyone think he is exempt from this condition. A stranger. I abandon my kingdom for yours. A sojourner. Not yet choosing for myself a seat here. Forgive me. The same. Here he asks for himself to be forgiven, that he may come to judgment secure.
39.1: 39.1 Unto the end, a psalm. Cassian. First he introduces the Church as having waited for the Lord, and received him, and from him the New Testament, which many are also to follow: hence he strikes down all superstitions and invites to the wonders of God. The same. Here is Christ with his members.
39.2: 39.2 Waiting, I waited. The same. He waits, and is ungrateful: but waiting he waits. Augustine. Authority from the ancients, in Abraham and the rest, etc., down to who is ours by worship, not of others. The Lord. The same. Not a man, who can deceive and be deceived, and who is in need along with me. He gave heed. The same. To me, that he might profit me: not to me, that he might also profit the wicked.
39.3: 39.3 From the pit. The same. The darkness of iniquities, namely of unbelief and ignorance, etc., down to the rock against the mire. Jerome. In the pit and the mire, the nations that worship idols: or, all who love earthly things.
39.4: 39.4 A song. Jerome. Not shameful, not theatrical, but through the New Testament. They shall see. Cassian. The wonders done at the time of the incarnation. Augustine. They shall see: what he first said of the former, many later peoples shall see.
39.5: 39.5 The name. The same. Which is Savior. As if: Blessed, etc., is he who hopes for nothing temporal from him but salvation, which his name indicates. In Hebrew genitives are often doubled in this way: or, blessed is he whose name is, that is, in whom is the praise of God, so that he believes salvation to come from him alone, whence also is his hope. Follies. Cassian. Idols, which deceive from the truth: or follies, in deceptive spectacles. Therefore in the plural, that it may be understood of all. These are false, but your works are wonderful; heaven and earth overthrow the superstitions.
39.6: 39.6 Your wonders. Augustine. Peter walking upon the waters is in a sign, not in the world, that is, in the fruits of the world. Augustine. Salvation is true, folly is false; it is not what it is thought to be. Jerome. Earthly things are vain: follies, angers and quarrels, etc. There is none like you. Augustine. None are the authors of the arts. I have announced. Here Christ speaks in the head and the members. These are the wonders of God, these the thoughts to which none is like. Cassian. Behold the wonders: the incarnation, the justice of the preaching, the deliverance of men from iniquities, the confusion of enemies, the joy of those who hope. First, the unlearned and unformed were prepared, that they might gladly receive the words of Christ. Augustine. See the wonders of God. I announced first through the Prophets, and afterward I myself spoke. They are multiplied above number. Jerome, Augustine. Above the number of those to be saved: or, above what anyone can count: or, as I speak, more have believed than formerly.
39.7: 39.7 Sacrifice and offering you did not desire. Augustine. As the matter came, he did not desire them, as though they were words of promise, etc., down to but he who poured it out is deaf and does not hear. But you have perfected ears for me. That is, you made me understand perfectly what you willed. Or, you have fitted a body for me, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews (Heb. 10), that is, you gave me a body fit for offering.
39.8: 39.8 Holocaust. You also did not ask for holocausts for sin. For sin. Which is above the offering; as of the goat, that is, the scapegoat, which was sent into the desert with the sins of the people: or, the two words may be for sin. Behold, I come. Cassian. Since the sacrifices cease, it is established that Christ comes.
39.9: 39.9 In the head of the book it is written of me. Behold, at once I come to do your will, because it is in the head of this book. Or, so it was determined beforehand with God the Father, who is my head, and I who am the book, that is, the pattern of justice for men.
39.10: 39.10 In the great Church. Augustine. In the whole world, not small as before: and if fear should rise, it will not prevent speaking. Lord, you know. The same. My lips sound to men, etc., down to that in this I may not be slothful.
39.11: 39.11 I have not hidden. Cassian. When I could profit, the truth, the promise, and salvation.
39.12: 39.12 Your mercy. Augustine. Love and fear bring me to you.
39.13: 39.13 Hairs. Augustine. Rightly, in comparison with offenses, the hairs are counted. For this reason in the Old Testament the priests were shaved, so as to seem to have laid aside the vices of the flesh.
39.14: 39.14 May it please. Cassian. May it please (Latin complaceat, in the subjunctive) signifies the Trinity of persons; you, in the singular, signifies the unity of essence. Augustine. May it please, he says, not doubting the power of God, if the will be present. As if: If you will, you can, Lord. Look. Cassian. His looking upon us is our help.
39.16: 39.16 Who say to me: Well done, well done. Augustine. Both he who says good things with an evil mind, and he who praises deceitfully to say evil things, are each evil and to be guarded against. Of the first he said: Who wish me evils; of the second: Who say to me: Well done, well done.
39.17: 39.17 And let them say. Cassian. This is their exultation: for this profession makes Christians rejoice forever.
39.18: 39.18 But I. Cassian. This is Christ speaking in the form of a servant: lest anyone arrogate to himself the glory of the joy foretold. A beggar, who does not suffice for himself. Do not delay. Augustine. Unless the days had been shortened, etc., down to those who now nourish what they have sought.
40.1: 40.1 Unto the end. Jerome. Understanding for the sons of Korah, that although poor and suffering, etc., down to the Apostle saying: But to me, etc.
40.2: 40.2 Blessed. He is mocked who honors a poor dead man; but blessed. Augustine. The Prophet extols the one who understands concerning the needy and poor. Jerome. First the Prophet speaks from himself, afterward he will introduce Christ. He who understands. Augustine. Note who understands, so that it is given even to those who do not ask: he who gives to one who asks does well; he who understands the one who is silent is without doubt blessed.
40.3: 40.3 May the Lord preserve him. The same. The Prophet rightly wishes this for the one who understands concerning the needy and poor, which is a sure promise. And give him life. The same. In the life to come, or here through justification.
40.4: 40.4 The Lord help. Cassian. Lest you think the blessed man has rest here: he softens his sorrows, and prays that human weakness may not be overcome by hardships; as though these temporal goods were a bed of rest: but God makes them full of sorrows, so that hope may not be placed in them. Bed. Augustine. For God providentially turns the whole couch, that is, worldly happiness, into straits. Cassian. Here he himself in fear asks mercy: for he who knew he had sinned feared to be justly handed over to these things: but so that the servants of God, afflicted by them, may not seem forsaken by God, since God himself endured such things; hence he says: My enemies have said. Or, the bed of sorrow. Augustine. The flesh, in which is sin, etc., down to when Adam was weakened by transgressing. Help. Augustine, Jerome. In the infirmity of the flesh, which weighs down the soul. Couch. Augustine. There is something earthly which the infirm man, etc., down to in place of the house of eternal dwelling.
40.6: 40.6 My enemies. Cassian. The Lord speaks of his passion, which was after the manner of the needy. Augustine. My enemies. These things are said specially of Christ, but can be said also of his members: and today tribulation is brought about so that the name of Christ may be extinguished: but through his death and that of his own the Church has grown the more.
40.7: 40.7 And if he came in. Cassian. Note that the wicked must be borne with. The same. Not only open enemies, but also those who pretended to be friends.
40.8: 40.8 He went out abroad. From the bosom of truth: wicked in entering, wicked in going out. Together. Augustine. That is, with one counsel all whispered against me. They whispered. Cassian. They do not dare to disclose the plan, because all are partners in the crime: though few are usually the authors of crimes.
40.9: 40.9 Shall he not. Augustine. He who has power to lay down his life, has he not also power to take it up again?
40.10: 40.10 I hoped. Augustine. In the members, because other brethren hoped something in him, because he seemed such as the rest. So too he says he hungers in the poor.
40.11: 40.11 But you, Lord. Augustine. Concerning the resurrection, which is the glory of the needy, to confirm the hope of the faithful. And I will repay them. Augustine. For because they are scattered throughout the world, it is for admonition, not yet for condemnation.
40.13: 40.13 But me. The same. He affirms that he prayed.
40.14: 40.14 Blessed. Cassian. A concluding praise, the passion and resurrection having been set forth. The God of Israel. Augustine. The Jews are our bearers of book-cases, who carry the books for us: we are Israel. Otherwise the pagans would have thought what is said of Christ and the Church to be fictions, but they are overcome by the testimony of enemies. From age, etc. Cassian. From when all things began to be governed until the age to come, where all things are eternal. So be it. Jerome. The doubling shows that this must be done by all. In place of so be it, in the Hebrew is written amen, amen, which Aquila translated truly, truly, or faithfully. And here ends the first book of the Psalter according to Jerome.
41.1: 41.1 Unto the end, for understanding. Cassian. Korah is interpreted Calvary. The sons, therefore, etc., down to which the insulting of the wicked opposes. Jerome. The sons of Korah, that is, the sons of the bald, etc., down to the word of the boys mocking Elisha.
41.2: 41.2 As the hart desires, etc. Augustine. This voice befits the catechumens, and also all who are still pilgrims. Hart. A hart weighed down by age, its hairs and horns growing out, draws a serpent out with its nostrils: then burning with the venom, it most ardently desires a fountain to drink; having drunk, it sheds its horns and hairs.
41.3: 41.3 It has thirsted. Augustine. He defines his desire, because it could be understood that the hart desires the fountain for the sake of drinking or washing; here all the desire is shown to be for God. When shall I come. What is quicker for God is slow for the desire of man. Such a hart, while it runs, suffers insulters; hence: My tears have been my bread. In prosperity too, which he despises, as in adversity. Bread. Cassian. Not bitterness or destruction, but bread.
41.5: 41.5 These things I remembered. Augustine. While they ask, Where is your God? I too have meditated through all these visible things, and through my very soul, that through these outward things I may find the invisible things of God. Behold the understanding of the title. I poured out. The same. To understand and reach, I stretched out above itself. I poured out. Cassian. Or I rejoiced. My soul melted within me; not outside, but pierced within itself it returns. Even if I do not see God visibly, I think nevertheless that through the Church, in which the saints are wonderful, I shall come to the heavenly Jerusalem, taken captive by the sweetness of angelic praise, which is received by the mind. To the place of the tabernacle. Augustine. The tabernacle of God on earth, etc., down to that is, of the eternal refreshment of those who rejoice. In the voice of exultation. The same. Of the eternal festival something sweet to the heart sounds: hence the hart is carried off to the fountains of waters, and is soothed. But because the world is noisy, and the flesh weighs down the soul: comparing this sadness with those joys, he says:
41.6: 41.6 Why are you sad? etc. Cassian. Concerning the disturbances against which reason strengthens the sensual soul by hope in God. Why do you disturb me? Augustine. If you investigate, there is nothing in the world for which you ought to do this: hope rather for the saving remedy yet, and if not now, fully in the future. Hope. Cassian. Or he can hope, because I shall still confess in the present, that is, do penance for my sins, that I may not stand against you.
41.7: 41.7 Within myself. Turned to God he says that the disturbances are from himself, their end from God: hence in him is his hope. And this is within myself, or from myself. Cassian. Behold, he who above was correcting the soul according to the condition of man, turning back says here that the soul is disturbed by himself, which would remain tranquil if there were not the vices of the flesh. Behold from what diversity man is made up. As if: therefore, that is, on account of the disturbances of the soul, I will remember. Augustine. That is, I hasten to you, because you shut out all evils. Behold the remedy by which he may escape the disturbances: hence he adds for which things he is mindful: From the land of the Jordan, where the Lord consecrated baptism, in which the humbled are washed, and become fruitful earth. Cassian. Mindful of these things, he is not disturbed by evils. Therefore I will remember. Augustine. Because the soul is disturbed toward myself, therefore I will remember, etc. No one runs to forgiveness except one who is displeased with himself, except one who confesses himself a sinner: which Hermon indicates; no one confesses unless he humbles himself, which is indicated in the little one. Jordan. The same. Descent. Descend, then, that you may be lifted up. Cassian. In the Jordan the Lord consecrated baptism, in which the humbled are washed and become fruitful earth, which yields fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold and a hundredfold (Matt. 13). Hermon. Augustine. A small mountain near the Jordan, etc., down to because God is mindful not in the proud, but in the humble.
58.8: 58.8 And a sword. That they may slay and eat. For who has heard? As if no one, so all will marvel, etc., down to you will bring to nothing or convert. Sword. The same. This is the twice-sharp sword cutting in both Testaments, with which Peter slays the creeping things shown to him in the dish, when it was said to him: Arise, Peter, slay and eat.
58.9: 58.9 You shall laugh them to scorn to nothing. The same. Those who say, Who has heard? Why? Because he will count it as nothing to convert all the nations, because all nations are to be Christian; and you say, who has heard?
58.10: 58.10 My strength I will keep for you, for you, O God, are my protector. The same. Even if I could destroy the Jews, who rushed upon me strongly, yet I permit them to live, keeping my strength for you, that is, for your disposition.
58.12: 58.12 He has shown. The same. That is, how much mercy he has toward me he showed me in those toward whom he has none; hence the Apostle: He endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, that he might make known his riches in the vessels of mercy (Rom. 9). Do not kill. It can be taken of the Jews, etc., down to it is shown what mercy there is for those grafted in. Cassian. To one considering what is to be done about them, if they are not witnesses of the law and of the death of Christ. Lest at any time they forget. Augustine. Even if they have not now forgotten, since they are not witnesses of the law and of the death of Christ. In your strength. Because you are strong, not they. Put them down, there was reproach to all. Or, put them down in that they are evil, that the good may rise: as in Paul, for Paul would not have risen unless Saul had first fallen (Acts 9).
58.13: 58.13 The sin of their mouth. The same. Kill not them, but the sin, that, he whom they wished to destroy being raised, they may be afraid. Cassian. And let them be seized when converted; because their deed, etc., down to but pardon wiped out the crime. In their pride. Augustine. Pride is the companion of envy: nor can it be that the proud man does not envy: hence also the devil envies man. And of cursing. Or malediction, which you thought a malediction, etc., down to because in these they were caught. They shall be announced in the consummation. Or, the consummations shall be announced, that is, it will be preached by the Apostles: Where sin of exercise and lying abounded, the grace of perfection has superabounded; and it pertained to the medicine of humility and of man's weakness. In the wrath of consummation. For there is a wrath, that is, a vengeance of God, of consummation, because at times God avenges so as to perfect; and there is one of consumption, as when he will say: Go, you cursed, into everlasting fire. And they shall know. For before, the Jews seemed just to themselves: but it is shown them that it is not without Christ, who rules Jacob: and pride being laid down, they know themselves equal to the nations, because all have sinned.
58.15: 58.15 They shall be converted at evening. Cassian. Diapsalma. The salvation of the Jews is affirmed, and the two walls being gathered, thanks are given.
58.16: 58.16 They shall murmur. The same. Or, they shall murmur, that is, they will grieve, that even now they are so much scattered; or, they shall murmur against the slothful, that is, they will rebuke others unwilling to believe.
58.17: 58.17 But I. The same. Here the psalm is concluded, where, the two walls being joined in the cornerstone, the whole Church now rejoices. And I will exalt. The times having passed, when the night of the world has passed, as Christ also rose in the morning: hence At evening weeping shall abide, and at the morning joy. The Apostles wept in the evening for the dead one, in the morning rejoiced at the risen. Mercy. Because you give all freely: though he has said many things, not all, in this one he comprehends all.
59.1: 59.1 Unto the end for those. Augustine. In the histories it is not read, etc., down to man to faith; earthly men, that they may live as heavenly. Basil and Theodoret. The history of the kings describes these things. But he foresees that the people will transgress, be led captive, and be brought back repentant. Therefore he inscribed: For those who shall be changed. Doctrine. Augustine. They are changed into doctrine, etc., down to Edom, earthly, into heavenly life. And he struck. When he struck Edom with the sword of the spirit, etc., down to he teaches that blessed is the contrition through which he proves they are to be changed to eternal things.
59.3: 59.3 O God, you have cast us off. Cassian. First are related the blows inflicted to avoid eternal punishments: You have cast off. In Adam. And you have destroyed us from immortality. Because you were angry for sins, and yet had mercy, through the Son, so that you moved us from error: And you troubled us, to penance: as therefore you have begun, finish, heal.
59.5: 59.5 You have shown. Augustine. For man being changed for the better, etc., down to to bear adversities to the end. Hard things. Cassian. That is, the miseries of time, which are delightful to us through charity, and grievous through the weakness of the flesh. With wine, that is, tribulation, by which the sufferer is purged, as a wound with wine: with spiritual wine, whence not vices but compunction.
59.6: 59.6 A bow. Augustine. The more it is drawn back, the more impetuously the arrow is borne forward, that is, the more the judgment is deferred, the heavier it will be when it comes. And that they may be delivered. Cassian. Diapsalma. Of the deliverance which he prays for and affirms, for which the blows are welcome.
59.7: 59.7 Your right hand. Augustine. That we may stand at the right hand, etc., down to of earthly things only usefully.
59.8: 59.8 God has spoken. The same. With this confidence I pray, which God promised in Christ, etc., down to it is the voice of the Church: I will rejoice. Shechem. It is interpreted shoulders, that is, the burden of Christ, etc., down to let others bear the yoke of Christ. The valley of tents: on account of the sheep of Jacob it signifies the Jews, who are also divided; because some believe, others do not, that is, from the Jews I shall have not a few.
59.9: 59.9 Manasseh. The same. Or, Manasseh is everyone who, forgetful of his former life, etc., down to: and you shall not remember the reproach of your widowhood. Ephraim. Fruitfulness: and this is the strength of the head, that is, of Christ: for a grain dying has power in itself to bear fruit.
59.10: 59.10 Moab the pot of my hope. The same. The daughters misusing their father, etc., down to when charity burns against the pot of iniquity. Cassian. Moab the pot of my hope. Or by Moab, etc., down to whence there is hope of life for me. Jerome. Pot, whence: I see a boiling pot, etc., down to: From it, then, the pot of tribulations boils over in the Church.
59.11: 59.11 A fortified city. Cassian. The future Jerusalem. Into Idumea, that is, even to the earthly, that, the number being filled, they might come together to blessedness.
59.12: 59.12 You will not go out. Augustine. But within you will work, and so he will lead better, because so he seems to fight not for temporal life, but for the future.
60.3: 60.3 I cried while my heart was in anguish. Cassian. In anguish, etc., down to there follows the hearing of the cry in the rock Christ. You have exalted me. Augustine. From the depth of vices. Cassian. And exalted you have led me. Augustine. On the rock, and therefore I am not overcome; You have exalted: by the example of this man great hope of being heard is given to others. You have led me. The same. Through yourself the way, to yourself the truth and life.
60.5: 60.5 I will dwell. Cassian. He trusts in the benefits of God, that against the dangers of the world he may persevere safe in the tabernacle of God. Forever. Until the ages are accomplished; because even if many are against: I shall be protected under the covering. I shall be protected under the covering of your wings. Which neither burden and turn away every harm. Forever, not one man forever, but the Church, which dwells on earth to the end of the world, and is never uprooted through adversities.
60.6: 60.6 For you, my God, have heard my prayer, etc. The same. Diapsalma. Now what has been heard concerning the inheritance held or to be held, he affirms, whence he promises praises. You have given. Nor will I say, you will give: so certain am I, as though I were already in it.
60.7: 60.7 Days upon days. Augustine. Whatever you say of eternity, etc., down to but let the saints reign with him forever. Or you will give an inheritance. Cassian. This, namely, because above the days of Christ, etc., down to because that king remains forever, so also they. Mercy and truth. Augustine. It is mercy, because not by merits but by goodness he forgives sins and promises life. Truth, because he does not deceive but renders what he promised. We ought to follow mercy toward the weak and toward enemies. Truth, by not sinning, that one may be just. Cassian. Mercy and truth. Here is the conclusion of the psalm, etc., down to: who will seek for him? Augustine. That no one may seek to learn these things in books, and afterward live for himself, not for him.
61.1: 61.1 Unto the end, for Idithun. Augustine. The one who leaps over, seeing so many things confronting him, submits himself to God, who is higher than he; and to those below, as from on high, he replies by rebuking. The one who leaps over answers the envious, who wish to deceive.
61.2: 61.2 Shall not. The same. That is, let not the foot of pride come to me. I shall not be moved any more, that is, and let not the hand of the sinner move me. Always subject to God, desiring nothing besides him. It will be so, because from him is my salvation, from the Father the Son, author of salvation, because he is also God, lest he be thought less.
61.4: 61.4 How long do you rush upon? The same. Or, according to another reading: How long do you lay upon, and the same sense. For the wicked lay upon man, that is, upon the Church, the burdens of sufferings: that to the end each of the faithful may fill up in his body what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ. All of you. Cassian. Or, according to another reading: All you, as though you all kill that man, as to the man, not all one, but the Church; but because God is protector I shall not be moved. Augustine. How long, from the blood of Abel, etc., down to namely not, which is the most high founder. Upon a man. Cassian. Power over the body has been given you, not over the soul. You rush upon. Not lightly, but you kill the innocent; you think he is without a defender, and that he easily falls, like a leaning wall, which would fall even if not pushed. And like a wall, which is a construction of stones without the binding of mortar; and lest you think it firm from its very newness, he adds pushed, or, you ought not to rush, because you kill yourselves, all of you, even by consenting.
61.5: 61.5 The price. Cassian. To take away Christ, that he not be worshipped, or, blessedness. They thought. Augustine. Note the different kinds of enemies, etc., down to of this the prophet says: Glorious things are said of you, O city. I ran in thirst. Because even if he always drinks them, yet he always thirsts further. With his mouth. Because they cannot by open evils, they try by flattering.
61.6: 61.6 But to God, etc. Cassian. Diapsalma. Again he urges himself, that is, his soul, to be subject, and admonishes the rest. My soul is subject. This petition fixes strength in our mind.
61.8: 61.8 In God is my salvation. The same. Then safe and glorious in him: now what? God himself is the help.
61.9: 61.9 Hope. The same. His faith being made known, he admonishes all who labor under superstitions to hope in the Lord. Pour out. Augustine. Through tears the heart is poured out, etc., down to: Whence, Prick the eye, and it brings forth a tear; prick the heart, and it brings forth knowledge (Sir. 22). Hearts, etc., wicked thoughts.
61.10: 61.10 But vain. Jerome. Or join thus, God is our helper; and although he so cooperates with us, yet the sons of Adam are vain and liars in the scales, perverting the Scriptures by which they prove falsehoods. Cassian. Diapsalma. He reproaches those who err, and admonishes to trust in God, not in perishable things, which the psalm intends. Liars in the scales. Who deceive by buying with unjust weights, or wish to seem just when they are deceitful. In the scales. In the balance of justice, by which they deceive more easily. Together, that they may be believed equitable.
61.11: 61.11 Do not hope in. Augustine. As if he said: Neither hope for nor desire what is gathered and then seized by others. Do not, the thirsty one turned to them. Do not. Plunder. The prey you want to seize is in a trap, you hold and are held; you hold what is another's, and are held by the devil. O ruinous gains! you find money, you lose justice. Let them flow. Do not set your heart. Cassian. He does not say: Do not have, for he does not condemn riches, by which we purchase heaven; but the heart set upon them, which does not spend but hoards.
61.12: 61.12 God has spoken once. Augustine. Do not set your heart. Why? because the power of judging belongs to the Son of God, etc., down to nor should one despair of mercy because of power. The power is God's: there is no power in anyone except from the just God, even if the justice is hidden from you.
62.1: 62.1 A psalm of David. Cassian. He speaks of the Church, which in the dryness of the world thirsts, and asks for mercy until she receives the eternal, teaching how to live well in the midst of a perverse nation. Augustine. A psalm in the person of the head and the members; his voice is ours, and ours is his.
62.2: 62.2 O God, my God, to you from the light, etc. The same. How the bride conducts herself in the desert, she desires to see God, whom she both praises and wishes to do so the more. God. The same. The common God, my God in a somewhat more special way; see the affection of pious entreaty through this doubling. From the light. Or at dawn, when Christ rose, that the Church may then praise him when by the example of his resurrection he roused her to rise. I watch, even while I sleep, not loving the things of the world. Cassian. And I thirst in mind and body. From the light. Augustine. For you would not be awake, unless the light arose that would rouse you. My soul has thirsted for you: and here my flesh for God, while it seeks from him here the necessities.
62.3: 62.3 Desert. The same. Where no saint dwells. Pathless, because there is no way by which to leave. Waterless, because even where you linger there is no water. But God here made a way, Christ, and sent water, filling the preachers with the Holy Spirit of his Word: That there might be in them a fountain of water springing up unto eternal life (John 4). So in the holy place I appeared before you, to see, etc. Augustine. To whom God does not appear let him be in holy desire, etc., down to For the sun by its own light makes us see, so also God.
62.4: 62.4 Above lives. The same. Of humanity, which are many, as of a soldier, a farmer and the rest: better is what you give to the corrected than what the perverse choose. My lips. After the benefits of God he promises praise. They shall praise, toward the neighbor, for whom also I am solicitous, because unless your mercy had come before me, I could not praise you, and as with lips, so let them bless in life. Or thus, Because above lives.
62.5: 62.5 So will I bless. The same. As you have given me by mercy to praise you, so I will bless, that I may ascribe to mercy the life in which I praise. In your name I will lift up my hands. The same. He lifts up his hands who, persisting in good works, adores God with hands stretched out in the figure of the cross; hence the Apostle: Lifting up pure hands in prayer, without anger and dispute.
62.6: 62.6 With fat. The same. In the inward parts. The fatness in the flesh, that is, wisdom, which is in the hidden, and strength of spirit. I will lift up my hands. The same. In Exodus, Moses, when he lifted up his hands to the Lord, etc., down to he who works for earthly things is overcome by Amalek.
62.7: 62.7 If I have remembered. Cassian. He sets forth the goods and evils of both parties, etc., down to except him who works in Christ. Cassian. In the mornings, that is, in the light of Christ, as above, I watch for you from the light, that the son of light, that is, of Christ, may watch for the author of light, for God.
62.8: 62.8 Helper, etc. Augustine. In the dangers of Idumea, etc., down to because your right hand received me from dangers, that is, propitiation.
62.10: 62.10 But they in vain sought my soul. But the king. In these two verses he compares the goods and evils of the different parties. Into the lower parts of the earth. Cassian. Because they were not carried up to the heavens. Evil thoughts are swallowed up by the earth, because born of earth, they tend to the depths of the earth, as into mire.
62.11: 62.11 They shall be portions for foxes, etc. Cassian. The beginning of the world, etc., down to while they join themselves to the deceitful by a perverse will.
62.12: 62.12 In God. Cassian. The Father, whence: I in the Father, and the Father in me. They swear, not by him, lest he command the oath, but in him, promising him obedience.
63.1: 63.1 Cassian. This psalm briefly treats, etc., down to that in sufferings we may hope in the Lord. Augustine. As our head, so let us pray in tribulations.
63.2: 63.2 Hear, O God, my prayer. That you may exalt, and deliver, because I entreat. From the fear of the enemy. Cassian. But not from the fear of death.
63.3: 63.3 You have protected me. Augustine. This was done in the head, and the members also experience it: by this example the rest are strengthened.
63.4: 63.4 For they have sharpened their tongues like a sword. Or those, namely, who are malicious and work iniquity. A bow. Hidden snares, as through a disciple, which is a bitter thing, that a table companion should be the betrayer. Bitter.
63.6: 63.6 Suddenly they will shoot. The same. Insidiously, as at one who does not know, as it seems to those who believe they deceive God. They will not fear. The same. O hard heart! to kill the man who raised the dead, and not fear for it. They have strengthened. Cassian. The speech, by obstinacy, not by truth. He is guilty of death: or, It is expedient that one man die. For themselves. The same. Not for the Lord, but for themselves, when they say: His blood be upon us and upon our children. That they might hide. The custom of the wicked; he who prepares a trick thinks he deceives.
63.7: 63.7 They have searched. Cassian. How they might accuse the just one, or how they might destroy him, lest the world go after him. Augustine. Searchings, that is, bitter and hidden counsels; but the more sharply they think, the more they fall away from truth and equity, and are plunged into darkness: for since they do not see God, they think they are not seen by God. Man shall come. Cassian. For he who searches out iniquities, etc., down to but in the heart of man it grows great. Augustine. They searched, but in vain, because man will come of his own accord to the passion. To a deep heart. The same. It was so for him, because he did this according to a deep counsel. The arrows of children are made. Cassian. He mocks the enumerated perversity of the Jews, who were the more troubled when the resurrection was announced, while the just rejoiced.
63.9: 63.9 Troubled. The same. There were those who, seeking counsel for their salvation, said: What shall we do, brethren?
63.10: 63.10 And all men feared. Augustine. If man fears, let not man terrify him from announcing, like the Apostles, whom the chief priests threatened, saying that they should not preach in the name of Jesus. And they understood his deeds. The same. Why did he suffer? why did he not come down from the cross? because he had to die and rise: which was not then understood.
63.11: 63.11 The just shall rejoice in the Lord. Cassian. A conclusion from what was said before, and the promise of the just is shown. All. The same. Lest you think it is said of the Apostles alone.
64.1: 64.1 Unto the end. Augustine. Jeremiah prophesied (25, 29) that after seventy years the people would return. Among the captives were Ezekiel and other prophets. When the seventy years were completed the temple was restored. It is a figure of us, who sigh from Babylon to Jerusalem, from the world and the body of sin to heaven. Of Jeremiah. Augustine, Jerome. Exalted; and it signifies those who say: Our conversation is in heaven. Haggai, festive. It signifies those who rejoice in hope, who in the remnants of their thoughts keep a feast day to the Lord; Ezekiel, the Lord strengthened me, and it signifies those who are strengthened in the Lord; these prophesied the return to Jerusalem. Of the people of the transmigration. Augustine. That is, who migrated from heaven to earth, from perfection to misery and confusion. When it began. The same. He who begins to love begins to go out; charity makes a citizen of Jerusalem, cupidity of Babylon: and so, mingled in body, they are separated in desire. Cassian. Consolation in exile; lest anyone despair: for it assures the return, and through whom, and what riches there are for those who return. He affirms the return, and prays.
64.2: 64.2 A hymn befits you. Not the gods of the nations and not elsewhere, but in contemplation, that is, faith, and there from good works the vow will be paid in the heavenly Jerusalem, which they used to pay to Mars after battles, and to the other gods in this manner. Sion. The heavenly homeland is Sion, the same is Jerusalem.
64.3: 64.3 Hear my prayer. Cassian. First he does what he says the others must do, namely, hear. All flesh. Augustine. That is, man, that is, of every kind: poor, rich, men, women, learned, unlearned, boys, old men.
64.4: 64.4 The words of the wicked. Cassian. With what hope do you pray this? Because to you all flesh will come, not only the soul, but also the wicked man. You must hear. For the words of the wicked, of the devil and of the first parents Adam and Eve. Have prevailed. That is, have cast into exile, or the pagans persuaded their children of their rites, but you will be propitiated in the sacrifice of Christ. Augustine. The words of the wicked, that is, the evil rites and customs of our parents, which we followed as children, who excel in age as in authority. You will be propitiated. Augustine. Propitiation is made through sacrifice, which Christ the priest offered. The same, then, is priest and victim.
64.5: 64.5 Blessed is he whom you have chosen, etc. Cassian. And blessed is everyone whom you have chosen from the mass of the perishing. You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you (John 15), and you have taken him into your lot, into eternal rest. Augustine. Or thus, you will be propitiated through the blessed man: etc., down to which cannot be told. In the good things. Cassian. Which good things are holiness in oneself, equity toward the neighbor. Temple. The Church, or the flesh of Christ.
64.6: 64.6 Wonderful. Augustine. Not in outward things, like an earthly house, but in justice, which is more beautiful to the inner eye, and more lovable than that which we now ought to hunger for, that we may then be filled with it. In equity. Cassian. When he will render to each what is worthy, to whom he also will say: Hear us, who are Savior. The hope of all. He describes the praises and powers of God. And in the sea afar off. Augustine. Therefore afar off, because in the sea. The sea is said in figure of the world, bitter with the falsehood of iniquities, and stormy with the gales of temptations, where fish devour one another.
64.7: 64.7 Preparing the mountains. Augustine. For fitting uses. In your strength. Because through them he worked miracles. How did he prepare? Girded with power, that is, with Godhead, because the humanity of the Word was girded with majesty, that what man did not have the Godhead might give. Girded. The same. Christ in the midst girded on every side, because we all who believe in him have him in common, but because faith is not from us but from him, he is said to be girded with his might.
64.8: 64.8 Who trouble the depth of the sea. Behold him who through those prepared worked, troubling to penance. The depth of the sea, not the surface, but hearts sunk deeper, or the hearts of princes. These were troubled when they saw both their gods and their hopes come to nothing. The sound. Augustine. Sounding with contradiction, tossed with persecution, etc., down to while they perceive these to be worth more than their gods.
64.9: 64.9 The morning and the evening. Augustine. Morning is prosperity, because morning is glad after the sadness of night. Evening adversity; in these man is tried, but it is given him to go out from them, lest he be captured by gains, he to whom God is riches: lest he be terrified by adversities, he for whom the Lord suffered. You will delight. You will make them delightful already in this life. For if the going out itself does not delight man, he does not labor to go out, but is captured by gains, he who is not pleased by the promise of Christ. And he is terrified by adversities, whom he does not delight who willed to suffer for him that he might make a way out for him.
64.10: 64.10 You have visited the earth and inebriated it. You will do this through the preachers, for within you teach those to whom they preach. The river. The depth has been filled with waters to receive, with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, for you prepared the food. The river of God. Cassian. The mercy of God is compared to a full river, etc., down to as it is disposed by him, without whom nothing is done there.
64.11: 64.11 Its streams. The Apostles and others who drank of the river. Inebriate, that they may suffice for themselves and others. Multiply, that through successions the preaching may not fail. The crown of the year, the whole world, where the Church is. Its streams. The same. You prepared, etc. And, O Lord, etc., down to by which the Word of God grows. The crown of the year. The same. Because the glory of victory belongs to him who conquers the devil. Of your kindness, etc. Augustine. Lest anyone glory in his merits. Your fields shall be filled. Cassian, Augustine. Men, on account of equality, that is, the just. The hills, because God raises the humble. The desert: all nations, to whom no prophet was sent.
64.13: 64.13 The beautiful places of the desert shall grow fat. When the Apostles came to them, through whom they were made comely.
64.14: 64.14 The valleys. The same. The humble peoples will bring much fruit. They shall cry out. The same. Not in blasphemy but in a hymn, whence they abound in grain. This psalm is sung at the funerals of the faithful, because it treats of the return from the Babylon of this world to the heavenly homeland, to which the saints, led out of the flesh at death, happily migrate, receiving the single robe, until in the resurrection they are glorified with the robe of double blessedness.
65.1: 65.1 Unto the end. Augustine. The Jews hoped for themselves temporal goods and resurrection from the justice of the law, etc., down to for the faith of the nations he would call to the same hope of resurrection. Shout joyfully to God, all the earth, etc. Cassian. First he admonishes all to rejoice in the resurrection of Christ, which gives life to all.
65.3: 65.3 Give glory. Augustine. Not as the Jews, who ascribe justice to their own merits and envy the nations grace. How terrible. The same. If you rejoice, also fear, lest what was given to the humble be taken from the proud: as happened to the Jews. Do not therefore insult the broken branches, but fear lest perhaps he not spare you either. Your works, O Lord. Cassian. Briefly he calls the mysteries of the incarnation works: that God is man, that he suffered, died, and the like. In the multitude of your power. Augustine. Here he hints at the resurrection, to which, the lying Jews being excluded, the nations are admitted. Bede. The Lord rose; many believed in him, etc., down to drank through grace. They shall lie. The works are of the earth, which the enemies lie about; against the liars, let all the earth adore, etc. Augustine. They shall lie. Enemies are wont to lie, etc., down to let all the earth adore.
65.5: 65.5 Come. Cassian. Diapsalma. He invites those beginning to consider the works of God, that one faith may join those whom one reward awaits: where, setting forth those works, he plainly says that the resurrection belongs to the nations, the Jews being put down.
65.6: 65.6 Who turns the sea. The same. The works in which he is terrible, and what they are, he adds: Who turns the sea. Literally, in the river Jordan; mystically, in the passing world. In the river. The same. Although sins are forgiven, yet in the course of mortality they are still present, for immortality does not come at once. In the river. Augustine. The river is the mortality of the world, where some come, others depart: but he who believes in Christ crosses on foot, humble in himself, not proud on a horse. There we shall rejoice. The same. Or thus: Terrible are the works, etc., down to and in these Christians rejoice. In him. The same. When he will be all in all, or in him who rules in his power.
65.7: 65.7 Let them not be exalted. The same. On account of the law, as if more were owed to them. For all have sinned, etc. (Rom. 3).
65.8: 65.8 Bless. Cassian. Diapsalma. He admonishes the nations to bless God, who though he tries with tribulations yet leads to the kingdom; for these things seem to oppose the promised resurrection. Make heard. Augustine. Openly, since he who loves God loves also his neighbor. The voice of his praise. Which the Father speaks of the Son: This is my Son.
65.9: 65.9 Who has set my soul. The same. Here he enumerates for what causes he ought to be proclaimed.
65.10: 65.10 For you have proved us. Augustine. You have not given us to be moved. Because you have proved us, you did not give us headlong, you proved us by adversities, by the fire of charity, which does not let torments be felt, or, you have tested us by the fire of tribulation, etc.
65.12: 65.12 A snare. Augustine. Not one who deceives, but one who tests. We passed through. Cassian, Augustine. You, all these things, and we, etc., down to this happens to us in temptations.
65.13: 65.13 I will enter. Cassian. Behold the goods against the preceding evils, to strengthen. In holocausts. That is, that I may offer myself to your sight, etc., down to but withdrew himself, which is dearer.
65.14: 65.14 They have distinguished. Augustine. He distinguishes who says he is nothing, God all; and that he needs him, not he me. And my mouth has spoken. Whom above all I have made manifest as prevailing over all other vows in my tribulation, not conquered by tribulation.
65.15: 65.15 Holocausts full of marrow. Myself with the marrow of inmost love. With the incense of rams. The same. Or, with incense, which is prayer; and rams, because the leaders of the flock pray most for the flock. With incense. Jerome, Augustine. With the prayer of the Apostles, because what is done by their tradition pleases God. Or with the burning and destruction of bestiality and resistance. Oxen: stubbornness; with goats, wantonness; these vices I slay in myself. I will offer you oxen. Augustine. If threshing oxen are offered, sinners do not remain so: but healed through penance they are offered; and they not by themselves but rather joined to the oxen, because they made friends for themselves of the mammon of iniquity.
65.16: 65.16 Come, hear. Diapsalma. All having now been set forth, he again admonishes not so much the unlearned as the devout, that by the example of his deliverance they may trust more in the Lord: blessing him for the hearing. So I do, and you, O nations, come.
65.17: 65.17 To him I cried with my mouth. Cassian. He sets forth how great things he did for his soul, adding: To him, etc. This he did for my soul, that I cried to him, while the nations cried to idols: and what I speak outwardly I have within, and not iniquity, because so purity of prayer is heard. I cried and exalted in my heart. Augustine. That is, I preached him publicly, and confessed him in secret. What I have in my mouth I have also in my heart: yet I will offer holocausts full of marrow. By these two the Christian is perfect.
65.18: 65.18 Mine. What is not perverse is his own; he sets it forth as a merit, that they may learn to labor before seeking the reward.
65.20: 65.20 My prayer, etc. These two are connected; if the prayer is not suspended, neither is mercy delayed.
66.1: 66.1 Unto the end. Cassian. After the canticle of the resurrection the Prophet adds his supplication, that the blessed may be led to the knowledge of God. He prophesies the blessing of all through the coming of Christ. Augustine. Because in the preceding psalm he had admonished us to bless God; which we cannot do unless he himself first blesses us; therefore he prays that this be blessed, saying: May God have mercy on us and bless us, etc.
66.2: 66.2 May God have mercy. The same. The blessing of God is first, which is like rain irrigating the earth of our mind: then we bless him, which is like fruit, and in both we grow, not he. Let him say therefore, desiring the rain of the Lord's blessing: May God have mercy, etc. May God have mercy on us and bless us. Cassian. But those who want many things, etc., down to and because Christ is known among the nations: Let them confess, etc. Bless us. The same. The Creator blesses the creature, by multiplying in number and merit. The creature blesses the Creator, by praising him with heart, voice and work, and ascribing to him every good it has.
66.4: 66.4 Let the peoples confess to you, O God. The same. After the knowledge he exhorts to confess for the direction and judgment.
66.5: 66.5 Let them rejoice and exult. Augustine. Because, now having confessed, they do not fear the judgments to come, those for whom Christ is advocate, not judge, let them rejoice.
66.6: 66.6 Let the peoples confess to you, O God. Cassian. The same admonition tending to something else, because the earth has given its fruit, and though the beginning of the sense is the same, yet it tends to different things.
66.7: 66.7 The earth has given her fruit. Jerome. Of Mary, Christ, etc., down to: But she alone ought not to have this, rather, Let him bless us also. God, our God. The same. Three times the Trinity, him, the unity. And let all fear him. Cassian. Fear is asked among benefits, that the things entrusted may be cautiously guarded: the fear of God begins and consummates; he who knows how to fear does not cease to love.
67.1: 67.1 Unto the end. Cassian. A psalm of David the prophet on the exultation of Christ and the Church here and in the future, that all may sing to God. At the rising of Christ, as the ark lifted up, etc., down to Moses is said to have used words like these.
67.2: 67.2 Let God arise and let them be scattered. The same. He confidently wishes what he knows will be. And let those who hate him flee. Jerome. Or it can be read of the penitent, etc., down to that by the tears of penance, the fire of the Holy Spirit being applied, their hardness may be dissolved. Who hate. Augustine. Let the obstinate be taken from the presence of him who is present everywhere; a grievous curse, that they wish and try what can in no way be done.
67.3: 67.3 As smoke vanishes. Cassian. Smoke from a flame vanishes as it rises; so sinners produce smoky actions from the flame of wickedness, and fail by their very loftiness. As wax melts. Augustine. It can be said of the penitent; or in the judgment the wicked will be taken away from the face of God: who will be a fire for the punishment of the impious, and a light for the just.
67.4: 67.4 Let them feast. Cassian, Augustine. In delights, which are in the sight of God. And let them be delighted, this can delight them, that they are glad because their gladness is not to be ended.
67.5: 67.5 Sing to God. Augustine. He turns to those to whom he gave so great a hope and exhorts them. Who ascends. The new life will not receive him unless the old has died; or, by rising he overcame the fall of the body. Above the west. Cassian. The setting of death falls upon him over whom the sun of justice rises. And that you may not doubt who this is, the Lord is his essential name, whom the Jews killed as a common man. In his sight. The consideration of the future reward softens hardships.
67.6: 67.6 Of the orphans. Augustine. Those whose father has died, the world and the devil, and whose mother is concupiscence. The widows, whose husband, error, dies; in whom God dwells, whom he gathers, whom he draws, because from widows and orphans he makes for himself a temple in which he is.
67.7: 67.7 God who makes dwell. Jerome. In the Hebrew it has: But the Lord makes monks dwell in a house, with whom sin does not dwell. Of one manner. Augustine. Of one mind, thinking one thing, etc., down to not by merits, hence he adds: Who leads out the bound. Leads out the bound. Cassian. From hell, the devil being bound. Who provoke. Blasphemers against God. Or by persecuting in the tombs, buried in carnal stinks, so that they neither wish nor are able to walk. Provoke. Augustine. By resisting justice, since they are altogether dead in dead works; but the bound wish to walk and cannot; these are loosed by grace, those are raised.
67.8: 67.8 O God, when you went forth. Cassian. Diapsalma, on the word of the Gospel through the going forth of Christ. O God, when you went forth. Truly you lead out, because his going forth was prefigured before Israel, when he appeared in the pillar of cloud and fire in the desert, and satisfied them with manna. Augustine. The going forth, when he appeared to men through humanity, or when he leads out the bound, that is, raises them. He passed through the desert, when he came to the nations. Basil. When you went forth. As if he said: when you were about to pass through that solitude which had not yet received the splendor of light, you shook the earth and moved it, but from heaven you distilled the drops of your grace.
67.9: 67.9 The earth was moved. Because then earthly men were moved on seeing such wonders. The heavens dropped at the presence of God: Manna, when manna came down as a dropping from the presence of God, whose presence was known by the pillar. Augustine. Mount Sinai smoked at the presence of God, according to another reading, when Moses received the law there.
67.10: 67.10 Rain. This is what the heavens dropped, manna, a voluntary rain which satisfied the will of that nation in eating eagerly. You will set apart, O God, for your inheritance. Because he did not give to other nations what he then gave to the Jews. Weakened, etc. For a time, while it did not believe in Christ. Cassian. God has perfected his inheritance, while he admitted the nations in supplement. He adds whereby he perfected it.
67.11: 67.11 Living creatures. That is, your nations, while they believe, dwell in the inheritance, that is, in the Church. He sets forth who the living creatures are. You prepared: he means the predestined, because they were prepared from the origin of the world. Augustine. Or, Mount Sinai at the presence of the God of Israel, understand it dropped, etc., down to in which grace abounded. Cassian. These things mystically, but according to the figure, etc., down to he sends therefore to the mystery. Augustine. Some books do not have mount, but at the presence of God, Sinai of Israel; that is, who gave the law to the people of Israel: because he who gave the law through Moses, by which to terrify, gave also the blessing through the Apostles, by which to set free. In sweetness. Cassian. It is sweetness by which good is done, not from fear of punishment, but from delight in justice.
67.12: 67.12 The Lord will give the word. Many powers to those who preach the word.
67.13: 67.13 The king of hosts. Jerome. Of the Apostles, or of the beloved. Cassian. The Father is king of the angels, whom he and the beloved command. Augustine. The king of hosts of the beloved. Of the Son, that is, the Father, or in the manner of the old Scripture Christ the king of hosts; of Christ, that is, of his own, as Moses did, as the Lord commanded Moses. Of the beloved, of the beloved. Cassian. The repetition of beloved is for commendation; but this repetition is not in all books, but whether it is or not, this is the sense, beloved not only for other things but also for dividing the spoils, which by dividing he made the Church beautiful.
67.14: 67.14 If you sleep. Augustine. To sleep among the midst of the lots is to rest in the authority of the two Testaments and to acquiesce peacefully. The wings of the dove silvered, the preachers by whose preaching the glory of the Church is borne to heaven. Dove. Augustine, Cassian. The dove is the Church, etc., down to is borne to heaven by preaching. And the hinder parts. Augustine. Where the roots of the wings, etc., down to the vigor of wisdom is charity. Among the midst of the lots. Augustine. In the Latin language it would be among the lots, etc., down to you shall have wings is ambiguous.
67.15: 67.15 Cassian. Diapsalma, as he distinguishes, on the gifts of Christ ascending, who alone can, and no other. Augustine. While by the grace of the Holy Spirit kings are distinguished, etc., down to and those who believe in him are protected.
67.17: 67.17 The mountain of God, a fat mountain. Augustine, Cassian. He adds the commendation of the mountain, etc., down to For this is the mountain which in Ezekiel wounds the prince of Tyre. It is well pleasing to God, etc. Augustine. For the Lord will dwell in it unto the end, that is, to the limit of his majesty, which is the end without end, and the fullness of all things. For the Lord has dwelt. None like this one, because this mountain, namely the Lord, will dwell in those mountains until he leads them to the end, that is, to contemplate God in himself. But other mountains are the chariots by which God is carried into the whole world. Chariot, because united with one mind by charity, whom God directs to the service of his will, with ten thousand, with innumerable peoples; the multitude of the saints. Unto the end. Because he is personally united to him, in whom dwelt all the fullness of the divinity bodily.
67.18: 67.18 Thousands of those who rejoice. Augustine, Cassian. It signifies a great multitude of the saints, etc., down to and therefore they rejoice. Sinai in the holy place. Cassian. It is the mountain on which the law was given. It is called the commandment in which the Lord rests, because in his holy commandments his presence is wont to be beheld. In Sinai. Jerome. Or in holy Sinai, that is, he who on mount Sinai once gave the law is the same in the holy one, that is, in Christ, who is the Holy of holies.
67.19: 67.19 You have ascended. Augustine. He who descended for our instruction. On high. Above all the heavens. You have led captivity captive. Cassian. First those held captive in hell: these are the spoils, the likeness of a triumph; you have received gifts among men from the Father, that is, men. Or you have given, as God, gifts to men, which is also done in triumphs. You have led captivity captive. Augustine. Hence they are called captives, because caught by the nets of Peter and put under the light yoke: hence in this chariot are thousands who rejoice; not who weep. You have received. Paul by apostolic authority, etc., down to: What you did to one of the least, you did to me.
67.20: 67.20 Daily. The same. Because daily he takes captive the captives to the end of the age. And because he leads that chariot to the end, he adds a prosperous journey. Journey. The course of life, which is truly prosperous, since the leader is the savior.
67.21: 67.21 Our God. Cassian. Diapsalma. He sets forth the operations which result from what was said above: the shattering of enemies, the conversions of sinners; martyrdoms of both sexes. Of saving. Augustine. He commends grace, because none is saved but through him; but lest you say, Why then must we die? bear it patiently, and do not be indignant at death, because even the Lord's departure, who was without sin, was no other than that of death, yet by will, that man might not fear death. Departures of death. Cassian. That is, the resurrection, do not complain of death, because Christ went out from it, and gave to go out from it. Lest you believe the evils of the obstinate go unpunished, he adds, but heads, pride, or the authors of the Jewish sect, or sedition, or heresy.
67.22: 67.22 The hairy crown of the head. The same. The cunning of empty questions, which seek such hostilities of calumnies that they seem to search out hairs.
67.23: 67.23 From Bashan. Augustine. That is, from confusion, etc., down to to those who were most desperate.
67.24: 67.24 Your foot. The same. That is, that those who were formerly enemies may become your foot, preaching even to blood, namely to death: and dogs, barking for God, who eat of the crumbs, etc. Your foot. Only those are to be taken up to the office of governing who preach to others what they receive, who carry out with the hands of good works what they preach or teach with the mouth; hence in Leviticus: The head of the turtledove is twisted back to the armpits. In blood. Basil. Because he shows God, etc., down to: and when I conquered them, my garments were sprinkled. Of the dogs. Augustine. In a great sacrament Gideon was ordered to lead out those who lapped water like dogs, three hundred only and no more, in the sign of the cross because of the thau, which signifies three hundred. From him. As if you ask whence so great a good, that they become dogs of him whose enemies they were? he says: From him, that is, by his grace, not from themselves.
67.25: 67.25 They have seen your goings, O God. The same. Or your steps have been seen, O God, by which you came into the world. This grace lay hidden in the Old Testament: now it is evident, when the Son who was sent is proclaimed among the nations. Who. God. Is in the holy place, the body, although the faithless do not see him, according as he suffered. In this too, by suffering or believing, the princes came before them, or came before to praise you.
67.26: 67.26 Princes. Basil, Euthymius. He calls the Apostles Princes, etc., down to and by preaching they followed them. In the midst. The ministers set over the new churches praising God, the flesh tamed and the skin dried from the moisture of sin, and stretched from the wrinkle of duplicity.
67.27: 67.27 Bless in the churches. Cassian. Diapsalma. He prays and affirms that this beginning be extended and confirmed, for which the heretics too are destroyed. Augustine. In the churches. These are the young women timbrel-players, lest anyone think carnally of choruses of luxury. For the churches are young maidens adorned with new grace. In the churches, not elsewhere, not in other little assemblies. From the fountains of Israel. Cassian. That in imitation of them you may preach what is fitting: because they are princes of faith, hope and charity, and through this Benjamin, that is, son of the right hand.
67.28: 67.28 There Benjamin, etc. Princes, etc. The same. Through the names of the tribes he indicates Christ and the Apostles. There, namely in the temple of Jerusalem or in the Church. The interpretation of the names also befits the Church. Cassian. Perhaps the Apostles were from these tribes, etc., down to: confession in faith, strength in hope, breadth in charity. In ecstasy of mind, or, as the Greek word properly is, etc., down to as a faithful and prudent steward, he divided.
67.29: 67.29 Command, O God, to your strength. The same. O God, make known the Son, as if to bring about what I announce as to come. Or, to your strength, that is, enjoin it on your strong ones, to announce you. Or, O Father, entrust your work to your strength, the Son, or the Holy Spirit. Augustine. For God commends his charity toward us, since, while we were sinners, Christ died for us: which he prays well and confidently. Confirm this, O God, which you have wrought. By beginning.
67.30: 67.30 From your temple in Jerusalem. Which is free, our mother, which is the temple, from which comes every best gift; from that temple, then. The kings of the earth. Or special ones will offer you gifts, that is, sacrifices of praise. But because heretics clamor against this praise.
67.31: 67.31 Rebuke the beasts of the reed. Augustine. That is, those who are moved by every wind of doctrine. That they may shut out those who are proved.
