This is what the Apostle says: Those who are proved, let them be made manifest (1 Cor. 11); or let the proved shut them out from the cows. For the steady, strong and grave do not allow themselves to be seduced: In a grave people I will praise you. Scatter. Rebuke the beasts, and also scatter the dissenters. The nations that desire wars. Heretics and others who consent to them, whom he calls nations on account of the kinds of diverse sects, lest the series of successions there confirm error.
67.32: 67.32 Out of Egypt, Ethiopia. Augustine. By the name of Egypt or Ethiopia he signifies the faith of all nations, the whole from the part. Not therefore from the Jews alone, but from the nations he prophesies there will be heralds. Jerome. Ethiopia, the nation black with sins, hastens to give its hands to God. A likeness from the conquered, who, laying down arms, give them to the victors lest they perish. His hand shall come before. The same. That is, his vengeance, through confession, lest they be punished remaining in sins.
67.33: 67.33 To God the kingdoms. That To God may be at the beginning of the following verse. Or rather To God is at the end of the preceding verse. And faith is commended, as it were, man is not justified by preceding works, but by faith which begins to work through love. Ethiopia, therefore, will believe God, and so will come before his works, that is, Ethiopia's, which in the Greek is not ambiguous, that is, by believing in God, it will come before its own works. Or his of Egypt, to God, that is, in God. Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God. Augustine. All having run its course, which we now see fulfilled, he exhorts to the praise of Christ, and foretells his coming to be. Sing psalms. Cassian. Diapsalma. Sing psalms: he will come who ascends, where he will consummate the saints.
67.34: 67.34 He ascends. The same. As man. For as God, equal to the Father, he is above the heaven of heavens, the higher creatures, so that he has nothing above himself. Jerome, Cassian. East. The Word begotten of the Father. And he ascends from the east by the power of the Word. Toward the east. He expressed the place where he rose and whence he ascended. Augustine. Toward the east, of our illumination. Or because Jerusalem is in the East. To his voice. The same. He who was humble in the passion will give the voice of power in the common resurrection. The voice of power. Cassian. The efficacy of raising all the dead.
67.35: 67.35 His magnificence and power. Augustine. Since then there will be no mixing with the wicked, hence his magnificence over the true Israel will be evident. In the clouds. Because he will come to judgment not alone, but with the elders of the people, who are the clouds: lest you take it otherwise, he adds: Wonderful in his saints. Euthymius. By the clouds. Here he understands the Apostles themselves, as being above and eminent over earthly affairs, and as full of spiritual water, which they drew from the depths of the Holy Spirit, to irrigate the fields and plains of souls, that is, the believers themselves.
67.36: 67.36 He will give power and strength to his people, blessed be God. Cassian. He promised great things, lest anyone, because of human weakness, despair of reaching such rewards.
68.1: 68.1 Unto the end. Augustine. Adam was changed from the form of God for the worse, etc., down to to suffer according to the Greeks. Cassian. The fourth psalm which treats more broadly of the passion and resurrection. It treats of the cause of the change, that is, the passion of Christ. Here Christ speaks, head and body. Save me. First, he prays to be saved, because he suffers much, as far as concerns himself freely, but what another seized, he himself pays. This is the voice of the despised grain of mustard seed, while it is buried in the garden, which grows into a great plant: this is dark and altogether contemptible. So also Christ, of whom: We saw him having no beauty nor comeliness, yet he filled the face of the earth, made a great mountain. The waters even to my soul. Augustine. That is, the crowds, etc., down to beyond which the wicked have nothing they can do to them.
68.3: 68.3 In the mire. Augustine. Man was made from the mire of the earth, etc., down to that is, the power of the flesh to escape the passion. Substance. Riches are meant, etc., down to that is, I did not find in them what I did. I came. Because willingly. Into the deep. The depth of the insane people.
68.4: 68.4 I have labored. Augustine. He cried long: Woe to you! scribes and Pharisees, so as to be hoarse as far as they are concerned, because he was not understood by them. Crying, etc. Cassian. He labors whose wish is not fulfilled. My eyes. Like the eyes of the two on the road not recognizing him, to whom what was within was made external, that is, the blindness which was made in the heart and in the eyes. For they said: We hoped that he would redeem Israel (Luke 24). Augustine. But he gave them hope back, etc., down to because they would have been lost. While I hope. Cassian. The cause is added: I wait for mercy, I do not entreat power.
68.5: 68.5 They are multiplied. Augustine. What he said before in type, he now says openly in fact. More than the hairs. For the infinite, or they are more than those which are for ornament. I took by force. They wished to seize divinity, and lost felicity: Adam seized it, presuming, like the devil, upon divinity.
68.6: 68.6 O God, you know. Cassian. Because he pays for others, he prays that those who wait, the ancients, and those seeking others, namely the moderns, may not be frustrated in him, since he bears so much so evenly. My foolishness. Augustine. From the members. Or, what is foolish of God is wiser than men. What they mocked in me, who seemed wise to themselves, you knew why the mockery happened, namely, such a death too. Cassian. My foolishness. That those ignorant of God about me are the ones who are changed into wise and just men.
68.7: 68.7 Let them not be ashamed. The same. He sets forth what he has paid; here he shows what he had said above of the members. Augustine. Let them not be ashamed, that is, let it not be said to them: Where is your Christ? or let the Church not be pressed, so that the children be ashamed. Who wait. Cassian. What the prophets and the just could not see with the eyes. Lest therefore it turn out otherwise than the Holy Spirit foretold through them, there follows: God of hosts, to whom nothing is impossible. God of Israel. Augustine. That those who can gaze on his Godhead may not be led astray by his carnal weakness.
68.8: 68.8 Because for your sake I have borne reproach. Cassian. He gathers into one the many things he endured, to arouse indignation against the Jews; reproach: he casts out demons by Beelzebub, a drinker, a glutton (Matt. 11). Has covered. This usually happens to those torn apart for good, who are wont for a time to become the more sad the more they know untruths are fabricated against them.
68.9: 68.9 A stranger. Or a guest, who is received in a house for a time; not as a most dear brother, which I was.
68.10: 68.10 The zeal of your house has eaten me up. When he drove out the sellers with a cord. What follows this zeal he adds: And the reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me. Because the rebuked Jews sent insults like darts upon him, such as: Is not this the son of Joseph? (Luke 4). Of those who reproached you. When they said: Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? (Ps. 77). These are your gods, Israel (Exod. 32). Hence he now says that the same insults fall on him which they once reproached, so that you may see that from impious custom they did this and not newly. Have fallen. Cassian. Evils fall upon us when we cannot avoid them: they have fallen, therefore, that is, they have had effect.
68.11: 68.11 And I covered my soul in fasting, etc. Augustine. I preferred to fast rather than receive gall and vinegar; that is, the old and bitter, who do not enter into his body. Cassian. And I covered. I did not exercise power by avenging. And it was made, which appeared in the spittings, a reproach. Augustine. Of detractors and mockers.
68.12: 68.12 And I put on. Augustine. I put on them flesh on which to vent their rage, and hid the Godhead. Sackcloth. Augustine, Jerome. Mortal flesh, that from sin he might condemn sin. Sackcloth, mourning flesh, as when he wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19), and for Lazarus (John 11). For a parable. Augustine, Jerome. A mocking one, so that in cursing anyone they would say: May it happen to you as to the crucified. Or, because I taught them in parables; hence: To you it is given to know the mystery of the Word of God, but to the others in parables. And then they spoke against me.
68.13: 68.13 They who sat. Cassian. They sit in the gate who mingle in the assemblies of men with diligent curiosity. He says, then, that his passion was a tale of the Jews, so that no one was exempt who was a stranger to such talk; hence Cleophas says: Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and do you not know, etc. (Luke 24). In the gate. Of the city: where judges are wont to sit to judge cases, that is, in public judgment. Jerome. Like the scribes and Pharisees having the key of knowledge: but neither entering nor allowing others to enter. And against me they sang. Cassian. They spoke of me in public assemblies, and sang at banquets: my mockery was their psaltery. Who drank wine. Augustine. Who are made drunk with temporal pleasure. Or, Cassian, let those who drink spiritual wine sing in praiseworthy work to God.
68.14: 68.14 But I. Cassian. To the evils mentioned is opposed prayer on his part, that we may learn to oppose not quarrels but prayers to disputes. A time of good pleasure. Augustine. Therefore now is the time of good pleasure and reconciliation, through the incarnation, the blood, the death; then he explains how this time came: In the multitude of your mercy. In truth. He put mercy first, now adds truth, because all the ways are mercy and truth: mercy, by forgiving sins; truth, by rendering what was promised.
68.15: 68.15 That I be not stuck fast. Augustine. In mind; above he said fixed in body; this is said from the weakness of the members. Out of the mire, that is, muddy desires. Out of the depths of the waters. Cassian. The Jews are deep in malice of counsel, turbulent in seditions.
68.16: 68.16 The deep. Cassian. Of sins, which swallows souls; hence: When the sinner comes into the depth of sins, he despises (Prov. 18). These dangers threaten his members. Neither let it press upon me, etc. Augustine. Even if you have fallen, the pit does not close its mouth over you, if you do not close your mouth; but confess and say: Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord, and you will escape. It closes over him who in the depth despises, from whom, as dead, as if he were not, confession perishes.
68.17: 68.17 Hear me, O Lord, etc. Cassian. The dangers of men having been set forth, he prays with their voice: Hear me, O Lord, for kind is your mercy, not because I have deserved. Kind. Augustine. Mercy is sweet to the afflicted, as bread to the hungry. Tribulation comes; God delays to help, to stir desire and make the help sweet; when that happens, there is no longer anything to delay.
68.18: 68.18 From a boy, etc. Augustine. From any saint, small, not proud; from whom the discipline of tribulation takes away pride.
68.19: 68.19 Because of my enemies, etc. Augustine. That they may be confounded by my deliverance, etc., down to hence Nebuchadnezzar himself converted preaches God. Because of my enemies. The same. This is plain, that the flesh rises, and ascending sends the Spirit; hence the enemies were converted, to whom it will not profit if you deliver only the soul.
68.20: 68.20 You know my reproach. The same. Because why these things are for me you know, they do not know. And because they themselves are in your sight, not knowing these things they cannot be confounded or corrected unless you openly pluck them out. And therefore he says: Because of my enemies. The same. Reproach, or disgrace, etc., down to but by helping may perfect. Reverence. The same. Others read ignominy, such as blows, scourges, and that he was handed over to Pilate as a guilty man: these he endured not for his own guilt but for us, to instruct us in such things.
68.21: 68.21 In your sight. Cassian. He arouses indignation against them, that they committed so great a crime with God present. My heart. Because he bore it willingly, according to that: With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you. Who might grieve together with me, and there was none; and who might comfort, and I found none. Augustine. The disciples and the women who wept over him were saddened, but not together. For they grieved carnally over mortal life, which was to be changed by death, when they ought to have grieved with him over the rest, who were killing the physician, which no one then did.
68.22: 68.22 And they gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. Augustine. That I did not find those who grieved together and those who comforted was for me bitter gall on account of the sorrow. Vinegar, etc. That is, sour, on account of their age. In the Gospel gall is read to have been offered to him, but in drink, not in food. It is said mystically, then, that is, upon the sweet food which he had taken with his disciples, which is the food of the unity of Christ, they cast gall: which they do to this day, and he sins more gravely who despises him sitting in heaven than he who crucified him walking on earth. They give a bitter drink, who by living badly make scandal for the Church, like heretics. The Lord tasted, teaching us also to taste, that is, to suffer such: but he did not drink, because such cannot be received into his body. This is foretold mystically, as it was also done mystically in the passion. Cassian. And they gave. This is the consummation of the passion; when he had said: I thirst, they offered gall with vinegar, by this deed showing their most bitter ways.
68.23: 68.23 Let their table become. Cassian. A prophecy against adversaries. Augustine. Let their table become. The table is Scripture: the Jews had it while they kept the commandment of God; after they became fasting from the law, this table was given before them to the nations, that they might grieve the more. Into a snare. That those who bound others with the letter of the law might fall bound in it. For retributions. Because it was taken from them and given to the nations. It was a retribution of evils, since, unwilling to feast on it, they were shut out from it. For a scandal. Because forsaking the author of peace, they stir up quarrels and perverse works for themselves.
68.24: 68.24 Eyes. Augustine. The teachers who lead the way. Let them be darkened, that is, lose the light of knowledge. And their back, etc. That is, the lesser. For when those who lead lose the light of knowledge, the followers are bent to carrying the burdens of sinners and to seeking earthly things; or, the back, the mind of the same. Always this is of those who do not repent.
68.25: 68.25 Pour out, etc. Cassian. That it may be copious after the manner of a river. Let it take hold. That it may not be possible to escape.
68.26: 68.26 Let their habitation become. Augustine. This now openly, etc., down to in which they were proud against God. In the tents. Cassian. The temple and the royal palace. To this he puts to dwell, which is done by the affection of a devout mind; to dwell in houses, which is done by bodily abiding.
68.27: 68.27 You have struck. Cassian. Not by his own fault: you struck by the passion, for the salvation of the nations; this they fulfilled by that cruel desire. And upon the sorrow. Because it was for their destruction. They added. To inflict death. Or upon the sorrow of my wounds, that is, which the lance and the nails had fixed in me, the guards of the sepulcher added.
68.28: 68.28 Add iniquity upon their iniquity, etc. Augustine. Their iniquity was to kill a man, and God added upon this that they should kill his Son, so that as they had killed the servants sent before, so also the heir himself.
68.29: 68.29 Let them be blotted out, etc. The same. Because they think themselves written, etc., down to and to stand at the right hand. Out of the book of the living, etc. Cassian. The knowledge of God, who predestined and gave life to those whom he foreknew to be conformed to the image of his Son. It is not, however, to be understood as if God writes anyone in this book whom he afterward blots out: but according to the hope of those who think themselves written.
68.30: 68.30 I am poor, etc. Cassian. Here he sets forth the dispensation of the incarnation and the holiness of his purpose, saying: What is the end of the passion? Sorrowful. Augustine. This according to the head, he sorrows for all: hence: He himself bore our sorrows (Isa. 53), which no other did. Therefore he says:
68.32: 68.32 And it will please. Cassian. The praise of a pure heart pleases more than the slaughter of cattle. A young calf. Augustine. For sins a young calf was offered, which signified the newness to follow; which has defense in its horns, protection in its hooves by which to tread down the roughness of the world; bringing forth, because the faithful man is increased daily by the power of God. Augustine. The calf stirs the earth with its hooves, so he who does not contradict, yet savors earthly things abjectly, is to be stirred up with hooves: and above this calf my praise will please with the angels, where neither will an adversary have to be driven off, nor a sluggard be roused from the earth.
68.33: 68.33 Let them see. Cassian. Because the offering is now in the mind, not in things, where the poor are made equal to the rich. And, O poor, yet do this with regard to God, seek the Lord. Or, that you may see, seek God, the food of the mind. The bound. Augustine. He who seeks beyond necessities loads himself with fetters; but sufficient for the day is its own evil. The bound. The same. Those bound by mortality, with which the offended Lord shackled his servants: but from it he hears them crying.
68.35: 68.35 Heaven, earth, sea. Cassian. Literally, that is, heavenly things, earthly things, and swimming things, these praise, while the Creator is praised from them. The same. It is the riches of the poor to see created things, and from them to praise the Creator. Let them praise him, etc. The same. What he said before together, he now admonishes singly; or, let the heavenly, earthly, swimming praise. And, to conclude everything perfectly, he adds: All that are in them: so all creation is invited to praise. Jerome, Cassian. As if he said: Let every knee bow, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth (Phil. 2). And all the creeping things in them. Cassian. All monstrous kinds, clinging to earthly sins.
68.36: 68.36 For God will save Sion, etc. Augustine. In the hope of the faithful people the building of the Church is completed: hence all creation is admonished to praise.
68.37: 68.37 And they that love his name, etc. Cassian. What in particular? all who love your name will dwell. Augustine. These are the seed of his servants. For this verse explains the preceding.
69.1: 69.1 For remembrance. Cassian. Memory in two ways, etc., down to and take up the hope of resurrection. Augustine. The voice of the afflicted for Christ, etc., down to first asking to be helped, the wicked to be ashamed.
69.2: 69.2 O God, come to my help. He admonishes that we glory in God, not in ourselves. Cassian. Here every petition is an affirmation, hence tribulations are not to be feared. This verse is said before all the hours at the beginning, because when we are wont to pray the devil especially strives to tempt, as dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment.
69.3: 69.3 Let them be confounded. Cassian. To be confounded is to be troubled by perversity. Let them be abashed, lest punishment follow the offspring from justice. Who seek, etc. Augustine. The times in the Church are different: at first there was the assault of the persecutors, hence, who seek; now there remains the ill will of the thinkers, hence, who wish. The same.
69.4: 69.4 Let them be turned back. The same. There are two kinds of persecutors, etc., down to he goes out whole who is caught by neither.
69.5: 69.5 Let all exult and rejoice in you. Cassian. He admonishes the good to rejoice, whom God helps and delivers as needy. Always. Because one ought never to cease from his praise. Let God be magnified. Cassian. Said after our manner, where someone grows by praises; for it is not God but we who profit by praising.
69.6: 69.6 But I am needy. Cassian. What I exhort, I do, etc., down to where there is a rich man, he always aims, desires and receives. Do not delay. The same. It seems slow, what is sought with great desire. Augustine. Let it not seem to me slower that you are to come, which is done through patience; he who lacks it finds it slow, and is turned aside from it: like Lot's wife, who became a pillar of salt to season you: for she is an example to you not to look back.
70.1: 70.1 Unto the end. Augustine. On the commendation of grace, etc., down to almost in single syllables grace is commended. Of the sons of Jonadab. The same. For willing sons, etc., down to who are evil of themselves. Cassian. Or thus, we are admonished in the title to have the devotion of the sons of Jonadab, etc., down to but they in their accustomed malice remained in obstinacy.
70.2: 70.2 In you, O Lord, I have hoped. The general just man speaks, from the beginning of the world to the end: placing all hope in God, he commends his grace, lest we presume falsely in ourselves. Cassian. Or the first are captive in the world, from which one can escape: the second in hell. Or, of the first, that is, of those who were captured by vices before the sons of Christ. This whole psalm with supreme intent commends the grace of God, which is given freely.
70.3: 70.3 Be to me a God, a protector, and a fortified place, etc. He promised two things, he renders two others.
70.4: 70.4 Of the sinner. Augustine. There are two kinds of sinners: some received the law, like the Jews and Christians; others did not, like the pagans.
70.5: 70.5 From my youth. Cassian. That is, from conversion, or from when I began to fight against the devil. Augustine. From my youth, from when I began to hope in you, etc., down to a young man fights, but falls, unless God is his hope.
70.7: 70.7 In you is my song. Cassian. It is a delight to me to be in you. Always. That the benefits may be continual. Always. Augustine. Both in the present, etc., down to against which nothing stands.
70.8: 70.8 Let my mouth be filled. Cassian. He has spoken of the benefits, now he asks that he may be able to give thanks. For if God does not fill the mouth, desire does not burn. All the day your greatness. Augustine. That is, without interruption, etc., down to by the name of greatness, therefore, he includes everything.
70.9: 70.9 Cast me not off. Cassian. Concerning the grace to be given in the time of old age and senility. Of old age. Augustine. Old age in Christ, when he was made a prodigy, when weakened on the cross and mocked; which is called old age because he took it from the old nature, hence: Our old man was crucified together with him (Rom. 6).
70.10: 70.10 For my enemies have spoken. Augustine. This is said of Christ, who among the hands of his enemies was made weak, and seized as though he could do nothing. But here it is said of his members, because he had such things from our person.
70.11: 70.11 God has forsaken him. Augustine. Hence elsewhere: Why have you forsaken me? that is, why do they think me forsaken, to their own harm. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.
70.12: 70.12 Be not far from me. Cassian. They think him far off, when he delays; be not far, that he may not expose to heavier things.
70.13: 70.13 Let them be confounded, etc. Cassian. Because the dispositions of God are not changed. Those who detract my soul. Another reading, those who commit my soul. Augustine. That is, provoking us to resist God, which is to wage war against God; as do those who are displeased with God in their adversities, which is to hold him unjust. The soul is also committed if it hates those by whom it suffers. Who seek. The same. As Job's wife did, who said: Say something against God and die (Job 7). As also the wife of Tobias said: Where are your acts of justice? (Tob. 4, 2). She said this so that God might displease him.
70.14: 70.14 And I will add. Augustine. It is an addition of praise, after the creation of all things, the praise for the incarnation and resurrection, which the lower things teach. All. Augustine. Because if he is praised in all other things, not yet in that he raised our flesh to eternal life, which is the praise added for the resurrection of Christ. Or there would be all praise, and nothing would be lacking to praise, if he condemned sinners, because it would be justice; but because you free these too: I will add above all your praise.
70.15: 70.15 My mouth shall announce your justice. Christ, but lest you take it otherwise, he adds: Salvation. Why? because it is not approved that anyone is justified by the works of the law. And this is: For I have not known literature, that is, the figures of the law by which I might become powerful. All the day. Augustine. Or thus, etc., down to may serve justice. For I have not known literature. The same. I will preach your salvation all the day, etc., down to because he was found in habit as a man (Phil. 2), and rises dead.
70.17: 70.17 You have taught. Cassian. Through the books, or by inspiring up to now: through the spans of time doctrine grew. Wonders. That of the unjust a just man. Wonders. Augustine. What is more wonderful than to raise the dead? etc., down to this is from youth and now. Youth. The same. Some note four times of the Church, some distinguish only three, signifying the same by now and old age. Hence the youth of the Church was when the virtue of the martyrs fought. Cassian. But the time proceeding, now, when faith advances through the Churches. Augustine. Old age, that is, the grave age, when the charity of many will begin to grow cold, when the times of the world decline. Senility. Cassian. The setting time, etc., down to against whom the Lord: I am with you even to the consummation of the age, etc. (Matt. 21).
70.19: 70.19 Even to the highest. And lest you think that man alone needs grace, etc., down to it contains in that they are. Even to the highest. Because the man-God sits at the right hand of the Father reigning with him. The great things you have done. Both are wonderful, that by grace man is redeemed who by justice had been condemned. O God, who is like you? How many tribulations, many and evil, have you shown me, and turning you gave me life, and from the depths of the earth, etc. To which person what grace there is, the captive namely, each resurrection, of mind and body; hence he promises thanksgiving.
70.22: 70.22 In the instruments of the psalm. Cassian. In the quickening of the spirit or the contemplative life.
70.23: 70.23 My soul which you have redeemed. Augustine. With the very inner lips with which it silently cries to God.
70.24: 70.24 When they shall be confounded and abashed. Then is the place of true and secure exaltation, when it is not permitted to the impious to rule.
71.1: 71.1 For Solomon, etc. Augustine. The true peacemaker, etc., down to who is commended here according to both natures. Cassian. The fourth psalm on the two natures of Christ admonishes us to believe Christ true God and true man as king, and it is a prophecy about Christ.
71.2: 71.2 Give the king your judgment, O God. Cassian. On judgment, wishing it to be given to the Son. Your justice, etc. Augustine. Note the repetitions of the same thing, or in other words, which greatly commend the divine utterances, especially in the psalms: and in that kind of speech by which the affection of the soul is to be moved.
71.3: 71.3 Mountains. Augustine. The prophets, the Apostles, who by height are near to heaven; to announce peace to the faithful people, Christ. And hills. Let them receive justice, that is, Christ, or the mountains peace for the people: and the hills he says of both preachers, preceding and following. Or let the mountains receive, that is, the greater. Peace. The word of reconciliation, namely the word of the Gospel, that they may announce it to the people. And the hills. That is, the lesser; justice, that is, obedience, that they may obey the doctrine of truth. By saying yours and your, he shows that all things which are the Father's are the Son's, and conversely.
71.4: 71.4 He shall judge the poor of the people. Cassian. He treats of the same judgment by affirming. After the wish, by the power of prophecy, he says what is to be provided by the coming of the Lord. Augustine. Or according to another reading: Justice will judge the poor. But the codices that have it in the letter are more approved. The poor of the people. That is, those who are poor in the people, in which good and bad are mingled. He will humble the calumniator. For while he helps by his grace, etc., down to who strives to draw the innocent into guilt. Jerome, Augustine. Or, he will humble, and, the devil being conquered, splendor will remain with the sun; that is, the Son with the Father, sitting at the right hand of the Father forever, this is before the moon, from generation to generation.
71.7: 71.7 He shall come down like rain, etc. Cassian. Behold who and what sort that king is who is to judge. Augustine. It alludes to the deed of Gideon, etc., down to and afterward the Gentiles would be rained upon, the fleece of the Jews being dry. Cassian. Christ will come down, etc., down to who then, after such plain similitudes, would doubt of the Virgin's childbearing? Upon the fleece, and as drops. Augustine. The fleece, Judea, which by the authority of doctrine was to be stripped, like a sheep of its fleece: or, because it held back the rain of doctrine, which it would not preach to the nations.
71.8: 71.8 And he shall rule from sea to sea. Cassian. He shows how great the extent of the kingdom is. From the river. Augustine. From the Jordan, where the voice: This is my beloved Son. From there his teaching began: from there the authority of the master is extended to the ends of the earth, the Gospel of the kingdom having been preached. Cassian. From there the rule of baptism flowed through the whole world. In few words he teaches great sacraments
71.10: 71.10 The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts. Cassian. The enemies are called obstinate, etc., down to or, historically it can be taken of the kings who came to adore Christ.
71.12: 71.12 For he shall deliver the poor from the powerful, etc. Cassian. He treats of his works, etc., down to in participation of justice.
71.14: 71.14 From usuries. Augustine. Usuries, sins, etc., down to helping by grace to do justice. Or, from usuries, of the future, that is, eternal punishments; and from iniquity, that is, from the sin itself, for which punishment was due. The name. Christian. Before him. Because in his kingdom they are to live before him.
71.15: 71.15 And he shall live, and to him shall be given of the gold, etc. Cassian. On the honor of the king. Of Arabia. Augustine. By Arabia, the nations; by gold, wisdom, which excels among doctrines. Of him always. The same. By multiplying, or attaining, or from his institution, because he himself taught to pray.
71.16: 71.16 Firmament. Augustine. It belongs to the prophets, because what they foretold he fulfilled. On the tops of the mountains. The same. The authors of the Scriptures, the Prophets and Apostles; whom he confirms, because all that was foretold by them was fulfilled in him. On the earth. Because for the sake of those who are on earth all things were written. Hence he himself came to earth to fulfill them. Above Lebanon. Augustine. As Lebanon produces lofty cedars, so Christ produces saints for heaven. Like grass. Cassian. Not the age of old grass but the greenness is compared to the saints. The good, migrating from this city of the present Church, will flourish in that blessedness. Augustine. In Genesis by the name of grass grain also is understood, etc., down to and whatever is held great in the world will be compared to the grass of the earth.
71.17: 71.17 May his name be blessed, etc. Cassian. He admonishes all to give him praises, because all shall be blessed in him. Before the sun. The same. That is, before every creature, lest you think the Son of God temporal. All nations. Augustine. Lest you take it of the twelve tribes, he adds all nations.
71.18: 71.18 Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, etc. Augustine. He praises for his part. Note the exclamatory blessing, with admonition and prophecy. So be it, so be it, etc. Cassian. It is magnificent that he concludes thus: It belongs to one who wishes to say it once, to one who greatly desires to repeat it. As if he said: What you have commanded, Lord, so be it, so be it, until what began from the river reaches to the ends of the earth. Jerome. It must be known that the seventy-first psalm is the end of the second book: hence at the end it has: So be it, so be it, for which in the Hebrew is said: Amen, amen.
71.20: 71.20 The praises have failed. The same. This also is to be observed more carefully, that the phrase: The hymns of David the son of Jesse have failed, belongs to the end of the seventy-first psalm. But what follows: A psalm of Asaph, is the beginning of the next. A hymn has three things: the praise of God with a song: for unless it is sung joyfully it is not a hymn: and one does not sing who does not love. If it is praise, and not of God, it is not a hymn: and if it is of God, and not with song, not a hymn. Beyond the usual he adds: Son of Jesse; for David, a man, a certain son of Jesse, reigned in Israel in the time of the Old Testament, in which the New was, but hidden: as Christ also in David and in Abraham, but hidden, as fruit is in the root, but does not appear. But a few prophets knew both Christ and the New Testament, namely in secret, and proclaimed that it would be revealed. In that time, therefore, for that kingdom where a man, the son of Jesse, reigned, for such carnal things the carnal people praised God. But that kingdom and others like it failing, the praise fails, not of the Son of God, but of the son of Jesse. These things failing, which God withdrew so that the things hidden under them might be sought, Asaph speaks, that is the Synagogue, but the faithful one, which piously worshipped God, although on account of earthly things, which it sought from God, not from demons, as the nations did. But observing that blasphemers abounded in these things, for the sake of which it served, it began to waver, not knowing what lay hidden in these figures, as though there were nothing better that God would give: but admonished through these withdrawn things to seek what it does not hold in common with the wicked, chastising itself with wonder, it says: How good is Israel! But to whom? To the upright of heart. First, therefore, describing the wickedness of the wicked, he says he envied their prosperity; yet corrected from it, and corrected he corrects others. Cassian. Here it is treated that praises have failed: because God no longer gives flattering things, as to boys to be enticed to serve, and the Synagogue says this, which now bears witness against what it formerly did, that it may be the more credible.
72.1: 72.1 How good. Cassian. He admonishes that we praise God not for temporal things but for eternal.
72.2: 72.2 Feet. Cassian. According to the judgment of the mind, which differed from the truth. Steps, hasty acts; almost, because it soon returned.
72.3: 72.3 The peace of sinners. Augustine. Temporal, flowing, perishable. Seeing. Not understanding. Because this peace is seen, not understood, it deceives the eyes, for it is flowing and perishable. Cassian. The peace of sinners because there is no turning aside in their death. That is, they do not die soon, but live long; although a stroke is at times not firm, as the scourge of correction lasts. And firmness in their stroke. God does not have mercy by consolidating their wounds: or, by likeness incurable, for whom nothing is forbidden.
72.6: 72.6 They are covered with their iniquity and impiety. Cassian. Lest they come to their senses; not clothed, that they might at least have the head free, but wholly covered.
72.7: 72.7 Their iniquity came forth as, etc. Augustine. There are some wicked from leanness, that is, necessity: others from abundance, as a poor man steals from want, a rich man from cupidity. They have passed. Cassian. As from the straight paths.
72.8: 72.8 On high. Augustine. Openly, in the manifest: or blasphemers against God.
72.9: 72.9 Against heaven. The same. As if they were gods; or against God, whom they blaspheme, saying that God either does not know their evils or does not punish. Their tongue has passed through the earth, etc. The same. Which speaks beyond the measure of humanity, etc., down to but their tongue goes beyond human frailty.
72.10: 72.10 Therefore my people shall return here. Cassian. Asaph explaining, etc., down to will return to it. Here. Augustine. In this opinion in which I now am. Full days shall be found in them. Jerome. They are found perfect, even if it does not now appear. Cassian. Or, the days are full, when Christ came: these then are among the Jews, who knew Christ.
72.11: 72.11 And they said. Augustine. Whence shall they be converted? etc., down to this is why it seemed to them that he did not know this. How does God know. The same. He does not say, he does not know: but still hesitates and is near to health: and from so grave an infirmity health is nearer, as the sick burn the more when near to recovery.
72.13: 72.13 And I said: Then in vain have I justified my heart, etc. Cassian. These are the things they said, to refute which I say these things: or still from the person of one doubting. He says he was deluded by foolish thoughts, so that when he has rejected these he may have provided better for us.
72.14: 72.14 And my chastisement. Another reading, and my judge in the morning. Cassian. Behold now the remedy, Christ the judge, who pointed out the way of truth, and, rising in the morning, transferred our hope from the world to the heavens.
72.15: 72.15 If I said. The same. Behold now he restrains himself by the authority of the saints, and now, truth being near, he deliberates thus: If I said. Behold the nation. Augustine. He begins to resolve another inconvenience. I have rejected; I judged what is not. I supposed; by what was said I wish to prove God not just; but in this way I think, I do not absolve. Before me, that is, as regards present things; or greater than I, surpassing me, unless God open. Or, behold the nation of your sons, to whom I disposed and sang, understand, it meets and confronts me, that is, there meets me the earlier preaching which I made to the Israelites, that they should worship God who created all things and restores to all according to their works: the doctrine meets me, to which I am fitted and accommodated. But lest I reject the nation of the earlier fathers, or contradict my earlier doctrine: I supposed, etc. Of your sons. For all, Abraham and the rest, teach otherwise, whom I ought to believe: for I am not wiser than all. But lest I reject: I supposed, or, I undertook to know; he is now recalled from the fall, who does not presume to be knowing against the saints. That I might know the truth of this matter, which not before, while he said God did not care for these things. I was thinking that I might know this: the first step of knowledge, when one knows that he does not know what he formerly seemed to know: but he repudiates the earlier opinion while he seeks another.
41.8: 41.8 Deep calls to deep. The same. It is fitting that I be mindful, etc., down to and on account of all these things I pray in adversities, and this is: With me is prayer. The same. Or deep calls to deep, that is, the judgment which God brought upon the sinner, etc., down to because he fears the judgments. Of the cataracts. Cataracts, literally, are the mouths of rivers.
41.9: 41.9 In the day. The same. That is, in prosperity, etc., down to whence we may live in adversity. With me is prayer. The same. Prayer in disturbances is mine, and this is with me.
41.10: 41.10 Why have you forgotten? Cassian. Why do you now allow me to be vexed by these miseries? He saw the sweetness of the homeland, and shuddered at the dangers of the world.
41.11: 41.11 While my bones are broken. Augustine. The bones are broken, as it were, while the virtue of patience is afflicted, which the wicked deride. This is that reproach: While it is said to me: Where is he? either he does not exist, or he does not care for you.
42.1: 42.1 Unto the end, a psalm of David. Augustine. Of the body of Christ, which groans here among the tares, that is, among the wicked, having many things in common with them: to be born, to die, prosperity and adversity: with whom, because it has no common cause of merits, it cries out: Judge me, etc. The same. This psalm is against pressures, lest they too draw us back from God. Cassian. He complains of the mingling with the wicked, and prays for separation. Judge me. The same. He does not ask that his own sins be examined, which is dangerous, but that his cause be prepared against the impious, that he may be with the elect: hence he adds: And distinguish. The unholy nation is the unjust and deceitful man, from whom he is separated in judgment: but here too, that he may not be corrupted by them.
42.2: 42.2 Why do I go about sad? Augustine. He seeks the cause of sadness, which is sin, as the cause of joy is justice. Isaiah, on account of sin: For a little while I made him sad, for so God punishes.
42.3: 42.3 Send forth your light. Cassian. Because, when it comes, all sadness of confusion will be taken away. Augustine. Because we now have the pledge of certainty, since these very things, that is, light and truth, have led the present Church, which is the tabernacle, away from sins.
42.4: 42.4 And I will go in. As the high priest to the Holy of Holies. Cassian. And I will go in. Of the final joy, for which he praises in tribulation, he who above was sad, whence he also comforts himself.
42.5: 42.5 I will confess to you on the harp. Augustine. He who does the commandments of God and does not suffer confesses on the psaltery; but he who does and suffers, which is from the lower nature, confesses on the harp, which sounds from below, as the psaltery from above. On the harp. Cassian. Behold, he who above was sad over the evils of the world makes joy for himself from good understanding. Why do you disturb me? The same. Often and strongly he persuades that the sadness of the world must be fled, which extinguishes patience, charity and hope, and confounds the whole life. The salvation of my countenance. Augustine. And elsewhere: Have mercy on me, etc., down to almsgiving, and prayer, which flies to God on those two wings.
43.1: 43.1 For understanding. Augustine. Let them not so seek that things be done for them, etc., down to and that these things not be loved. Cassian. He distinguishes the benefits of God, which were given to beginners in the world, to the perfect in heaven. That it may be the more wonderful that the present are abandoned, he recalls the past.
43.2: 43.2 O God, with our ears. Augustine, Cassian. First he says: O God, as one is accustomed to do when glad or gravely afflicted. We have heard. That the faith in the matter may be greater, lest it be thought doubtful. Our fathers. Not young men, that they might seem our own, who would speak of certain things as their own. The work which, etc. The same. Even if he works always, yet he is said to work when he shows some sign of newness.
43.4: 43.4 But your right hand. Augustine. That is, the good success which you gave them. And your arm, etc. The same. That is, strength; and the light, that is, wise counsel: all of which you did out of your goodwill.
43.5: 43.5 You yourself are my king and my God. Augustine. The times have changed; the author is not changed.
43.7: 43.7 For I will not trust in my bow. Cassian. Man's lesser strength, because it avails less in war. The sword. The greater strength, which is believed to avail more in war. Augustine. Or, my sword shall not save me, but you, because in this age too you saved us, lest they draw us after them, and you made them ashamed: and therefore we shall then be praised.
43.8: 43.8 You have saved, etc. Augustine. Note that things said in the past are also to be taken for the future.
43.10: 43.10 But now you have cast us off. Cassian. Diapsalma. He enumerates the evils which the good have suffered here, not forgetful of God for all that. Cassian. He heightens the evils, that he may obtain the goodwill of the judge. You have confounded, while here they are held in reproach by the unjust. Augustine. These things truly to come, etc., down to this is a fast not of abstinence but of luxury.
43.11: 43.11 You have turned us back. Cassian. For those who fail. Or, to turn back is to flee the enemy; hence: If they persecute you in one city, flee to another. They plundered. This happens to the fugitives, that those who cannot resist the enemy fall into plunder.
43.12: 43.12 You have given us like sheep for food. Cassian. Those who persist in faith. Here are diverse martyrs, that is, diverse kinds of martyrdom: some as food for beasts, others handed over to the nations in slavery; hence he says: Like sheep for food, where the slaughter of some is noted.
43.13: 43.13 You have sold your people without price. Augustine. While they are given to foreigners and no one acquires them: which is done for testing or correction; or no one is gained for them, or if anyone, few.
43.14: 43.14 A reproach to our neighbors. Cassian. A grievous affliction is laid upon us by neighbors, because what is inflicted by those standing around is not said to be transitory. A derision to those who are round about. Cassian. Derision is a confused voice of joy, announcing insult with immoderate mirth. Contempt is abject worthlessness.
43.15: 43.15 In the likeness of the nations. The same. In the likeness of Christ they were set among the nations, when they inflicted on them equal punishments.
43.17: 43.17 Of one who reproaches. The same. To reproach is to curse to the face; to speak against is to detract from one who is absent, and to bite deceitfully.
43.18: 43.18 All this has come upon us. The same. Because they were not in us through fault.
43.19: 43.19 Our heart has not drawn back. The same. So that it should go backward, even if at times it comes down from the contemplation of the Godhead. You have turned aside. Augustine. Our paths were in the pleasures and prosperities of the world: but you took them from their way, and showed the narrow way that leads to life. Jerome. Or and you have turned aside, that is, you made our works depend on your law. Or, you have not turned aside, with another letter, that is, you did not allow our paths to turn aside and go astray. Paths, that is, works; from your way, that is, from the law; because you have humbled us.
43.20: 43.20 The shadow of death. Augustine. Or, this mortality is the shadow of death: but true death is damnation with the devil.
43.21: 43.21 If we have forgotten the name of God. The same. This is the understanding of the sons of Korah, who on account of all these evils do not forget God, knowing that God will require these things.
43.22: 43.22 He knows. The same. God is said to know both what he knows and what he makes you know. He knows, for he will require it for your sake, that you may find yourself, and give thanks to him who made you, as was done in Peter, who proved what he could do. For your sake we are put to death. Cassian. Not for our crimes, but that your faith may be increased among the nations.
43.23: 43.23 Arise. The same. He prays for help, that he may aid the afflicted here at the time of the resurrection. Augustine. Thus far we have not forgotten; and that we may persevere: Arise, for for your sake we are put to death. Augustine, Jerome. Even if they know that Christ does not sleep, and has risen for himself, they pray nevertheless that he rise again through faith, not for themselves, but for the nations, which think him dead. For if they too believed he had risen, those who believe in him would not be persecuted, but they too would believe. Augustine. Or arise, strengthen. You sleep. You seem to neglect. Wherefore, even if we do not know, you know why: whether for fault, or for benefit. But if for fault, would that it were absent; if for benefit, would that it were present. Some you cast off, because you withdraw your face, that is, your knowledge, from them: you sleep to some who groan over their evils.
43.24: 43.24 Why will you forget? That is, you do not give the spirit of fortitude, without which they are destitute. And of tribulation. Cassian. Because you do not soften it, etc., down to who easily yield to unlawful motions, and cling to earthly things.
43.26: 43.26 Arise, Lord. Here arise is put without sleeping, which belongs to the resurrection, in which is the hope of all the faithful; in which human captivity is destroyed; through which we are helped and set free. Our belly on the earth. Augustine. He who fixes his knees to the earth has something by which to be humbled more: but he who is humbled so much that even his belly cleaves to the earth has nothing beyond by which to be humbled more. He expresses, then, extreme humiliation, so that since he has come to the utmost, the mercy of God may now be present. Or he laments those who are the belly, that is, the carnal, and who have clung, that is, consented to the unjust.
44.1: 44.1 Unto the end, etc. Augustine. An epithalamium, that is, a praise of the bridal chamber. A canticle for those who shall be changed, and for the beloved, that is, the bride and bridegroom, is written for the sons of Korah, that they may revere. For here is described him through whom they will be changed, because the praise of the bridegroom and bride is sung here. Cassian. The Prophet promises that he will utter forth the proclamations of God.
44.2: 44.2 My heart has uttered forth. Augustine, Jerome. For the Prophet speaks within, etc., down to before it is what he is going to do. But the counsel of the Father is the Word. Good. By whom all good things were made. I speak. That is, I bring forth the Word: the same here as before; but he says that in the Word itself are all the works of God; hence: What was made in him was life, so that nothing is in the work which was not first in the counsel. Of this it is said: God has spoken once. A reed. He compares the Word not to a sound, which passes, but to writing, which remains. Or, swiftly, because not one thing after another, but all things at once in the one eternal Word. Swiftly. The power of prophecy, which does not think under human torment what it makes known to others from the hidden things of the Godhead.
44.3: 44.3 Beautiful in form. Cassian. He begins the praise of the bridegroom, first from his form. He has blessed. The Prophet said the former things in the person of God, these in his own; or all from himself. Or, he utters the word who says a hymn to God. I speak my works. Augustine. To the praise of him who is from him. Tongue, reed. Because what I say, I also write. Or, swiftly: because what I write will come quickly. Cassian. In your lips. Because, as he speaks, the world has received the grace of reconciliation.
44.4: 44.4 Gird yourself. The same. Here he praises him for power; and such as you are, gird yourself.
44.5: 44.5 With your comeliness and beauty. Comeliness refers to the humanity in which he appeared to the world; beauty to the Godhead, by which he adorns all things. Look. Have pity and look upon perishing man. Prosper. Setting men free. Proceed. From the womb of the Virgin, as a bridegroom: or from these conquered to others to be conquered. Reign. Show your power in the faith of men, you who have always reigned. And by this, because both through yourself and through your own you teach the truth, by which you destroy our falsehood. And because he is meek in bearing with the wicked, as when he prayed for enemies, so also his own: And because he showed the justice of life. And because he will lead you without offense through the course of the whole life, or from people to people. Wonderfully. Because all will marvel, or because he will work miracles.
44.6: 44.6 Peoples shall fall under you. Augustine. That is, many of his enemies will submit themselves to him, and this by reason or by will. This is what the title said: For those who shall be changed, of the sons of Korah. Into the hearts. Cassian. Of your enemies, that they may be friends, like Saul.
44.7: 44.7 Seat. The same. Here from judgment: seat belongs to judgment. Rod. The same. The rule of divine equity, which is truly straight and is never bent: this rules the just, strikes the unjust. Augustine. Let no one presume much on mercy, nor flatter himself: because the rod of direction, if it rules some, crushes others: it rules the spiritual, crushes the carnal.
44.8: 44.8 You have loved. The same. Or, because you have loved justice, etc., these rewards have been given: he made you king, giving the name which is above every name. And you have hated. If a man hates iniquity in himself, he acts with God: God hates iniquity, you also should hate it. O God. Augustine. In the Greek it is plainly put twice, one a vocative, the other a nominative. This one is anointed, that other is the stone which Jacob anointed.
44.9: 44.9 Myrrh, etc. Cassian. Here the Prophet praises the bridegroom from the wife and the adornment; first from the adornment. Augustine. Myrrh and drop. Perfumes are fittingly applied to the nuptial chamber, etc., down to that is, redemption, through the water of baptism. From ivory houses. Jerome. In ivory there is chastity, for what was first dark becomes bright by saws and files; so the saints, polished by the cutting and rubbing of diverse torments, become bright with a variety of virtues. Daughters of kings. Augustine. Of earthly ones, not caring for the honor of their fathers, etc., down to and for raising up offspring they undertook.
44.10: 44.10 The queen stood, etc. Cassian. Here he commends the bridegroom from the wife. In variety. The same. Even if there is unity in charity, nevertheless she is adorned with gold, that is, the teaching of the Apostles, with scarlet of the martyrs, with the jewels of virgins, with the purple of the penitent.
44.11: 44.11 Hear, O daughter. Cassian. The praise of the bride is more subdued, but fourfold: from form, from glory, from the maidens, from offspring. Augustine. Hear, O daughter. The Prophet addresses the queen, like one of the fathers. The Jews saw and killed; you hear the Gospel, and by believing you will see God: here through an image, in the future face to face. Or, Hear the prophecies which foretold the incarnation, and see them fulfilled.
44.12: 44.12 And the king will desire. Cassian. Here he praises her from form.
44.13: 44.13 Of Tyre. Cassian. By Tyre, neighbor to Judea, the nations are designated; hence the Canaanite woman is a figure of the Church. Cassian. Of Tyre, of the nations, the whole from the part. With gifts. Augustine. That they may offer themselves, etc., down to the nations, namely, which are in the straits of sins.
44.14: 44.14 All glory. Cassian. From the glory of the bride, as above from the power of the bridegroom. From within. Augustine. Or inwardly. Let almsgiving therefore be in secret, where God sees. Or not in circumcision made by hand, as in the old law, but in spiritual things. In fringes. Cassian. The end of a garment signifies the end of the world or of man. Golden. Not gilded, as above, but golden, because at the end is all perfection, where charity is found full.
44.15: 44.15 They shall be brought to the king. The same. Here the bride is praised by her companions, as above from judgment. The same. They shall be brought, by timely preaching. After her. The same. First unity is spoken of, afterward an enumeration of parts is distinguished, when it says: Virgins and her neighbors.
44.17: 44.17 Instead of your fathers sons are born to you. The same. Or instead of the ancient fathers, worshippers of idols, the Apostles are born, the princes of preaching. Augustine. Or after the prophets, the Apostles; after the Apostles, others. This psalm is sung for the feast of the Blessed Virgin Mary, because what is said here generally of the Church can be referred specially to Mary. It is also sung for virgins, because there it is said: Virgins shall be brought to the king. And for the Apostles, because where it is said: Sons are born to you. Likewise for the Nativity of the Lord, because there the praise of the bridegroom and bride is treated, and the wedding of Christ and the Church, whose betrothal was made in the incarnation of the Word.
45.1: 45.1 Unto the end. Cassian. A psalm of David, of some faithful man of Judea, that the testimony may be more certain. For hidden things. For the manifestation of hidden things: that God is man, that salvation is promised to both peoples, that blindness has befallen Israel, that the Apostles passed to the Gentiles, that there is peace on earth; hence: They shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into sickles (Isa. 2). For the sons of Korah. Cassian. Sons of the cross. He speaks of hidden things, that is, of the coming of Christ.
45.2: 45.2 Our God. Cassian, Augustine. In the coming of the Lord all hope is shown to be placed, even in the passing of the Apostles to the Gentiles. They have found us exceedingly. Augustine. For we were fleeing from them. Or, they found us exposed through Adam. Exceedingly: so much the more powerful is he who sets us free.
45.3: 45.3 The earth shall be troubled, and the mountains shall be carried over, etc. Cassian. Judea, as dry: without idolatry, surrounded by the bitterness of the nations. Or, the sea. Augustine. The world. The heart of the sea. The savagery of the nations
45.4: 45.4 They roared and were troubled, etc. The contradicting nations: or the Apostles by preaching. And their waters were troubled. The reference is to the sense, not to the word: that is, the waters of the sea, namely the peoples, or their doctrines, which were made foolish when the doctrine of the Savior shone forth; hence: They were swallowed up, etc. And this is the rod of Moses, which devoured the rods of the magicians.
45.5: 45.5 The rush of the river. Cassian. Diapsalma. Because the Church is founded on Christ, to whom nations and kingdoms are subjected. Augustine. As if he said: So the sea rages; but amid these waves and noises they do not fear who have fled to that refuge.
45.6: 45.6 God will help it. Cassian. Or, with his countenance, that is, by the showing of his help, when by helping he makes himself known. In the morning. In the very beginning of the good work; and this at daybreak, that is, through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, who is the light as of the day.
45.7: 45.7 He gave. As a great reward. His voice. The preaching, at which the earthly man trembled. The earth shall quake with the fear of the judge.
45.8: 45.8 The Lord of hosts. The same. He briefly defines what Christ is. With us. As if: He who sent angels now comes himself, and is with us, because he is our protector with us; therefore: Come, as though I invite you now secure. Our. Only of the sons of the cross. The God of Jacob. Who has given us as much as he gave Jacob: for he is not God of him alone.
45.9: 45.9 Come and see. The same. Diapsalma. The great works of the incarnation. He has set. As signs, to call the people. Wonders. Such as the birth from the Virgin, and the star, and the rest. Taking away wars. Augustine. Because by his coming the idolatry and superstition of the whole world perished, or, at that time, by his presence the world was pacified.
45.11: 45.11 Be still. The same. If the weapons are burned, be still, having nothing with which to fight.
46.2: 46.2 All nations. Augustine. As if he said: the boys insult, saying: Bald head, bald head; you, all nations to whom grace has passed: Clap, etc. The nations to whom grace has passed, and whom in the previous psalm he called to faith, he invites to praise.
46.3: 46.3 The Most High. Jerome. Powerful in what he wills. Terrible. Remigius. Because he is to judge in power.
46.4: 46.4 He has subdued peoples to us. Cassian. This befits the faithful, to whom all outsiders are subjected, or, he has subjected to himself those to be joined with us. Peoples, the Jews. To us. The same. Namely to the universal Church; it befits all the faithful to say this, to whom outsiders are subjected. Under our feet. The same. By the feet understand the preachers, to whom the peoples are subjected. Augustine. Under our feet. So exalted is the Church that it has those not yet believing under its feet.
46.5: 46.5 He has chosen for us, etc. Or in the person of the Apostles, he chose to give us his inheritance, of many peoples, that we may cultivate it, striking their hearts with the sword of preaching and destroying malice. Inheritance. Augustine. The heavenly inheritance is the beauty of the Christian people, in which he who is now despised will be beautiful, shining like the sun. The beauty of Jacob which, etc. That is, those like Jacob or marked through Jacob, who give earthly things for heavenly, as Jacob did, which was the grace of God, because he loved him, Esau being rejected.
46.6: 46.6 God is gone up. Cassian. In the diapsalma the ascension and kingdom of God are described, hence he urgently admonishes to sing psalms. With a shout. Augustine. The joy of the Apostles marveling, etc., down to which can neither be kept silent nor be expressed.
46.7: 46.7 Sing psalms. Cassian. Praise with works: it is greatly salutary that it is so often repeated, because it is God who creates, and the King who governs what is created.
46.8: 46.8 All. The same. Not as Jupiter of Crete, Mars of Thrace. Wisely. He teaches how psalms are to be sung. Formerly they sang without sense, while they worshipped stones. Augustine. No one does wisely what he does not understand.
46.9: 46.9 He shall reign. The same. Now this prophecy is fulfilled: God sits upon his holy seat. Holy seat. Augustine. The Thrones, Virtues, and saints.
46.10: 46.10 The princes of the peoples. Cassian. The first-fruits of all the nations have gathered by believing in Christ, because, the Jews being driven out, the nations succeed as sons of Abraham, having the promise, because the Jews grew proud. Jerome, Cassian. Or the strong gods, namely the Apostles, whom neither death nor life will separate from the love of Christ. Lifted up, by miracles and doctrine.
47.1: 47.1 A psalm, or praise of a canticle, for the sons of Korah, the second day, etc. Augustine. On the first day God made light, etc., down to of which it is sung here for the sons of Korah. Cassian. Of the founding of the city, which he describes in commendation. Augustine. He commends the city, etc., down to from eternal stability.
47.2: 47.2 In his holy mountain, etc. The same. This is that mountain, etc., down to upon which the Church is founded.
47.3: 47.3 It is founded in exultation. Jerome. As if he said, which was before subject to curses, etc., down to he is Christ, who spreads joy through the whole Church. Mount Sion, the sides. Augustine. Whoever cling to someone are called his sides, etc., down to likewise from the north all evil will be opened, etc.
47.4: 47.4 In its houses. Or, in its steps, that is, according to the degrees of merits, because in each one distinctly he will give knowledge of himself. When he receives it. To be defended, and what need is there? For the kings against. But seeing by faith, namely that this city is so worthy, they marveled, etc.
47.5: 47.5 The kings. Augustine, Cassian. The princes of the Jews. Gathered. By Herod inquiring about the place of the birth. They came together. Agreeing in saying: In Bethlehem of Judah, according to the Scriptures.
47.6: 47.6 Seeing. What they had read in the prophets. They marveled. At so great a glory, not lightly or idly. But they were troubled. For sin, and They were moved. To faith, and so great was the fear that the body trembled.
47.7: 47.7 There were pains as of a woman in labor, of penance, seeing thus; but:
47.8: 47.8 With a vehement wind, of Herod. You shall break the ships of Tarshish. Because in Tarsus, the ships of Cilicia which were believed to have carried the Magi back to their own country were broken by Herod. Tarshish. Augustine. Cilicia is a region from Tarsus, etc., down to when all has run its course he concludes. Therefore:
47.9: 47.9 As we have heard. In the city of the Lord of hosts, because there he assigns guardian angels. He repeats. In the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God. That is, the Catholic Church, lest an assembly of heretics usurp this name for itself. But lest it be thought temporal, he adds: God has founded it forever. Not for an hour, as the earlier tabernacle of Moses
47.10: 47.10 We have received your mercy, O God. Cassian. Giving thanks for the coming of Christ, he admonishes concerning the degrees of the Church to be distributed, by which the Savior may be recognized. In the midst of your temple. Jerusalem: those are more gravely accused who despise him who was seen in their midst. By this is noted the incarnation of Christ, who, according as he is man, was presented in the temple.
47.11: 47.11 The right hand. Cassian. On this side the just are placed. Augustine. We have received, O God. In what order it was founded, or what we have heard and seen. Of your temple. The same. That is, of the people not receiving mercy, who among many: so that there seem to be no grains, yet some, because according to the name. According to your name. Cassian. Which is spread everywhere, because there is no one, even if he does not know the worship, who does not submit to this name. Or according to the name. That is, as the reverence of your name, etc., down to your propitiation justified many, who all praise.
47.12: 47.12 Let mount Sion rejoice. Augustine. Even if the just labor among thorns, etc., down to theirs it is now to gather, God's to separate. Mount Sion and let them exult. Cassian. The Church, which is on the watchtower of the people. The daughters of Judah, because of your judgments, O Lord. Holy women. By Judah their nation is shown, which is for Christ's sake, who is from Judah, and let these exult, that the Church may be in both sexes. Augustine. The cause of joy is the judgments to come, where they know they will come to blessedness. Let those who are inside rejoice; you who are outside, surround.
47.13: 47.13 Surround it. By showing honors. Embrace it. In charity. Tell in its towers. Set your hearts. Cassian. Preach to others in the concord of the Apostles, etc., down to lest through joy they grow lax and slack.
47.14: 47.14 In its strength. Augustine. The strength of the city is charity, which nothing overcomes; hence Solomon: Love is strong as death. Cassian. He admonishes to set the hearts in the strength of the Church. Distribute its houses, that you may tell it to another generation. That is, the distinct offices, etc., down to whom the Lord first chose.
47.15: 47.15 For this is, etc. This is what is to be told, a brief statement, but one that concludes everything. Forever, against those who made temporal men gods.
48.1: 48.1 Unto the end, a psalm, etc. Cassian. The Prophet treats of the lovers of the world, and of Christ the redeemer, not of those, but of the despisers of the world, so that one cast down in the world may not value the proud. Augustine. Those who worship God, etc., down to he makes them attentive to new and mighty things.
48.2: 48.2 Hear this, all you nations. Cassian. I except no one, etc., down to namely when the tares will be separated from the wheat, the sheep from the goats.
48.3: 48.3 And you earth-born. Augustine. I withhold speech from none; let the heir of the earth hear, for judgment: the just, for the kingdom.
48.4: 48.4 My mouth shall speak. Cassian. He commends what is to be said. Wisdom for divine things, Prudence for forming morals; in these two all divine discourse is indicated.
48.5: 48.5 I will incline. Jerome. I will humble myself to the truth speaking within, which teaches to speak in parables, lest it lie open to all.
48.6: 48.6 Why shall I fear? Cassian. He begins to tell what he promised, saying that Christ will not redeem the impious; here the prophet, treating the general cause in his own person, seeks the cause of the condemnation and fear of the wicked, which is iniquity. Augustine. Why shall I fear? as though there is nothing for me to fear, since avoiding iniquity is in my power; for which alone there will be fear on the last day, which will be evil for the condemned, not for the just. Of my heel. The same. He plays on the words, etc., down to that is, will oppress and cause fear.
48.7: 48.7 Who trust. These, namely, who trust, etc., down to in which they are so foolish.
48.8: 48.8 A brother does not redeem. If a brother, that is Christ, does not redeem, etc., down to because such a one does not give God propitiation.
48.9: 48.9 And shall yet live. The same. After the end of life he will live according to the soul, because the soul will not perish with the body, but will be preserved for sorrow, until, the body being taken up, he is tormented in both.
48.11: 48.11 He shall not see. The same. That is, he does not understand, etc., down to when the wise man passes through life. Or, the senseless. The same. He who does not attend. The fool. He who, if he attends, does not take care. Riches. Cassian. For which they did evil. Their own: which are not according to God.
48.12: 48.12 They called their names. Augustine. The heirs, who at the tombs of the dead make themselves drunk in their memory, but not a drop reaches the tongue of the one burning in hell.
48.13: 48.13 And man when. And in this as in the rest, man does not understand; or, God is not to be blamed for it: he did not understand his dignity, he did not act with understanding, but, reason being lost, was compared to beasts, not in anything else but in wisdom.
48.14: 48.14 This way. Cassian. Here he now gathers all that has been said into one. The way, that is, the life, because it leads to death. Scandal. Goad and pain, etc., down to: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. They shall be pleased with their mouth. Augustine. Since they are such, etc., down to and they are worse than open evils.
48.15: 48.15 Like sheep. Cassian. Diapsalma. What distress is to be repaid to the impious. They boast, but it is already clear to me that they are placed in hell. Sheep, their wool lost, remain; so in these, without consumption of substance, the punishment finds something to torment. Death. Augustine. As Christ is life, so the devil is death; he is a shepherd to them as to sheep, whom he draws to the pastures of death. Shall feed upon them. Cassian. From the likeness of beasts, etc., down to will lead from punishment to punishment. In the morning. Augustine. Because now it is night, while the merits of the just do not appear and the happiness of the impious is, as it were, named. Their glory shall grow old in hell, etc. Augustine. How great glory he seemed to have, etc., down to: They have been driven out from their glory.
48.17: 48.17 Do not fear. Cassian. Diapsalma. An admonition not to fear the powerful, who leave all things with the light. For why these things are permitted to sinners is a common complaint. When a man is made rich. For the despised have these things too. Glory. In the honors of the world. House. Because not only himself, but all who belong to him.
48.19: 48.19 He shall be blessed. The same. Not for a good act, but for delights he shall be blessed, by the favor of the luxurious, who among feasts wish well to the shepherds. He will confess to you when you have done well to him. Augustine. Scorn the confession which prosperity makes; but that is of great merit which the force of sorrow does not take away.
48.20: 48.20 To the generations of his fathers. The same. Those who follow the worst fathers are to be condemned by their fellowship. And man. Cassian. He repeats the ugliness of man, that the wicked may rest from the wicked.
49.1: 49.1 A psalm of Asaph. Jerome. Asaph, in Latin congregation; in Greek, synagogue, which here speaks faithfully, which awaits Christ, through which the unbelieving Jews are the more refuted. Cassian. Asaph, about to introduce the voice of God concerning the change of sacrifices, first treats of both comings, inviting through the first, terrifying through the second. The God of gods. Cassian. Lest anyone think meanly of the incarnation, etc., down to by name, like false gods, Jupiter, Venus. He has spoken, and called the earth. Augustine. Through himself, through heralds. From the rising of the sun to the going down. Cassian. As if he said, etc., down to: out of Sion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.
49.2: 49.2 Out of Sion, the loveliness of his beauty, etc. Augustine. The glory of the Gospel began, etc., down to that they might be witnesses in Jerusalem and in all the earth.
49.3: 49.3 A fire shall burn before him and round about him. The same. It will go before him; therefore let punishment terrify those whom rewards do not invite, etc., down to it will accompany the wicked to hell. A mighty tempest. He shall call heaven from above, and the earth. Cassian. Not a wind, etc., down to first he called all in common, then he will call in order to discern. To discern his people. Augustine. First he called them mingled from the rising of the sun to its going down, but then to discern.
49.5: 49.5 Gather together his saints to him. The same. The Prophet, seeing things to come, etc., down to it is said of the wicked, of whom he did not fill his hand. Who set his covenant above sacrifices. The same. The New Testament above the Old, etc., down to who value works of charity more than the sacrifices of cattle.
49.6: 49.6 And the heavens shall declare his justice, etc. The same. Already the heavens have declared to us this justice of God, etc., down to and if now mixed, because God is a just judge.
49.7: 49.7 Hear, my people, etc. Cassian. The voice of Christ, that, sacrifices of cattle being left, a sacrifice of praise may be made. Augustine. Or, he repeats under another word, Hear as Israel, that is, as one seeing God, and I will testify, namely this: I am your God. Your God. Augustine. First he says simply: I am God. And afterward he says: I am your God. As if he said: Even if I am not your God, yet I am God. For to my good I am God, but to your harm I am not your God. I am. Cassian. To be is proper to the Godhead. Hear, Israel. The same. As if he said: If you are Israel, that is, if you see me, you do not neglect to hear. That God is God in general, your God in particular.
49.8: 49.8 But your holocausts. Augustine. If the soul is inflamed, and seizes the members for its own use, that they may not serve cupidity: hence in Leviticus it is commanded that they offer the fat with the kidneys, by which inner charity is signified.
49.9: 49.9 I will not take, etc. Cassian. Even if you do so: I will not take calves from your house, as though I took what is signified, not those from the house. For mine: as if he said, because they are not yours but mine. For mine are, etc. Augustine. Mine are the things you do not possess, namely the untamed: the beasts of the woods, the cattle, the oxen, etc. Cassian. By these similitudes he figures the Church, etc., down to: He does not want the flesh of bulls in sacrifices, but in the poor.
49.11: 49.11 I know all the fowls. Augustine. All things are with him, by a certain knowledge of ineffable wisdom.
49.12: 49.12 If I shall hunger, I will not. The same. If you give these things, perhaps you think I hunger, which is madness?
49.13: 49.13 Shall I eat the flesh of bulls? Formerly these were sacrificed, not because God was delighted by them, but lest they be offered to demons, and they were sacrificed to God alone, in whom there was some significance. Offer to God. Cassian. He does not say to me, but speaks of himself as of another, as also afterward: But to the sinner God said, not I.
49.15: 49.15 Of tribulation. Augustine. Our tribulation is properly out of fear for salvation, not for carnal things.
49.16: 49.16 But to the sinner. The same. From whom he wants sacrifice, where the sinner's wickednesses are charged against him. Cassian. These things he said to his people, etc., down to For reading is not denied to those who are to be corrected.
49.17: 49.17 But you have hated. The same. You say with the mouth, but deny discipline by deed: if I correct you, you murmur. A thief, you ran. The same. In these he thunders against all vices; the whole from the part, or a thief of the sound understanding of Scripture. With adulterers. Who put the false, taking away the true.
49.19: 49.19 Your mouth has abounded, etc. The same. He accuses the conscience and the tongue, etc., down to not by chance does he disparage another, but by zeal.
49.20: 49.20 Sitting. The same. What he does passing by or standing, he does not do with will. Your brother. The same. Every man. And against the son of your mother, the Church, to whom we are joined by charity. You set a scandal, heresies or other things by which the innocent may be caught. You spoke against. Augustine. While one who seems learned detracts, etc., down to by the food of stronger doctrine. Like yourself. Cassian. By consenting to the wicked. I will set it against you. Augustine. What you put behind your back, I will place before your face.
49.22: 49.22 Lest he seize. Cassian. God, to punishment, and there be none to rescue. When the devil seizes, God rescues; but when God seizes, no one can set free.
49.23: 49.23 The sacrifice of praise. Cassian. What the wicked sing is not a sacrifice of praise, nor are animals. And this is the way to God, the ladder of Jacob, on which the angels, that is, the faithful, ascend to the praise of the divinity, and descend to the praise of the humanity. There is the way in which, etc. The same. In the sacrifice of praise. The salvation of God. Augustine. Christ, who came with grace, whom he knows who attributes anything to other than the grace of God.
50.1: 50.1 Unto the end, a psalm. Cassian. When Nathan reproved him, the king was not ashamed to confess his sins publicly, etc., down to which is available from God to the penitent. David. Augustine. He is set forth as an example, not of falling, but that, even if you have fallen, you should not despair of rising again. Cassian. First is the supplication, etc., down to full remission of sins is granted.
50.3: 50.3 Have mercy on me, O God. The same. This penitential psalm, etc., down to because he foresaw that through this psalm many would perish. According to your great mercy. For a grave sin one would have to despair, were there not great mercy. How great the great cannot be defined. Great mercy. The same.
