Great mercy brought God down from heaven, etc., down to when God is asked to forgive according to himself? Of your mercies, etc. Cassian. He asks through mercy and compassion. And mercy is in nature, compassion in effect.
50.4: 50.4 Wash me yet more. Cassian. He adds the manner of blotting out that he wants: Cleanse me, etc. Jerome. Wash so as to cleanse, for some things are washed which are nevertheless not clean.
50.5: 50.5 For I know my iniquity. Augustine, Cassian. Whose mercy he asks that he forgive, because he knows it is just that he punish sins, he adds: Do not you punish, because I punish. For I know my iniquity, etc. Against me. Augustine. He had sin behind his back, when the king, forgetful of himself, gave judgment against the rich man who took the poor man's sheep.
50.6: 50.6 Against you only have I sinned. Jerome. For he alone punishes justly who has nothing in himself to be reproved; this among men is Christ alone. Against you only. Cassian. Because the king, superior to all, is to be punished by God alone. Before you. Because he knows that he is everywhere, he accuses himself because, in his presence, he was not ashamed to sin. That you may be justified, etc. Whose words do not pass away but are fulfilled. And may overcome when you are judged. God is of such justice, etc., down to that he may prevail between himself and him, if they are judged. Against you only. Augustine. To Christ, who has no sin, etc., down to because he had so gravely offended God. And may overcome. Augustine. Or you are so just that you overcome the devil, and death, and the Jews, when you are judged: and in the judgment in which you were judged.
50.7: 50.7 In iniquities. Cassian. The odium of the sin is lessened, etc., down to he is accused of one and confesses all.
50.8: 50.8 For behold, etc. Augustine. So he gives mercy as to keep the truth, so that neither are the sins of him whom he forgives left unpunished. For he forgives the one who punishes himself. Mercy, then, is that man is set free; truth, that sin is punished. Truth, etc. Cassian. Because in confessing he spoke the truth, which God seeks above sacrifices, he begs to be helped. The uncertain and hidden things. Augustine. There are also hidden things in such, etc., down to whence he ought to have guarded himself the more from sin. Hidden. Cassian. From the authority of him who reveals, the confidence of washing and whitening.
50.9: 50.9 You shall sprinkle me. Cassian. The second is confidence in the mercy of God, which is very useful: lest despair creep in, which is graver than all sins. With hyssop. The same. Dipped in the blood of the sacrificed victim, it was sprinkled over the body of the leper, signifying that the stains of sins are to be washed away by the blood of Christ. Augustine. Hyssop is a lowly herb, etc., down to in which is swelling, so humility cures pride. Above snow. The same. Beyond comparison: hence also on the mountain the garment of Christ shone like snow.
50.10: 50.10 To my hearing. Augustine. Note the humble man. I shall hear you, etc., down to and because now humble, now the humbled bones exult.
50.11: 50.11 Turn away. Cassian. Secure from confidence, he asks the blotting out of all sins and full restoration.
50.12: 50.12 In my inward parts. The same. Whence the adultery came forth. In both parts, soul and body, he asks the remedy of healing, because in them he sinned. He so desires to be cleansed that he seems to wish to commit nothing such thereafter.
50.13: 50.13 Cast me not away from your face. Cassian. Turn your face from sins, but not me from your face, whence light and health come.
50.14: 50.14 With a princely spirit. Augustine. Some here note the Trinity in God, who is spirit, since he is not body; by the right spirit, the Son; by the Holy Spirit, by his own name; by the princely spirit, the Father. Cassian. The spirit of prophecy, which is more precious to him than all, he asks only that its strength not be taken away, saying nothing of the rest.
50.15: 50.15 I will teach. The same. What the restored man repays; first weeping, now he becomes a teacher.
50.16: 50.16 From blood. The same. Because many are the carnal sins, etc., down to which come from the corruption of flesh and blood. Your justice. The same. He praises justice, when he ought to give thanks to piety; but it was also of justice to receive the confessing one; and these two things are always joined in the judgment of the Lord.
50.17: 50.17 Your praise. Augustine. That you created me; that you did not abandon me when I sinned; that you urged me to confess; that you cleansed me.
50.19: 50.19 A sacrifice to God. Cassian. What at that time was offered for expiation. Troubled. The same. A glad and wanton spirit binds to sin. The promise of this sacrifice follows: A contrite heart.
50.20: 50.20 Deal kindly. The same. Now rejoicing, he prophesies of the building of Jerusalem, where is the sacrifice of justice. The walls. Augustine. Let the bulwarks of our immortality be built in faith, hope and charity.
50.21: 50.21 Then you shall accept the sacrifice. The same. Now a sacrifice for iniquity, etc., down to then justice will be the sacrifice, the offerings lesser saints, the holocausts the perfect. Then they shall lay. Cassian. Priests, innocent calves, etc., down to the faithful suffering for your name will be acceptable to you. Altar. Augustine. The heavenly Jerusalem.
51.1: 51.1 Unto the end for, etc. Jerome, Augustine. Doeg betrayed David, etc., down to This is not a prayer for the wicked, but a prophecy of what will be to them.
51.2: 51.2 Doeg. Cassian. The adversary of David signifies Antichrist, who will stir the whole world; who will come through signs and miracles before the coming of the judgment, and, seeking help from Saul, that is, from the devil, will announce that David, that is, Christ, has come into the house of Ahimelech, that is, to the Church, which is the kingdom of the Father. Abimelech. Jerome. He says, in Hebrew Ahimelech, etc., down to therefore Abimelech, my father's kingdom, and it signifies the Jews.
51.3: 51.3 Why do you glory in malice, etc. Cassian. The first is an invective against Doeg, to strengthen the faithful against Antichrist and his accomplices.
51.4: 51.4 He has thought. The same. A light mind, a hasty speech, does not think before it speaks, hence: The heart of fools is in their mouth. Like a razor, etc. The same. While it promises renewal, so that deceitful one, namely Antichrist, cuts off blessedness, and kills.
51.5: 51.5 You have loved malice, etc. Cassian. He does not forsake evil who loves it above kindness; and if kindness touches the soul, he shrinks back.
51.6: 51.6 A deceitful tongue. The same. That is, deceitful words, ministers of falsehood, of those who carry one thing in the heart and bring forth another in the mouth.
51.7: 51.7 Therefore God. Cassian. Of the swift end of the unjust. And your root out of the land of the living. Augustine. Our root is charity, etc., down to for this is the dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth. The same. The root of evil is cupidity, which bears no fruit in the land of the living. Or, he speaks of Antichrist, whose root is his ministers, who will have nothing with the saints.
51.8: 51.8 The just shall see. The same. For his casting down, derision. The same. The just shall see. What is for the wicked, etc., down to because he will deceive the faithful more than all other evils.
51.10: 51.10 But I, etc. The same. How the good man conducts himself against him. Cassian. Thus far the censure of him; here the praise of the opposite party: behold the perfect demonstration. A fruitful olive tree. Augustine. The people of God is an olive tree, from which the proud branches, that is, the Jews, were broken off, and the wild olive from the Gentiles was grafted in. Cassian. A fruitful olive tree, from whose shoot the Lord Christ blossomed forth, who was anointed with spiritual oil above his fellows. Forever and ever. Augustine. What he said forever, he repeats as forever and ever: that by repeating he may confirm how firmly he is founded in the love of the kingdom of heaven.
51.11: 51.11 You have done it, and I will wait for your name. The same. Namely the things foretold, that I am an olive tree, that I have hoped in mercy forever.
52.1: 52.1 Unto the end for, etc. Cassian. The understanding of David the prophet, etc., down to here of the coming of the judgment. Augustine. Or for Mahalath, etc., down to consolation at the end of the psalm. The fool said. The same. A rebuke of the wicked. The same. The fool is everyone who lives badly, etc., down to he says, There is no God.
52.3: 52.3 God from. Cassian. Or from heaven, that is, he has admonished through holy souls, that he may see, etc. If there is, etc. The same. Or if he does not understand, if at least he is seeking to understand God.
52.4: 52.4 All have turned aside. The same. A fitting order. First they turn aside; then they are useless; hence there is none who does good.
52.5: 52.5 Shall they not know. The same. A threat to the wicked concerning the end. Augustine. He threatens them, etc., down to But deservedly this to them, because:
52.6: 52.6 They have not called upon God. The same. He consoles those who groan, that they may not imitate the prosperous, because they have not called upon God, whence they are soon to perish, the consolation of the faithful. The bones of those who please men. Cassian. The good displease themselves while they chastise the flesh: the wicked please. They are confounded. The same. That is, they shall be confounded, separated, so that it may be read generally of all the wicked, but Israel shall be saved.
52.7: 52.7 Who will give out of, etc. Augustine. But salvation for the Church in labor.
53.2: 53.2 The Ziphites. Jerome, Augustine. They are interpreted as flourishing, etc., down to he admonishes to praise God in adversities.
53.3: 53.3 O God, in your name. Augustine. He prays among the Ziphites. Augustine, Jerome. Here save in your name, afterward I do not fear to be judged in your strength. Augustine. O God, in your name, the words of the Church hidden among the Ziphites, whose good is within and reward hidden: others ask to be set free by others; I in your name.
53.4: 53.4 O God, hear. Cassian. Again O God, a name of power, he repeats lest help be delayed. Give ear. Augustine. The Ziphites, even if they hear these things, do not understand, who know only temporal things.
53.5: 53.5 Strangers. Augustine. Ziph was a small village which belonged to the tribe of Judah, whence the Ziphites.
53.6: 53.6 For behold. Cassian. Diapsalma. What God does for himself and the Ziphites, whence he renders praises. He helps. Augustine. Which they themselves do not know, among whom I lie hidden; but that he helps me, they would see, if they set God before their eyes.
53.7: 53.7 Turn back evils upon my enemies. The same. Or turn away, he prays for those to be converted: and this is the sacrifice he pays for deliverance. In your truth. Augustine. Or according to another reading: In your strength, destroy those whom you have borne with in your weakness. Willingly will I sacrifice. The same. Because for himself, not for another thing which I might want from him. He who praises for the sake of another thing praises from necessity; if he had that, he would not praise. But to me, even the things he has given please for the sake of the giver.
54.1: 54.1 Unto the end, in songs. Augustine. Understanding. With great care the Church ought to understand, etc., down to who for the troubles of citizens fled into solitude.
54.2: 54.2 Hear my prayer, O God. Cassian. A prayer, set forth against evils, or the waves of the world. Do not despise my supplication. The same. For if God gives temporal things to someone who asks, yet his prayer is not accepted by him, because it lacks the due end.
54.3: 54.3 In exercise, etc. Augustine. Every wicked man lives either to be corrected or that through him the good man may be exercised. I am troubled at the voice of the enemy. Augustine. In the very fight, while he wishes both to love his enemies and, with the abundance of warfare, begins to hate, and so begins to be sunk in the waves. Jerome. Troubled. Or, I am troubled at the voice of the enemy, who said I was a Samaritan and had a demon.
54.5: 54.5 My heart is troubled. Cassian. By the law of the flesh the mind is troubled in me, it does not go out from me
54.6: 54.6 Fear and trembling. The same. It is the property of death that we first fear it, whence we tremble. Darkness has covered me. Jerome. The darkness is wicked men, who persecute the Church, and who cover it: he who hates his brother is in darkness.
54.7: 54.7 Who will give me wings like? Augustine. But in this weakness what does he say? Who will give me wings? He wishes to be separated for a time from so many scandals, lest, being weak, he increase his sins by remaining among them. Like a dove, etc. The same. Not like a raven, etc., down to but it is necessary to remain for your sake, and so there is merit from desire. Cassian. Dove. Or the dove sent out, finding muddy places, returned to the ark; so Christ, finding the hearts of the Jews muddy, flew away to the Gentiles.
54.8: 54.8 Behold, I have gone far off. Cassian. He touches on what Christ avoided, the persecutors, to remove an occasion of anger, and he remained in desert places praying: in which he taught us to pray and rest in the secret of conscience when we are pressed by the wicked. And I remained in solitude, of the Gentiles; hence: Let the desert rejoice and blossom like the lily. And elsewhere: Rejoice, barren one, that do not bear (Isa. 35, 54).
54.9: 54.9 I waited for him. Diapsalma. Now in solitude, safe, he hopes for the help of God, and calls down a curse on the citizens. Cassian. I waited, so that it may be read in the person of Christ in solitude, secure I sustained not from myself the protection of the Father, who saved me from faintness of spirit, that I might not fall or yield to evils in the passion, from the tempest that I might not grow angry.
54.10: 54.10 Cast down. Cassian. Lest they fortify their thoughts by plotting. Divide. The same. Lest the unity be proud, lest malice have effect. In the city. This is the city of which the Lord says through the prophet: I am God and not man, and I do not enter the city. Yet there is another which God inhabits, of which it is said: A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden.
54.11: 54.11 And toil in the midst of it, etc. Augustine. Already toil in the midst, because iniquity: but rest in humility.
54.12: 54.12 Usury, etc. The same. Because he demands more with injury. Or in whatever thing he has received, he does not forgive, that it may be forgiven him.
54.13: 54.13 For if an enemy. Cassian. A reproach of Judas, when read in the person of Christ; or, thus far the Church has dealt with open enemies, now with hidden ones. I would perhaps have hidden myself from him, etc. The same. Great patience would so give place to words as to hide itself so as not to see the adversary.
54.14: 54.14 But you, O man. Augustine. Formerly, because at one time you gave good counsel. Of one mind. Cassian. Because among the Apostles he was a leader, sent ahead to the strongholds and villages. Known, because he foreknew the betrayer, so that Christ speaks specially against Judas. Jerome. Or thus, generally against any Jewish man, etc., down to the ordinances of the law or the morsel. Of one mind. Augustine. You who once admonished well; Leader: I made you leader over my people. Known, of the same nation. My acquaintance. Who together. The same. Who were with me in the same Church.
54.15: 54.15 Meats. Cassian. Bodily ones, which could be sweet only to the unjust. The man of iniquity is wont to be softened by banquets, so that the guilt is heavier for him.
54.16: 54.16 Let death come. The same. As above against open enemies, so here he calls down a curse on the hidden. And lest it be thought that it is one man he was speaking of, he shares the punishments among the Jews, that is, he calls down a curse in common on the Jews with others. Augustine, Jerome. Let death come. He touches here the beginning of schism, etc., down to and Christ and the Church speak in the same voice. Augustine. Let it come: As upon those who were the beginning of schism and proudly separated themselves, a new death came; for the earth opened and swallowed them alive. Let them go down alive into hell. The same. As the earth swallowed the leaders, etc., down to so these who sin knowingly go down. Alive. The same. Knowing that they perish, and yet perishing they are swallowed by the gaping of earthly cupidity. In their dwellings. They are foreign, not natural, but received as guests, as it were newcomers, or first in dwellings, that is, in secret, afterward in the midst, that is, in the open. But I, etc. Cassian. He affirms what is done to himself and to them, proceeding alternately.
54.18: 54.18 Evening and morning. Jerome. Because he saved, therefore evening, when he was taken; morning, when he was judged; noon, when he was crucified. I will tell, the works past. I will announce the powers and works which he will do: and therefore he will hear, etc. Augustine. Evening. I will tell of the past, etc., down to against those who do not love peace, because I loved peace. Cassian. To tell belongs to the evening, when he spoke all that Judas was arranging. To announce, of the morning, when he said to Pilate: For this I was born, that I should bear witness to the truth.
54.19: 54.19 They draw near to me. In name, not in divinity; in body, not in mind; in number, not in merit. For among many they were with me. Jerome, Augustine. Because in many things with me, that is, in the baptism of the Gospel, the reading, feasts and the like, but not in few with me. With me in all the sacraments, but not in faith, hope and charity, without which all are nothing. Augustine. Or, in many, that is, in the chaff, etc., down to so also they are with me in many.
54.20: 54.20 God will hear, etc. Cassian. At noon, when he gave up the Spirit. Behold how many mysteries in brief: or, you will save in the morning, and evening, and noon: hence be not ungrateful, tell and announce, and he himself will hear, etc. He will humble them who is before the ages. The same. Concerning pride, that they may believe. Or he will humble them to take away their place and nation. For there is no change for them, and they did not fear God, he stretched out his hand in repaying, etc. Augustine. Because the mind of the faithless is unchangeable.
54.21: 54.21 They have defiled: Cassian. because those defiled and were divided: the just are armed the more, the weak are set free, who have their care upon God.
54.22: 54.22 Wrath. The same. The vengeance of judgment, etc., down to appropriates to his own. Heart. Augustine. The secret will of God, which is contained in the Scriptures. Their words were softened. Cassian. Or this is for them, because they softened their words by flattering, which are darts when they say: He is guilty of death. Augustine. But if to you, a child nourished with the milk of lesser doctrine, they are still hard, do not be angry at the breasts of the Church; but cast it upon the Lord, not another, who is a harbor, or a rock to the ship, not a harbor tossed in the world. The words themselves, etc. Cassian. Because softened they do not lose their power, but the evangelists are armed with them, and strike the hearts of men to the love of peace, and free the weak from the tangled questions of heretics.
54.23: 54.23 Your care. The same. The care of the world, etc., down to so the sadness of a man harms the heart. The wavering. And if here, these were words of wavering: I was saddened in exercise, etc.
54.24: 54.24 But you, etc. Augustine. These then will not waver, etc., down to Woe to those who sin and do not repent. Their days, but I, etc. The same. Voluntary ones, not appointed by God.
55.1: 55.1 Unto the end, etc. Augustine. The people who is made far from the saints is in the inscription of the title: to whom contradicts both the Jew and everyone who does not wish to have Christ as king; and those who afflict the Church: against whom this psalm strengthens the Church. In the inscription of the title, when they held David himself. The inscription of the title, etc., down to the persecutors who tread the Church like grapes. Allophyli (foreigners). The same as the people who is made far from the saints. Gath, that is, in the winepress. David is read, etc., down to but, when it is pressed, it is not barren.
55.2: 55.2 Have mercy on me, O God. Cassian. The Church prays, touching summarily on the tribulations, in which through hope in God she ends by saying she does not fear, that is, at the end of the first part she says she does not fear. Fighting against me he has afflicted me, etc. Augustine. A man visibly: the devil invisibly, whence the tribulation is more dangerous.
55.4: 55.4 From the height. Cassian. The height of the day, the world, where is the swelling of pride: to make the tribulation heavier, he says he is trodden down by the proud. Augustine. From the height. Another reading, etc., down to he does not say: I will not fear, but, I will hope in you. Of the day. The Day is Christ, whose twelve hours are the twelve Apostles: hence he himself says: Are there not twelve hours in the day? The height of this day the enemies cannot reach, hence at the passion of Christ: Darkness was made.
55.6: 55.6 All the day, etc. Cassian. He enumerates the evils, by bearing which the conversion of enemies also comes about, hence also through hope in God he says he does not fear, as he had done before.
55.7: 55.7 They will dwell. Augustine. Or, some of those who are far from the saints, etc., down to for if they say false things about you, they do not take away heaven, nor do these do harm.
55.8: 55.8 For nothing. The same. Because there is no labor for you in it, as though it were nothing to you, because, even if they are despaired of, yet you heal by a word; or for none of their merits, but freely through piety. In anger you will break the peoples, while through the scourges of God they come to their senses, or while they foresee the wrath of God. In anger you will break the peoples. Because you terrify with tribulations, etc., down to and the wrath of consumption, by which the wicked are punished unto destruction.
55.9: 55.9 O God, I have declared my life to you. The life of man is threefold: of nature, by which we live and breathe; of grace, by which we live in Christ; of sin, which is lived in vices. Two are from God, because good, namely the life of nature and the life of grace: the third is from man, because evil. All these we ought to declare to God. Cassian. O God, my life. You will break, and I, for their instruction, my life before, which was always evil. He declares his life to God who confesses sin: not teaching God, but condemning himself, that he may be released. You have set my tears, etc. Augustine. Pious tears, which ask for enemies: and therefore acceptable to God, as he himself has promised.
55.10: 55.10 In whatever day, etc. Cassian. Whether in childhood, or in middle age, or at the end of life. Wonderful clemency, which awaits any time of our conversion, and whenever asked, forgives! You are my God. Augustine. Even if of all, mine properly, who help me, whom I worship and love. Others are strangers.
55.11: 55.11 In God I will praise the word. The same. The word, that is, the teaching and speech; whatever I shall say, I will praise in the Lord, that is, I will attribute it to him: and if anything presses, I have hoped, and therefore I will not fear. Augustine, Jerome. Or, in God the Father the Word, that is the Son, because whatever is said of the Father and the Son according to substance is said also of the Holy Spirit. This is said of the power of the Word, by which he is eternal and consubstantial with the Father, and afterward of the humanity, he adds: In the Lord, that is, in Christ, who is the Word made flesh. I will praise the speech, etc., that is, the preachings by which he gave the world a rule of living and salvation. This man preaches these two things, the power of the word and the humanity of Christ. In God I will praise. Or thus, that the Trinity of nature is personally through the three words which he sets. In God the Father I will praise the Word, that is, the Son; in the Lord, that is, in the Holy Spirit I will praise the speech, that is, the Son.
55.12: 55.12 They are in me. Within, things which never depart from us; The vows of praise, which will be rendered in eternity. Cassian. They are in me. The Church, now free from the evils of the world, says that in the future blessedness, or even here, she will sing the praise of God.
55.13: 55.13 For you have delivered. Cassian. Or it can be taken of the future thus, etc., down to where one also pleases God perfectly, hence he adds: That I may please, etc.
56.1: 56.1 Unto the end. Augustine. A psalm briefly of the resurrection and passion. The psalm does this, that you, Pilate, or whoever you are, may not destroy David, etc., by denying the king, because, covered with flesh, he fled from the knowledge of the Jews. The same. No title is inscribed for David, etc., down to where Christ lay hidden, unknown to the Jews.
56.2: 56.2 Have mercy on me. Cassian. The Prophet in the person of the Lord, because in him the Lord, as though amid evils, cries out, and foretells deliverance. Cassian. Christ, as man, prays, so humble in the passion that he is thought to be one of the faithful crying out. And in the shadow. The voice of the body is joined to the head: and speaking in the person of the members and his own, he will say how he can be delivered, he sent the Word.
56.4: 56.4 He sent his Word from heaven. Augustine, Jerome. From his hidden essence, etc., down to whom they thought they had extinguished. He sent from heaven. Jerome. Diapsalma. Now he declares what he sent and from whom he delivered, and speaks in the person of the members. He delivered. The same. Because he has already sent the Word, it is certain, as though he who delivered already existed, that is, he will deliver: and he gave, that is, he will give, to reproach those who trample on me. God sent. Augustine. The Word, in which he acted mercifully, in which he also fulfilled the promises. Mercy, because out of mercy he died for us. Truth, because as he foretold, he rose, to justify us. His mercy, etc. Jerome, Augustine. For both are contained in him. For if there had been mercy alone, we would have license to sin; if truth alone, man could not have endured.
56.5: 56.5 I slept. Augustine. Easily to be roused from deep rest: Disturbed by the passion, I slept. David did not sleep in the cave, but Christ in death. Cassian. Disturbed, according to the flesh, by the memory and anguish of the passion, whence: My soul is sorrowful, etc. And Jesus began to be weary and to fear. Sons of men. The order is correct: the sons of men prepared snares; but he inserts how they troubled. Tongue. Those voices, Crucify, crucify, and the like, also wrought death, like a sharp sword (Matt. 26; Mark 14).
56.6: 56.6 Be exalted. The same. In the person of the prophet, the injuries having been seen, and having seen that in the resurrection the Jews were made empty, the man on the cross cries out rejoicing: Be exalted, O God, above the heavens, that he may judge the Jews on earth. Be exalted. The above words of the Lord, the prophet indeed, but in the person of the Lord, because the Lord speaks in the prophet. Even when the prophet speaks from his own person, the Lord speaks through him, who dictates to him. Augustine. Be exalted. The words of Christ. But, O Father, etc., down to because the whole world is subject to him.
56.7: 56.7 They prepared a snare. An exaltation being interposed, he goes on with the narrative begun. For my feet. Cassian. The rebukes of the wicked and the promises to the faithful are the Lord's, with which they prepared deceits, as concerning the adulteress. They bowed down, while, feeling compassion for them, he was made barren by them. Before my face a pit, etc. While they said to his face: He is guilty of death.
56.8: 56.8 Ready. The same. Diapsalma. After the resurrection he promises praises. Or, ready to give thanks for what he shows there, I will sing.
56.9: 56.9 Arise, my glory. The same. And therefore, O flesh, who are the cause of my glory, Arise, mightily, as a congratulation for working a miracle, he who is certain, repeats it, affirming the same. I say arise, because I am certain also of the hour, for I shall arise at dawn. Arise, psaltery and harp. Augustine. One flesh of Christ rose, etc., down to the psaltery and harp rose, therefore, and confesses to the Lord.
56.11: 56.11 Unto the heavens. The same. Who is above the clouds, where is the seat of the angels, etc., down to mercy ascended to the heavens.
57.1: 57.1 Unto the end, destroy not, of David in the title, etc. Cassian. He warns that no one should contradict the kingdom of Christ. The first part is a reproach of the Jews, that we may not do similar things.
57.2: 57.2 If indeed you speak justice. Augustine. It is easy for all to speak justice, etc., down to because I am your king, as the title says: Rightly. The Jews so judged concerning Christ that they are proved to have spoken falsely of him.
57.3: 57.3 Your hands. The heart follows the hands: whatever you wish and cannot do, God counts as done. They weave. Or they join together, namely adding one thing to another, etc., down to whence the Lord with a scourge of little cords struck those buying and selling in the temple.
57.4: 57.4 The sinners are estranged from the womb. Or, they are estranged from the womb of the Church, etc., down to the abortive are cast out.
57.5: 57.5 Fury is theirs. The same. The thing itself is not praised by Scripture, wherever a likeness is given, as of the unjust judge, who scarcely heard the pleading widow. Of the deaf and stopping her ears. Cassian. Not only do they not do, but they do not even wish to hear. Augustine. The earth, present things, in which man delights; the tail, things past.
57.6: 57.6 Of the charmer who enchants. The same. Or according to another reading: Of a remedy prepared by a wise man. A prepared remedy, etc., down to this, then, is the wise man by whom the remedy is prepared.
57.7: 57.7 God shall break. Cassian. What recompense for them. Augustine. Asps, the Jews, while they tried insidious things; lions, when they cried out for death; their Molars broken, when Christ rose. Teeth. Deceitful words. In their mouth. He will take them by their own words. The Lord will break the molars of the lions. They shall come to nothing: the outcries for death. He will break, lest they come to effect; which he explains by saying: To nothing.
57.8: 57.8 Like water. The same. They are also compared to torrents, because sounding against the rocks of pride they are unforeseen and headlong, but quickly pass. They are compared to so many evils. He has bent his bow. Vengeance until within and without they are weakened and taken away from the sight of God, sent into Gehenna, here in the present, from their own land.
57.10: 57.10 Before your thorns. The same. That is, before they understand sins. The bramble, that is, sharp condemnation, at the last the fire of vices swallows them, that is, devours them. Bramble. A kind of plant, at first soft, but which afterward turns into thorns: so also sins now delight, but afterward prick. As the living, so, etc. Because the life of the impious is not true but false: they seem to live, and do not live. So in wrath he swallows them, because God judges calmly, or because there is no wrath in comparison with the future one.
57.11: 57.11 The just shall rejoice when he sees vengeance. Cassian. The correction of the just from the punishment of the unjust.
57.12: 57.12 And man shall say. Augustine. As is done by the just judgment of God, etc., down to and because fire swallows the wicked, therefore there is a God judging them on earth.
58.1: 58.1 Unto the end, destroy not. Cassian. In vain does anyone try to destroy what divine authority so often forbids. Destroy not. Augustine. When Pilate said: What I have written, I have written, etc., down to and to have fame among all the nations. Cassian. He prays first to be delivered by ascending from the lowest to the highest: he prays also for the salvation of the nations. Augustine. Here the whole Christ speaks, namely head and body.
58.2: 58.2 Deliver. The same. While he who is without stain asks this, he shows what we ought necessarily to ask. From my enemies. Cassian. There are four kinds of adversaries, etc., down to of these then he says: Deliver me, etc.
58.4: 58.4 The strong. Augustine. There are also those who presume on their own justice, etc., down to but those hoping in riches prevailed in their vanity.
58.5: 58.5 Iniquity. Cassian. Ill will: sin, of the deed.
58.6: 58.6 Arise. Augustine. Because you seem to sleep. To meet me. As though I run to you by deserving: And you, meet me, that is, repay according to merit. See. The same. That is, make it seen how I run to you, etc., down to after you have seen me die, you believe me equal to the Father.
58.7: 58.7 They shall be converted. Cassian. Diapsalma. The salvation of the nations having been prayed for is affirmed, and the salvation of the Jews who will pray. Toward evening, that is, later, after the ascension and the sending of the Spirit, etc., down to I fast twice on the sabbath. They shall go round about. Augustine. They will fortify the Churches against heretical assaults. And, behold, they will speak openly.
